initiatives.title: Assertions.eth: Transactions that check themselves, ensuring simulation outcomes
initiatives.summary: An assertion checks the outcome of a transaction on-chain, and a failed check reverts it. Assertions protected the $220M TheDAO Security Fund launch. This grant makes them easy to use from any account, a Safe, a DAO vote or a wallet: checks can use values read while the transaction runs, and a new Assertion Viewer shows signers each assertion as a plain sentence. A public board measures the money each protected transaction moves and the money its account holds and controls.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Safe owners, DAO voters and wallet users approve calldata, and the result can differ from what they expected: state moves after signing, and calldata can hide what it does. An assertion writes the expected outcome into the transaction, such as a minimum balance after a swap, and the transaction reverts when the outcome is different. Signers are protected from a wrong result even when they cannot read the calldata.

OP Mainnet's next upgrade ([superchain-ops eth/084](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/superchain-ops/tree/main/src/tasks/eth/084-U21-op-ink-soneium-uni)) is one Safe transaction that gives 25 contracts new code across four chains, including the vault holding over 180,000 ETH of bridge deposits. Its signers see a delegatecall and a wall of hex, and the task's README lists checks to run after it executes. We wrote those checks into the transaction instead, with the ones the Builder reads from the chain: 60 checks, all passing on a mainnet fork, and if one fails nothing executes.

Two gaps remain, and this grant closes them:

- **Signers take the author's word.** The description of the checks comes from whoever built the batch. The Viewer rebuilds it from the transaction.
- **Checks compare against fixed numbers.** Notations records a value while the transaction runs, so a check can say "this transaction takes out at most 50,000 USDC" whatever the balance is.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
**[Blossom Labs](https://blossom.software)**, the team behind EVMcrispr and Assertions, carries out all the work in this grant.

- [Sem](https://github.com/sembrestels), lead engineer: author of the Assertions contracts, the EVMcrispr compiler and the Assertion Builder, and of the [launch transaction](https://etherscan.io/tx/0x462475a38cd8a3b75b2732db28ea21a7addfce059af03ea4f638f461c707bf10) of TheDAO Security Fund.
- [Rodrigo Castillo](https://www.linkedin.com/in/rodrigo-castillo), designer at Giveth: designs the Builder and Viewer interfaces.

Blossom Labs is the round operator of TheDAO Security Fund Round 2, and Rodrigo works at Giveth, which administers the fund, so the independent technical reviewer for these milestones is named in the grant agreement and is not Blossom Labs.

No other funder pays for this scope. TheDAO Security Fund Round 1 [paid about $7,186](https://thedao.fund/transparency/assertions-eth-on-chain-transaction-guards-for-ethereum) for the existing contracts.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
- [Four contracts](https://assertions.eth.limo/docs/contracts/deployments/) live on Ethereum mainnet, with tests and symbolic proofs. The new work builds on them as deployed, so none is changed or redeployed.
- The Assertion Builder and docs at assertions.eth, which already build protected batches for a [Safe](https://assertions.eth.limo/docs/guides/safe/), a [DAO proposal](https://assertions.eth.limo/docs/guides/dao-proposals/) and a [wallet](https://assertions.eth.limo/docs/guides/wallet-batches/).
- EVMcrispr's Safe module, still experimental.
- A [Notations](https://github.com/BlossomLabs/Assertions/issues/10) prototype in its spec.

This grant pays for what is left: Notations on mainnet, our review of EVMcrispr's Safe module, the Builder changes, the board, and the Viewer, built from scratch.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- **[Notations](https://github.com/BlossomLabs/Assertions/issues/10)**: the contract that records a value while a transaction runs, for later checks to compare against, and deploys the compiled assertions.
- **[EVMcrispr](https://github.com/BlossomLabs/Assertions/issues/10)**: a `set` whose value is read when the batch executes, which a Safe and a DAO vote need because sometimes they execute days after they are written. Our own review of the Safe module, so it leaves experimental status.
- **Assertion Builder**: adapted to use the new features.
- **Protect your transactions**: a public board at assertions.eth listing every mainnet transaction checked by the Assertions contracts, with three values measured from onchain data: the money the transaction transfers, the money the originating account holds, and the money that account controls (for a bridge admin, the assets in the bridge it can upgrade). Each value links its addresses and its query.
- **[Assertion Viewer](https://github.com/BlossomLabs/Assertions/issues/13)**: open a pending or executed transaction and read each assertion as a plain sentence, checked against the calldata and deployed code.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Guards and policies that check transactions an account did not build with assertions.
- Frame transactions ([EIP-8141](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-8141), [EIP-7906](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7906)), planned for Assertions v3 ([#16](https://github.com/BlossomLabs/Assertions/issues/16), [#17](https://github.com/BlossomLabs/Assertions/issues/17)) once both drafts are final.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- Contracts, Builder, Viewer and board are MIT licensed. The EVMcrispr changes are released under EVMcrispr's license, AGPL-3.0.
- Blossom Labs maintains the contracts, the Builder, the Viewer and the board for 12 months after the last milestone at no further cost: assertions.eth stays online and reported bugs are fixed. EVMcrispr consulting funds it.
- Pinned target: at least 10 outside accounts, holding at least $3,000,000 combined, execute a transaction checked with what this grant builds.
- One exception: Notations ships labeled unaudited until an audit is funded or we can formally verify it, as we have started to do for the existing contracts ([140 of 326 claims so far](https://github.com/BlossomLabs/Assertions/blob/master/docs/claims.md)).

initiatives.title: Blobscan: Decentralized Archive for Ethereum Blob Data
initiatives.summary: The blob archiver that Optimism's documentation recommends to rollup node operators was archived on Oct 9, 2026 and is no longer maintained, while Ethereum nodes prune blobs after 18 days. Blobscan already serves its full mainnet blob archive from IPFS. This grant adds three-node redundancy, lets community DAppNode operators pin copies, and serves the archive through the beacon blobs endpoint rollup nodes already call. It also decodes Base, Arbitrum One, OP Mainnet and Mantle blobs, and funds paid API tiers that cover the running cost.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Ethereum nodes prune blob contents after 18 days by default, and with PeerDAS nodes sample availability without storing full blobs. Older blob data then lives only in a few archives.

Who is safer: users of rollups whose state can only be rebuilt and checked from blob data. From what: losing that data when a single archive fails. Base ($14.15B), Arbitrum One ($9.35B), OP Mainnet ($1.48B) and Mantle ($1.21B) alone secure about $26 billion, according to L2BEAT on 6 November 2026.

Rollup software already depends on these archives:

- **Optimism:** a node that syncs from data older than 18 days needs an archive source, and a fault-proof dispute over a block older than the retention window needs a blob archiver.
- **Arbitrum:** new nodes, and nodes back from a long time offline, need historical blob data.
- **Aztec:** its documentation points operators to archive services such as Blobscan.

Our own logs show the same. Between 7 October and 6 November 2026, 92% of the 3.9 million distinct blobs requested from Blobscan's API were older than 18 days, data Ethereum's own nodes had already deleted. Live nodes of at least three L2s read new blobs from it within the hour, and today all of that depends on a single node.

The archiver Optimism's documentation recommends, base/blob-archiver, was archived by its owner on Oct 9, 2026. Our endpoint serves the route op-node requests (`/eth/v1/beacon/blobs/{slot}`), so an operator can add it as a fallback beacon URL.

EthPandaOps also runs a blob archive endpoint. Both add resilience, and ours lets anyone keep their own copy.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
- **Paulo Colombo**: web3 developer, 6+ years, DAO tooling and dApp UIs (Gardens, EVMcrispr, TEC Hatch). https://github.com/PJColombo
- **Pablo Castellano**: senior DevOps engineer, 15+ years running scalable systems. https://github.com/PabloCastellano

EF funded the analytics workstream of the same Blobscan project; its Dagster pipeline also computes the archive-health metrics in this grant. No other funder pays for this scope. Blobscan is the team's own codebase.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
Built with the team's own funds:

- The Blobscan explorer and API are live: about 6.5M API requests a month, excluding retry loops, and about 1.2 TB served.
- An IPFS (Kubo) node runs in production. All mainnet blobs are migrated to it, the backend writes new blobs to it, and Blobscan users download blobs from it.
- The IPLD generator builds a deterministic DAG per epoch and exports CAR v2 archives: https://github.com/Blobscan/blobscan-ipld

That single node is the only copy today, so our own archive is a single point of failure. This grant fixes that first.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- Two more archive servers hosted by supporters in other locations, so every mainnet blob sits on three Blobscan-run nodes in different places
- A public CID registry with the network root published via IPNS, and a status page with archive-health metrics (pinned coverage per epoch, copies per blob) and a public alert when any blob falls below 3 copies
- A DAppNode package: independent operators pin the rollups and the disk space they choose
- A beacon-API-compatible blobs endpoint (`/eth/v1/beacon/blobs/{slot}`, `genesis`, `spec`) with a free rate-limited tier and paid tiers (API keys, quotas, x402 payments): an archive sync tier for history syncs, and a rollup node tier with an SLA, sold as an independent fallback next to a team's main beacon provider
- Paid full and custom CAR exports (by rollup or date range) over HTTP; the full mainnet archive is close to 3 TB
- Paid bulk metadata exports: per-rollup index, KZG commitments and decoded batch metadata
- Explorer decoders for Base, Arbitrum One (and Orbit chains such as Robinhood Chain), OP Mainnet and Mantle blobs
- Analytics: new blob metrics, dashboard and address pages (funded by EF)

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Gnosis Chain and any other non-Ethereum chain
- Mantle data from before its Arsia upgrade (16 April 2026), when it posted to EigenDA

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- Code stays AGPL-3.0.
- Each blob is stored as one raw IPFS block (CIDv1, sha2-256, the full 131,072 bytes), so its CID matches any other archive that stores blobs as raw blocks.
- The free tier, including the blobs endpoint at a rate limit, stays free. Any blob can also be fetched free from IPFS by its CID in the public registry.
- The Blobscan team maintains the archive, the blobs endpoint, the DAppNode package and the decoders after the last milestone, paid for by API tier revenue.

initiatives.title: Blockscout: Address Poisoning Detection and Public API for Ethereum and L2s
initiatives.summary: Blockscout scores every token transfer for address poisoning and serves the score through a public API. A working draft is open as PR #14931. This grant funds tuning, a backfill, Metadata reporting, and outside wallet adoption.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown: Address poisoning plants dust transfers from look-alike addresses in a victim's history, hoping they copy the wrong one. Scam Sniffer tracked a $50 million loss in December 2025 and a $12.2 million loss in January 2026 ([Cointelegraph](https://cointelegraph.com/news/over-62m-lost-address-poisoning-since-december-scam-sniffer)). Blockscout offers only an admin-managed scam badge today. Afterwards, any wallet can check an address against a public score before a user sends funds.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown: Blockscout does the work: Victor Baranov, lead engineer; Nikita Savik, product and API manager; Nick Zenchick, DevOps; Tom Goriunov, front end; Yan Yaskov, Lead QA. Track record: [Victor](https://github.com/vbaranov), [Nikita](https://github.com/NikitaSavik), [Nick](https://github.com/nzenchik), [Tom](https://github.com/tom2drum), [Yan](https://github.com/yvaskov), [Blockscout](https://github.com/blockscout/blockscout). No other funder pays for this scope.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown: [PR #14931](https://github.com/blockscout/blockscout/pull/14931) is a working draft: a weighted rule engine, a realtime indexer fetcher, a storage table, a `poisoning` field on API v2 token transfers, and tests. It lacks a backfill and Metadata reporting, so this ask covers tuning, backfill, reporting and adoption.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- Tune rule weights and thresholds on a labeled sample, and publish precision.
- Harden the realtime fetcher and backfill past transfers.
- Report flagged addresses to the Metadata microservice.
- Document the public `poisoning` field for Ethereum and the L2s Blockscout hosts.
- QA and staging at mainnet scale.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Chains other than Ethereum and its L2s.
- Wallet interfaces, which integrators build.
- Blocking or reversing transfers.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- The current Blockscout repository license applies.
- Blockscout maintains the feature set after the money is spent, committing at least 5 engineering hours per month from paid API plan revenue.
- New requests are funded by the projects that ask for them.

initiatives.title: BlockThreat: Weekly Threat Intelligence That Keeps Ethereum Teams Ahead of Attackers
initiatives.summary: BlockThreat is the weekly briefing 13,000+ blockchain security professionals, DeFi projects, exchanges, law enforcement, and many financial institutions read to keep up with attackers by learning their tactics, what was hacked and how, which vulnerabilities and techniques are new, what DPRK is doing, and what to change in their defenses this week. This grant funds 12 months of its Ethereum and L2 coverage and, for the first time, tracks what teams do with it. It pays in full only if at least 10 outside teams apply a recommendation, at least 3 stop a real attack with one, and outside organizations put in $20,000 of new revenue so BlockThreat keeps running without the fund.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
BlockThreat told teams where the attacks were going before they got there:

April 2026: after the KelpDAO and Drift hacks, it told teams to treat nodes, relayers and signers as part of the protocol, and to "stop using every day machines to sign multi-million-dollar transactions" (April).
July 2026: its outlook named the next target: "the next likely frontier will be signer infrastructure", the systems that approve and sign high-value transactions (July).
September 2026: it predicted that the next big exchange hack would start with social engineering, and told teams to audit their signing services and treat source control access like signing keys (September).
October 29: attackers went from a fake job interview to an engineer's laptop to Binance's wallet signing service, which signed 50 EIP-7702 authorizations and emptied its main Ethereum hot wallet. The loss was $6.3B (Cointelegraph, Week 44).
First week of November: 9 of the 13 incidents BlockThreat tracked across the industry, and about 97% of the $53.2M lost, came from outside smart contracts, led by $48.6M of validly signed withdrawals at one exchange (Week 45).

An audit covers none of this, and a defense built for last quarter's attacks is already behind. The warnings are public but scattered across hundreds of blogs, X threads, chatrooms and disclosures that no security team has time to read. BlockThreat reads them, re-ranks the threats every week and month, and says what to change.

Who is safer: security teams at Ethereum and L2 protocols, exchanges, custodians and wallets, against the attack vectors in play right now, such as compromised signing infrastructure and keys, fake-interview malware, frontend and DNS hijacks, and known bugs in forked code. Afterwards, anyone can point to teams that changed a defense because of a BlockThreat recommendation, and to teams that stopped a real attack with it.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
Peter Kacherginsky (@iphelix) does the work: editor of BlockThreat since 2019, sourcing, analysis and impact tracking. He has more than 20 years in security and founded Coinbase's blockchain security team. He has spoken at DeFi Security Summit for the past four years, most recently on "The State of DeFi Security - 2026", and seven years of his editions are public at blockthreat.com.

BlockThreat earns money from reader support, advertising, Enterprise subscriptions and Peter's advisory work for protocols (blockthreat.com/vciso). The Ethereum Foundation and TheDAO Security Fund each sponsored it once before, and neither funds this scope. No other funder pays for this work.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
* Seven years of weekly editions without a gap, plus monthly outlooks with loss statistics, the top 10 attack vectors and emerging threats, all free to read since November 2026.

* The readers are the defenders: 13,000+ subscribers at 1,900+ organizations, among them exchanges, custodians, protocols and audit firms. Past advertisers include Immunefi, Chainalysis, Trail of Bits and OpenZeppelin.

* One edition covers a defender's whole week. Week 44 had 30 incidents, 5 vulnerabilities and 18 research papers and tools, plus DPRK, malware and scam reporting.

* The sourcing: 294 feeds, 972 X accounts, 48 chatrooms and 15 newsletters. That is 32+ hours of reading a week, filtered with an in-house classification tool, reviewed by hand, and delivered as a 10-minute edition.

* The data behind the statistics: 2,313 incidents tracked, growing by 10 to 15 a week.

A new threat intelligence desk would have to build all of this first. Here the fund pays $6,000 a month for the Ethereum share of one editor's time, and readers and sponsors pay for the rest.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
* 12 months of weekly briefings: the attack vector behind every Ethereum and L2 incident, the vulnerability disclosures, research, tools and threat-actor reporting that matter to Ethereum teams, and what to do about them (what to patch, what control to add, what to test for, who is on notice)

* 12 monthly outlooks: Ethereum loss statistics, the re-ranked top 10 attack vectors, and the threats to prepare for next

* Impact tracking, which is new work: a reporting link in every edition, follow-up with teams that act on a recommendation, and a quarterly impact report

* Building the sponsor base that pays for BlockThreat after the grant, at prices already published.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown: Live exploit monitoring, incident response and audits. The focus of the newsletter is on deep analysis of past incidents, extraction of emerging threats and lessons, and consistently accurate future outlook to point out future incidents.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
* Every weekly briefing and monthly outlook stays free to read, with no paywall, and may be quoted with attribution.

* Peter keeps publishing BlockThreat for at least 12 months after the last milestone, paid from reader support, advertising and Enterprise.

* Pinned targets: at least 10 outside teams applying a recommendation and at least 3 stopping a real attack.

* Sponsors and advertisers never shape coverage and paid placements are labeled.

initiatives.title: colibri: Know What You Sign, Verified Simulation Against Blind Signing
initiatives.summary: A secure key does not help when the signer is shown one transaction and authorizes another effect. The Bybit attack demonstrated the scale of this failure mode. This grant turns colibri's verified local simulation into an open pre-sign security layer: independently reconstruct transaction effects from cryptographically verified state, apply deterministic security policies, and return machine-readable block/warn/confirm decisions that wallets can enforce before signing. The result must ship in at least 5 production signing flows.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown: The signing interface is itself part of the security boundary. In the February 2025 Bybit incident, compromised Safe infrastructure presented signers with a benign-looking operation while malicious transaction data changed control of the wallet; about $1.46 billion was stolen (https://www.a16zcrypto.com/posts/article/bybit-hack-lessons). Hardware wallets protect keys, but they cannot protect a user who authorizes a malicious effect they cannot independently understand. colibri can simulate locally on verified state, independent of the dApp or RPC that constructed the transaction. This grant makes that independent check enforceable before signing and deploys it in real signing flows.

sections.markdown:

- **Simon Jentzsch, Chief Architect.** Worked on TheDAO (2016), co-founder of slock.it, built the Universal Sharing Network and Incubed (IN3), the first minimal verification client for Ethereum. Co-author of EIP-1186 (eth_getProof), the Merkle-proof standard most Ethereum light clients use for state verification.
- **Steffen Kux, Vision & Product.** Head of the project business at slock.it from 2017, with industrial clients such as Siemens and Energy Web Foundation. Worked on Incubed, CEO of dm3, Co-founder of corpus.ventures.
- **Jork Leonhardt, Business & Ecosystem.** COO at slock.it, co-founder of Tokenize.it and corpus.ventures.
Track record: colibri has been in production since November 2025 and is integrated in the Ethereum Foundation's Kohaku wallet SDK, the Freedom browser, Ambire and beel.com (formerly Tokenize.it).

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown: colibri already executes eth_call locally on verified state. A transaction-security prototype runs on top of it: local simulation and evaluation by a small local model, fully in the browser, already integrated in the Kohaku wallet SDK (https://github.com/ethereum/kohaku-extension/tree/HEAD/src/web/modules/sign-account-op/components/ColibriSimulationResult). This grant turns the prototype into an open foundation: structured effects, a deterministic rule engine, a wallet-facing policy interface and test vectors. A team starting from scratch would first need a client that verifies state locally, because a simulation on unverified data inherits the same trust problem.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- Local transaction simulation on verified state. 
- Structured effect extraction: token transfers, approvals, NFT movements, balance changes, ownership and upgrade changes, reverts. 
- A baseline deterministic rule engine with an extensible rule and policy interface. 
- A machine-readable result that wallets use to block, warn or require extra confirmation, demonstrated in a reference signing flow.
 - An open interface for local explanation components, with a reference integration of a local model. Security decisions never depend on the model, and transaction data never goes to a hosted LLM. 
- Reproducible test vectors for normal, suspicious and malicious transactions. 
- Integration support for wallets and signing tools adopting it.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Advanced commercial transaction-security capabilities: domain-specific language models, model weights, training data, specialized analyzers and rule sets, threat intelligence. corpus.core may license these separately. 
- Training custom models. The reference integration uses an existing local model runtime. 
- Hosted or managed services. 
- The verification core, new chains, general dApp integrations and PAP. Companion initiatives cover them.

sections.markdown:
- **License:** local simulation, effect extraction, the baseline rule engine, the policy and explanation interfaces, the reference integrations and the test vectors are released under an OSI-approved open-source license. Commercial extensions built on top are not covered. 
- **Maintenance:** corpus.core maintains the open foundation after the grant, funded by commercial transaction-security products built on it. 
- **Pinned targets:** at least 5 new wallets or signing tools show colibri’s verified simulation results in their production signing; at least 2 from the list in the adoption milestone or teams whose multisig governs over $100 million onchain.
- **Exception requested:** a merged upstream pull request counts toward the target when the integrating team's own release schedule delays production use.

initiatives.title: colibri: Make dApps Verify What They Show in Wallets, DeFi and Web3 Apps
initiatives.summary: A wallet can protect keys perfectly and still show a user false blockchain state. This grant moves colibri's local cryptographic verification into production wallets, DeFi frontends and other Web3 applications, so balances, allowances, contract state, logs and calls are verified before an application acts on them. It funds a Go binding, a drop-in provider and at least 12 new production integrations across at least 3 application categories.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown: The security boundary of a wallet or dApp does not end at key custody. Applications continuously make security-relevant decisions from RPC data: balances, allowances, bytecode, storage, logs, name resolution and eth_call results. If those reads are manipulated, the application can display false state, route funds incorrectly or construct a transaction from a false premise. colibri replaces the RPC provider as a source of truth with locally verified proofs. Manipulated reads are a proven attack path: in April 2026, compromised RPC infrastructure (https://www.corpuscore.tech/blog/the-code-was-fine-thats-the-problem) fed false chain data to KelpDAO's bridge verifier and released about $292 million (https://unchainedcrypto.com/layerzero-links-292-million-kelp-dao-bridge-exploit-to-north-koreas-lazarus-group/). Every wallet that trusts its RPC provider depends on the same kind of infrastructure.

initiatives.title: colibri: Trustless Across Ethereum, Verification for L2 Networks and Bridges
initiatives.summary: colibri turns blockchain reads from a trust assumption into a cryptographic check. This grant makes that security model reusable across Ethereum’s L2s a production multi-chain verification framework, a public capability table for L2 networks, and an explicit capability/fallback model with no silent downgrade. Success means at least 5 L2 networks use colibri verification in their own production products and at least 3 cross-chain protocols use it where a false read can move real value. Chain-specific engineering that can be funded by a chain foundation is explicitly excluded.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown: Ethereum's security model is based on independent verification, but most applications abandon that property at the RPC boundary. The problem becomes more severe across L2s and bridges, where one application may trust several independent read infrastructures. The April 2026 KelpDAO incident (https://www.corpuscore.tech/blog/the-code-was-fine-thats-the-problem) showed the direct consequence: compromised RPC infrastructure caused a verifier to attest to a non-existent source-chain event, releasing about $292 million on the destination chain (https://unchainedcrypto.com/layerzero-links-292-million-kelp-dao-bridge-exploit-to-north-koreas-lazarus-group/). colibri moves verification to the application edge: data is accepted only together with evidence that the client verifies locally.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
corpus.core (Germany) does the work.
- **Simon Jentzsch, Chief Architect.** Worked on TheDAO (2016), co-founder of slock.it, built the Universal Sharing Network and Incubed (IN3), the first minimal verification client for Ethereum. Co-author of EIP-1186 (eth_getProof), the Merkle-proof standard most Ethereum light clients use for state verification.
- **Steffen Kux, Vision & Product.** Head of the project business at slock.it from 2017, with industrial clients such as Siemens and Energy Web Foundation. Worked on Incubed, CEO of dm3, Co-founder of corpus.ventures.
- **Jork Leonhardt, Business & Ecosystem.** COO at slock.it, co-founder of Tokenize.it and corpus.ventures.
Track record: colibri has been in production since November 2025 and is integrated in the Ethereum Foundation's Kohaku wallet SDK, the Freedom browser, Ambire and beel.com (formerly Tokenize.it).
https://github.com/corpus-core/colibri-stateless
https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1186
https://medium.com/corpus-core-insights/colibri-stateless-production-release-8d5a88c116d1
https://github.com/ethereum/kohaku/blob/HEAD/packages/provider/README.md
https://github.com/AmbireTech/ambire-common/blob/HEAD/src/controllers/verification/verification.ts
https://github.com/solardev-xyz/freedom-browser/blob/HEAD/src/shared/chains.json

Other funding for this scope: none.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown: colibri has been in production since November 2025 and runs on Ethereum, Gnosis and the OP Stack. The verifier, the execution and consensus proofs, and a zk-compressed consensus proof already exist. Bindings are available for JavaScript/TypeScript, Swift, Kotlin/Java, Python, Dart/Flutter and Rust. This grant pays for what is missing: the chain adapter framework, the per-network support table, the fallback protocol and the new networks. A team starting from scratch would first have to build the verifier itself.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- Hardening only the reusable multi-chain verification components required by this grant: common proof interfaces, explicit verification/trust modes, cross-chain conformance tests, live-chain testing and reproducible CI. General Ethereum-core work unrelated to multi-chain adoption is excluded.
- A public, machine-readable support table for every network (the Verification Capability Model): what colibri verifies natively, what it verifies only partially, and where it relies on the fallback. Applications read the active mode for each request. 
- A chain integration framework: standardized chain/consensus adapter interfaces where possible, reusable L2 verification components, an integration SDK, conformance and live-chain tests, test vectors, compatibility checks, and a documented process for adding a network.
- A witness-based verification fallback protocol for networks without native proofs yet: defined security assumptions, integration with the Capability Model, applications always able to identify fallback use, no silent downgrade, a migration path to native verification, reference implementation, test vectors, and documentation.
- Integration support for L2 teams and cross-chain protocols adopting colibri verification.
- At least 2 reference network integrations on materially different architectures, selected only where their chain-specific engineering is not being paid by another foundation, grants program or commercial integration budget.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Integrations into wallets, DeFi protocols and other dApps. A companion initiative covers them.
- Networks that are not Ethereum or one of its L2s, this grant covers Ethereum L2s and bridges only. 
- New language bindings such as Go. They belong to the companion dApp initiative. 
- Pragmatic Adaptive Privacy (PAP). A companion initiative covers it. 
- Transaction simulation and the open transaction-security foundation. A companion initiative covers them, built on the verified data this grant delivers. 
- Commercial vRPC, prover services, and integration work for RPC providers.
 - The full integration cost of chains that have their own foundation, grants program or integration budget. They may pay separately for chain-specific engineering, support and maintenance beyond the reusable components funded here.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- **License:** the verifier, chain adapters, support table, fallback protocol and test suites are released under an OSI-approved open-source license. Commercial vRPC and prover services built on top are not covered.
- **Maintenance:** corpus.core maintains the chain integrations and the support table after the grant, funded by commercial products built on the open core.
- **Pinned targets:** a public support table covering at least 6 Ethereum L2 networks and at least 5 L2 networks using colibri verification in a production product run by the chain team, 2 of them from the named list, and at least 3 cross-chain protocols using colibri verification in production.
- **Exception requested:** a merged upstream pull request counts toward the bridge target when the bridge's own release schedule delays production use.

initiatives.title: DappFence: Verifiable Frontend Security
initiatives.summary: DappFence is an open-source, client-side security system designed to protect users from compromised web frontends. The February 2025 Bybit theft, in which attackers manipulated the Safe wallet interface to deceive signers and steal approximately $1.5 billion, demonstrated why Ethereum security must extend beyond smart contracts to the interfaces people use to interact with them. DappFence verifies frontend assets against an authenticated integrity manifest and blocks resources that do not match the version defined by that manifest. Coinspect will bring the implementation to production-ready, validate it in production deployments, finish and publish its integration tooling, and drive adoption by dApps.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Smart contracts can be decentralized and independently verified, while the frontend used to interact with them still depends on centralized infrastructure. An attacker who compromises a dApp's domain, DNS, hosting platform or CDN can serve modified code that alters transaction parameters, and browsers do not check that the code they receive is the code the dApp team published. In February 2025, attackers modified the JavaScript served by the Safe wallet interface used by Bybit and drained its cold wallet without exploiting any contract bug ([Sygnia](https://www.sygnia.co/blog/sygnia-investigation-bybit-hack/), [NCC Group](https://www.nccgroup.com/research/in-depth-technical-analysis-of-the-bybit-hack/)). Frontend compromises also hit BadgerDAO ([TRM Labs](https://www.trmlabs.com/resources/blog/trm-investigates-badgerdao-defi-protocol-hacked)) and KyberSwap ([CoinDesk](https://www.coindesk.com/tech/2022/09/01/defi-platform-kyber-network-discloses-265k-exploit-vows-to-reimburse-all-funds)).

Gateways that serve dApps from IPFS face the same risk: in April 2026, attackers hijacked eth.limo's DNS for about five hours ([eth.limo post-mortem](https://discuss.ens.domains/t/eth-limo-dns-hijack-post-mortem/22079)), and a compromised gateway can serve modified code for every site it delivers.

DappFence protects the users of every dApp that deploys it, including dApps served through IPFS gateways. Wallet defenses such as transaction simulation and clear signing check the transaction; DappFence checks the code that builds and presents it, so a modified interface is blocked before the user is asked to sign.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
**Coinspect** does the work. Andres A., the main author of the current DappFence codebase, leads development and works full-time on this grant (https://github.com/a-d-j-i).

Coinspect is a security research and auditing firm founded in 2014: https://www.coinspect.com.

Coinspect develops and owns the DappFence repository and has pledged $27,000 of the funding goal. There is no other funding for this work.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
DappFence already has a working implementation. Automated browser tests show that a modified page, script or external resource, including the DappFence script, is blocked, that new signed releases load without being blocked, and that attempts to wipe DappFence from the browser are detected.

On a user's first visit, the site installs a Service Worker that the browser keeps between visits. On later visits, that Service Worker verifies the frontend's code against manifests signed by the dApp's publisher and blocks any file that does not match. No external service, browser extension or dedicated infrastructure is involved: the script and the signed manifest are served from the dApp's own hosting, and an attacker who controls that hosting cannot forge a valid manifest without the publisher's private signing key. An attacker who tries to remove DappFence has to replace a Service Worker script whose expected hash is in the signed, public manifest, so such an attack is straightforward to monitor.

The repository contains:

- The Service Worker runtime (@dappfence/core), with a report-only mode for gradual rollout.
- A warning page and emergency panel shown when tampering is detected, and a status endpoint with verification results and block history.
- Manifest tooling (@dappfence/manifest-tools) that hashes a build, signs the manifest and verifies signatures.
- Initial build integrations for Next.js and Vite.
- A test application and an end-to-end browser test suite.

The current implementation remains a prototype and requires hardening before production use. The grant pays for hardening, release and adoption, not for building what already exists.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- Runtime hardening: Close the known gaps in the verification runtime, including stronger verification of a dApp's own Service Worker.
- Signing and release workflow: Harden manifest generation, signing and verification.
- Integration tooling: Finish and publish the Next.js and Vite integrations and extend them where production deployments require it.
- Compatibility: Run the end-to-end test suite on Chrome and Firefox, and against sample applications built with each supported integration.
- Production deployments: Deploy in live, publicly accessible dApps, starting with one and growing to the adoption target, and resolve the issues each deployment surfaces.
- Support: Direct assistance to dApp teams integrating DappFence.
- Documentation: Integration, onboarding, signing and release guides for dApp teams, and a threat model stating what DappFence protects against and what it does not.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- First visits and the protection window: Trust is established on a user's first visit. The browser downloads the DappFence script again once 24 hours have passed since its last check, so returning users have a protection window of up to 24 hours when the script is served with a long cache lifetime. Two cases are therefore not covered: a user whose first visit happens while the site is already compromised, and a compromise that persists beyond the protection window, after which the attacker's script can replace the Service Worker on returning users' browsers.
- Supply chain and signing keys: Verification confirms that users run the release the publisher signed. It does not assess whether that release is safe: malicious code added before signing, through a compromised dependency or build pipeline, passes verification, as does code signed with a compromised key.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- Code published under the MIT license, with development public in the repository.
- Coinspect maintains the public repository for 6 months after the last milestone, at no further cost: reviewing and merging contributions and publishing releases to npm.
- DappFence has no business model yet; further development after the grant will need new funding.

initiatives.title: Dedaub: Free, Backtestable Onchain Monitoring on 13 EVM Chains
initiatives.summary: Dedaub runs a monitoring platform where anyone can write unlimited onchain queries in DedaubQL and run up to 2 alerts, free of charge, on 8 EVM chains. This grant buys the storage to expand to at least 13 chains, add at least 5 Ethereum L2s, and keep 12 months of uncompressed history on every newly supported chain (24 on Ethereum mainnet), so any alert can be replayed over past exploits before a team relies on it. It also buys one analysis server that runs the Gigahorse decompiler on the new chains. The free tier stays free, SEAL and SEAL 911 members get unlimited access for 36 months, and Dedaub launches a new paid offer for its monitoring infrastructure to sustain it.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Two gaps, one cause.

- Coverage: the platform indexes 8 chains, and the same attackers, the same bytecode and the same Ethereum-issued assets are on dozens more. Ethereum L2s with billions in value, such as Mantle, is not covered by the platform today.
- Backtesting: an alert that has never been run against a real attack is an untested guess. Replaying an alert over history needs call traces and logs in a form that can be scanned quickly. We compress older data to stay within capacity, and a backfill on compressed data slows from milliseconds to tens of minutes per day of history.

The cause is storage. Adding chains without more disk makes the compression problem worse. Adding disk without more chains leaves the ecosystem's value uncovered.

Who is safer: any team on the covered chains, whose alerts can be replayed over past exploits before they rely on them, and incident responders, who get the decoded internal-call trace of an attack transaction the same day on chains whose explorer shows no traces. Every new chain is an Ethereum L2 whose value settles on Ethereum. Attackers reuse Ethereum exploit code across all of them.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
Dedaub does the work. This is a grant, not a competition: the platform, the decompiler and the CLI named below are Dedaub's own, and the hardware extends them.

Drafted by Giorgio Bonuccelli with the Dedaub engineering team. A Dedaub team member, Yannis Bollanos, holds an ETHSecurity Badge and will abstain from ranking this initiative.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
Everything this grant extends is Dedaub's own and in production:

- The monitoring platform at https://app.dedaub.com, live on 8 EVM chains, with DedaubQL queries, alerts, backfill and email, webhook and Telegram notifications.
- The CLI and agent skill, MIT-licensed, with reference notes for 95 protocols: https://github.com/Dedaub/monitoring-cli
- The Gigahorse decompiler, free since 2018, more than 16,000 registered users across ten EVM chains.

There is nothing else to build on. The grant buys the storage and one analysis server; the software, the chain data feeds and the people are Dedaub's.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
What the money buys. Every item is an example; the purchase may be of analogous hardware.

- 8 Memblaze PBlaze7 7A40 61.44 TB NVMe drives, $24,950 each, $199,600 (Bytehaus written quote to Neville Grech, 27 May 2026, to be re-quoted)
- One analysis server, current-generation CPU, at least 1 TB of RAM, $50,000 (Dedaub target figure, quote pending)
- One 24-bay NVMe enclosure, $10,229 (Serial Cables list price, 28 September 2026)
- One external HBA with four cables, $1,707 (Serial Cables list prices, 28 September 2026)

What gets delivered:

- At least 5 new Ethereum L2s. At least 3 of them from: Robinhood Chain, Mantle, World Chain, Ink, Linea, ZKsync Era, Celo, Ronin. Any other L2 counts only if L2BEAT shows at least $200M in value secured when it goes live. Every chain gets traces, logs, and token transfers indexed, DedaubQL alerts, email, webhook, and Telegram notifications, the CLI, and agent skill.
- Decompilation on every new chain: the analysis server runs the Gigahorse decompiler, so every EVM bytecode contract on them becomes readable without source, free.
- A backtesting storage tier: 8 drives in mirrored pairs (about 246 TB usable) attached to Dedaub's existing database server, keeping 24 months of uncompressed history for Ethereum mainnet and 12 months for the other chains. Backfill becomes a normal step when creating an alert, from the web app and the CLI.
- Decoded traces for responders: the internal-call trace of any transaction on a funded chain, queryable in DedaubQL and exportable from the CLI.
- Unlimited access for SEAL and SEAL 911 members: unlimited active alerts with backfill and decoded traces without rate limits, for 36 months from the first new chain going live.
- A new paid offer: a new way to pay for Dedaub's monitoring infrastructure (for example self-serve subscriptions for teams and/or protocol maintainers), so the service is sustained by its users.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Archive nodes. Dedaub sources archive data from RPC providers at its own cost.
- The network, data centre space, RPC subscriptions and bandwidth, and the people who onboard chains and run the platform. None of this is billed to the grant, now or later.
- Alt-L1s (for example Arc, Monad, Plasma, Gnosis). Dedaub may add them, paid for by the chain or the apps on it, not by this grant.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
1. The CLI and its agent skill stay MIT-licensed. The platform remains Dedaub's hosted service, free at the tier described above.
2. The free tier (unlimited queries, 2 active alerts per user, no time limit, no credit card) is live on every funded chain, and Dedaub keeps it after the grant as its own policy, as it has with the decompiler since 2018.
3. SEAL and SEAL 911 members get unlimited alerts with backfill and decoded traces without rate limits for 36 months from the first new chain going live. Dedaub carries the compute cost.
4. 12 months of uncompressed history on every covered chain, 24 on Ethereum mainnet. If measured volumes or drive prices force a cut, Arbitrum and Optimism shorten first to 6 months; Ethereum mainnet and the new chains never shorten.
5. Dedaub owns and runs the equipment, keeps every funded chain live through the last milestone and beyond, and provides invoices and serial numbers for every item to the technical reviewer.
6. Dedaub re-quotes every line in writing before signing and covers any price rise between signing and purchase up to 15% of the quoted price. Every item may be replaced by analogous hardware; the analysis server may be a refurbished unit with equivalent specifications.
7. Dedaub staff and contractors never count towards any milestone.
8. If the round funds less than the full amount, the number of new L2s drops with it.

initiatives.title: Defimon Rescue Agent: Autonomous Whitehat Rescues for Safe Harbor Protocols on Ethereum
initiatives.summary: Defimon detects DeFi exploits in under a second and has returned over $2.5M to victims. This grant turns that into an autonomous rescue agent for the 33 protocols that adopted the SEAL Whitehat Safe Harbor: a rescue playbook per adopter, verified with the protocol, and an agent that identifies the root cause and the funds still at risk within minutes and moves the remaining funds straight to the protocol's registered recovery address, with no human in the loop. Safe Harbor bounties pay for running it after the grant.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Most exploits drain a protocol over several transactions, across minutes or hours. The funds still in the contract after the first transaction can be rescued, but only by someone who sees the attack at once, understands the bug fast enough to reuse it defensively, and has legal cover to do it. That almost never happens. The SEAL whitehat rescue list records 25 rescues worth about $80.7M since 2022, and only 5 of them were done under Safe Harbor, although 33 protocols holding $60.7B have adopted it (safeharbor.securityalliance.org). Whitehats hold back because reusing the attacker's path is legal risk, and because nobody runs rescue capacity as a standing service.

Who is safer: users of Safe Harbor adopters on Ethereum mainnet, Arbitrum One, OP Mainnet and Base (Aave, Lido, Sky, Uniswap, Pendle, Euler, Balancer, Polymarket and 25 others). From what: an exploit in progress, while part of the funds is still in the contract. What anyone can point to afterwards: at least 5 adopters that verified their rescue playbook and know Defimon as a responder, a published benchmark of minutes from attack transaction to root cause, a public incident log, and, when an exploit hits an adopter, funds returned to its on-chain recovery address, confirmed by the protocol and by SEAL 911.

The money at stake, from the DefiLlama hacks dataset (api.llama.fi/hacks, pulled November 11, 2026; DeFi protocols on Ethereum mainnet or an Ethereum L2, centralized exchanges excluded):

- 2025: 70 incidents, $447M lost, of which 56 contract-level exploits worth $364M.
- 2026 to date: 130 incidents, $557M lost, of which 111 contract-level exploits worth $414M.
- Three Safe Harbor adopters were exploited in the last 12 months: Balancer V2 ($128M, November 2025), Makina ($4.2M, 2026, $3.4M returned under Safe Harbor), Lazy Summer ($6M, 2026).

How much of that is rescuable: Decurity reconstructed the per-transaction drain timelines of 10 multi-transaction exploits from 2022 to 2026 (rescue-window.decurity.io). In 6 of the 10, more than 80% of the funds at risk were still on the contract 5 minutes after the first attacker transaction, and 6 of the 10 drains lasted longer than an hour. Where a bot acted inside that window (Squid, Foom), 81% to 82% of the funds at risk came back the same day; where nobody did (CrossCurve, $2.76M), less than 1% came back.

Why the rescue has to be autonomous: 49% of vulnerable contracts are exploited within 30 days of deployment and 85% of vulnerable proxy implementations within 30 days of the upgrade (time-to-hack.decurity.io). Incidents are spread evenly across all four 6-hour blocks of the UTC day, so a human responder misses most of the 5-minute windows, and a playbook written once goes stale at the adopter's next upgrade.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
Decurity does the work. The rescue is fully autonomous: Defimon's agent detects the exploit, identifies the vulnerable function and the funds still at risk, and moves them to the protocol's registered recovery address from the playbook, so the protocol holds its funds again before anyone at Decurity is awake. People do the follow-up, none of it time-critical: notifying SEAL 911 and the protocol's security contact, the incident log entry, and KYC where the agreement requires it for the bounty. Arseniy Reutov, CTO and co-founder, leads the program (QuickNode case study: https://www.quicknode.com/blog/real-time-defi-exploit-detection). Arseniy holds an ETHSecurity Badge and will abstain from rating and ranking this initiative.

Public cases where Defimon rescued funds or warned the team before the drain:

- Foom.cash, February 26, 2026: $1.84M rescued on Ethereum and returned the same day; Foom.cash paid a 10% security fee:
    - https://defimon.xyz/blog/foom-cash-whitehat-rescue-february-2026
- Squid Router, April 7, 2026: $512K rescued:
    - https://x.com/DefimonAlerts/status/2041530294369386806
- Veil.cash: 2.025 ETH rescued
    - https://x.com/Veildotcash/status/2025293773891404225
- Secured.finance: alert 45 minutes before the hack
    - https://x.com/DefimonAlerts/status/2096855557575458950
- Ajna.finance: team alerted one hour before the hack
    - https://x.com/DefimonAlerts/status/2093632180656263283
- Guru.fund: team alerted before 85% of funds were drained
    - https://x.com/DefimonAlerts/status/2080679061265739844
- Olas.network, Yam.finance: governance takeovers reported
    - https://x.com/DefimonAlerts/status/2096432367908933790
    - https://x.com/DefimonAlerts/status/2095019159847313766
- Kpk.io: proxy backdoor reported
    - https://x.com/DefimonAlerts/status/2079618207569133651
- CPIMP: several projects notified
    - https://x.com/DefimonAlerts/status/2003167362829418679

No other funder pays for this scope. Defimon's paid feed ($200 per month) and Signals channel ($50 per month) fund detection today; nothing funds standing rescue capacity.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
Everything the grant extends is live:

- Detection on Ethereum, Arbitrum, Optimism, Base and Polygon with an LLM-verified confirmed-attacks stream and early detection of attacker contracts, proxy upgrades and malicious governance proposals.
- An AI agent that, given an attack transaction, identifies the vulnerable function and the balances still exposed, and executes the rescue. Measured on real incidents: Squid Router was rescued 4 minutes after the first attacker transaction, $512K of $623K at risk (82%); Foom.cash 16 minutes after the first exploit transaction landed on Base, which included recognizing the same flaw in the separate Ethereum deployment, $1.84M of $2.26M at risk (81%).
- The operational experience of those rescues. Foom.cash also showed the gap this grant closes: the protocol had no Safe Harbor terms, no recovery address and no responder it knew, so the return relied on goodwill on both sides.

The grant pays for the part nobody funds: per-adopter rescue readiness (registry data, recovery addresses verified with the protocol, pre-written rescue paths), benchmarking the root-cause agent, private transaction submission, legal review of the runbook against the Safe Harbor terms, and running the agent and its follow-up process for 12 months. A from-scratch build of detection plus rescue capacity would cost several times this budget.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- Covered chains: Ethereum mainnet, Arbitrum One, OP Mainnet and Base. These are the chains Defimon runs detection and rescue on today.
- A rescue playbook for every Safe Harbor adopter with at least $10M on a covered chain: recovery address and scoped assets read from the SafeHarborRegistry (0x326733493E143b8904716E7A64A9f4fb6A185a2c), bounty and identity terms, security contact, and a pre-written rescue execution path. A public index shows the terms; the execution paths stay private.
- Playbooks kept current: every implementation upgrade of an adopter's scoped contracts, which Defimon already detects, triggers a re-verification of that adopter's playbook within 7 days.
- Playbooks verified with the adopters themselves: recovery address, scoped contracts and security contact confirmed by the protocol, and Defimon introduced as a responder it should expect to hear from. Where an adopter's agreement requires Named identity (Aave, Sky, Euler, Balancer, Silo, Makina, Origin, Reserve and others), Decurity completes KYC and sanctions screening at payout, as the agreement requires.
- The root-cause agent benchmarked on replayed historic exploits, with the replay set and results published.
- Private transaction submission (Flashbots Protect or equivalent) and the go/no-go checklist from the SEAL Whitehat Rescue Guide: active or imminent exploit, independence from the attacker, net benefit, return within the agreement deadline, SEAL 911 notified.
- The rescue agent running against every covered adopter for 12 months, and a public incident log: every rescue-candidate event on an adopter is logged with acted or not acted, and why.
- Free rescue-grade alert feed for SEAL 911 members for the grant period.
- Outreach to protocols holding over $100M that have not adopted Safe Harbor, to add them to the registry.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Rescues on protocols that have not adopted Safe Harbor. Those are legal risk for the whitehat; a legal destination for such funds is the subject of the separate RFP "An Open Bug Bounty Program for All of Ethereum: White Hat Rescued Funds Distribution Service" on this board.
- Initiating an exploit, acting on a known vulnerability before an attack starts, or bug bounty reporting. Rescues start only during an active or imminent exploit.
- Any chain other than Ethereum mainnet, Arbitrum One, OP Mainnet and Base. Defimon also runs detection on Polygon PoS, BNB Chain, Avalanche and Hyperliquid, and nothing on those chains counts toward any deliverable or milestone.
- Tracing or freezing funds the attacker already moved, and negotiating with attackers.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- The rescue runbook, the adopter index, the replay benchmark set and the incident log are published under CC BY 4.0. The rescue execution tooling stays closed, because it would help attackers as much as defenders.
- Every rescue under this program returns funds to the protocol's registered recovery address within the agreement deadline and is reported in the public incident log. Decurity keeps only the bounty the agreement defines. Rescues are rewarded by Safe Harbor bounties, never by this grant.
- Decurity keeps the rescue agent running against every covered adopter for at least 12 months after the last milestone, paid from Safe Harbor bounties and feed revenue, at no further cost to the fund.
- Decurity staff, affiliates and Decurity's own contracts never count toward any milestone.

initiatives.title: Echidna: Fund Development Through 2027
initiatives.summary: Fund Gustavo Grieco, Echidna's creator and maintainer, to carry out Echidna's 2026 to 2027 roadmap during 2027: keep EVM execution current, improve campaign and worker architecture, strengthen symbolic verification, turn agent control into a dependable workflow and optimize execution performance. At minimum, the period produces three tagged maintenance or minor releases, at least two substantial roadmap outcomes delivered in tagged releases, three technical posts, and a public SKILL prompt and MCP workflow for AI agents.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Smart contracts can pass large unit test suites and still fail after an unexpected sequence of calls, actors, prices, timestamps, upgrades, or token behaviors. Echidna attacks that gap with stateless and stateful property-based testing. It generates transaction sequences from a contract ABI and searches for inputs that falsify user-defined properties or Solidity assertions.  
Echidna already combines coverage guidance, corpus mutation, source integration, automatic test minimization, Foundry reproducers, hevm cheatcodes, and optional symbolic execution. Its next challenge is reliability at the seams: EVM behavior changes, campaign and worker coordination, symbolic-execution edge cases, agent control and improved performance. Those are the areas that determine whether auditors can trust a long-running campaign and reproduce what it found.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
Gustavo Grieco does the work, in the public [Echidna repository](https://github.com/crytic/echidna).  
He was the lead developer of Echidna and the lead author of [the ISSTA 2020 paper](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3395363.3404366) that introduced it. He was a security engineer at Trail of Bits from September 2017 to April 2025, junior to principal, across blockchain audits, fuzzing, and tool development, and has been independent since. He has been [elected Audit Committee Technical Expert for the Arbitrum DAO since July 2025](https://snapshot.box/#/s:arbitrumfoundation.eth/proposal/0x131574819442cb6da293795ee9faeec4754a5af664b535b654b3d9d3d53f47e1). He co-authored the [Slither paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.09878) and echidna-parade, and before Echidna he built another fuzzer: [QuickFuzz](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2976002.2976017). Echidna lives in the crytic GitHub organization, which Trail of Bits runs. Even after he left Trail of Bits, Gustavo is still a volunteer to keep Echidna maintained.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
The recipient has the decisive head start. The work touches Echidna's Haskell engine, release process, hevm and Slither integrations, symbolic execution, Foundry compatibility, and the existing MCP preview. A new vendor would first spend months on implementation details and EVM edge cases.  
The [2026-2027 roadmap discussion](https://github.com/crytic/echidna/issues/1612) is the maintainer's planning thread, where users prioritize the goals. The 2.3 [releases](https://github.com/crytic/echidna/releases) added optional symbolic verification, multiple SMT solvers, Foundry reproducers, and an experimental MCP interface. The [public fuzzing campaigns list](https://github.com/perimetersec/public-fuzzing-campaigns-list) shows the tool in real audit work, and Recon Invariant Testing Extension and scfuzzbench are external users or integration targets.  
**Example roadmap outcomes**, to show the expected scope. The milestones name the class of outcome, so the issue can change.

> * Fork support like [issue \#1623](https://github.com/crytic/echidna/issues/1623): the relevant fork's execution-layer changes supported in hevm and Echidna, with fork-specific and conformance tests.  
> * Symbolic verification like [issue \#1625](https://github.com/crytic/echidna/issues/1625): difficult properties proved by combining fuzzing and symbolic execution, with replayable counterexamples.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
> * EVM and toolchain compatibility: hevm, Slither, new Foundry cheatcodes, crytic-compile, SMT solver configuration, packaging, and operating-system support  
> * Campaign and worker architecture and execution performance  
> * Symbolic execution for verification, exploration, and counterexample discovery, with bounds and unsupported cases reported plainly  
> * Continued development of the MCP integration so agents can inspect and direct live fuzzing campaigns  
> * A public versioned SKILL prompt that teaches an agent Echidna's capabilities  
> * Fixes and feedback sent upstream to hevm, Slither, and Foundry  
> * Support for users running long and complex campaigns, on Telegram, Discord, and GitHub

Six months of maintainer time at $8,000 a month, spread over the 12-month grant and including VPS capacity and frontier-model access, is $48,000.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
> * Rewriting Echidna in another language  
> * Building a general autonomous auditor or claiming that an LLM replaces a security engineer  
> * Writing a complete fuzzing harness or invariant suite for one protocol  
> * Performing an audit or formal-verification engagement for a specific protocol  
> * Supporting non-EVM chains except through the normal EVM-compatible stack

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
> 1. **Open source and public development.** All grant-funded code, tests, documentation, and examples are published under AGPLv3 or another OSI-approved license, through public issues, pull requests, and tagged releases.  
> 2. **Roadmap delivery.** Each roadmap outcome ships in a tagged release whose notes explain the improvement and link to the test, reproducer, or benchmark behind it.  
> 3. **Substitution and 2026 carry-over.** A blocked roadmap item may be replaced by one of equal or greater security value and scope, with the reason, the replacement, and its acceptance evidence published first. Unfinished 2026 roadmap work counts if it happens in 2027, was not funded elsewhere, and is of comparable scope and importance.  
> 4. **Current EVM support.** Finalized EVM and toolchain changes in the work period are covered by public regression tests. No milestone depends on an Ethereum upgrade shipping on a fixed date: if a fork slips, the fork-dated target moves with it.  
> 5. **Honest output.** Agent controls are documented. Symbolic results state the mode, solver, bounds, timeout status, unsupported operations, and caveats, and incomplete analysis is never reported as verified. Release artifacts tie to public source tags, and installation paths are tested in CI.  
> 6. **Post-grant maintenance.** The recipient keeps maintaining Echidna after the grant (releases, triage, security reports, user support on the public channels), without follow-on funding and at a pace set by his other paid work.  
> 7. **Pinned targets, counted from the first payment.** EVM fidelity and campaign reliability: within 90 days after the next Ethereum mainnet fork activates. Symbolic verification and agent workflows: within 7 months. Roadmap completion and handoff: within 10 months. Adoption: within 12 months.

initiatives.title: EEZ: Making Its Contracts Safe for Chains to Adopt
initiatives.summary: EEZ extends Ethereum, and Ethereum's security with it. EEZ turns cross-chain execution into an Ethereum primitive: rollups and L1 call each other in one transaction, checked on Ethereum with no bridge in between, and a protocol deploys once instead of on every chain. This grant takes EEZ from audit to adoption: an independent audit and fixes, a testnet where outside chains can try the audited contracts, and a final payment only when outside chains and protocols run EEZ on mainnet. Our mission is to deliver an open-source model, within a non-profit framework, that is secure enough for everyone to use; its adoption rests on shared risk, which requires shared security, shared funding, and shared collaboration.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Some of the largest losses in Ethereum's history happened at its bridges: honeypots of locked funds guarded by small signer sets that rely on reputation rather than contract logic or validity proofs, prioritizing UX over security. Ronin, Poly Network, BNB Bridge, Wormhole, and Nomad all sit near the top of the [Rekt leaderboard](https://rekt.news/leaderboard/), and each broke the layer that decides which cross-chain messages are valid. 

EEZ turns cross-chain execution into an Ethereum primitive. A contract on one rollup calls a contract on another rollup, or on L1, and uses the return value in the same transaction, with the result checked on Ethereum. That takes the bridge out of these flows:

- Moving assets between rollups no longer needs a third-party contract holding pooled assets, so there is no bridge pool for an attacker to drain.
- Atomic multi-chain actions, such as a swap funded from another rollup, complete fully or revert together, within one L1 block, provided a builder includes the bundle.
- A smaller attack surface. Today a protocol copies itself onto every network it reaches, and duplication breeds bugs: version drift, per-chain initialization mistakes, maintenance across every copy. The Balancer v2 exploit drained the same code chain by chain. With EEZ a protocol deploys once, where it is easiest to audit and secure, and a fix applies everywhere. 

Every Layer 2 becomes a true extension of Ethereum: one account and one contract address across connected chains, with wallets routing sends so funds sent to the wrong chain can stop being lost. Ethereum L1 stays as secure as it is today, since its consensus does not depend on EEZ. What changes is the layer above it: cross-chain validity is decided by checks on Ethereum instead of by a signer set's reputation, the locked-fund pools that made bridges worth attacking disappear, and the code that can lose user money across chains collapses to one set that Ethereum can see and everyone can audit.

**What each rollup keeps.** Each rollup declares the proof systems it accepts and how many must agree, and every cross-chain outcome is checked on L1 against them; the composer that builds each bundle can at most stall calls. Based rollups, like the first Gnosis deployment, go further: sequencing happens inside the L1 block, and anyone can rebuild the chain from L1 data alone. Today one attestation signer runs the check by re-executing each block window, so until more proof systems are added, a chain's safety rests on that signer. The audit covers the signer, the multi-prover design it plugs into, and how each rollup locks its configuration down.

**What independently tested guarantees change.** Every rollup that adopts EEZ inherits the same contract set on Ethereum. Its cross-chain attack surface becomes that reviewed set plus its own configuration, instead of a bridge it built and audited alone. Every later adopter shares one review, and a fix reaches all of them at once. The same sharing is the risk: a flaw in the shared set is a flaw everywhere, which is why no chain should adopt it on the EEZ team's word alone. The audit turns these guarantees from a design claim into something a rollup can rely on; the testnet lets outside chains verify it, and mainnet adoption shows they did.

With audited EEZ, users and teams will be able to:

- Move assets between rollups with no third-party pool holding funds for an attacker to drain.
- Run atomic multi-chain actions, such as a swap funded from another rollup, that complete fully or revert together within one L1 block, provided a builder includes the bundle.
- Deploy a protocol once, where it is easiest to audit, and serve every connected chain from that one deployment, so a fix applies everywhere.
- Use one account and one contract address across connected chains, with wallets routing sends so funds sent to the wrong chain can stop being lost.
- Adopt a shared, independently audited contract set instead of building and auditing a bridge alone, with every later adopter sharing the same review and every fix reaching all of them at once.

EEZ is not a dapp and not a product. It is an Ethereum public good: an open, permissionless protocol for synchronous composability between Ethereum rollups. The core EEZ contract has no admin role. Each connected rollup keeps its own contract, whose owner sets the accepted proof systems, verification keys, and threshold. That design puts the security of the whole system on its smart contracts, which is exactly what this grant puts under independent review.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
The EEZ Association does the work and is accountable for the outcome.

* [Jordi Baylina](https://x.com/jbaylina), core contributor
* [Friederike Ernst](https://x.com/tw_tter), co-initiator
* [Eduardo Antuña](https://x.com/eduadiez), core contributor
* [Jesús Ligero](https://x.com/JesusLigero3), core contributor
* [Armagan Ercan](https://x.com/epochzer0), coordinator

Other funding: Gnosis commits $30,000 to this goal and hosts the testnet nodes; the $10,000 milestone covers the contract deployment, documentation, conformance suite, and reference integration built on top.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
* The protocol is built and public at [eez-core-protocol](https://github.com/eez-association/eez-core-protocol): contracts, specifications under `docs/`, end-to-end test scenarios, and open findings from internal review. The contracts are prepared for devnets and ready for audit.
* GnosisDAO [approved GIP-153](https://snapshot.org/#/s:gnosis.eth/proposal/0x5522f4cbd034c966a08d6901b05c7ad7300041b3e0d75a0ad3da868af1a98b98), making Gnosis Chain the first governance-backed adopter.
* [Celo](https://celo.org/), [Polygon](https://polygon.technology/), and [Linea](https://linea.build/) have agreed in discussions with us to test the audited contracts.
* Vitalik Buterin stress-tested the design with Jordi Baylina at ETHPrague 2026 ([fireside](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=prgWmgUbSVQ)) and called EEZ "a quite helpful effort" at Dappcon Berlin ([panel](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gfG-R8AOu0E)). Joseph Lubin supports EEZ publicly ([post](https://x.com/etheconomiczone/status/2052390993610133513)).

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
* **Independent audit** of the EEZ core contracts at one pinned commit, including privileged roles, cross-chain behavior, and the single attestation signer live today with the multi-prover design it plugs into. Fixes by the EEZ team, re-review by the auditor. About 8 to 10 senior-auditor-weeks; report within 2 months of the auditor's appointment.
* **Integration environment:** the audited contracts on a public testnet, integration docs, a conformance suite, a reference integration, and a support channel. Celo, Polygon, and Linea build their own integrations; this grant pays none of that.
* **Integration support** for the first outside chain or protocol that goes to mainnet.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
* Rollup node software, provers, sequencers, and other off-chain infrastructure
* The internal economics of connected rollups
* Re-auditing changes made after the pinned commit

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
* **License:** MIT, with a LICENSE file at the repository root.
* **Maintenance:** the EEZ Association maintains the contracts and the public security record after the grant; the testnet stays public for at least 12 months after the report.
* **Pinned target:** at least 2 outside chains and 4 dapps from the adoption lists run EEZ on mainnet within 6 months of the audit report. If the condition is met earlier, the adoption milestone is disbursed earlier.
* **Independent auditor:** we publish a shortlist of at least 2 firms and why we chose one; the auditor has no ties to the EEZ Association, its contributors, Gnosis, or ZisK.

initiatives.title: ETH Daily Security: Getting Ethereum Users to the Tools That Protect Them
initiatives.summary: Ethereum security builders ship good tools, and most users never hear about them. Under this initiative, ETH Daily will transition from a general news briefing to a security-focused publication, and will use its existing audience to send users to Ethereum security tools. Every link to external tools will be tracked, so the clicks sent to each tool can be counted and reported publicly.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Builders keep shipping tools that stop attacks: approval revokers, wallets that check signatures and transactions. A tool only protects the users who find it. Users have no central place to learn what exists and how to use it. They scramble to search X, GitHub and Reddit.

Wallet drainers took $494 million from 332,000 addresses in 2024 and $83.85 million from 106,106 wallets in 2025 (Scam Sniffer annual reports, drops.scamsniffer.io). Users who revoke bad approvals, check signatures and verify addresses they interact with can avoid these attacks. The best security layer is the preventive layer.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown: ETH Daily (pseudonymous): solo producer of a daily Ethereum news podcast, newsletter and social feed for over 4 years. Track record: https://x.com/ethdaily

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown: The distribution exists: 10,000 combined newsletter and podcast subscribers and 26,000 combined followers on X, Lens, and Farcaster (https://ethdaily.io/ads). Four years of coverage and a security archive are public. Nobody else funds this scope, which is why the price is $2,900 a month.

sections.heading: In scope

- ETH Daily becomes a security-focused Ethereum publication for the grant period

- Guides and podcast episodes that send the audience to the hub
- A published neutrality policy

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:

- Paid referrals and sponsored listings are disclosed inline and never change what we recommend
- The hub is maintained for 12 months after the last milestone at no further cost
