initiatives.title: EthSec: AI Security Review of the Ethereum Ecosystem
initiatives.summary: EthSec will run Argus, its AI security system (https://ethsecurity.org/content/argus/), as an ongoing review of the Ethereum ecosystem: all Ethereum DeFi, all Ethereum layer 2s, and base-layer and client code. This grant pays $200,000 for Argus token credits used in that work. EthSec will publish a report; when appropriate, that report is an aggregate findings report without technical details. Adoption is acknowledgment from the affected teams. A public acknowledgment is not required, but EthSec will ask for one where possible. After the grant, EthSec keeps running the reviews from its own budget, which it intends to keep raising money for.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
The problem is larger than DeFi protocol losses alone. Argus covers the Ethereum ecosystem: DeFi on Ethereum, Ethereum layer 2s, and the base-layer clients that run the network.

As of 13 November 2026, Ethereum DeFi has about $39.4 billion locked (https://defillama.com/chain/ethereum). Ethereum layer 2s secure about $35.1 billion (https://l2beat.com/scaling/tvs). Those figures move day to day; they show the scale of funds that sit on live contracts, on layer 2s, and behind the clients that process them.

Losses span more than one layer. Immunefi's 2026 Ecosystem Vulnerability Scoreboard puts DeFi protocol losses at $680 million in 2025, and says 89% of those losses came from protocol logic exploits (https://immunefi.com/blog/research/the-ecosystem-vulnerability-scoreboard-6-years-of-defi-loss-data/). One of those incidents, the Balancer V2 composable stable pools exploit, lost $128 million across Ethereum and several layer 2s. That same report keeps centralized exchange failures separate: exchanges absorbed over $1.6 billion in infrastructure-class losses in 2025, led by the $1.5 billion Bybit compromise. Chainalysis counted over $3.4 billion stolen across the industry from January through early December 2025 (https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/crypto-hacking-stolen-funds-2026/). DeFi protocol losses are only one slice of that picture.

The Glamsterdam gas changes (Ethereum Improvement Proposal 8037 and 8038) showed the same gap at the base layer. ChainSecurity and the Ethereum Foundation found deployed contracts that rely on gas invariants the upgrade would break (https://blog.ethereum.org/2026/11/06/glamsterdam-8037-8038).

After this work, users of Ethereum DeFi, layer 2s, and the base layer are safer because confirmed bugs in live systems have been reported to the teams that run them. Anyone can point to a report, and to acknowledgment or other proof that outside teams accepted those issues, plus a public fix when possible.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
EthSec (Eth Security Inc, a Delaware nonprofit being formed) does the work. It is an AI security lab for Ethereum. Argus is EthSec's AI security system (https://ethsecurity.org/content/argus/).

David Theodore, executive director and a board member, is the proposer, the contact, and the lead for this work. He is also an ETHSecurity Badge holder for TheDAO Security Fund. He was a founding member of the Ethereum Foundation Protocol Security Team. He was a founding board member of SEAL and is its longest-serving director, still active on the board. He has been a Lead Security Researcher (LSR) at Cantina/Spearbit and a Lead Senior Watson (LSW) at Sherlock.

Before that, he was a security engineer at Google and an exploit developer in the US defense industry.

EthSec is hiring security researchers and analysts. No candidate is pre-assigned to this grant. Joe Lubin is giving $100,000 as the initial match in TheDAO Security Fund. This initiative asks TheDAO Security Fund for the remaining $100,000.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
EthSec's public site is https://ethsecurity.org. Argus is already in use internally for AI-driven security review (https://ethsecurity.org/content/argus/). A fuller public track-record page will be built there; today the site is the public link.

This grant buys Argus token credits to run reviews at scale. It does not fund a new scanner, a new model, or a from-scratch tool. Adjacent approved initiatives already cover a proprietary Solidity scanner and CI integrations (Kann AI, https://initiatives.thedao.fund/initiative/scaling-kann-ai-for-ai-smart-contract-security-2), AI-guided checklist reviews inside Remix (https://initiatives.thedao.fund/initiative/ai-guided-smart-contract-security-checks-in-remix), security rules for coding agents rather than audits (https://initiatives.thedao.fund/initiative/shift-left-security-for-ethereum-open-source-agent-enforced), a map of every Ethereum DeFi protocol's audits to live code (SEAL Audit Transparency, https://initiatives.thedao.fund/initiative/audit-transparency-for-ethereum-every-defi-protocol-s-audits), and live monitoring and circuit breakers (Glider Monitor, https://initiatives.thedao.fund/initiative/glider-monitor-circuit-breakers-for-ethereum-defi). This work is a live review service across DeFi, layer 2s, and the base layer, not a tool for other teams to run themselves.

The $200,000 pays for Argus token credits used in those reviews, private disclosure of confirmed findings, and a report.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
Argus reviews the Ethereum ecosystem: all Ethereum DeFi, all Ethereum layer 2s, and base-layer and client issues (execution and consensus clients and related core protocol code). The work is AI-driven vulnerability discovery, triage, and review of live systems in that scope.

The $200,000 is spent on Argus token credits (frontier model APIs and other inference) used in those reviews.

What that money produces:

- Argus-driven vulnerability discovery, triage, and review across that scope
- Every confirmed finding reported privately to the affected team. Where a Glamsterdam gas-invariant break is confirmed, it is also reported to glamsterdam@ethereum.org.
- A report. When appropriate, that report is an aggregate findings report, with counts of high and critical findings per sector, and with no technical details
- Acknowledgment from outside teams. A public acknowledgment is not required, but EthSec will ask for one where possible
- After the grant, EthSec keeps running the reviews from its own budget, which it intends to keep raising money for

EthSec will assist every affected team through the fix and will verify fixes are implemented when possible. This is a firm commitment. Payment does not depend on a fix shipping.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Training a new foundation model, or building a new public scanner product
- Hardware, lab fit-out, or general EthSec operating costs already covered by existing lab funds
- Contracts, clients, or chains other than Ethereum and its layer 2s
- The November 2026 Glamsterdam decision process itself. This grant cannot start until the initiative is fully funded, so those dates are context, not deliverables.
- Publishing technical details of a finding before it is fixed
- Counting token usage, model calls, or internal reviews as adoption
- Guaranteeing that every review finds a bug, or that a reviewed system is free of bugs

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
EthSec will publish a report. When appropriate, that report is an aggregate findings report without technical details.

Until a finding is fixed, a public report may be aggregate only: counts of high and critical findings per sector, with no technical details. Detailed write-ups may be published after a fix, under CC BY 4.0. Payment does not depend on those write-ups.

A disclosure policy stating that rule is published before the first report. Confirmed findings are reported privately to the affected team.

EthSec will assist every affected team through the fix and will verify fixes are implemented when possible. This is a commitment. Payment does not depend on a fix shipping.

After the grant, EthSec keeps running Argus reviews from its own budget, which it intends to keep raising money for, at no further cost to TheDAO Security Fund.

Pinned target: a report covering Argus reviews of at least 100 already-deployed Ethereum or Ethereum layer-2 contracts, Ethereum layer 2s, Ethereum client codebases, or other node software, and acknowledgment of at least 20 high or critical findings by at least 10 outside teams, as set in the adoption milestone (this is the minimum target: some form of proof that teams accepted our issues, plus a public fix when possible).

initiatives.title: ForensIQ: Faster Ethereum Incident Response Through Evidence Reconstruction
initiatives.summary: ForensIQ is building an open-source module that connects off-chain incident evidence (logs, files, transaction hashes) with Ethereum activity to reconstruct attack timelines, trace fund flows, and flag transfers to attributed exchange addresses. It replaces the manual handoffs between logs, block explorers, and attribution tools with one evidence-linked workflow that produces a verified response package faster. The grant funds the missing connective layer on top of ForensIQ's existing MVP (case management, Crystal and Etherscan integrations), not a rebuild of the platform. Success is measured through pilots with protocol, exchange, and law-enforcement investigators, tracking time to a verified timeline and correctness rather than a promised percentage improvement.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
During an Ethereum security incident, time is a critical resource. Responders need to establish what happened, identify the affected assets, follow the funds, and prepare the evidence needed for their next action. Every manual handoff between logs, transaction views, attribution results, and investigation notes consumes part of that response window. Funds can move again while the team is still assembling its first coherent account.

This initiative funds an open-source module that reduces the work between receiving incident evidence and producing a verified response package. It connects off-chain evidence with Ethereum activity, reconstructs the attack timeline, maps supported fund movements, and flags transfers to attributed exchange addresses. The intended users are protocol and exchange security teams, incident-response firms, and law-enforcement investigators.

**Less time assembling evidence. More time to act on it.**

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
The proposed recipient is the ForensIQ team, backed by HackenProof. The proposer reports an existing MVP with user and role management, case creation, file uploads, AI file analysis, and integrations with Crystal and Etherscan. These components provide a head start; the grant pays for the additional investigation module and its validation, not rebuilding the SaaS foundation.

The head start combines working ingestion and analysis components with existing blockchain integrations and access to prospective pilot users through HackenProof. Reuse should let the team spend the grant on cross-source reconstruction, response exports, and field validation. Before the agreement is finalized, a baseline demonstration and reuse inventory will make those savings checkable. The module is at MVP stage; measured investigation outcomes will come from the pilots.

HackenProof's existing relationships provide a route to pilot users. The proposer identifies law-enforcement partners in Ukraine and the Netherlands as intended first testers and plans to invite Hacken and other cybersecurity partners.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
[Crystal](https://crystalintelligence.com/crystal-expert-for-law-enforcement/) provides blockchain investigation capabilities, including fund tracing and case organization. These are substantial existing capabilities; neither timeline visualization nor transaction tracing alone is the novelty proposed here.

The proposed advance is an independently deployable, evidence-linked workflow connecting selected incident logs to Ethereum transfers and response preparation, evaluated against investigators' existing processes. The first milestone will document feature overlap, identify components worth reusing, and fix the specific workflow improvement to be tested.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- Ethereum mainnet, native ETH movements, and ERC-20 transfers; support for relevant execution traces must be documented against the selected data provider.
- Two or three log formats chosen with pilot users during the first month, plus supporting file evidence with stable source references.
- A shared timeline with normalized timestamps, original timestamps retained, and explicit handling of unknown time zones or uncertain ordering.
- Fund-flow views linking transfers to transaction hashes and addresses, with documented tracing assumptions.
- Crystal attribution integration and Etherscan transaction-data integration, with documented access requirements.
- Incremental case updates and configurable polling alerts for supported transfers to addresses attributed to exchanges, including source, retrieval time, and uncertainty. Provider delays and polling intervals are visible.
- Evidence-linked attack hypotheses, human-reviewed containment recommendations for agreed scenarios, and an exportable investigation package. Exchange action remains at the recipient exchange's discretion.
- Standalone deployment, public documentation, reproducible test fixtures, and independent pilot evaluation.

**What this pays for:**

Consider an illustrative investigation: a team provides access logs, incident files, and suspicious transaction hashes. The module places relevant events on one timeline, links each finding to its source, traces supported transfers, and checks available address attribution. If funds reach an address attributed to an exchange, the investigator gets an alert and an evidence package to review for an escalation request. The team can start reviewing supported findings while the broader investigation continues.

The funded contribution is the connection between those steps: evidence normalization, traceable correlations, incremental updates, and a consistent response export. Existing blockchain intelligence supplies attribution. AI helps organize evidence and propose explanations; an investigator verifies conclusions and chooses actions. Recommendations will cover a small set of incident scenarios agreed with pilot users, rather than promise a reliable diagnosis for every attack.

Success means shorter time to a verified timeline and a usable escalation package, with correctness measured alongside speed. Pilot results will establish whether and where the module saves time; no improvement percentage is claimed in advance.

The open-source core will ingest supported logs and supplied Ethereum data, produce timelines and fund-flow views, and export evidence without a ForensIQ account. Commercial attribution is an optional enrichment using the operator's own credentials. Without it, exchange identity can remain unknown. Public fixtures allow the complete workflow to be evaluated without purchasing third-party access.

**On the milestone plan:**

The six-month plan allocates roughly four months to development and two to pilots and refinement. Pilot recruitment and data-access arrangements start in month one. The proposed cost basis is $120,000 for team work ($20,000 per month), $10,000 for infrastructure and external services, and $5,000 for independent review, all included in the milestone amounts. Team work covers backend and data integration, AI/evidence analysis, investigator-led validation, and pilot delivery. Staffing allocations will be fixed in the final plan; these figures do not imply four full-time hires. Service costs and reviewer fees must be validated before contracting. Payments are tied to acceptance, not monthly payroll.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Other chains and L2s, cross-chain bridge tracing, and claims to resolve movement through mixers.
- A proprietary address-labeling database or redistribution of third-party data without permission.
- Universal log ingestion, autonomous remediation, automatic freeze-request submission, or guaranteed recovery.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
1. **Open source and independently usable.** All code developed for the funded module is released under an OSI-approved license. The license is fixed in the agreement. No paid ForensIQ account is required, and necessary reused dependencies must permit standalone distribution.
2. **Evidence before conclusions.** Findings include source references. Observations, hypotheses, and attribution are distinguishable. Missing evidence and unresolved paths remain visible.
3. **Safe handling of case material.** Deployment documentation explains where data is processed, external-provider access, and retention settings. External AI processing requires explicit configuration. Untrusted file contents cannot trigger external actions.
4. **Reproducible acceptance.** Public fixtures, commands, expected outputs, and evaluation reports let an independent reviewer reproduce the core workflow. Sensitive investigation materials are not published.
5. **Independent adoption.** At least three external teams use the module on investigation material and publicly confirm use, or authorize a named independent reviewer to confirm use publicly with identifying details omitted. Attendance at a demo does not count.
6. **Maintenance.** ForensIQ maintains the module for at least 12 months after completion of the pilot phase, covering bug fixes, security updates, and integration compatibility. HackenProof's own budget backs this commitment. Future grants may support expansion but are not a condition of maintenance.

**Note on the adoption milestone**

Public confirmations disclose no sensitive evidence. Participation and publication arrangements must be agreed with pilot teams. Private cases can use the independent attestation route; other qualified teams can also satisfy the criteria. The independent reviewer must be able to verify that the three teams are distinct and external to the recipient. The final milestone accounts for approximately 37% of the budget.

initiatives.title: Kann Audits: Scaling Kann AI for AI Smart Contract Security
initiatives.summary:
Kann AI is a proprietary, Solidity-focused AI security model developed by Kann Audits to identify vulnerabilities and security issues in Ethereum smart contracts. An Alpha version is already publicly accessible at https://scan.kannaudits.com, supported by a specialized vulnerability dataset and practical security research.

This $50,000 grant will fund improvements to the model's detection accuracy, reasoning capabilities, and dataset quality, alongside CI/CD integrations that enable Ethereum developers to automatically scan smart contracts during development. Our goal is to make AI-assisted vulnerability detection more reliable, accessible, and actionable across the Ethereum ecosystem.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Security remains a major challenge for Ethereum developers. While professional smart-contract audits are essential, they are expensive, time-consuming, and typically conducted at specific stages of development. Existing automated security tools help identify potential vulnerabilities, but often produce false positives or struggle to recognize issues requiring deeper contextual reasoning. This creates a gap between basic automated scanning and the security analysis developers need throughout the development lifecycle.
Kann Audits is addressing this gap through Kann AI, a proprietary AI model developed specifically for Solidity vulnerability detection and supported by a specialized security dataset. Rather than simply adding an interface to a general-purpose AI model, we are developing and improving the underlying security-focused model itself. With grant funding, we will improve detection accuracy, reduce false positives, strengthen vulnerability reasoning, and introduce CI/CD integrations that enable automated security scanning on code changes and pull requests. This will help Ethereum developers identify potential vulnerabilities earlier, investigate findings more efficiently, and incorporate security checks into everyday development workflows without replacing professional manual audits.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
Kann AI is developed by Kann Audits, a smart-contract security firm combining hands-on security research, professional auditing experience, and AI engineering expertise.

Erkan Alaydinov - Founder, Kann Audits

Erkan has worked in smart-contract security since 2023, with experience in professional security audits, independent security research, public audit contests, private code reviews, and large-scale AI-generated finding triage. He leads the security research direction of Kann AI, including vulnerability analysis, dataset quality, and the practical evaluation of model-generated findings.

LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/erkan-erolov/

Kann Audits track record

Kann Audits has completed 71 smart contract security audits and secured more than $2 billion in TVL.

Our AI security tooling has also been used by projects including Manifest Finance, HyperLend, and Mystic Finance.

This combination of practical security research and AI engineering gives Kann Audits the expertise needed to develop a specialized vulnerability detection model and evaluate its performance against real-world smart-contract security issues.

Funding and relationships

The protocols mentioned above are examples of previous users of our security tooling. Their inclusion does not imply that they are funding the initiative or formally endorsing this application.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
Kann AI is already an operational product rather than a concept awaiting initial development.

Kann Audits has developed a proprietary AI model specialized in detecting security vulnerabilities in Solidity smart contracts. The model is supported by a dedicated vulnerability dataset informed by real-world security research, historical vulnerability patterns, audit findings, and manually reviewed security issues.

An Alpha version of Kann AI is already deployed and publicly accessible at:

https://scan.kannaudits.com

Developers can use the existing platform to submit Solidity code for AI-assisted security analysis and review potential vulnerability findings.

Our advantage comes from the security expertise supporting the model. Kann Audits has conducted 61 security audits involving protocols representing more than $2 billion in TVL. This experience helps us understand real vulnerabilities, distinguish meaningful findings from noise, and continually improve the quality of the model's training and evaluation process.

The grant will not finance development of a new product from scratch. The initial model, core infrastructure, security research methodology, and public scanning platform have already been established through Kann Audits' own investment.

Instead, grant funding will accelerate improvements to the existing model, expand and refine the vulnerability dataset, strengthen evaluation against previously unseen contracts, improve inference reliability, and introduce production-ready CI/CD integrations.

This existing foundation allows the requested $50,000 to be concentrated on measurable technical improvements and practical developer adoption rather than initial product research and infrastructure development.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
The initiative will focus on improving Kann AI's Solidity vulnerability detection capabilities and making automated smart-contract security analysis easier to integrate into Ethereum development workflows.

Solidity AI model improvement

We will expand and improve the proprietary vulnerability dataset using real-world Solidity vulnerabilities, exploit examples, secure contract implementations, and difficult negative examples. The improved dataset will support further model training, with an emphasis on increasing vulnerability detection accuracy, strengthening contextual reasoning, and reducing false positives and false negatives.

Development will prioritize major Solidity security risks, including access-control vulnerabilities, reentrancy, unsafe external interactions, accounting inconsistencies, and complex authorization issues.

Evaluation and benchmarking

We will establish a held-out security benchmark containing vulnerable and non-vulnerable Solidity contracts excluded from model training.

The current Kann AI Alpha will serve as the baseline for measuring improvements. Evaluation will report precision, recall, false-positive rates, false-negative rates, and performance across relevant vulnerability categories.

We will document important failure modes, publish the evaluation methodology, and share benchmark results so that improvements can be assessed independently.

CI/CD security integrations

We will develop integrations that allow Ethereum development teams to run Kann AI vulnerability scans automatically within their existing development workflows.

The initial integration will target GitHub Actions, enabling scans during pull requests and code pushes.

The integration will support:

Automated Solidity vulnerability scanning.

Security results associated with code changes.

Machine-readable findings suitable for CI/CD pipelines.

Configurable severity thresholds.

Automated warnings or failed checks when configured security thresholds are exceeded.

Integration guides, configuration examples, and developer documentation.

Production infrastructure and adoption

We will improve the reliability and scalability of the existing Kann AI scanning infrastructure and deploy updated models through the publicly accessible platform.

We will support adoption by independent Ethereum development teams, with a target of at least 20 projects or teams successfully integrating Kann AI into real CI/CD workflows.

Use of funding

Grant funding will support AI model development and training, security dataset curation, benchmarking, CI/CD engineering, inference infrastructure, developer tooling, testing, and documentation.

All funded work will directly support the improvement and practical adoption of Kann AI as a Solidity smart-contract security tool.

sections.heading: Out of scope

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
Kann Audits commits to making Kann AI a practical and accessible AI-assisted security tool for Ethereum developers while maintaining clear boundaries around proprietary technology and public deliverables.

Public access

Kann AI will remain publicly accessible through https://scan.kannaudits.com throughout the funded development period and for at least 6 months after completion of the final milestone, subject to reasonable usage limits, infrastructure capacity, and operational safeguards.

The improvements developed through this grant will be made available through the public Kann AI scanning platform.

Open-source commitments

We will publish relevant security evaluation methodology, benchmark results, and technical documentation so developers and security researchers can understand the system's capabilities and limitations.

Proprietary technology

The core Kann AI model weights, proprietary training methods, and privately curated vulnerability dataset will remain the intellectual property of Kann Audits.

We request an explicit exception to any grant requirement that would otherwise mandate publication of the underlying model weights or complete proprietary training dataset.

Where licensing, confidentiality, and security considerations permit, we will publish relevant research findings, benchmark artifacts, and supporting evaluation materials.

Maintenance

Kann Audits will maintain the publicly deployed Kann AI platform and funded CI/CD integrations for at least six months following acceptance of the final milestone. Maintenance will include reasonable bug fixes, operational support, and compatibility updates.

initiatives.title: Kleros x Seer: Open Risk Pricing for DeFi, a Public Price for Default Risk
initiatives.summary: A DeFi rating is one firm’s estimate of how likely an asset is to fail; the firm has no skin in the game, and nobody can take the other side. Seer prices that probability in an open prediction market, following Vitalik Buterin’s design for trading on many highly improbable events, and the result is a probability of default, free to read, so any lender or depositor can check it. The markets run on Ethereum Mainnet, open at Credora by RedStone's probability of default ratings and are settled by the Kleros oracle. They will also deploy on the Ethereum Economic Zone, a ZK rollup settling on Ethereum, once it is live.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Depositors and lenders lose money when an asset they hold or accept as collateral fails, and nothing liquid or transparent prices that risk. Here, an asset defaults under Credora’s definition: holders cannot redeem it for 14 days, or its reserves fall 1% or more short for 7 days. A hack counts when it causes either.

On 18 April 2026, an attacker forged a cross-chain message on KelpDAO’s rsETH bridge, which relied on a single verifier, took [about $292 million](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/kelpdao-bridge-exploit-april-2026/) of unbacked rsETH and borrowed real ETH against it, leaving Aave facing [$124 million to $230 million](https://www.coindesk.com/tech/2026/04/20/aave-could-face-up-to-usd230-million-in-losses-after-kelp-dao-bridge-exploit-triggers-defi-chaos) of bad debt. That verifier setting was readable on-chain: in an rsETH market, whoever noticed it could have been paid to price the risk higher, warning lenders and DeFi users before anything was lost.

A market pays for finding weaknesses: whoever spots a risk first profits by moving the price, and loses money if wrong. A protocol that reduces its risk sees its price fall, in public.

The price serves DeFi users comparing vaults before depositing, curators and lending protocols setting caps and collateral, insurers testing a rating’s probability of loss, and risk-scoring platforms, one of which has already asked to show it next to its own score.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
- [Clément](https://x.com/clesaege), Co-founder and CTO. Reviews the market mechanics.
- [0xAlex](https://x.com/alex__eth), Integration Lead. Leads this initiative.
- [JuanRah](https://x.com/JuanRah), Oracle Lead. Point of contact for this initiative.
- [Minh](https://github.com/nvm1410), Engineering, Seer. Builds the market and its interface.
- [Facundo](https://x.com/facundo_trotz), Legal. Drafts the default event rules that resolve the market.

Kleros and Seer pay the development costs; no other grant funds this work. Credora supplies the ratings.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
- The interface is live at [risk.seer.pm](https://risk.seer.pm) with its code in a [public repository](https://github.com/seer-pm/risk-pricing-ui).
- The mechanism is implemented. Each asset has a token paying out if it defaults, plus a "no default" token that pays out if no listed asset does.
- The interface shows Credora’s probability of default, fetched live through its API, next to the market’s, which moves with every trade.
- Seer and Kleros have run and settled markets with a similar stack. [Gitcoin's GG24 Deep Funding round](https://gov.gitcoin.co/t/deep-funding-gg24-web3-tooling-and-infra-round/25040) used Seer's markets to help allocate $350,000 across 98 open-source repositories.
- The user guides are [written and public](https://jagged-ironclad-e1b.notion.site/Default-Risk-Prediction-Markets-Beginner-User-Guide-35da95a2cc7d80fba056c16d17e99303).
- The default event rules are being finalized. With vague rules, traders price the risk of a dispute instead of the risk of failure, so every edge case, such as a failure that starts in one quarter and is confirmed in the next, is settled before trading starts. Kleros Court jurors apply these rules when a payout is disputed.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
A new market opens every quarter and asks which listed assets will default during that quarter, so a live price always exists and traders return each quarter. It lists 33 DeFi assets in 4 categories.

Liquidity is the hard part of any prediction market. The pool takes the other side of every trade, so when a better-informed trader moves the price, the pool has sold at the old price. A default costs most, because the pools sold that asset's default token cheaply before the news.

The grant asks $90,000 for liquidity. Each quarter's liquidity is deposited at the rating firm's probabilities, Credora's today, so no market opens at an exploitable price. Kleros Cooperative owns the positions and bears the impermanent loss.

In [Gitcoin's Deep Funding trial](https://gov.gitcoin.co/t/deep-funding-gg24-web3-tooling-and-infra-round/25040) on Seer, about 14% of $44,000 was lost this way, which the round's operators called "the cost to obtain information".

When each market settles, Kleros redeposits what remains in the next quarter's market, including after the program ends. The first milestone’s advance seeds the first quarter’s market with $15,000; the rest of the liquidity follows with the milestones, $20,000, $20,000 and $35,000, each deposited in the following quarter's market.

The grant also asks $10,000 for trading credits for DeFi risk teams and communities, vault curators, security researchers, and traders from earlier Seer markets, usable only in these risk markets.

Deliverables:
- An application to trade the probability of default of 33 DeFi assets, with the grant’s liquidity and trading credits deployed.
- A public API of current and historical market-implied probabilities that anyone can read without an account.
- A quarterly public report: each asset's opening and closing probability and whether it defaulted, plus volume, traders, cost of liquidity and every divergence from the rating, and what followed it.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown: Producing initial ratings (Credora does), underwriting cover, or any claim that a listed asset is safe.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- Grant funds go only to liquidity and trading credits.
- Kleros publishes its liquidity, trading and credits addresses, so third-party activity can be told apart on-chain.
- Kleros Cooperative maintains the markets, the public API and the report for 12 months after the final milestone at no further cost.
- The interface code is open source under the MIT license in its public repository.

initiatives.title: LeakDetectAI: Detecting and Eliminating Side-Channel Vulnerabilities in Ethereum Wallets and AI Agents
initiatives.summary: LeakDetectAI is an AI-powered security initiative that detects and helps eliminate side-channel vulnerabilities that can expose private keys, signing secrets, cryptographic operations, and sensitive transaction data across Ethereum wallets, protocols, and autonomous AI agents. The project will deploy LeakDetectAI in real-world Ethereum security workflows, working directly with ecosystem developers and maintainers to identify, reproduce, and remediate vulnerabilities. Its success will be measured through independently verifiable adoption, maintainer-accepted vulnerabilities, merged fixes, and regression tests across the Ethereum ecosystem.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Ethereum wallets, protocols, and autonomous AI agents handle sensitive information, including private keys, signing secrets, cryptographic operations, and transaction data. Yet timing variations and other side-channel signals can expose this information even when software behaves as designed. Conventional security testing often overlooks these vulnerabilities because it focuses on functional correctness rather than unintended information leakage.

LeakDetectAI closes this gap by bringing AI-powered side-channel detection into real-world Ethereum security workflows. It enables developers and security teams to identify and reproduce hidden vulnerabilities, validate fixes, and introduce regression tests that prevent them from returning. This makes it possible to detect and remediate security weaknesses that conventional testing may miss, strengthening the protection of Ethereum wallets, protocols, and AI agents.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
LeakDetectAI is led by Manu Gupta, Project Lead, and Dr. Pritha Gupta, Research Lead. Together, they bring complementary experience in open-source infrastructure, decentralized systems, AI, cryptography, side-channel analysis, and automated security testing.

Manu Gupta: Project Lead | Open-Source Security and P2P Maintainer
Manu brings over 20 years of open-source engineering experience, with a track record spanning decentralized networking, cryptographic infrastructure, distributed systems, and security engineering. He is a Technical Lead and Maintainer in the libp2p ecosystem and has contributed to IPFS, IPLD, and Multiformats, including work across Go, Rust, JavaScript, and Python implementations, interoperability, protocol specifications, and network security. For LeakDetectAI, he leads project delivery, Ethereum and wallet ecosystem integration, open-source development, adoption by external projects, and coordination with maintainers to turn identified vulnerabilities into verified fixes.
Profile: https://github.com/seetadev

Dr. Pritha Gupta: Adoption and Research Lead | AI, Cryptography and Side-Channel Security
Dr. Pritha Gupta brings research experience in AI, cryptography, side-channel analysis, and automated security testing, including work associated with Ruhr-Universität Bochum and Software Innovation Campus Paderborn. She leads the technical methodology underpinning LeakDetectAI, including adversarial inference experiments, machine-learning and neural architecture search (NAS) pipelines, detection methodology, and security benchmarks. She also supports the translation of research capabilities into reproducible testing workflows and practical adoption by wallet and agent developers.
Research profile: https://sec4ai-ai4sec.github.io/

Existing funding and technical foundation
LeakDetectAI has previously received community support through the Giveth / Ethereum Security Quadratic Funding round, including community contributions and matching-pool support. This provides an initial community-backed funding foundation. The present request is for dedicated funding to support Ethereum ecosystem adoption, integrations, remediation engineering, and verification of security improvements. No additional grant amount or funding commitment is being represented here beyond that community support.

The initiative builds on existing side-channel analysis and automated security-testing work, including AutoSCA, developed in the context of Achelos. AutoSCA demonstrates the practical application of automated analysis and machine learning to identify cryptographic side-channel vulnerabilities, including Bleichenbacher-style TLS vulnerabilities. The underlying research direction is documented in the ACM AISec paper, Automated Detection of Side Channels in Cryptographic Protocols: DROWN the ROBOTs! LeakDetectAI extends this technical direction to Ethereum wallets, transaction signing, hardware-wallet workflows, and AI-agent applications.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
LeakDetectAI has an existing open-source foundation in automated side-channel analysis, machine-learning-based leakage detection, and hardware-wallet security testing. This is not a proposal to build side-channel analysis from scratch: the team has already published and made available the underlying research code and experimentation infrastructure. Public work includes:

Hardware-wallet testing and Ethereum/Web3 security: https://github.com/SEC4AI-AI4SEC/autosca-hw-wallet-tester 
The active development repository for automated side-channel security testing, including hardware-wallet analysis.

Deep-learning side-channel analysis: https://github.com/SEC4AI-AI4SEC/deep-learning-sca
An existing research and reproducibility codebase for automated side-channel analysis.

Quantitative information-leakage detection: https://github.com/SEC4AI-AI4SEC/AutoMLQuantILDetect 
An existing package applying AutoML and information-theoretic methods to detect and quantify leakage.

Project resources and demonstrations: LeakDetectAI project github site, project dashboard and and public research discussions: 
https://github.com/SEC4AI-AI4SEC/deep-learning-sca/discussions/3 and https://x.com/libp2p/status/2119770702907871743 

Partners: https://leak-detect-tooling.lovable.app/#partners 
Giveth Update: https://leak-detect-tooling.lovable.app/#giveth 
Devcon Update: https://leak-detect-tooling.lovable.app/devcon 
 
Prior ecosystem validation: LeakDetectAI was selected for the Ethereum Security Quadratic Funding round, with support from Giveth and TheDAO Security Fund. The selection and community discussion are publicly documented at https://x.com/manusheel/status/2054083699298472238 and https://github.com/SEC4AI-AI4SEC/deep-learning-sca/discussions/3 

The grant is priced below a from-scratch build because it reuses existing research, code, experimental methods, and testing infrastructure rather than funding the development of foundational side-channel analysis and AutoML capabilities again. The requested work is the focused next step: adapting and validating these capabilities against Ethereum wallet and agent threat models, building reproducible Ethereum-specific benchmarks, and working with ecosystem projects to turn findings into verified fixes and regression tests. The existing repositories provide a starting point; the Ethereum-specific integrations, validation, and adoption outcomes remain the work to be delivered by this grant.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
LeakDetectAI will deliver the adoption of an open-source security testing and remediation capability across Ethereum wallets, hardware wallets, AI-agent frameworks, and Layer 2 ecosystems. The funding will support the integration of LeakDetectAI into the actual security-testing and development workflows of participating projects, collaboration with their maintainers to identify and reproduce exploitable side-channel weaknesses, and engineering support to implement and verify fixes. The central deliverable is not simply a tool that detects potential information leakage, but demonstrable security improvements in Ethereum projects that use it.

Adoption will be pursued across six areas. First, LeakDetectAI will be adopted for desktop, mobile, and hardware-wallet security testing, covering real-world key-management, transaction-signing, and authorization workflows. The work will engage relevant wallet developers and hardware-wallet testing environments to identify reproducible weaknesses, provide actionable remediation guidance, and support fixes and regression tests. Second, the existing Ethereum field deployments, including the Ethereum Layer 1 and 2 based hardware-wallet testing workflow using Ledger, will be used to apply LeakDetectAI in practical environments. The objective is to translate findings from these deployments into documented, actionable security improvements in the participating applications and their associated workflows.

Third, adoption will extend across Ethereum agent and protocol ecosystems, including relevant teams and applications within Optimism and Arbitrum. LeakDetectAI will be applied to agent execution, transaction authorization, signing, and protocol-integrated workflows, with participating developers supported in reproducing and remediating confirmed weaknesses. Fourth, we will work with Ethereum wallet developers, with prospective targets including MetaMask, Rabby Wallet, and Safe, to identify side-channel vulnerabilities affecting wallet security and support maintainers in implementing fixes. Fifth, we will engage Ethereum agent-framework developers, with prospective targets including Coinbase AgentKit and ElizaOS, to identify weaknesses in agent execution and transaction workflows and support code-level remediation and regression testing. These are prospective adoption targets, not confirmed commitments; engagement and remediation will be pursued in coordination with the relevant maintainers.

The sixth area will consolidate these efforts into ecosystem-wide adoption and verified security remediation. We target adoption by at least three named Ethereum wallet or agent-framework projects and at least three implemented security improvements in participating codebases, including wallet and agent-framework environments. Each counted improvement must be linked to a reproducible weakness identified through LeakDetectAI and supported by verifiable evidence of remediation, such as a merged patch, released fix, downstream code change, or equivalent maintainer-confirmed implementation, together with a regression test or repeatable validation showing that the weakness has been addressed. Deliverables will include documented integrations, vulnerability reproduction reports, remediation records, regression tests, and a public adoption report, subject to responsible-disclosure requirements.

The $60,000 requested will fund the adoption work required to achieve these outcomes: deployment and testing across desktop, mobile, and hardware-wallet environments; integration into existing Ethereum field deployments; engagement with Ethereum and Layer 2 agent and protocol teams; direct collaboration with wallet and agent-framework maintainers; vulnerability reproduction and remediation support; implementation of security fixes and regression tests; and independent verification and documentation of the resulting improvements. Of the total request, $50,000 (Milestones B to D) pays only on outside teams using LeakDetectAI and merging its fixes. This allocation will support the engineering effort and maintainer coordination needed to move identified vulnerabilities through to implemented fixes.

The success of the initiative will be measured by security improvements in real Ethereum projects, rather than downloads, user counts, demonstrations, or the number of testing runs. By completion, participating projects will have used LeakDetectAI to identify actionable side-channel weaknesses and address them through implemented fixes and regression tests. This will make Ethereum safer by reducing opportunities for attackers to exploit observable execution behaviour to infer sensitive information, strengthening the protection of wallet keys and signing operations, improving transaction authorization security, and reducing the exposure of AI-agent workflows to side-channel attacks. All non-sensitive tooling, remediation guidance, and verification evidence will be published as reusable open-source resources so that other Ethereum developers can adopt the same protections.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
LeakDetectAI will not undertake general-purpose privacy research, academic research without a direct Ethereum security application, or the development of new foundational machine-learning or side-channel analysis algorithms unrelated to the project's defined objectives. The initiative is not intended to build a general-purpose privacy auditing platform, surveillance or user-monitoring system, or a commercial security product. It will not cover non-Ethereum ecosystems, or other unrelated blockchain networks; the scope is strictly limited to Ethereum, its Layer 2 ecosystems, and the wallets and agent frameworks serving them.

The grant will not fund the development of new wallets, blockchain protocols, consensus clients, agent frameworks, or general-purpose AI infrastructure. It will not include broad penetration-testing engagements, smart-contract auditing unrelated to the identified side-channel risks, formal verification of entire applications, or remediation of vulnerabilities outside the project's defined threat model. It will also not fund speculative vulnerability research that cannot be connected to a concrete Ethereum security risk or actionable remediation.

Finally, the project will not publicly disclose exploitable vulnerabilities before maintainers have had a reasonable opportunity to address them. Sensitive findings, exploit details, and affected code will be handled through responsible-disclosure processes. Funding is specifically for the development and application of Ethereum-focused detection capabilities, vulnerability validation, maintainer-supported remediation, and independently verifiable improvements to Ethereum wallet and agent security; activities outside these boundaries are excluded.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
LeakDetectAI commits to releasing all grant-funded, non-sensitive software, detection tooling, benchmark suites, test cases, documentation, and integration examples under an OSI-approved open-source license, preferably Apache-2.0, with source code and development history publicly available in the project's GitHub repositories. Any existing components with different licenses will retain their original licenses, and their licensing compatibility will be reviewed before integration. No grant-funded core functionality will be made exclusively available through a proprietary service.

We commit to maintaining the open-source repositories after the grant period, including preserving documentation, addressing critical bugs, reviewing community contributions, and keeping the detection and regression-testing infrastructure usable. We will make reasonable efforts to coordinate ongoing maintenance with the relevant Ethereum wallet, agent-framework, and open-source maintainers. The project will also document installation, testing, and integration procedures so that other developers can independently use and extend the work without depending on the original team.

For ecosystem adoption, we commit to pursuing the named targets MetaMask, Rabby, Trust Wallet, Safe, Coinbase AgentKit, and ElizaOS. The adoption objective is verified remediation in at least three named projects, including at least one Ethereum wallet and one agent framework. Evidence will consist of publicly verifiable issues, maintainer-reviewed fixes, merged pull requests or downstream commits, and regression tests, subject to responsible-disclosure requirements. These projects are pinned adoption targets for engagement and evaluation, not claimed partnerships or guaranteed commitments from their maintainers. Where a target has no reproducible vulnerability within the project's scope, or its maintainers decline participation, we will document the outcome and pursue another relevant Ethereum wallet or agent framework with equivalent adoption potential.

We are not requesting an exception to the open-source licensing or public-goods commitments. The only qualification is that existing third-party components retain their original licenses and security-sensitive vulnerability details may remain confidential until responsible disclosure permits publication. We will not use confidentiality as a reason to withhold non-sensitive grant-funded deliverables or the evidence needed to verify completed security improvements.

initiatives.title: mab.xyz: Reproducible Builds for the 12 Main Ethereum Clients
initiatives.summary:
Ethereum runs on client software such as Geth, Lighthouse and Prysm, which node operators download from each client's repositories.
Today, operators have to trust that each download was built from the public source code untampered.
This proposal aims to make the 12 main clients reproducible: anyone can rebuild a release from its source, and get exactly the same binary as the one in the repository.
We work with the client teams to achieve reproducibility, and we publish a webpage explaining how anyone can verify a release themselves.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
- **Who is safer:** validators and node operators who run official client releases, and the users who rely on them.
- **From what:** an attacker who breaks into a client team's build machine or release account and ships a tampered release, while the public source code still looks clean. The xz-utils backdoor in 2024 worked this way: the malicious code was only in the release files, not in the public repository [1].
- **What anyone can point to afterwards:** official client releases that rebuild from source to exactly the same file, the accepted fixes in each client's repository, and a public webpage that explains how to repeat the check.

We found no client whose official releases are checked by anyone outside its own team. Two clients check their own builds, some say their builds are reproducible without anyone verifying it, and the rest have done part of the work or none. No tampered client release is known so far. These clients secure all staked ETH.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
- [Vivi Andersson](https://github.com/vivi365), engineer: PhD student at KTH. Built Geth Rebuild, a tool that checks whether official Geth releases match their source code [2].
- [Sofia Bobadilla](https://sofiabobadilla.github.io/), coordinator and engineer: PhD student at KTH and member of mab.xyz, works on Ethereum and smart contract security.
- [Raphina Liu](https://github.com/Stamp9), engineer: PhD student at KTH. Took part in Ethereum Protocol Fellowship cohort 7.
- [Julien Malka](https://luj.fr/), engineer: postdoc at KTH. Studies build reproducibility across whole software distributions, and showed how one tampered build tool can infect an entire Linux distribution [8].
- [Martin Monperrus](https://www.monperrus.net/martin/), advisor: Professor of Software Technology at KTH.
- [Javier Ron](https://github.com/javierron), advisor: postdoc at KTH. Researches how running several different clients keeps Ethereum resilient [4].
- [Aman Sharma](https://github.com/algomaster99), engineer: PhD student at KTH. Studies why building the same software twice gives different files, and how to fix it [3].

Other funding: CHAINS, a KTH research project financed by the Swedish Foundation for Strategic Research, funds the PhD research of the four KTH students. It does not pay for this engineering work, so this grant pays for the engineers' time. The Ethereum Foundation funded our earlier research on client diversity [5].

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
Our team has already done this for Geth, the most used execution client, and has studied the problem at scale:

- **Geth:** Geth Rebuild checks whether an official Geth release matches its source code [2]. While building it, Vivi Andersson reported two problems to the Geth team: file paths from the build machine were left inside the release, and the wrong compiler version was used. The Geth team fixed its builds in 2024 and tagged her on the fix [6][7].
- **Attacks on build tools:** with Julien Malka, we showed that a single tampered build tool can silently spread to nearly all the software of a Linux distribution [8]. It is the kind of attack that hides in the build, not in the source code.
- **Java clients:** our published study of thousands of Java packages explains the common reasons builds differ and provides a tool that removes some of them [3]. The clients Besu and Teku are written in Java.

What is missing is the same work for the other 11 clients: finding what makes their releases differ and getting the fixes accepted. Some client teams have started on their own, such as Reth and Lighthouse [9][10], but none has yet reached an official release that anyone outside the team can rebuild and check.

**References:**

[1] Report of the xz-utils backdoor. https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2024/03/29/4

[2] Geth Rebuild: Verifiable Builds for Go Ethereum. https://www.diva-portal.org/smash/record.jsf?pid=diva2%3A1908608

[3] Causes and Canonicalization of Unreproducible Builds in Java. https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21679

[4] Proving and Rewarding Client Diversity to Strengthen Resilience of Blockchain Networks. https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.18401

[5] Ethereum Foundation 2024 Academic Grants. https://blog.ethereum.org/2025/01/17/academic-grants-recipients

[6] Geth issue on reproducible builds. https://github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/issues/28987

[7] Geth fix for reproducible builds. https://github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/pull/30321

[8] Trusting-Trust Attack against an Entire Linux Distribution through Binary Manipulation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24888

[9] Reth: reproducible build profile. https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/10459

[10] Lighthouse: reproducible builds. https://github.com/sigp/lighthouse/pull/6799

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- Fixes to each client's build process, so its official Linux release can be rebuilt exactly from source. We contribute them to the client's own repository.
- A public webpage that explains the work and, for each client, how anyone can verify a release themselves.
- Working with each client team until the fixes are accepted. This is where most of the effort goes.

By official release we mean the file operators download from the client's release page.

The 12 clients: Geth, Nethermind, Besu, Erigon, Reth and Nimbus-eth1 (execution), and Prysm, Lighthouse, Teku, Nimbus, Lodestar and Grandine (consensus).

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Reviewing the client source code itself. This work proves that a release matches its source, not that the source is free of bugs.
- Operating systems other than Linux.
- A service that rebuilds and checks every new release automatically (this is an initiative itself).
- L2 clients and validator tooling.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- MIT license for the webpage, the how-to guides and any scripts. Fixes use each client's own license.
- The fixes live in the client repositories, where the client teams maintain them.
- MAB maintains the webpage and the how-to guides for 12 months after the last milestone.

initiatives.title: mab.xyz: Reusable Security Workflows for Triage of Vulnerability Reports
initiatives.summary: This initiative will research, develop and validate reusable workflows for Ethereum vulnerability triage and patch validation. Rather than building another standalone AI security agent, we will investigate how existing tools, agent skills, automated checks and human review can support trustworthy decisions. Audit firms, bounty platforms and protocol teams will be able to adapt the open workflows to their own tools and infrastructure. Independent teams will test them on real security work.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
- **Who is safer:** Ethereum and L2 protocol users whose security teams must investigate reported vulnerabilities and assess proposed fixes.
- **From what:** False or inconclusive vulnerability reports, ineffective fixes, regressions that disrupt legitimate transactions, and new vulnerabilities introduced during repair.
- **What anyone can point to afterwards:** Openly documented workflows, reproducible evaluations on Ethereum incidents, and evidence that independent auditing teams used the workflows on real findings.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
- **Sofia Bobadilla, lead:** PhD student at KTH, member of CHAINS and mab.xyz, with expertise on smart contract security, particularly on exploit validation, automated vulnerability repair and transaction replay. Homepage: https://sofiabobadilla.github.io/
- **Martin Monperrus, advisor:** Professor of Software Technology at KTH and co-founder of mab.xyz. Homepage: https://www.monperrus.net/martin/

Other funding: WASP (Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation) and the Swedish Foundation for Strategic Research support Sofia's PhD research. This grant supports applied workflow research, portable implementation examples, reproducible evaluation and external adoption, distinct from the existing research funding.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
Our team has already published research and developed open tools addressing three stages of smart contract vulnerability response:

- **Behavior preservation:** PonDeReplay, our open-source replay framework, compares patched contract behavior with historical Ethereum transactions [1]. This mechanism is key for revealing unintended effects; for example, a tested guard that stops an attack on Yearn yDAI also blocks 88 legitimate keeper calls [2].
- **Exploit validation:** PoCo studies how AI agents turn vulnerability reports into runnable Foundry proofs of concept and how to verify that those tests actually demonstrate the reported issue [3].
- **Patch effectiveness:** Our study of automated smart contract fixes evaluated whether patches stopped real exploits, showing why passing conventional checks is not sufficient evidence of security [4].

These results are publicly available, and our work on exploit validation and automated repair has been peer-reviewed. Our findings have also informed AI-related guidance for Ethereum Foundation grants [5].

The missing piece is not another standalone agent or replay tool, but independently evaluated guidance for combining these checks in real audits. We will study which workflows improve decisions across different setups, where they fail, and when human review is necessary. We will publish reusable specifications, integration examples, and evidence of adoption by independent auditing teams.

**References:**

[1] PonDeReplay (open-source replay framework).
https://github.com/ASSERT-KTH/PonDeReplay

[2] Smart Contract Invariants Protect Against Cybercriminals.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13191

[3] PoCo: Agentic Proof-of-Concept Exploit Generation for Smart Contracts.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.02780

[4] Do Automated Fixes Truly Mitigate Smart Contract Exploits?
https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.04600

[5] Ethereum PhD Fellowship on AI-Powered Protocol Security: Research, Auditing, and Vulnerability Detection.
https://web.archive.org/web/20260211213355/https://esp.ethereum.foundation/rounds/phdfp26/phdfp-rfpd1

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- Workflow specifications for three decisions: whether a vulnerability is reproducible, whether a patch stops the exploit while preserving expected behavior, and whether a patch introduces security regressions.
- Explicit inputs, outputs, verification steps, uncertainty states, escalation criteria and evidence formats for each workflow.
- Portable agent skills and reference examples that can be adapted to different models, agent frameworks, and existing auditor toolchains.
- Reproducible empirical evaluation on public Ethereum cases, including failure analysis and comparisons with existing individual-tool approaches.
- Hands-on integration and feedback with independent audit firms and security teams using real Ethereum or L2 findings.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Building a hosted service or requiring teams to adopt one agent framework or vendor.
- Guaranteeing that all workflows outperform existing practice; negative and inconclusive findings will be documented.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- MIT for code and agent skills; CC BY 4.0 for workflow specifications, public benchmarks and published evaluation results.
- Sofia Bobadilla will maintain the published reference materials and fix reproducibility-breaking issues for 18 months after the final milestone.
- Public benchmarks will use public incidents. Confidential adopter cases can be validated using redacted evidence supplied to the independent technical reviewer.

initiatives.title: Nethermind: Formally Verified EVM for Ethereum
initiatives.summary: Nethermind will extend LeanCIL to verify the Amsterdam EVM in its zkVM guest. The proof will link Ethereum's rules in Lean to compiled .NET CIL and optimised RISC-V. Nethermind will check EthLib definitions before reuse and publish proofs tied to the guest's exact build, identifying methods shared with the regular client. Adoption requires two independent operators publishing mainnet block proofs for 30 consecutive days and 20% of observed Ethereum execution nodes running a release with the shared methods.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
A zkVM proves that a guest program ran. It cannot show whether the program implements Ethereum correctly. Wrong opcode results, gas charges or state updates can produce valid proofs of invalid Ethereum results. Bugs in EVM code shared with the regular client may also affect ordinary nodes.

Nethermind will prove its Amsterdam EVM against an independently reviewed Lean specification, through CIL and optimised RISC-V. The team will check EthLib definitions against Ethereum specifications and fixtures before reuse. A public manifest will identify proved methods that also appear unchanged in regular-client builds. The proof excludes production-only methods and JIT-generated code.

LeanCIL could also help verify C# components of other Ethereum projects. Nethereum provides .NET libraries for transaction signing, wallets and EVM interaction, alongside tooling for Solidity development in VS Code. Applying LeanCIL to Nethereum would require separate work beyond this grant.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
- **Ben Adams, Principal Engineer (LeanCIL & Nethermind):** Nethermind EVM, state and zkVM contributor; co-author of 15 Core EIPs; .NET runtime and ASP.NET Core contributor; twelve-time Microsoft MVP. Leads compiled CIL proofs. [Contributions](https://github.com/NethermindEth/nethermind/pulls?q=is%3Apr+is%3Amerged+author%3Abenaadams) · [LeanCIL](https://github.com/NethermindEth/LeanCIL).
- **Maxim Menshikov, Senior Engineer (il2rv64):** Security researcher and .NET Runtime contributor with completed doctoral studies focused on abstract interpretation and model checking of real-world applications. Developer of Nethermind’s [bflat-riscv64](https://github.com/NethermindEth/bflat-riscv64) compiler supporting ZisK, SP1 and OpenVM. Leads machine-code refinement proofs. [Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=pSDXCfIAAAAJ&hl=en) · [GitHub](https://github.com/maximmenshikov).
- **Julian Sutherland, PhD, Head of Formal Verification (EVMYulLean):** Imperial College London PhD, with publications at ECOOP, ESOP and ACM TOPLAS. Leads the Amsterdam semantics work. [Imperial profile](https://vtss.doc.ic.ac.uk/people/sutherland.html) · [EVMYulLean](https://github.com/NethermindEth/EVMYulLean).
- **Łukasz Rozmej, Ethereum Core Developer:** Nethermind contributor and AllCoreDevs participant. Reviews Amsterdam requirements and shared EVM integration. [GitHub](https://github.com/LukaszRozmej) · [Contributions](https://github.com/NethermindEth/nethermind/pulls?q=is%3Apr+is%3Amerged+author%3ALukaszRozmej).

Previous Ethereum Foundation funding supported Cancun formalisation.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
LeanCIL is being built to verify compiled .NET code, including Nethermind's EVM. It proves supported CIL methods and composes contracts. Its instruction model, runtime support and proof automation do not yet cover the full EVM. This grant funds the missing capabilities and the EVM proofs.

EVMYulLean and `il2rv64` provide starting points for the other proof stages. EthLib defines and proves EVM rules in Lean, with some Amsterdam gaps. Nethermind will review these components before reuse, reducing duplicate work.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- Extend EVMYulLean to Amsterdam using reviewed EthLib definitions and lemmas. Check fork rules, gas charges and state changes against Ethereum specifications and fixtures.
- Extend LeanCIL for the CIL instructions and .NET runtime behaviour reached by the EVM. Bind proofs to method bytes and metadata, automate checks and prove all reachable EVM-owned methods.
- Extend `il2rv64` to prove that the optimised RISC-V code matches the compiled CIL, then compose the refinement proofs.
- Prove precompile dispatch, gas charges, return data and failures under explicit contracts, excluding their algorithms.
- Publish proofs, coverage, assumptions, build identities and comparisons of proved methods shared with the regular client.
- Measure independent Ethereum nodes running a release containing those methods.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Formal verification of the entire regular Nethermind EVM or its JIT-generated code. Production CIL that differs from the guest is excluded.
- Precompile algorithms, the full stateless guest, witness and SSZ processing, tries, block orchestration and zkVM provers.
- Completion of LeanCIL for arbitrary .NET programs, all EthLib modules, other clients, L2 plug-ins or native targets.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- Publish all Nethermind-owned project code, specifications and proofs for LeanCIL, EVMYulLean and `il2rv64` under dual MIT OR Apache-2.0 licensing, at the user's choice. Record the pinned EthLib revision; reused upstream EthLib code retains its CC0-1.0 licence.
- Nethermind will maintain LeanCIL and the EVM correctness proofs after the grant and update coverage for later Ethereum forks.
- Prove the complete Amsterdam zkVM EVM, including precompile invocation, and publish trusted assumptions and external contracts.
- Review reused EthLib components and report discrepancies, test results and proof assumptions separately from evidence of Ethereum conformance.
- Describe regular-client benefits only for identical, proof-covered methods. Exclude duplicate node observations and known Nethermind-operated nodes from adoption counts.
