initiatives.title: NorthScan: DPRK IT Worker Screening for the Ethereum Ecosystem
initiatives.summary: NorthScan will provide approved Ethereum organizations with a controlled service for screening GitHub profiles for behavioral, identity and network signals associated with DPRK IT worker activity. The six-month pilot will combine automated assessments with selected human review, practical integration resources and measurable adoption across the ecosystem. The grant will also validate a sustainable freemium and paid-access model for trusted organizations.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Ethereum organizations often evaluate remote contributors through fragmented checks that miss coordinated GitHub activity, fabricated professional identities and network patterns associated with DPRK IT worker operations. General KYC and background-check services rarely provide this GitHub-specific threat context.

After this pilot, approved organizations will be able to submit a public GitHub profile before hiring, funding or granting technical access and receive a structured, evidence-based assessment with confidence levels and selected human review. This will support better-informed decisions while treating the results as risk signals rather than definitive attribution.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
NorthScan is led by Heiner García Pérez, an independent cyber threat intelligence researcher specializing in DPRK IT worker activity, OSINT, HUMINT, financial crime and GitHub-based investigations. Heiner will lead the research, product direction, screening methodology, pilot operations, human reviews and participant support. Limited specialist support may be contracted for discrete engineering or infrastructure tasks, but Heiner remains accountable for every milestone.

Relevant work and track record:

* NorthScan: https://northscan.co/
* About NorthScan: https://northscan.co/about
* The GitHub Diaries: https://northscan.co/articles/github-diaries
* ANY.RUN investigation, Part 1: https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/lazarus-group-it-workers-investigation/
* ANY.RUN investigation, Part 2: https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/lazarus-group-it-workers-investigation-part-two/
* Insomni’hack presentation: https://insomnihack.ch/talks/smile-youre-on-camera-livestreaming-from-north-koreas-it-workers-laptop-farm/
* Security Alliance contribution: https://radar.securityalliance.org/from-north-korean-it-workers-to-it-recruiters/

NorthScan previously received approximately $2,000 in community funding through Giveth and TheDAO Security Fund. The remaining development and research have primarily been self-funded, and there is no other committed funding for the work described in this proposal.

NorthScan owns and operates the private screening platform, intelligence registry and detection methodology used for this initiative. ANY.RUN and BCA LTD were research collaborators on the linked investigations but are not recipients of this grant. NorthScan does not own or maintain GitHub, Giveth, TheDAO, ANY.RUN or Security Alliance codebases, and no external organization named above controls the proposed service.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
NorthScan is not starting from a concept. A working private intelligence platform already stores and connects GitHub accounts, public commit-email observations, sources and provenance; performs GitHub profile lookups; preserves profile snapshots; maps follower and following networks; identifies network communities and evidence similarities; and supports analyst review and exportable assessments. The underlying database, investigative rules and detection logic are private, but designated TheDAO curators can receive a supervised live walkthrough without receiving access to the source code or intelligence database.

This foundation was developed from more than two years of direct research into DPRK IT worker operations. Public evidence of that work includes:

* NorthScan research: https://northscan.co/
* The GitHub Diaries: https://northscan.co/articles/github-diaries
* ANY.RUN investigation, Part 1: https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/lazarus-group-it-workers-investigation/
* ANY.RUN investigation, Part 2: https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/lazarus-group-it-workers-investigation-part-two/
* Security Alliance contribution: https://radar.securityalliance.org/from-north-korean-it-workers-to-it-recruiters/

The grant therefore pays to harden and adapt an existing research platform into a controlled screening service: secure API access, documentation, a lightweight SDK, pilot operations, selected human review and adoption validation. The $50,000 price is below a from-scratch build because the core platform, intelligence corpus, investigative methodology and working GitHub-analysis workflows already exist. Public release of the internal codebase, database or detection logic is not included because these are NorthScan’s core security and investigative assets.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
* A secure, access-controlled screening API for approved organizations. It will accept a public GitHub username or profile URL and return a structured JSON assessment containing relevant behavioral, identity and network signals, supporting evidence and confidence levels.

* Secure pilot infrastructure, including API-key authentication, rate limiting, usage logging, credential revocation, persistent database hosting and a documented process for escalating selected assessments to human review.

* Public integration resources: API documentation, JSON schema, synthetic examples and a lightweight open-source SDK that participating organizations can use from their own environments.

* A controlled pilot with at least 10 independent Ethereum ecosystem organizations, at least 100 non-test profile assessments and at least 10 participant-submitted cases receiving human analyst review.

* Demonstrated technical adoption, with at least five participating organizations using the documented API or SDK from their own environments and at least three participants providing documented feedback.

* A whitelisted freemium model for trusted organizations, including a small allowance of free screenings, proposed paid tiers and access safeguards.

* Commercial validation of the service, including a concise sustainability plan and evidence of initial organizations paying for screening capacity.

* A concise public GitHub screening guide describing defensive indicators and appropriate interpretation of results without disclosing NorthScan’s private detection logic, database or sensitive intelligence.

The funding pays for engineering and security hardening, hosting and database infrastructure, API and SDK development, documentation, pilot onboarding and support, human analyst time, participant coordination, and validation of a sustainable operating model beyond the grant.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
* No public dashboard or unsupervised access to NorthScan’s internal intelligence platform.

* No public release of NorthScan’s private source code, intelligence database, detection rules, scoring methodology or sensitive investigative material.

* No ATS, HRIS, KYC provider, identity-verification or background-check integration during this grant.

* No access to private GitHub accounts or repositories, compromised credentials or non-public platform data. Assessments use publicly available information.

* No mass collection or enrichment of personal information, broad email discovery, wallet tracing or continuous monitoring of every assessed profile.

* No public bulk IOC feed or commitment to produce recurring threat-intelligence reports. Public reporting is limited to the concise screening guide and approved aggregate pilot findings.

* No unlimited human investigations. Human review is limited to the cases specified in the milestones.

* No automated hiring rejection, legal determination or definitive attribution of a person to the DPRK. NorthScan provides evidence-based risk signals to support decisions made by participating organizations.

* No 24/7 incident-response service, guaranteed detection of every DPRK IT worker or guaranteed prevention of infiltration.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
Licensing

* The lightweight client SDK and synthetic integration examples will be published under the MIT License.
* The API documentation, JSON schema and public GitHub screening guide will be published under CC BY 4.0.
* Published materials will remain publicly accessible after the grant.

Maintenance

* NorthScan will maintain the published SDK, documentation and examples for at least 12 months after the final milestone, including critical security, compatibility and documentation fixes.
* The hosted screening service will remain available to approved organizations for at least six months after the final milestone while the validated freemium and paid-access model supports longer-term operation.
* This maintenance commitment does not include major new features, unlimited screenings, unlimited human investigations or 24/7 support.

Pinned targets

The milestone amounts and acceptance targets are fixed as submitted. In particular, the adoption payment remains conditional on evidence of at least 10 participating organizations, 100 non-test assessments, 10 human-reviewed cases, five organizations using the API or SDK from their own environments, documented feedback from three participants, and at least three participating organizations purchasing additional screening capacity at the published pilot price.

Requested exception

NorthScan’s internal platform source code, intelligence database, detection rules, scoring methodology and sensitive investigative material will remain private and proprietary. The hosted API will remain restricted to approved organizations rather than becoming permissionless or publicly accessible, because unrestricted access could expose investigative methods, enable evasion or create privacy and abuse risks.

initiatives.title: OKcontract: Onchain Risk Map, an Open Operational Incident Graph for Ethereum Security
initiatives.summary:
Onchain Risk Map converts documented security incidents into reusable evidence for
Ethereum builders. It maps failures across software delivery, wallets, signing, account
authorization, infrastructure, and execution using typed relationships and explicit
evidence confidence.
This grant will fund an open, versioned Ethereum dataset with at least 30 independently
reviewed incidents, 30 defensive-control assessments, and tools for comparing failures.
External use will be documented through public work products from at least six
organizations.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Ethereum applications depend on interacting technical and operational systems.
A security failure can begin in a software dependency or operator session, alter
transaction construction, pass through legitimate signing, and reach onchain execution.
Understanding those relationships is necessary to design effective protections.

Historical incident reports contain valuable evidence, but comparing them requires
repeated interpretation of terminology, system boundaries, causes, and consequences.
Onchain Risk Map will share that work through a maintained reference model and
reproducible dataset.
Auditors, wallet developers, projects, and incident responders will be able to find
comparable incidents, inspect affected trust boundaries, and assess proposed defenses.
The scope addresses wallet experience, smart contract security, infrastructure, and
incident response in the Ethereum Foundation’s linked Trillion Dollar Security report.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
OKcontract Labs initiated the project and owns the existing package.
Proposed responsibilities and person-month allocations are:

- Ida Swarczewskaja, proposer and project manager: coordination, user research, and
  external adoption, 2 person-months.
  OKcontract Labs co-founder, previously Head of UX/UI at Mirakl.
  [Track record](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/opa-up-and/9781449328849/author_bios.html).
- Shahaf Nacson, security contributor: incident analysis, account authorization, and
  control assessment, 2 person-months.
  Co-author of ERC-4337, formerly with the Ethereum Foundation.
  [Track record](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-4337).
- Henri Binsztok, technical lead: schemas, tooling, and releases, 1
  person-months. OKcontract Labs co-founder, previously at WALLIX.
  [Track record](https://github.com/wallix/awless/blob/master/README.md).
- Anonymous contributor, former academic researcher, 1 person-month.

No external funding for this scope has been reported.
No previously funded milestone or companion-project cost is included in this request.
The team will benefit from using the dataset in its own security tooling; that internal
use is excluded from adoption counts.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
The [public preview](https://map.okcontract.com) provides the starting point.
OKcontract Labs’ existing package includes typed topology definitions, incident
annotations, source snapshots, explicit merge and exclusion decisions, catalog
validation, and deterministic generators.
The source package is currently private.

The grant pays for publication, stronger provenance, independent review, and external
use. Completed prototype work is excluded from the budget.
A from-scratch build would also need to create the existing model, catalog, and
generators. The first milestone makes these foundations publicly inspectable through a
versioned source release.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
1. Publish the graph specification: node and relationship semantics, incident surface
   roles, confidence levels, and primary-cause assessment rules.
   Include JSON schemas, TypeScript interfaces, migration guidance, and examples.
   Distinguish architectural relationships, observed incident relationships, and analyst
   hypotheses.
2. Strengthen provenance and incident identity.
   Attach references and review rationale to individual surface, relationship, and cause
   assertions. Record reviewer identities, dates, disagreements, and corrections.
   Normalize chain identifiers and support multiple transactions per incident.
   Separate source observations from canonical incidents to prevent duplicate incident
   counts and loss totals.
3. Publish a reviewed Ethereum L1 and L2 corpus spanning contract exploitation, signing
   deception, supply-chain compromise, governance, custody, bridges, and delegated
   authorization. Publish selection criteria and coverage gaps.
   Preserve unknown and disputed findings.
4. Assess defensive controls, including transaction verification, restricted delegation,
   release integrity, independent approval channels, and upgrade restrictions.
   Record enforcement location, assumptions, and whether each control prevents, detects,
   or limits the failure mechanism.
   Separate demonstrated protection from hypothetical applicability.
5. Release downloadable datasets, a query CLI, executable examples, and a small
   reference viewer. Publish mappings to [OAK identifiers](https://onchainattack.org/)
   and a field-level
   [STIX 2.1](https://docs.oasis-open.org/cti/stix/v2.1/os/stix-v2.1-os.html)
   compatibility note, including unmapped fields.
   Link available upstream exploit reproductions.
   Include machine-readable query outputs for defensive AI-agent workflows.
6. Recruit external users, support use in their work, and compare source-only and
   graph-assisted workflows.
   The grant covers onboarding, workflow support, evaluation design, and public evidence
   collection. Publish completion time, factual errors, missing evidence, and feedback,
   including neutral or adverse results.

The planning budget is $42,000 for 7 person-months at $6,000, $6,000 for independent
incident review and technical verification, and $2,000 for hosting and releases.
Milestone allocations are: specification, $9,000 labor, $2,000 review, $1,000
operations; corpus and tools, $9,000 labor, $3,000 review; viewer and handoff, $8,000
labor, $1,000 operations; adoption, $16,000 labor and $1,000 evidence verification.
These are planning allowances.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
Exhaustive incident coverage, live monitoring, emergency response, newly developed

initiatives.title: Onay: Local signing companion
initiatives.summary:
Ethereum is built to be verifiable, and verification is cheap. Yet most users still sign transactions without independently checking what they are approving. A second sanity check on the tx is a low-hanging fruit and Onay makes that second check seamless: it verifies the transaction locally, explains what it does, and lets the user compare against their wallet before signing.

Onay is a local desktop app with a thin browser extension that sits between the dapp and the wallet. It intercepts the signing request, verifies chain state through an embedded Helios light client, recompiles and verifies the source code locally, simulates the transaction, renders its intent in readable form with ERC-7730 clear signing, and finally displays the ERC8213 calldata digest for an equivalence check.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Ethereum is built around verification. In practice, transaction signing still depends heavily on blind trust.

Before approving a transaction, a user typically trusts an RPC for chain state, a verification service or explorer for the ABI, the dapp for what the action means, and often a remote tx simulator for what the transaction will do. The wallet eventually asks the user to approve bytes, but the context that makes those bytes understandable usually comes from external systems, if it comes at all.

Independent verification is already possible, easy, and cheap. So why not add a second or third factor check to what you are about to sign, and check if they agree on everything? We are used to have 2FA in every parts of our lives but not in the most sensitive step in crypto.

The problem is usability. Doing it properly today means stitching together several tools and manual checks, so almost nobody does it for ordinary transactions. 

Onay turns that into a second sanity check that can run on every signing request. It independently reconstructs the facts the user needs before approving: the chain state, the code actually deployed, the contracts reached during execution, and the human-readable intent of the transaction. 

The application does not hold any keys and is view only. So it can safely leverage a multitude of services and display any information that will enrich the signing process. It does this locally, without replacing the wallet or taking custody of keys. 

This gives hardware-wallet users, multisig signers, treasury operators, and ordinary Ethereum users a practical way to compare what a dapp is asking them to sign against an independently verified view.

Ethereum already makes verification possible. Onay makes it easy enough to actually use.

Onay puts every security-relevant fact through the user's own machine, or highlights what’s missing:

- Chain state is proof-verified by a local Helios client where the chain supports it (Ethereum, the OP Stack family, Linea), and read from an RPC the user chooses everywhere else, with a permanent notice about the trust that implies.
- Sourcify's verification claim is not trusted blindly. The app downloads the sources, recompiles them with the pinned solc binary, and compares the result byte for byte with the on-chain code.
- The transaction runs in a local EVM to reconstruct the call tree, so every contract it touches goes through the two checks above, and ERC-7730 descriptors turn the verified ABI into readable intent. It does full ABI decoding with NatSpec comments when clear-signing is not possible.
- After confirmation the app shows the ERC-8213 digest. A wallet that implements the standard shows the same hash, which proves the wallet received exactly the bytes the user reviewed, and that the dapp or the transport was not compromised in between.

Afterwards a multisig signer, a treasury operator or any hardware wallet user can check what they sign with no trusted intermediary and no hosted service.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
**Sourcify** does the work: Manuel Wedler, Kaan Uzdogan and Marco Castignoli, all full-stack developers on the Sourcify team, which runs the verification service and its libraries (lib-sourcify, the clear-signing library) at a scale of millions of requests. Sourcify is part of the Argot Collective.

Track record: 
- https://sourcify.dev
- https://github.com/argotorg/sourcify
- https://github.com/manuelwedler
- https://github.com/kuzdogan
- https://github.com/marcocastignoli.

Relationships to codebases named here: the team maintains Sourcify, lib-sourcify as well as the ERC-7730 clear-signing library and the ethereum/clear-signing-erc7730-registry repo that Onay recompiles and renders with.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
A working prototype exists and anyone can run it: https://github.com/sourcifyeth/project-independence, a Tauri desktop app with an embedded Helios light client, the local Sourcify verification gate, proxy and diamond resolution, ERC-7730 clear signing, local EVM simulation, Ledger signing, post-mining verification, activity history and an address book. The browser build runs at https://explorer.sourcify.app against live contracts on mainnet.

The prototype was written quickly to prove the idea end to end and none of its code is trusted as-is. We received positive feedback from our close circle of external stakeholders and want to continue shipping this into production.

The rebuild plan, the full UX mock of release 1 with fake data, and the transport design (native messaging with encrypted pairing) are done. Two of the four libraries the verifier depends on, lib-sourcify and the clear-signing library, are the team's own code.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
Release 1 is the transaction verifier. This grant pays for:

- **The extension.** A hand-written, zero-dependency script that wraps the page's EIP-1193 provider, catches eth_sendTransaction and signing requests, and forwards them to the app over native messaging. The host manifest allows only this extension, the channel is sealed with X25519 keys exchanged on first approval, and the app verifies the browser binary before accepting.
- **The app.** Helios light-client state for supported chains and user-chosen RPC state for every other EVM chain, the local EVM call-tree reconstruction, the local verification gate over every contract in the tree, ERC-7730 rendering, the confirm-or-reject review, and the ERC-8213 digest display after confirmation.
- **Other ways to input a transaction.** Not through the browser extension. Raw transactions, calldata and EIP-712 payloads pasted by hand, and ERC-4527 animated QR codes from air-gapped wallets (Keystone, OneKey, AirGap).
- **Supply-chain hardening.** Pinned and release-age-delayed dependencies, lifecycle scripts disabled, cargo-deny and cargo-vet, Socket and OSV scans in CI, hash-checked solc binaries, reproducible extension builds diffable against the git tag, releases built only from CI, and a software bill of materials with every release.
- **Distribution.** Signed desktop builds, and the extension published on the Chrome Web Store.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Holding keys. The verifier never generates or hold the user's key; the user's wallet does.
- Any hosted service. Nothing runs on a server the team operates; Sourcify and the ERC-7730 registry are untrusted download sources that the app re-verifies.
- Effects preview (balance changes, storage writes, events), the transaction builder, Ledger signing, post-mining verification and the Firefox port. They belong to later releases.
- Non-EVM chains.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- License: the app, the extension and the relay published under GPL3, with the repository public from the first milestone.
- Maintenance: the Sourcify team maintains Onay after the last milestone as part of its tooling, for at least 12 months at no further cost.
- Pinned target: release 1 available for download, with the extension on the Chrome Web Store, within 6 months of the first payment.
- Analytics are off by default and switched on by one explicit toggle. They exist to measure usage for this grant (below) and for nothing else. They send only a random per-install id, the chain id and a verified-transaction counter, never an address, a transaction, an IP address or any personal data, and the aggregates are published on the public metrics page. The prompt that offers the toggle says exactly this.

We want this tool to be really used so the grant payout is heavily skewed on the adoption goals.

initiatives.title: Ostros: an open-source hardware wallet on CrossBar's security chip, against screen implants and blind signing
initiatives.summary: Ostros™ is CrossBar's hardware wallet, open from the chip to the apps. It runs on Daric, CrossBar's open-core RISC-V security chip, and the Rust-based Xous operating system. This grant adds chip attestation, clear signing, a recovery phrase a screen implant cannot read, an owner check that firmware and chip are genuine, an independent security review, and an app loader for outside security apps. The grant is paid out as wallets add Ostros support, owners verify their own devices, and outside teams build security apps on it.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
- **Screen implants.** In October 2026, Ledger confirmed a hidden implant in at least one device sold through a reseller. The implant read the recovery phrase off the Ledger device's screen during setup and sent it out over a mobile network. Reported losses exceed $86 million (BleepingComputer, Ledger).
- **Blind signing.** In February 2025, Bybit lost about $1.5 billion after its Safe signers approved a malicious upgrade they could not read on their devices (BlockSec).
- **No way to check.** Most hardware wallet owners cannot verify that their device runs the published firmware on a genuine chip.

After this grant, an Ostros owner creates a recovery phrase that a screen implant never sees in full, reads Ethereum transactions in plain language before signing, and confirms their firmware and chip are genuine.

This grant is one step toward a goal of a hardware wallet that owners can verify end to end, from an open-source chip through open software to a device they can open and inspect. CrossBar builds both the chip and the wallet, so this goal can be reached. Any hardware wallet can reuse the split recovery phrase method, the attestation design and the owner verification tool, the way distributions build on Linux. A follow-on initiative will (1) make the device openable, and (2) let owners inspect the chip inside their own wallet.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
CrossBar has developed ReRAM since 2008 and the Daric chip since 2021. It holds more than 200 patents and works with TSMC (chip manufacturing) and Foxconn (device design and assembly).

- **Mark Davis**, CEO, CrossBar: https://www.linkedin.com/in/mark-davis-16945b4/
- **Sung Hyun Jo**, CTO, CrossBar: https://www.linkedin.com/in/sunghyunjo/
- **Andrew "bunnie" Huang**, advisor; former Chief of Hardware Security at CrossBar; created IRIS chip inspection and co-created Xous: https://www.bunniestudios.com
- **Miriam Neubauer**, strategy, product and growth: https://www.linkedin.com/in/miriamneubauer/
- Plus more than 10 CrossBar engineers across chip design, hardware and firmware.

**Collaborators:** Nicolas Bacca (ZKNOX, co-founder and former CTO of Ledger, https://www.linkedin.com/in/nbasim/) develops the Ethereum signer Ostros runs and designed the split recovery phrase method. Nicolas is an ETHSecurity Badge holder. ZKNOX's own initiative (ZK Clear Signing) pays for different work, and ZKNOX does not count as an adopter. Sylvain Bellemare (Sureshot Labs) works on firmware and bootloaders: https://www.linkedin.com/in/sylvainbellemare/

**Other funding:** A previous Giveth round raised $20,047 from 147 contributors for SDK documentation and outreach. No other funder pays for this scope.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
- **The chip:** Daric, CrossBar's security chip with published RTL, SDK and documentation, features a 350 MHz RISC-V core with an MMU, 4 MB of ReRAM, crypto accelerators, a true random number generator, a key store, glitch sensors and a security mesh. Its post-quantum library (ML-DSA, ML-KEM) is NIST CAVP-validated on the RISC-V core.
- **The software:** Xous runs on Ostros with a fully open bootloader, core drivers, an e-ink UI, seed generation and key management. The firmware build is deterministic.
- **The Ethereum signer:** The shared Ethereum signer (https://github.com/ethereum/ethereum-app) runs on Ostros hardware with verifiable signing (ERC-8213), demoed at Devcon 8.
- **Developers:** The Founders Edition ships to developers in late November 2026, and teams have applied to build apps on it. At Devcon 8, 196 developers signed up for CrossBar's Dabao hackathon and picked up a free board with the same die, so they already use the RISC-V, Rust and Xous tools Ostros needs.
- **In use and openly reviewed:** Ostros builds on the open Xous environment (OS and secure boot), where findings from public reviews of the Daric die are fixed. The Baochip version of that die shipped in every DEF CON 34 badge (August 2026). At Devcon 8, CrossBar guided about 250 attendees one by one through IRIS inspections, on their own chip or on a demo chip.

The secure chip and the operating system already exist, so the grant covers the security features and their adoption.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- **Attestation:** Each Ostros can prove it carries a genuine Daric chip, set up in a new factory personalization flow. The split recovery phrase and the app loader both build on it.
  - Technical: A key generated inside the chip at personalization, checked against a published CrossBar root, as a per-device certificate or anonymous attestation (scheme chosen during the grant).
- **Clear signing:** Ostros shows Ethereum transactions in plain language (ERC-7730), or the verifiable digest (ERC-8213) when no descriptor exists.
- **Web companion:** Connects Ostros to any Ethereum app through WalletConnect.
  - Technical: USB or Bluetooth; the device decodes and displays each request itself, so the companion never decides what the owner sees.
- **Owner verification:** A public guide and tool to rebuild the firmware, match its hash and check the attestation.
- **Split recovery phrase:** Features a 24-word phrase: 12 words show on the Ostros screen and 12 go to the owner's computer over a connection the computer checks comes from a genuine Daric chip. An implant on the screen never sees the full phrase, so an attacker needs both an implant and malware on the computer (method by Nicolas Bacca, Devcon 8).
  - Technical: The computer accepts its 12 words only after checking that the session key is signed by the device's attestation key. The 12 words an implant could see leave more than 120 bits of the phrase unknown.
- **App loader and developer kit:** Outside teams install security apps without rebuilding the firmware, with an emulator and system API documentation.
  - Technical: Each app runs in its own Xous process, isolated by the MMU, under a permission model that limits what each app can reach.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Planned follow-on initiative: (1) the openable device, and (2) research into Daric chip inspection in the Ostros package.
- Drivers not needed for these features (power management, fingerprint, NFC, vibrator, LED), the app store website and MPC on the RISC-V core: CrossBar builds these with its own funds.
- Apps for other chains (Bitcoin and others).

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- Software under Apache 2.0; chip RTL and board design files under CERN-OHL-W, except the bus fabric, USB PHY and analog blocks, which do not process data.
- Pinned targets: Release firmware rebuilds bit-identically from source, the full recovery phrase never appears on the Ostros screen, and no secret is shared across devices.
- Ostros works with any Ethereum app and does not require a proprietary companion app.
- Public vulnerability disclosure process; fixes ship as signed, reproducible firmware.
- CrossBar maintains the grant deliverables for at least 12 months after the final milestone (security fixes, firmware updates, review of outside pull requests).
- CrossBar publishes the IRIS rig design, software and Devcon 8 reference images under open licenses.

initiatives.title: Owney: Trust and Security Assessment Framework for Agentic DeFi
initiatives.summary: Owney turns its Trust and Security Assessment Framework for DeFi agents (13 subcategories, 3 platforms assessed) into an open, machine-readable standard and a continuous assessment pipeline that agent platforms integrate with. Today no independent, public, versioned assessment tells depositors which agents are safe to use.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Autonomous agents move user liquidity across DeFi on Ethereum and its L2s. A model, a prompt, a hot key, an operator, every protocol touched: any one can lose the funds. Depositors (individuals and institutions) cannot tell a careful agent from a reckless one.

No agent has lost user funds yet. But during the KelpDAO rsETH exploit (April 2026, $124 million to $230 million of bad debt on Aave) and the Resolv USR depeg (March 2026, about $25 million extracted), Zyfai's agents exited early while depositors sat frozen in Aave (sources: https://www.bankless.com/read/agents-and-x402-make-defi-safer, https://x.com/Zyfai_/status/2036119040528375853). The same autonomy loses funds when screening, key management or incident response is weak. Afterwards, anyone can open the public board and see a current assessment of every integrated agent, re-checked at least every 14 days.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
- Wiebe Hendriks, Founder & CEO Owney, https://www.linkedin.com/in/wiebe-hendriks/
- Jeevesh Kuril, DeFi Researcher AtlasYield, https://www.linkedin.com/in/jeeveshkuril/
- Maciej Poszywak, Security Researcher CODESPECT, https://www.linkedin.com/in/maciejcodespect/

Framework v1 was co-developed with CODESPECT, Hacken and CORE3. Owney discloses any commercial relationship with the assessed platforms.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists

Zyfai, SurfLiquid and Yield Seeker are assessed, results at https://risk.owney.app/, and all three endorsed it publicly. The methodology is still private; publishing it is milestone 1. Rebuilding from scratch would take most of the grant.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
The board exists; this is not a website. The money buys:

- Framework v2: criteria, evidence and scoring for every subcategory, as an open specification plus agent skills a pipeline can execute, and a performance pillar: one reporting format in place of self-reported APY, one metric combining returns with risk. The draft is shaped together with DeFi agent teams before publication.
- A continuous pipeline: platforms integrate once, and re-assessment runs on a schedule and on change.
- Re-assessing the 3 existing platforms and onboarding new ones, with platforms showing their results on their own sites and a public metrics page tracking adoption and recognition.
- A maintenance and funding plan with a named maintainer, so the benchmark keeps running after the grant.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Building or operating any DeFi agent
- Audits of any protocols
- A returns leaderboard: the board never ranks agents by APY
- A heavy platform build

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- OSI-approved license for the specification, skills and pipeline code; methodology public and versioned.
- Re-assessment at least every 14 days and on every reported change; stale assessments marked stale.
- Identical fees, process and criteria for every platform; conflict-of-interest rules published.
- Owney maintains it after the grant, funded by fees from connected platforms and assessment work.
- Pinned targets: 6 platforms assessed, 3 integrated with over $200,000 of user funds each and over $10,000,000 together, and 3 platforms fixing a finding from their assessment.

initiatives.title: Proof of Audits: Proof Before Sign for Ethereum Wallets and Agents
initiatives.summary: Wallets ask users to approve transactions without showing whether the code they will run is the code that was audited. Proof Before Sign shows, inside the wallet and before signing, which calls in a transaction match reviewed code, which are only inside an audit's scope, and which have no matching public audit evidence. AI agents that sign for their owners can be held to the same evidence rules.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
An audit tells you which code was reviewed. Your wallet asks you to approve a transaction using the code deployed today, and it doesn't tell you whether they're the same.

We analysed 12 Ethereum transactions involving 97 contract calls (https://proofofaudits.com/demos/proof-before-sign). Only 2 calls had a recorded byte-for-byte match to a reviewed build. Another 74 ran code in files named in audit reports, and 21 had no matching public audit in our records.

Those are very different levels of evidence, and none of that difference is visible when someone presses Confirm.

Proof Before Sign brings that evidence into the wallet. Before the user signs, it shows what matches reviewed code, what has changed and what remains unverified. AI agents can also be required to follow the owner's evidence rules.

A matching audit is not a guarantee of safety, but users should at least know what they are relying on.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
I'm M K Veerendra Vamshi, founder of Proof of Audits and a smart-contract security researcher. I placed first in Sherlock's Allbridge Core Yield audit contest in 2025.

I started Proof of Audits to solve a problem I kept seeing in Web3 security: teams spend heavily on audits, but users still cannot tell whether the contracts they're interacting with are the code that was reviewed.

We've built a working transaction-analysis service, a MetaMask Snap and a public Ethereum evidence explorer. We've also started onboarding auditors to the platform, so we're building both the technology and the researcher network behind it.

At Devcon and DSS Mumbai, I connected with people from Sigma Prime, ChainSecurity, corpus.core and other Ethereum security teams. These conversations opened opportunities to explore integrations, share audit evidence and work together. They are relationships we're developing, not partnerships we're claiming are already signed.

I lead the product, security research and engineering. The grant will allow us to bring in specialist engineering and independent security review capacity, while I remain responsible for delivery and adoption.

**Track record:**

https://audits.sherlock.xyz/watson/veerendravamshi

https://github.com/MKVEERENDRA
https://proofofaudits.com

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
We've already done the work needed to show this problem can be solved. Now we need to make the solution reliable enough for other teams to use, and get it into the wallets where it matters.

Our live analyzer has checked 12 real Ethereum transactions involving 97 contract calls. Only 2 had recorded byte-for-byte matches to reviewed code. Another 74 were linked to audit scope, while 21 had no matching public audit evidence.

We've also built an explorer covering 656 functions across ten major Ethereum protocols, reproduced deployed Aave V4 and Uniswap V2 code from reviewed commits, and developed a MetaMask Snap that displays this evidence before signing. The code is public, although the independent evidence release process and ordinary MetaMask distribution are not complete.

We're not starting from zero on distribution either. Auditors have already joined our platform, we have an API for audit firms to publish their evidence, and Devcon gave us direct connections with security researchers, audit firms and Ethereum infrastructure teams interested in exploring the product.

**The next challenge is getting this into everyday use.**

The grant will fund three things:

- **Finish the product:** Complete the difficult execution-path checks, strengthen evidence verification, commission independent security reviews and prepare the wallet and agent integrations for production use.
- **Bring in the evidence:** Work with auditors, audit firms and protocols to connect reviewed source code, findings and fixes to the contracts running on Ethereum.
- **Get it into wallets:** Turn our Devcon connections into technical pilots, give external wallet and agent teams integration support, and prove that they use the checks in real Ethereum workflows.

We already have the product foundation and the relationships to begin this work. A new team would need to build that foundation before attempting the same integrations.

The final $25,000 of this grant is tied to adoption: at least two independent wallet or agent teams must use the evidence checks in live Ethereum workflows for 30 days, including at least one established provider. An independent reviewer will verify that use.

We're not asking TheDAO to fund another audit dashboard. We're asking it to help put existing audit evidence in front of people at the moment they are about to trust a contract with their funds.

**Existing work:**

https://proofofaudits.com/demos/proof-before-sign

https://proofofaudits.com/explorer/functions

https://github.com/ProofOfAudits/proof-before-sign-snap

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- Reproduce the proposed transaction at a pinned Ethereum mainnet state, naming the external calls, proxy implementations and dependencies it reaches.
- Match the code that runs to the reviewed source revision with reproducible compiler inputs and bytecode comparison.
- Attach the audit report, reviewed commit, scope, relevant findings and fix rechecks to each claim.
- Flag changed implementations, unresolved calls, code outside any audit scope and who holds upgrade rights, without producing false matches.
- A wallet evidence panel and a versioned integration API.
- An agent adapter that enforces the wallet owner's own approval rules. An AI model cannot override them.
- Published evidence fixtures, test results, known limits and integration documentation.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Audit contests or researcher payments, which are a separate initiative.
- Auditor bonds, slashing or loss compensation.
- Any claim that an audited transaction is safe.
- Chains other than Ethereum mainnet.
- A promise that a simulated transaction will run the same way once included onchain.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- Code funded by this grant is released under Apache-2.0 and evidence data under CC BY 4.0.
- Proof Before Sign stays free for wallet users. Published evidence stays free to read.
- Paid integrations for AI APIs, agents and other high-volume services are planned to cover hosting after the grant. Exact rates are in each customer's commercial terms and can be shared with the technical reviewer.
- Proof of Audits maintains the released components and ships security fixes for 12 months after the final milestone.
- Every result is one of MATCHED, CHANGED, PARTIAL or UNKNOWN. UNKNOWN is never treated as approval.
- Payment never changes what the evidence says.

initiatives.title: PRSpec: Spec-to-Client Verification for Ethereum Execution Clients
initiatives.summary:
Ethereum relies on multiple independent execution clients implementing the same protocol specifications consistently. Yet specifications evolve, implementations differ, and conventional tests only cover explicitly defined scenarios.
PRSpec adds a complementary verification layer that connects EIP requirements directly to client source code, combining deterministic checks with LLM-assisted semantic analysis.
Its V2 release introduces deterministic witnesses, specification change tracking (Fork Watch), adversarial verification, and reproducible evidence tied to exact specification revisions and client commits.
PRSpec already supports Besu, Geth, Nethermind, and Reth, with a working CI pilot demonstrated on a Besu fork.
This initiative will turn the existing implementation into a practical, privacy-conscious workflow that client teams can independently evaluate and integrate.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Ethereum already has extensive testing infrastructure. PRSpec does not replace EEST, Hive, or existing client tests.
The missing piece is a practical way to connect specification requirements with their corresponding implementation points across independent clients.
When an EIP changes, engineers must manually trace affected requirements, identify relevant code paths, and determine whether each client has implemented the change consistently.
PRSpec helps automate this process through three complementary capabilities:
- **Deterministic checks:** Extract measurable requirements from pinned EIP revisions and verify them against client-code anchors, without requiring an LLM.
- **Fork Watch:** Compare specification revisions, identify changed parameters, and map their impact to relevant verification rules and client files.
- **Semantic analysis:** Use LLM-assisted analysis and adversarial verification to identify potential implementation divergences. Findings remain candidates for engineering review, not automatic bug confirmations.
The goal is to help client teams identify issues earlier, investigate them with reproducible evidence, and decide where additional tests or implementation changes are needed.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
**Safi El-Hassanine — Founder and Lead Developer**
PRSpec is independently built and maintained by Safi El-Hassanine, a software developer focused on Ethereum infrastructure, protocol verification, and developer tooling.
He designed and developed the project's architecture, multi-client analysis engine, deterministic verification system, Fork Watch, and CI pilot.
PRSpec's public development history includes technical discussions with Nethermind, Ethereum Foundation execution-specs contributors, Besu, and go-ethereum.
The grant will directly support continued engineering and open-source development. Safi will be responsible for delivering the milestones and publishing their supporting evidence.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
PRSpec is a working open-source project, not a proposal to build a tool from scratch. Its V2 implementation includes:

**1. Four execution-client integrations**
Source-code mappings for Geth (Go), Nethermind (C#), Besu (Java), and Reth (Rust). The semantic analysis registry covers 10 EIPs across the clients, with Reth currently covering 7.

**2. Deterministic verification**
The witness engine currently includes EIP-1559 and EIP-4844 rulebooks.
- 34 cross-client checks: 34 matched, 0 mismatched, 0 incomplete.
- Two additional rule/client combinations are explicitly marked as lacking verified code anchors.
- A historical EIP-4844 replay correctly identifies three constants changed by a real specification commit.

**3. Fork Watch**
Implemented and tested against a historical EIP-4844 change, identifying modified parameters, affected verification rules, and relevant client files.

**4. Semantic analysis and adversarial verification**
A published mutation experiment tested 10 pre-registered implementation deviations:
- 6 confirmed, 1 flagged, 3 inconclusive.
- 0 missed and 0 errors.
The clean baseline produced 33 raw issues, all rejected during automated verification.
This is a single experiment on one pinned client revision, not a statistically established detection or false-positive rate.

**5. Working CI pilot**
On November 12, 2026, PRSpec completed an end-to-end GitHub Actions pilot on a Besu fork. It produced a report artifact and reproducible evidence, including a terminal transcript and screen recording.
The pilot is advisory and non-blocking. It is not installed in the official Besu repository.

**6. Engineering and reproducibility**
The V2 codebase includes:
- Installable CLI and Dockerfile with pinned dependencies.
- Local OpenAI-compatible model support and a `--no-cloud` privacy guard.
- Fail-closed exit codes.
- JSON, Markdown, and HTML reports.
- 210 passing automated tests, with 2 skipped tests requiring an API key.

**Explore the implementation and evidence:**
- GitHub: https://github.com/Fosurero/PRSpec
- Verification record: https://github.com/Fosurero/PRSpec/blob/main/VERIFICATION.md
- Roadmap: https://github.com/Fosurero/PRSpec/blob/main/ROADMAP.md
- Besu pilot evidence: https://github.com/Fosurero/PRSpec/tree/main/docs/evidence/2026-11-12/besu-fork-e2e

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
The initiative focuses on making PRSpec V2 independently deployable, reproducible, and practical for execution-client teams.

1. **Production packaging:** Finalize the CLI and Docker distribution, pinned environments, installation instructions, and reproducible examples.
2. **Deterministic verification:** Expand witness coverage beyond EIP-1559 and EIP-4844, improve fork-aware rules and client-code anchors, and evaluate EEST-format witnesses against EELS.
3. **Local model execution:** Validate open-weight models through OpenAI-compatible endpoints, publish hardware requirements and inference costs, and preserve the `--no-cloud` guard.
4. **Client CI integration:** Turn the Besu pilot into a reusable integration kit, add PR-level reporting, and work with client teams on advisory, non-blocking trials.
5. **Finding quality:** Maintain transparent triage records covering confirmed findings, disputed findings, false-positive candidates, and incomplete analyses.
6. **Maintainability:** Document how to add EIPs, forks, client mappings, and rules, and provide an integration guide and technical walkthrough.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
PRSpec is an additional verification layer, not a replacement for existing testing infrastructure.
This initiative does not promise:
- Complete EIP compliance or proof that an implementation is bug-free.
- Replacement of EEST, Hive, ethereum/tests, or existing review processes.
- Automatic confirmation of LLM-generated findings.
- Consensus-layer client support.
- Deterministic verification of every semantic requirement.
- Mandatory transmission of proprietary source code to external AI providers.
- Official client adoption or endorsement without public confirmation.
- Perpetual maintenance beyond the grant period.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
**Open source:** PRSpec and its documentation will remain available under the MIT license.
**Privacy:** Teams can run PRSpec in their own infrastructure. Local model support and `--no-cloud` will remain available, with external data flows and costs documented.
**Reproducibility:** Results will identify the relevant EIP revision, client commit, and model configuration where applicable. Incomplete analyses will not be presented as successful checks.
**Finding quality:** Findings will be reported as review candidates, with confirmed, disputed, false-positive, and incomplete results tracked separately.
**Adoption transparency:** Only publicly evidenced integrations will count as adoption. Trials and technical discussions will be reported separately.
**Independent review:** PRSpec will seek independent execution-client engineering review of its methodology, finding quality, and integration safety. Review will not be presented as endorsement.
**Continuity:** A public maintenance guide will explain how to extend coverage and reproduce existing results. The repository will remain publicly accessible after the grant period.

initiatives.title: RA2: Economic property packs for AMMs and lending markets, fuzz tests any protocol runs in its own CI
initiatives.summary: Open-source invariant properties that check the economics of AMM pools, lending markets and flash lenders under fuzzing: no withdrawal above its share, no redemption rounding in the user's favour, no healthy loan liquidated, no flash loan repaid short. 37 properties already exist, and they catch five seeded bug classes with no hints. This grant adds the bug classes behind the Euler and Cream exploits, position-based markets and Echidna and Medusa support. Its largest milestone pays only when at least 6 outside protocol teams run the pack in their own CI.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Depositors, liquidity providers and lenders on AMMs and lending markets lose money to economic logic bugs: rounding in the attacker's favour, an action that skips a health check, a share price moved by a donation, a flash loan that comes back short.

- **Euler** lost about $197 million in March 2023. A donation function skipped the health check, and the attacker then liquidated their own position ([Chainalysis](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/euler-finance-flash-loan-attack/)).
- **Cream** lost about $130 million in October 2021 to collateral whose share price a donation had doubled ([Immunefi](https://immunefi.com/blog/bug-fix-reviews/hack-analysis-cream-finance-oct-2021/)).

Each protocol writes these checks from scratch, or skips them. Public property packs cover token standards ([crytic/properties](https://github.com/crytic/properties), [a16z/erc4626-tests](https://github.com/a16z/erc4626-tests)), not the economics of pools and markets. On this board, the Community Fuzzing RFP funds fuzzing infrastructure and the Echidna grant funds the engine; both put writing protocol invariants out of scope. This fills that gap: a team writes one adapter (10 functions for a pool, 15 for a market) and gets every property.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
- **Jean Rausis**, co-founder: serial entrepreneur and cybersecurity specialist with a background in ethical hacking, architect of the team's DEX designs and delta-neutral synthetic assets ([LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jeanrausis/))
- **Eric Rabl**, co-founder: EPFL-trained mathematician with a background in quantitative finance and algorithmic market making, leads protocol math ([LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/eric-rabl-6708a570))

Both co-founded RA2 Capital. RA2 TECH SA (Montreux, Switzerland, registered since 2019) employs 25+ in-house engineers and researchers who build Everything (everything.inc), a DeFi protocol where lending, borrowing, leverage and swaps share a unified pool per asset pair, and the SmarDex ecosystem. Those engineers wrote and run the invariant suite this pack generalises.

RA2 has self-funded more than $20 million of R&D over five years. No other funder pays for this scope.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
- **The pack is built:** 37 properties across AMM pools (18), lending markets (17) and ERC-3156 flash lenders (2), MIT licensed. 24 generalise the invariant suite of Everything's UniPool v1 contracts; 13 are new. It already handles virtual-share markets (OpenZeppelin ERC-4626, Morpho Blue).
- **It is tested.** Three fuzz campaigns pass 16,384 calls each against reference pools. Five mutant contracts each carry one bug class (withdrawal rounding, redemption rounding, an unpaid flash fee, a flash loan repaid short, a missing health check). The fuzzer catches every one with no hints, within 35 calls, and CI checks both on every push.
- **It caught a bug nobody planted.** On its first run it flagged a stale `totalAssets` view in our own reference market, fixed before publishing.

This costs less than a from-scratch build because the property design, the adapter model and the mutant harness are finished. The money goes to the missing bug classes and to onboarding other teams.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- Position-based lending (Aave and Morpho style accounts) alongside loan-based markets
- Reference adapters for Uniswap V2, Morpho Blue and Euler V2, published in the repo and run in its CI
- New properties for the Euler and Cream classes: no user action leaves the caller's own position liquidatable, a donation cannot raise the value a market assigns to collateral, and a liquidatable position is always profitable to liquidate
- Echidna and Medusa entry points for every pack
- The money's main work: onboarding. An adapter guide, and hands-on help writing the adapter with each adopting team until it runs in their CI

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Auditing any protocol, or writing a protocol's full invariant suite beyond its adapter
- Fuzzing compute or hosting
- Formal verification
- Properties specific to Everything's design (virtual reserves, its vault routing), which stay in its private suite

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- All code, properties and adapters under MIT.
- We maintain the pack for 12 months after the last milestone at no further cost. Everything's own contracts run it in CI, so we keep it working for ourselves.
- Every new property ships with a seeded mutant that proves it fires.
- Pinned target: at least 6 outside protocol teams running the pack in their own CI.

initiatives.title: Remix: AI-Guided Smart Contract Security Checks
initiatives.summary: Remix is working to expand on Cyfrin's public Security Checklists, and make them more actionable inside the Remix platform. This grant funds the structured tagging of audit checklists, RemixAI integration for targeted security reviews, and automated Foundry fuzz test generation to verify findings with concrete execution traces.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
With the rise of AI-generated contracts, a growing number of non-developers and beginners are creating and deploying smart contracts. This expands the attack surface, as these users often do not know which security checklists apply to their code or how to fix flagged vulnerabilities. Historically, over $8 billion in user funds has been lost specifically to smart contract execution flaws, according to an empirical study in Science Direct.

Integrating a consistently maintained and tagged Cyfrin Security Checklist directly into RemixAI solves this. Users get automated, contract-specific filters (such as ERC-20, NFT, or staking), actionable AI-guided fixes, and automated Foundry invariant tests that validate checklist findings with counterexample execution traces.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
- **Yann Levreau**: Lead Dev, Remix (https://github.com/yann300)
- **Stephané Tetsing**: AI Dev, Remix (https://github.com/STetsing)

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown: This initiative builds directly on the proprietary integration of the existing Remix IDE and Cyfrin’s Security Checklists. Remix has already delivered initial scoping, architecture, and agentic workflows under a $15,000 internal commitment. As the maintainer of the platform, the Remix team possesses a decisive head start that cannot be replicated by a third party, and Remix's diverse user base is the ideal audience for this initiative's outputs.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- Tagging Cyfrin's security checks so they can be filtered by contract type (ERC-20, NFT mint, vault, staking, etc.), relevant code patterns, severity, and required Solidity knowledge
- Upgrading RemixAI to read these tags and filter checklists based on the specific contract
- Building tailored security reports with actionable, AI-generated fixes scoped to specific vulnerability types
- Developing and deploying x402 endpoints with enhanced audit capabilities
- Cross-model audits where two or more models audit the same code and propose a joint report
- Audits at runtime using the checklist combined with an execution trace and Solidity source code
- Publishing Remix plugins for Claude and OpenAI, making security checklists and runtime audits available as connectors
- Automated Foundry fuzz and invariant test generation from checklist items and static analysis findings, executing through the Desktop Foundry runner and recording traces to the run directory
- Driving adoption through quarterly community calls to review findings, plus educational efforts including documentation, six workshops, media support, and video tutorials

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown: - Performing traditional, manual audits on user contracts

- Main workflow code published under Apache 2.0 and MIT. x402 code under MIT.
- Remix maintains the tools and functionality for at least 12 months after the final milestone at no further cost to the fund.
- Cyfrin checklist updated quarterly with new findings for the duration of the initiative.
- The long-term funding model is sustained through tiered subscriptions, AI top-ups, and pay-per-use x402 revenue.
- Pinned targets: at least 5,000 unique users generating reports and 3 third-party integrations.

initiatives.title: Revoke.cash: Exploit Exposure Layer, Free Data on Every Wallet Still Approved to an Exploited Contract
initiatives.summary: After an exploit, the token approvals users granted to the exploited contract stay live and keep getting drained, sometimes for years. Revoke.cash will scan every supported chain for every contract on its public exploit list, compute which wallets are still exposed, and serve that data through a free API so any wallet or explorer can warn its own users. The multichain exploit check on Revoke.cash moves out of the paid tier and becomes free, and a public metrics page tracks exposure, revocations, and value at risk per exploit.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Exploited contracts do not stop draining when the news cycle ends. Radiant Capital's lending pools on Arbitrum and BNB Chain were taken over in October 2024, and the attacker's implementation is still installed. It still calls transferFrom on wallets with open approvals: about 2,200 wallets were drained in 2025 and about 170 more in 2026 through September 13, all to one receiver address (0x070ca92f568037d351666b3918a0f6ba7ad20ed1), with the latest drain two days before this was written. Radiant's DAO scoped these approval losses at $7.7M for 2024 and $1.2M for the first quarter of 2025 and did not compensate them. Revoking is the only protection those wallets have.

The same pattern repeats at every scale. Multichain disclosed a router bug on January 18, 2022 and asked users to revoke; the first drain came 16 hours later, and a month on 3,101 of 7,962 affected addresses still had not revoked (Multichain post-mortem). During that incident Multichain built an ad-hoc approval-revoke API that SushiSwap, SpookySwap and AAVE integrated to warn users. Multichain is gone and nothing replaced it. In January 2026 SwapNet drained $13.43M from 18 Matcha users, 17 of them in the 45 minutes between the first attack and the pause (Matcha post-mortem).

Today a user learns they are exposed only by opening the Revoke.cash page for that exploit, one chain at a time. Wallets and explorers have no data source to warn their own users. After this initiative, any wallet can tell a user "you are still approved to exploit X on chain Y" the moment they open it, and anyone can check the ecosystem-wide numbers.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
**Rosco Kalis** does the work. He created Revoke.cash in 2019 as the first token approval management tool and has worked on it full-time since 2022, growing it to 100+ networks, NFT and Permit2 support, batch revoking, and the exploit checker. He maintains the public exploit list and the spender data this initiative builds on. Revoke.cash received Optimism RetroPGF funding and is the tool protocols point their users to after an incident, most recently in Matcha's SwapNet post-mortem.

Track record: https://github.com/rkalis, https://x.com/RoscoKalis, https://revoke.cash/about.

No other funder pays for this scope. The Optimism Foundation and the Monad Foundation sponsor batch revoke fees on their chains, which is unrelated to this work.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
- The public exploit list: 67 documented approval exploits with contract addresses per chain, a submission template, and per-exploit pages with a single-chain checker at https://revoke.cash/exploits
- Chain coverage: Revoke.cash already indexes approvals on 100+ EVM networks, with the RPC, log-provider and block-range handling that a chain-wide scan needs
- An exploit fan-out already running in the Revoke.cash indexer for its automated revoking, which re-evaluates known wallets when an exploit is listed (open source in the repository, packages/core/lib/auto-revoke)
- The impact methodology: scripts that compute value exposed at exploit time, value protected by earlier revocations, and value still at risk, with a token price mapping built up over two years (apps/web/scripts/exploits)
- Spender risk data with exploit labels, and existing embeds in Ledger, Safe, World App and Farcaster that give direct lines to wallet teams

A from-scratch team would pay for chain coverage, the exploit list and the pricing work before writing the first line of exposure code. That is why this is $100,000 and not a from-scratch price.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- **Chain-wide exposure scan per exploit.** For every contract on the exploit list, all approval events across the whole chain are read, the set of wallets with a live allowance is computed, and it is kept current as users approve and revoke. Covers ERC-20, ERC-721 and Permit2 allowances on every supported network.
- **Public exposure API, free and unauthenticated.** Per exploit: exposed wallets per chain and the affected spenders. Per address: exposed to any listed exploit, all chains in one call. Rate limited, open data license, with integration documentation so any wallet or explorer can warn its own users.
- **Free multichain exploit check on Revoke.cash.** Any user checks any address against all listed exploits on every chain at once, backed by the same API. Today this is a Premium feature.
- **Public metrics page with an automated impact pipeline.** For every listed exploit, per chain and in total: wallets exposed, wallets that revoked within 72 hours of listing, time from exploit to listing, value exposed at exploit time, value protected by revocations made before the exploit, and value still at risk today. Prevention is counted ecosystem-wide, from any tool. The pipeline runs on listing and on a schedule, prices assets with a maintained source, and publishes its methodology. Results are also served through the API.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Push alerts of any kind from Revoke.cash for free users. Wallets deliver warnings inside their own UI. Revoke.cash's paid tiers keep push monitoring and automated revoking on top of the free layer.
- Automated revoking.
- Tracing stolen funds to attacker addresses. The metrics show exposed value, not confirmed theft.
- Attributing prevented value to Revoke.cash or any single tool.
- Changes to how exploits get listed. The public exploit list on GitHub and its submission template stay as they are.
- A general spender risk dataset.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- The exposure engine, API and pipeline are published under MIT; the exposure and metrics data under CC BY 4.0.
- We maintain the scan, the API and the metrics page for at least 12 months after the last milestone at no further cost.
- Pinned target: at least 3 third-party integrations in production within 9 months of the first payment.
- The free layer covers pull: any address, any chain, any listed exploit, with no subscription. No exception requested.

initiatives.title: RFP: A Bug Broker That Gets Ethereum Bugs Fixed and Researchers Paid, Bounty or No Bounty
initiatives.shortTitle: A Bug Broker That Gets Ethereum Bugs Fixed and Research…
initiatives.summary: In the age of AI, team inboxes fill with junk bug reports, so whether a real bug gets fixed comes down to who sends it and whether the team trusts them. This RFP seeds a for-profit broker that builds relationships with real bug hunters and validates their exploits. It takes serious findings to teams across Ethereum that trust it, sees them fixed and the researcher paid, and lives on its fees.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Every valid finding left unfixed waits for the next attacker to find it. Users are safer when someone both sides trust owns the job of getting it fixed.

- Bounties work where programs exist: [Immunefi](https://immunefi.com/) has paid researchers over $140M. Code with no bounty, no maintainer or a program that never answers has no such path.
- Without a broker we expect researchers to drop findings rather than chase unbountied teams, since a lone researcher asking for payment risks looking like an extortionist.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
The goal: validated findings get fixed, including in unmaintained code, and researchers get paid, bounty or no bounty. Bidders have complete freedom in how they get there, including their own milestones, within the hard requirements below. This RFP is a starting point and will change; the final milestones are agreed with the selected team.

One possible approach, the one the milestones below follow:

- Build relationships with real bug hunters, validate their exploits, and take each finding to the owner with the full details and an offer to help fix it.
- Charge for it: fees from teams, a cut of researcher payments, commissions on bounty submissions it files and defends, or another model.
- Keep a working line to SEAL's war rooms for findings that turn into live attacks.
- Use the security contacts published under the companion security-contact RFP without depending on them.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Bug hunting itself.
- Whitehat rescues of funds at risk ([separate RFP](https://initiatives.thedao.fund/initiative/an-open-bug-bounty-program-for-all-of-ethereum-white-hat-res) on this board).
- Bugs in shared code where several teams must fix together (the companion coordinated-patching RFP).

sections.heading: Existing work
sections.markdown:
- [Zero Day Initiative](https://www.zerodayinitiative.com/about/): Web2's trusted broker since 2005. It pays researchers, then gives the vendor the details and a 120-day deadline ([policy](https://www.zerodayinitiative.com/advisories/disclosure_policy/)).
- [SEAL 911](https://securityalliance.org/seal-911): a free emergency hotline that has coordinated over 200 war rooms for active or imminent incidents. The broker handles findings not under active exploit.

sections.heading: Who we expect to do this
sections.markdown:
An independent for-profit company: an audit firm with an AI bug-hunting pipeline, a bounty platform, or a new firm. The best pitch answers one question: why will researchers and teams both trust you? A clear connection to SEAL, whose war rooms bring together major security crews, is a strong plus. Nobody is pre-selected.

Drafted by TheDAO Security Fund from a conversation with EthSec (ethsecurity.org) and Consensys. Consensys Diligence may bid. A fix counts toward the milestones of only one initiative on this board. EthSec, TheDAO Security Fund and Giveth will not bid.

sections.heading: Hard requirements
sections.markdown:
1. **Disclosure never depends on payment.** The affected team receives the full finding at first contact, with no condition, before any payment request.
2. **Terms first.** Payment terms, the same for every team, are published before any team is contacted. A law firm's opinion on the model goes to the technical reviewer, with its summary published, before the first payment request.
3. A finding goes only to the teams that must fix it, never sold or licensed to anyone else.
4. Nothing about an unfixed finding is published, including which team is slow to respond.
5. Every finding is validated with a working proof of concept before any team is contacted.
6. Researchers may stay unnamed in public.
7. **Outside means unaffiliated:** no shared owner, staff or funding with the selected team. A payment or fix counts only when payer and researcher are also unaffiliated with each other, and each finding is a separate root cause.
8. Ethereum and L2 code only.
9. **A business that pays for itself.** The broker is a for-profit company that charges for its service, with a business model in the bid that covers its costs after the grant.
