initiatives.title: RFP: An Open Bug Bounty Program for All of Ethereum: White Hat Rescued Funds Distribution Service
initiatives.shortTitle: An Open Bug Bounty Program for All of Ethereum: White H…
initiatives.summary: Our industry's security holes fund North Korea's weapons programs, scam compounds full of trafficked people, and countless cybercriminals. Black hats find exposed money and take it, while white hats who find the same holes warn the team and hope the money stays there long enough to be rescued; with AI speeding up attacks, that is a losing strategy. This RFP funds a legal entity that takes what white hats rescue, gives them legal cover, pays them without KYC, and earns its fee only when owners get their money back. Our goal is an army of white hats rescuing money everywhere they can, in effect an open bug bounty on all of Ethereum.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
This protects people whose funds sit in exploitable contracts or on leaked keys: a white hat who finds them can take them first and send them somewhere lawful. Today we leave that money on the table for the worst people in the world. White hats hold back because they want legal cover first, someone else to do the work of returning the money second, and pay third. Give them a destination they trust and they will rescue funds like mad, many just for the lulz.

- North Korea takes billions from our industry ([FBI](https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA250226)). UN monitors found crypto theft brings in as much as half of its foreign income and helps bankroll its nuclear program ([NK News](https://www.nknews.org/2024/03/north-korea-relies-on-crypto-theft-for-up-to-half-of-foreign-income-un-report)).
- At least 220,000 people may be held in scam compounds in Myanmar and Cambodia alone, forced to run scams that include crypto fraud ([UN News](https://news.un.org/en/story/2023/08/1140187)).
- Anthropic measured the value AI agents could exploit from real, previously hacked contracts doubling roughly every 1.3 months ([Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/research/smart-contracts)). You fight AI with AI, once white hats have somewhere safe to send what they find.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
Legal setup (a new entity or an existing one), custody, an owner portal and a public case page, plus case work through month 12: outreach that brings rescuers' cases in, the operator's own rescues, intake, owner searches, ownership checks and returns. That covers known owners (a protocol, company or token holders), paid back within weeks, and unknown owners (weak or leaked keys), paid as they prove their claims.

The ideal service gives white hats legal cover when they hand funds over and pays their bounties without KYC. Where the law stops short of that, propose the design that gets closest and say where it falls short; once this RFP is funded, we pick the proposal that works and comes closest. The fee design here is a starting idea too: the team picks the legal structure, custody setup and tools, and may propose any design that solves the same problem, as long as owners pay for their rescue, the rescuer's bounty and operator's fee come only from returns, and unclaimed funds stay open to claims.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Rescues that need red-teaming or breaking into someone's computer or systems, this is not accecptable: rescues must start from public information, such as open-source code, onchain data or keys already published
- Tracing and freezing stolen funds
- Assets on chains other than Ethereum and its L2s

sections.heading: Existing work
sections.markdown:
- [SEAL Whitehat Safe Harbor](https://frameworks.securityalliance.org/safe-harbor/whitehat/) lets a white hat step in only during an exploit under way or imminent, on a protocol that adopted it, for a bounty usually 10% capped at $1 million ([SEAL](https://securityalliance.org/safe-harbor)). A good start with a narrow use: a white hat may not act on a known hole before an attacker does.
- [DART](https://assetrecovery.io/) (Digital Asset Recovery Technologies) and the independent Crypto Recovery Trust it works with are the closest model: a Wyoming statutory trust with an independent trustee takes crypto from white hats, gives them legal cover and returns it to verified original owners where the law allows.
- About 70,500 ETH from TheDAO's 2016 refund contracts is still unclaimed a decade later ([thedao.fund](https://thedao.fund)): even a famous refund never reaches every owner.
- [Kleros](https://kleros.io/) arbitration, for disputed claims.

This RFP aims to go further than Safe Harbor: if a white hat can take exposed money, they should.

sections.heading: Who we expect to do this
sections.markdown:
Nobody is pre-selected. A winning team pairs legal operations with BD and outreach people that white hats and incident-response groups already trust, since adoption pays only when rescuers hand funds over and owners are found. It needs no onchain engineering expertise.

Drafted with TheDAO Security Fund; the idea was built by Griff Green from conversations with SEAL 911, DART, TheDAO's lawyers and other teams. DART has a clear head start and may bid, as may TheDAO's lawyers.

sections.heading: Hard requirements
sections.markdown:
1. Victims pay for their rescue with a haircut on the return or a fee to collect it. That funds an equal rescuer bounty and operator fee, paid only on returns to verified owners: An example payout scheme could be: 2% each of the first $10 million, 0.25% to $100 million, 0.06% to $1 billion and 0.01% above (about $200,000 each at $10 million, $425,000 at $100 million and $1 million at $1 billion). Tiers apply per case, and a case is one incident with all its related addresses, chains and staged returns. Rates may rise case by case, within a published ceiling and set before the case is accepted, when few owners are likely to come forward. The proposal shows how the fee sustains the service after the grant, even with few claims and zero yield.
2. Published rules for proving ownership, including for leaked or weak keys (a signature from the exposed key proves nothing on its own), and a dispute path to a neutral arbiter.
3. A licensed firm's legal opinion covers custody, money transmission, sanctions, unclaimed property, how far rescuers can be paid without KYC, and what protection rescuers get when they hand funds over. Every return and bounty is sanctions-screened.
4. Funds nobody claims become an endowment: once they count as lost or abandoned under applicable law or a rule the operator publishes before the rescue, the operator may stake them or earn other low-risk yield and keep that yield, but every claim stays open and the principal stays available to pay it for at least 7 years from the rescue.
5. Rescued funds, including any staked under Hard requirement 4, sit only in audited code, such as an unmodified Safe, or with an independent trustee or regulated custodian, kept apart per case and from the operator's own funds, and the operator can't move them alone.
6. A public case page lists every deposit, return and endowment balance, each valued in USD at its block by a published onchain query: Chainlink feed, else relevant DEX TWAP (e.g. Uniswap v3 TWAP); anything else counts as $0.
7. Rescuers may stay unnamed in public. Where the law requires identity checks for bounties, the proposal says which checks and why, and the legal opinion in Hard requirement 3 confirms them. Owners' identities and evidence stay with the operator; the technical reviewer inspects counted case files and keeps no copies.
8. Code is open source, under a license the bidder states.
9. A case counts only if the funds were rescued after the award starts and its case page links the onchain trail from exploited contract or leaked address to owner. The technical reviewer also confirms the owner had the funds before the incident, no protocol could have recovered the funds itself, the owner is not the operator, its staff or an affiliate, the exposed contract or key was not deployed or funded by the rescuer, the operator or their affiliates, counted rescuers are not each other's staff or affiliates, and in each adoption milestone at most one counted rescuer is the operator or tied to it. Milestones count what owners receive, after bounty, fee and gas.
10. The operating legal entity signs an indemnification agreement with every white hat who hands it funds, so if a white hat is sued over a good-faith rescue handed to the service, the entity covers their legal defense.

initiatives.title: RFP: Clear Signing: Independent Attestations for the ERC-7730 Descriptors of Ethereum's 100 Most-Used Contracts
initiatives.shortTitle: Clear Signing: Independent Attestations for the ERC-773…
initiatives.summary: Pay one established security firm to review, under its own name, the ERC-7730 clear signing descriptors for the 100 most-used verified Ethereum contracts and publish a signed attestation for each one, so wallets can trust what they render. The registry holds 739 descriptors, 166 carry an attestation, every one of those is signed by a single firm, and none of the top 100 contracts has an attested descriptor. The firm keeps each attestation current for 12 months. A major wallet backs the firm from the start, and payment lands on published attestations and on wallets that act on them.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Clear Signing (ERC-7730) is the Ethereum standard for showing users a human-readable summary of what they are about to sign, instead of raw calldata. Descriptors for each contract live in the open registry at github.com/ethereum/clear-signing-erc7730-registry, and wallets read them. A wrong descriptor is worse than none: the user sees a confident summary that does not match what the contract does. The registry's own reviewing guide says its pull request review is a plausibility check, and that the trust layer is the signed attestation an auditor publishes after verifying the descriptor against the contract's source. Wallets choose which attesters to trust and can refuse to render a descriptor nobody has attested. Bybit lost about $1.5 billion in February 2025 after its signers approved a Safe transaction whose displayed contents differed from what they signed ([Bybit incident timeline](https://www.bybit.com/en/learn/this-week-in-bybit/bybit-security-incident-timeline), [NCC Group analysis](https://www.nccgroup.com/research/in-depth-technical-analysis-of-the-bybit-hack/)).

Attestation lags far behind authoring. On 2026-10-31 the registry had 739 descriptors and 166 attestations, all signed by one firm under Ethereum Foundation funding. Sourcify's live dashboard at erc7730.sourcify.dev ranks verified mainnet contracts by calls that are not plain ETH or standard token transfers: the top 100 carry 75% of those calls, 20 of them have a descriptor, and 0 of those descriptors are attested. Descriptor authoring for the rest is under way through the clear signing working group. Nobody is funded to verify and sign the result, and no second firm has put its name behind any descriptor.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
This RFP pays one security firm for verification and signature. The firm's reputation is the deliverable: every attestation is published under the firm's own key and name.

- Review each descriptor for a target contract against the registry's auditor guide
- Publish an EAS offchain attestation (ERC-8176 schema) for each descriptor that passes, as a PR to the registry's sigs folder
- For each descriptor that fails, post the defects on the registry PR or as an issue, and attest the corrected version once it is merged
- For 12 months after each attestation, review every fix, addition or change to that contract's descriptor and re-attest it, or post the defects, within 30 days, so the registry's dropped-attestations list stays empty for this batch
- Migrate every attestation the firm has published to a new version of ERC-8176 or of the registry's attestation format within 60 days of the registry adopting it, during the engagement or the 12 months that follow, at no extra cost
- Publish a batch page: each target contract, its descriptor, review status, defects found, attestation UID and date

The target set is the top 100 verified contracts on erc7730.sourcify.dev by calls that are not filtered out (ETH, standard token transfers, closed source, bots etc) 7-day window, archived on the day the firm starts (based on final agreement with argot to allow for small manual fixes to the list). Descriptors for those contracts are written by others; the firm attests what exists and what lands during the engagement, and keeps reviewing what changes for 12 months after each attestation.

ERC-8176 is being reworked to be easier for developers to use, so a new version may land during the engagement.

The submitter is allowed to update the list (with consent from TheDAO at milestones after 30 contracts attested and 80 contracts attested).

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Writing descriptors. The firm does not attest a descriptor it authored.
- Contracts without verified source, and contracts outside the agreed list
- Wallet-side code, schema changes, registry tooling

sections.heading: Existing work
sections.markdown:
- The registry's auditor guide (auditors/README.md): the 5-step review, the ERC-8176 hash, the EAS schema, and the sigs folder format, built on the clearsig CLI (github.com/Cyfrin/clearsig)
- The 166 attestations already in the registry, as the format and bar to match
- Sourcify's clear-signing library, which lets a wallet name trusted attesters and fall back to raw calldata when no trusted attestation exists

sections.heading: Who we expect to do this
sections.markdown:
Nobody is pre-selected. We want one firm whose whole business is security and whose name a wallet would accept as a trusted attester: a smart contract audit firm, or a firm in monitoring or incident response with published Ethereum work. Today one firm signs every attestation in the registry; this RFP adds a second, independent name. A strong bid shows at least 3 years of published Ethereum security work, names the reviewers who will sign, and comes with public backing from a major wallet that plans to accept the firm's attestations.

Co-drafted by the submitter with TheDAO Security Fund. The submitter is a listed co-author of ERC-7730, convened the clear signing working group meetings until the Ethereum Foundation took over that role. The submitter and his employer will not bid on this initiative.

sections.heading: Hard requirements
sections.markdown:
1. **Security firm, in public.** The bidder is a company whose primary business is security, with at least 3 years of published Ethereum security work and at least 20 public audit or incident reports, linked in the bid.
2. **By the book.** Every review follows the registry's auditor guide in full, and no attestation is issued for a descriptor that formats a function whose displayed intent the guide says v2 cannot express.
3. **Under its own name.** Attestations are signed with a key the firm publicly declares as its own, in ERC-8176 format, merged into the registry's sigs folder.
4. **Independent.** The firm attests no descriptor it wrote, and discloses any commercial relationship with a protocol whose descriptor it reviews.
5. **Defects in public.** Every failed review is posted on the registry PR or as a registry issue before any attestation of the corrected version.
6. **Support for 12 months.** For 12 months after each attestation, the firm reviews every fix, addition or change to that contract's descriptor, including changes that follow a contract upgrade, and re-attests it or posts the defects within 30 days, at no extra cost.
7. **A major wallet backs the bid.** The bid includes a public statement from at least 1 of MetaMask, Rabby, Trust Wallet, Ledger, Trezor, Phantom or Fireblocks that it plans to name the firm as a trusted attester, linked in the bid. A bid without it is ignored.

initiatives.title: RFP: Community Fuzzing Tooling for Ethereum Ecosystem Projects
initiatives.shortTitle: Community Fuzzing Tooling for Ethereum Ecosystem Projec…
initiatives.summary: The Ethereum ecosystem is lacking a solution for scalable, continuous, and compute-intensive fuzzing campaigns for projects. For each project to subscribe to their own solution would be costly and could have diminishing returns over time to make it a worthwhile investment of time, money, and human capital. We are requesting proposals from applicants who have developed or can develop tools to orchestrate fuzzing at scale, assign compute resources efficiently, and flex these resources up and down in an agile manner so that any team can orchestrate their own fuzzing campaign for themselves. A self-serve model. This RFP would fund the construction and maintenance of such a tool.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Security review has shifted a great deal of effort onto LLM-assisted tooling over the last eighteen months. That shift has been productive and remains accessible to teams through frontier models and private tools, but it is also incomplete. They are weakest precisely where fuzzing is strongest, particularly on regression detection and avoidance as developers ship new or harden existing code.

**Current state:**

Many teams know the above, but very few run fuzzing continuously. The reasons are mostly operational:

- Compute: Meaningful fuzzing is measured in sustained core hours. Most teams cannot justify that as a standing line item for a single codebase, so it never gets budgeted.
- Time: Someone has to write harnesses that generate inputs structured enough to reach deep code rather than bouncing off input validation.
- Software: Teams that do try usually run a fuzzer in GitHub Actions or a similarly time-boxed CI runner, yielding a few minutes of fuzzing per commit. That is only enough to replay an existing corpus and generate suitable code coverage.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- A documented CLI or front-end UI
- Running continuous fuzzing campaigns across multiple tenants in a secure manner
- Ability to allocate compute across multiple projects and scale it up and down efficiently and on demand
- Capability to hand off harnesses, corpora, and knowledge to users
- Documentation so teams can maximally self-serve

**On the milestone plan:**

Amounts below are shown as a share of the awarded budget, with an indicative figure at a $150,000 award.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Manual audits and code review. This program funds fuzzing infrastructure.
- Authorship of harnesses and tests
- Publishing exploit detail or proof-of-concept code for anything still unpatched
- A guaranteed bug count. Fuzzing finds what it finds; the commitment is to compute and process.
- Triage of findings
- Incident response
- Any other professional services

sections.heading: Existing work
sections.markdown: None named.

sections.heading: Who we expect to do this
sections.markdown:
The strongest bidder is a team that has run continuous fuzzing at scale before, over months rather than for the duration of an audit, and can show the following evidence: campaigns sustained, coverage figures, bugs found and disclosed. Proposals should be explicit about:

- Coverage of languages and frameworks
- Compute: State the sustained core hours you can field and where they come from
- User Experience: How does the user access the tool? Is it via service request only? A CLI? A dedicated User Interface? Briefly describe the user flow as it will exist should the grant be awarded.

The proposal will likely be best served by a single grant recipient, but the RFP can certainly be considered for multiple participants if that best serves the needs of the ecosystem.

sections.heading: Hard requirements
sections.markdown:
1. Aggregated results measured and published: Aggregate and abstracted statistics for coverage, findings, etc., updated at least quarterly on a public page. Bug counts alone are not an acceptable measure of a fuzzing program.
2. Siloed User Experience: Users may only see their own findings for security purposes. This must be available to be considered for the grant.
3. No user lock-in: Harnesses must build and run on standard open source fuzzing tooling. Every project keeps its harnesses, corpus, and documentation under an open license at no further cost, and must be able to keep running them without paying the grantee anything.

initiatives.title: RFP: Hunt Down Every Ethereum Team Until It Publishes a security.txt and Joins a Web of Trust
initiatives.shortTitle: Hunt Down Every Ethereum Team Until It Publishes a secu…
initiatives.summary: Ethereum is permissionless, so teams publish security contacts many ways or not at all, and researchers and their AI agents cannot reliably find where a bug goes or how to encrypt it. Of the 50 largest DeFi entries on Ethereum, 37 serve no security.txt, and only 2 publish one with an encryption key. AI is finding bugs fast, so this needs solving now. This RFP pays one person or a small team to get every team to publish one standard and to build, on what SEAL and other groups already have, a private web of trust that reaches each team's security lead fast.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Researchers need one clear pathway to every team. A report that never reaches the team leaves users exposed until an attacker finds the same bug.

- Researchers now hunt with AI agents. An agent can route and encrypt a report automatically only when every team publishes the same machine-readable record in the same place. AI can also chain low-severity bugs into critical ones, so every finding needs a route.
- The worst bugs need more than a public address: every extra hop is a chance to leak. In a web of trust a finding goes straight to a verified security lead, who knows the sender is real amid AI-generated junk reports.
- Our count (November 23, 2026) checked the website DeFiLlama lists for each entry.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
Bidders have complete freedom in how they get there, including their own milestones, within the hard requirements below. What matters is three outcomes: one agreed standard for what teams publish and where; every Ethereum and L2 team with real value at stake publishing it; and a private web of trust that reaches those teams' security leads fast. This RFP is a starting point and will change; the final milestones are agreed with the selected team.

One possible approach, the one the milestones below follow:

- Settle the standard: what every project publishes (a contact, a private channel such as an encryption key, and a vulnerability disclosure policy, or VDP, with scope, expected response and safe harbor) and where (security.txt, SECURITY.md with GitHub private reporting, an onchain record such as ERC-5437), endorsed by groups that send and receive reports.
- Hunt teams down one by one: direct outreach, pull requests to their repositories, whatever tactics work.
- Build the web of trust with SEAL: start from the contacts SEAL and other groups already have, verify each team's security lead and a backup on a video call, connect them over encrypted channels, let members vouch for researchers so teams know a report is real, and keep it current with call-tree drills.
- A public campaign, for example on X, naming who has published and who has not.
- A simple public tracker, a checkmark per record per project, mainly to track this grant's progress and give teams a gold star.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Running bug bounties.
- Validating or handling reports (the companion bug broker RFP).
- Emergency response to live hacks ([SEAL 911](https://securityalliance.org/our-work/seal-911) does that).

sections.heading: Existing work
sections.markdown:
- [RFC 9116](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116): security.txt, with fields for a contact, an encryption key and a policy.
- [SEAL's vulnerability disclosure framework](https://frameworks.securityalliance.org/vulnerability-disclosure/overview): tells teams to publish one consistent set of contacts everywhere researchers look, with a [SECURITY.md template and sample security.txt](https://frameworks.securityalliance.org/vulnerability-disclosure/security-contact) and a policy template. The natural starting point.
- [disclose.io's dioterms](https://github.com/disclose/dioterms): public-domain VDP and safe harbor templates.
- [ERC-5437](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-5437): an onchain contact with an encryption key, status Stagnant.

sections.heading: Who we expect to do this
sections.markdown:
One person or a small team that SEAL and researchers already trust, good at relentless, polite outreach and loud public campaigns. A strong bid shows SEAL will work with it. Nobody is pre-selected.

Drafted by TheDAO Security Fund from conversations with EthSec (ethsecurity.org) and Consensys. EthSec, TheDAO Security Fund and Giveth will not bid.

sections.heading: Hard requirements
sections.markdown:
1. **Verified means project-controlled.** A record counts only when the project publishes it itself: on its domain, in its repository or from its admin or governance address.
2. **Encrypted to count.** Only records with a published encryption key or a private reporting form the project controls count.
3. **Open and maintained.** The standard is published under CC0 or CC BY 4.0, and a home outside the selected team commits in public to maintain the standard and the web of trust after the grant. The tracker's data is open, each checkmark linked to the project's own record.
4. **Names only, never bugs.** Campaigns and the tracker show only whether a project published the records, never a vulnerability, finding or report.
5. **Private stays private.** Web-of-trust members' direct contacts are never published; only vouched members can use them, under access rules the bid states.
6. **Outside means unaffiliated.** An outside team shares no owner, staff or funding relationship with the selected team. Affiliates count toward no criterion.
7. Ethereum and L2 projects only.

initiatives.title: RFP: OpSec Ratings Coalition to Build & Maintain an "L2BEAT for OpSec"
initiatives.shortTitle: OpSec Ratings Coalition to Build & Maintain an "L2BEAT…
initiatives.summary: Every team says it takes OpSec seriously, but nobody can check. This RFP funds a neutral coordinator to get at least 4 OpSec audit firms working together, so more teams get OpSec audits and fix what they find, with a public board of the teams that did (every gap stays private). Then the list gets teeth: protocols, bridges, L2s, wallets and exchanges make a current listing on the board a condition of doing business.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Your keys, your devices, your multisig process, your access controls... these matter as much as your smart contracts:

- Bybit lost nearly $1.5B in ETH in February 2025 after attackers took over one Safe developer's computer ([Chainalysis](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/bybit-exchange-hack-february-2025-crypto-security-dprk/)).
- KelpDAO lost about $292M in April 2026 through compromised RPC nodes, "not a smart contract hack" ([Chainalysis](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/kelpdao-bridge-exploit-april-2026/)).

Serious teams already buy OpSec audits, and all of that work is invisible, while the findings often wait on a to-do list. After TheDAO hack, shipping an unaudited contract became negligent. OpSec audits need the same shift, and SOC 2 checklists were never built for stolen keys and tricked signers. Teams that complete an OpSec audit and fix what it finds get listed on a public board.

A rating only matters if missing it costs something, the way no bank works with a firm that fails compliance. Once the exchanges, protocols, bridges, L2s and wallets that move the money require a current listing, weak OpSec costs a team its listings and integrations, and users are safer from stolen keys, hijacked laptops, tricked signers and poisoned infrastructure.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
This RFP pays for coordination: getting the OpSec audit firms working together, then getting the businesses that move the money to require an OpSec audit. The board is the easy part.

Bidders have complete freedom in how they get there, including their own milestones, within the hard requirements below. What matters is three outcomes: more teams get OpSec audits, teams act on them by fixing what they find, and the OpSec audit firms coordinate as one coalition, ideally one that outlives the grant on member dues and runs shared services like red teaming. This money funds only the coordinator.

One possible approach:

- A simple public board of teams that completed an OpSec audit and fixed every critical and high finding, with their auditor and dates. It may also show facts anyone can check onchain, such as timelocks, multisig thresholds and outflow limits, the way L2BEAT Stages shows rollup trust assumptions.
- The founding firms list the teams they audit first, with a clear path for any qualified OpSec firm to join. The coalition decides.
- Shared outcome goals in place of one rigid checklist, such as "after a compromise, the team can trace affected systems and the root cause within 24 hours", built on SEAL's frameworks, with the auditor answering for the result.
- A six-month check-in, and a verification committee that spot-checks listings.
- Member dues, equal votes for founding firms and a neutral name. Fees from listed teams only if the coalition chooses, the same fee whatever the result.
- The first organizations that require a current listing.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Performing the OpSec audits (the OpSec audit firms do that)
- Requiring every firm to adopt one shared standard (the coalition may agree one if it helps)
- A heavy platform build

sections.heading: Existing work
sections.markdown:
- [SEAL Security Frameworks](https://frameworks.securityalliance.org/): SEAL's open OpSec, multisig, treasury and incident frameworks, the natural base for the standard.
- [SEAL Certifications](https://securityalliance.org/our-work/certifications): modular certifications assessed by auditors SEAL accredits, recorded as onchain attestations. Bids may build the standard and rater roster on it; a bid that starts fresh explains why.
- [L2BEAT Stages](https://l2beat.com/stages): the model, a public maturity rating for rollups.
- [Coinspect Wallet Security Ranking](https://wallets.coinspect.com/): a quarterly public security score for Ethereum wallets.

sections.heading: Who we expect to do this
sections.markdown:
Nobody is pre-selected. The dream candidate is a credible coordinator who can get 4+ OpSec audit firms to work together (if you have ever tried to get six companies to agree on anything, you know that's the real work here), then get the protocols and wallets that matter to write a listing into their policies.

A strong bid reads like a founder pitch: one credible lead or a lean team, its own plan, and why audit firms and protocols will take its call. The OpSec audit firms that back this RFP before the vote each name one ETHSecurity Badge holder to the panel that reviews bids, and the panel's majority picks the coordinator.

The longterm goal of this initiative is to bootstrap an organization that can make Operational Security Audits as necessary as smart contract audits. We expect in the long run for this organization to provide many shared services for the OpSec auditors, such as becoming a certification authority, red teaming projects on the board, etc. 

Drafted by Griff Green of TheDAO Security Fund, with feedback from several OpSec audit firms. Griff runs no audit firm and will not bid.

sections.heading: Hard requirements
sections.markdown:
1. Listing only. The board shows a team's name, its auditor, dates and facts already public onchain (timelocks, multisig thresholds, rate limits), never its gaps, findings or why a team is missing.
2. Fixed before listed. A team is listed only after its auditor confirms every critical and high finding is fixed.
3. Human-led audits. Only human-led, crypto-specific OpSec audits earn a listing; an automated or AI-only scan, or a generic SOC 2 or ISO 27001 report, never does.
4. Open and tool-agnostic. Any rules under CC BY 4.0, board code under MIT, and a listing is reachable with any tools or vendors.
5. Listings expire. A listing lasts at most 12 months and is suspended on a disclosed incident or material change until the team is re-audited.
6. Built to last. The coalition and board keep running after the final milestone on money other than TheDAO's, with a maintenance plan in the bid.
7. **Neutral coordinator.** The coordinator is not an OpSec audit firm, because whoever runs the coalition would gain an edge over the firms it convened.

initiatives.title: RFP: Production-Ready Local-First Safe UI
initiatives.summary: This RFP funds a production-ready, local-first Safe multisig UI, deployed to IPFS with reproducible builds, that anyone can run with nothing but an RPC endpoint and a wallet. It is an independent way to execute transactions if Safe for any reason becomes unreachable, and a tool to cross-check every hash before signers approve.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
A Safe is a contract on Ethereum. Its owners and threshold are on-chain, and anyone can execute a transaction once it carries enough owner signatures to meet the threshold. In the standard flow, everything before that step happens off-chain, through the hosted Safe{Wallet} frontend that Safe Labs operates and the Safe Transaction Service behind it. Self-hosting that stack means running the Client Gateway, the Transaction Service and a tracing archive node for internal-transaction indexing, so few teams do.

In July 2024, WazirX lost roughly $235M from a Safe multisig managed through Liminal Custody, whose interface showed a routine transfer while the signatures authorized a malicious contract upgrade. In October 2024, malware on the computers of Radiant Capital's signers showed a clean transaction while their hardware wallets received different calldata; the signers signed blind instead of checking the domain and message hash on the device, and lost roughly $50M. In February 2025, malicious JavaScript in the hosted Safe{Wallet} frontend showed Bybit's signers one transaction while their hardware wallets signed another, and roughly $1.5B left the Safe. These incidents are different manifestations of the same underlying problem: the software presenting a transaction to a signer cannot be treated as a trusted part of the signing boundary.

Assume Safe's hosted frontend and Transaction Service disappear tomorrow. A non-technical multisig signer should still be able to:

- open this UI from a local copy or the IPFS release
- connect a hardware wallet
- rebuild the transaction from the Safe's on-chain state (owners, threshold, nonce, contract version) and the parameters they were sent, then recompute its hashes locally
- verify exactly what they are signing
- exchange signatures with the other owners through ordinary files or links
- execute the transaction using only a JSON-RPC endpoint

No Safe account, Safe backend, project-operated server, indexer or technical help required. That is Vitalik's walkaway test.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
This RFP pays for finishing, hardening and maintaining a local-first Safe UI with minimal dependencies and trivial deployment. Optimise for the least technical signer rather than the developer running the UI. Deliverables:

- Ethereum Mainnet, Safe contract versions v1.3.0 and v1.4.1 at minimum
- Production hardening of an existing codebase, or a fresh build
- The full lifecycle against one standard JSON-RPC endpoint: load a Safe from chain state, propose, sign, exchange signatures, execute, manage owners and threshold, arbitrary contract calls
- Signature exchange without a server: signed transaction packages exported and imported through ordinary files or shareable links, with nested Safe (EIP-1271) support and approveHash as the on-chain alternative
- Verification: enter or import a transaction's full SafeTx parameters and recompute the EIP-712 domain hash, message hash and safeTxHash locally, with calldata decoded offline from a bundled selector database or a user-supplied ABI
- Hardware wallet signing on Ledger and Trezor at minimum, over WebUSB or WebHID or through a vendor library bundled with the app
- A command-line tool or local API that returns the hashes and decoded calldata for a given Safe address, chain ID and transaction parameters, for scripts and AI agents
- Reproducible IPFS builds with fixed import settings, an ENS name whose contenthash resolves to the current release, and docs for running locally and verifying a build
- 12 months of maintenance after the first tagged release (expected within 3 months of funding), and a business plan for the years after

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Full Safe{Wallet} parity (Safe Apps, swaps, staking, onramps)
- Hosted backends or indexers, including a team-run web server for this UI (the IPFS and ENS release is in scope)
- Chains beyond Ethereum Mainnet
- Mobile apps
- New smart contracts

sections.heading: Existing work
sections.markdown:
- [localsafe.eth](https://github.com/Cyfrin/localsafe.eth) (Cyfrin, MIT), live at [localsafe.eth.limo](https://localsafe.eth.limo). Its README calls it "still a project in early development": Safe v1.4.1 only, no transaction history; last release v0.3.1, June 18, 2026.
- [Eternal Safe](https://github.com/eternalsafe/wallet) (GPL-3.0), a Safe{Wallet} fork (app v1.26.2) that needs only an RPC URL. Received a Safe Grants Program grant; maintained by Devan Non; signature "smart links" are encoded rather than encrypted; v1.4.1 by default.
- [Safe's own monorepo](https://github.com/safe-global/safe-wallet-monorepo) (GPL-3.0). Self-hosting it means the [Client Gateway](https://github.com/safe-global/safe-client-gateway), the [Transaction Service](https://github.com/safe-global/safe-transaction-service) and a tracing archive node ([Safe docs](https://docs.safe.global/core-api/api-overview)).
- Hash-verification tools: [safe-tx-hashes-util](https://github.com/pcaversaccio/safe-tx-hashes-util), [OpenZeppelin Safe Utils](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/safe-utils), [Cyfrin safe-hash](https://tools.cyfrin.io/safe-hash). They verify hashes only.

A bid built on another codebase should show it meets these hard requirements with fewer runtime dependencies.

sections.heading: Who we expect to do this
sections.markdown:
Nobody is pre-selected. Teams that have already shipped Safe frontends or signing tools, including the people behind localsafe.eth and Eternal Safe, will be judged on that record, and the budget is $120,000 either way. Safe contributors are welcome to bid or to co-fund.

Co-drafted by Griff Green and pcaversaccio, both Curators of TheDAO Security Fund. pcaversaccio maintains [safe-tx-hashes-util](https://github.com/pcaversaccio/safe-tx-hashes-util), listed above.

sections.heading: Hard requirements
sections.markdown:
1. **Open source.** An OSI-approved license, MIT or GPL-3.0 expected, and a public repository from the first commit of funded work.
2. **RPC only, nothing project-operated.** Every flow works against a standard JSON-RPC endpoint. Runtime dependencies are minimised, with no dependency on a hosted SaaS, proprietary API, mandatory backend, indexer, telemetry service, analytics provider or project-operated infrastructure, and no analytics or telemetry in the UI.
3. **Signature exchange without a server.** Signed transaction packages export and import through ordinary files or shareable links. Imported signatures are checked against the transaction's safeTxHash and the Safe's current owner set before they are accepted: signature recovery for EOA owners, an isValidSignature call for contract owners. Off-chain signatures work for nested Safes through EIP-1271, and on-chain approval through approveHash is supported as an alternative.
4. **Hardware wallets.** Ledger and Trezor at minimum, over WebUSB or WebHID or through a bundled vendor library. Before signing, the UI shows the EIP-712 domain hash, message hash and safeTxHash. The device shows the domain hash and the message hash, and the signer matches those against the UI and an independent hash tool. Vendor libraries are bundled and served with the app, with no popup, iframe or metadata fetched from a vendor's servers and no separate bridge daemon to install.
5. **Undecodable calldata stays unverified.** Calldata the UI cannot decode is shown as raw bytes with an unverified label, never as safe to sign.
6. **Verifiable builds.** Reproducible from a tagged commit to the published IPFS CID with fixed import settings, by an unaffiliated user without the team's infrastructure; the ENS contenthash resolves to the current release.
7. **Trivial deployment.** Open a local copy or the IPFS release, connect a hardware wallet, and work. Nothing to install beyond that.
8. **A maintenance and business plan in the proposal.** Who maintains the UI for the 12 months after the first tagged release, and how it is paid for after that.
9. **Public evidence for every milestone.** Recordings, transaction hashes, CIDs, test runs and named parties confirming, all published.

initiatives.title: RFP: What Replaces Patch Tuesday? Coordinated Disclosure for Bugs Shared Across Ethereum
initiatives.shortTitle: What Replaces Patch Tuesday? Coordinated Disclosure for…
initiatives.summary: Ethereum is permissionless, so when a bug turns up in shared code nobody knows who else runs it or where. The best-known model for coordinated fixes is Microsoft's Patch Tuesday, one scheduled day a month, and the day after is known as Exploit Wednesday. With AI reading every patch, a scheduled day tells attackers when to look, and waiting for it leaves a known bug live. This RFP asks bidders how Ethereum should coordinate instead, and pays for hand-run disclosures first, then an open standard built from them.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Users are safer when every team running a buggy piece of shared code is warned privately and patches before the fix is public. Today nobody holds that list.

- Geth shipped a pre-announced fix for CVE-2021-39137 ([advisory](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9856-9gg9-qcmq)) on August 24, 2021. Three days later it was exploited on mainnet, splitting off nodes that had not upgraded ([Geth postmortem](https://github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/blob/master/docs/postmortems/2021-08-22-split-postmortem.md)).
- Vyper fixed a broken reentrancy lock in December 2021 without realizing its impact, so protocols on old versions were not explicitly notified ([Vyper](https://hackmd.io/@vyperlang/HJUgNMhs2)). In July 2023 attackers took $69.3M from pools compiled with them, $52M after returns ([CertiK](https://www.certik.com/resources/blog/2qbPMcyJpR5UfoKrcjWxlQ-vyper-incident-anaylsis)).
- In December 2023 an ERC-2771 and Multicall flaw affected thousands of contracts, and several pools holding almost 90 ETH were hacked before OpenZeppelin's full public disclosure ([OpenZeppelin](https://www.openzeppelin.com/news/secure-implementations-vulnerable-integrations)).
- In a 2024 study, a GPT-4 agent exploited 87% of 15 disclosed vulnerabilities when handed the public advisory, and 7% without it ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.08144)).

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
Bidders have complete freedom in how they get there, including their own milestones, within the hard requirements below. Each bid states a hypothesis and a plan of attack for three problems:

1. Who else has it: find who runs the vulnerable code (forks, deployments, chains, node operators) on Ethereum and its L2s.
2. A warning they trust: warn them privately, through a channel where each side can verify the other, so they act.
3. Going public in the age of AI: stage fixes so they land in public repositories without exposing the bug early, release them together, then push operators to update.

One possible approach, the one the milestones below follow: start by hand. The selected team runs real disclosures alongside the teams fixing each bug, races to reach every other affected team before the fix is public, then systematizes what worked. The target clock is 24 hours from bug confirmed to every affected team notified. Example hypothesis: a dependency map built before any bug lets one person list every affected team inside that clock. This RFP is a starting point and will change; the final milestones are agreed with the selected team.

The lasting output is an open, broad disclosure standard (process, comms templates, when and how to go public), informed by SEAL 911 and the cases run. Bugs can come from any source; bids say where. The selected team may use the security contacts published under the companion security-contact RFP and may pass researcher payment to the companion bug broker.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Finding bugs.
- Whitehat rescues.
- Findings only one team must fix (the companion bug broker RFP).

sections.heading: Existing work
sections.markdown:
- [Microsoft Patch Tuesday](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/msrc/faqs-security-update-guide) and [Exploit Wednesday](https://www.manageengine.com/patch-management/exploit-wednesday.html), the day after.
- [SEAL 911](https://securityalliance.org/seal-911) handles live incidents; SEAL's [disclosure framework](https://frameworks.securityalliance.org/vulnerability-disclosure/overview) covers one affected project and tells teams to warn forks before publishing. Bids say whether their standard extends it.
- [linux-distros](https://oss-security.openwall.org/wiki/mailing-lists/distros): Linux distributions' private embargo list, 14 days at most.
- [CERT/CC VINCE](https://sei.cmu.edu/news/certcc-releases-vince-software-vulnerability-collaboration-platform): one shared case space for many vendors.
- [Ethereum Foundation public disclosures](https://github.com/ethereum/public-disclosures): the EF cross-checks client bug bounty reports and shares them with affected client teams.
- [Project Zero's Reporting Transparency trial](https://projectzero.google/2025/07/reporting-transparency.html) targets the "upstream patch gap".

sections.heading: Who we expect to do this
sections.markdown:
A team that client, rollup and protocol security leads already trust with embargoed information: a security alliance, an incident-response firm or a consortium of those leads. Nobody is pre-selected.

Drafted by TheDAO Security Fund from a conversation with EthSec (ethsecurity.org) and Consensys. EthSec, TheDAO Security Fund and Giveth will not bid.

sections.heading: Hard requirements
sections.markdown:
1. Bug details go only to verified contacts at teams that must act. Bids say how they verify them.
2. A public log records each coordinated disclosure after release (what, when confirmed, when each team was notified, share patched), never before.
3. The disclosure standard is published openly for anyone to use.
4. Running costs come from the L2s and protocols served, or from a named home that funds it. Client teams are not expected to pay.
5. **Outside means unaffiliated.** An outside team shares no owner, staff or funding relationship with the selected team. Affiliates count toward no criterion.
6. Ethereum and L2s only.

initiatives.title: Runtime Capital: Safe Lockdown Guard, an Emergency Freeze for Kidnapping and Coercion
initiatives.summary: Kidnapping and physical coercion can force Safe owners to authorize transfers with perfectly valid signatures. Safe Lockdown Guard gives them a separate emergency action: freeze guarded transfers with a credential that cannot spend funds. Runtime Capital has built and published the open-source audit candidate; this $14,000 request funds the remaining independent audit cost, with a final milestone tied to verified use on Ethereum mainnet. The audit, fixes and installation documentation will be public for every compatible Safe operator.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
A Safe verifies signatures, not whether its owners signed freely. Physical coercion can turn a valid signing quorum into an attack path. Treasury operators need a separate emergency action that can interrupt transfers without giving another party custody or spending authority.

The guard lets a registered emergency credential start an on-chain freeze. With the required configuration, it blocks owner and module transfers and new ERC-1271 signature validation during the incident. A restricted recovery path lets owners replace a compromised signer with a pre-approved recovery owner. Normal operation resumes after the configured lockdown and recovery periods. An optional transaction delay provides time to activate the freeze before a coerced transaction executes. The contracts have no team administrator or privileged unlock key. The protection has documented boundaries, including existing token allowances and previously valid signatures; it does not guarantee an attacker's behaviour or a person's physical safety.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
The team behind Runtime Capital, a DeFi fund, developed the guard and funded its development. This is its contribution to Ethereum's public security infrastructure: reusable code, public specifications and an independent audit that any compatible Safe operator can use. Runtime Capital handles auditor coordination, remediation, release documentation and ongoing maintenance. Public project contact: contact@runtime.capital.

The project has been awarded a subsidy of up to $6,500 through the Ethereum Security Subsidy Program, a joint initiative involving the Ethereum Foundation's Trillion Dollar Security Initiative, Chainlink Labs, Nethermind, participating audit firms and Areta Market. The subsidy is delivered as a discount from participating audit providers, covering at most 30% of an eligible quote. At our $20,000 gross audit ceiling, it reduces the cost by $6,000, leaving $14,000 to fund. Participation is not an endorsement or recommendation by the program partners. This discount is already deducted from the amount requested here.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
The public v1.0.0-audit-candidate.3 tag contains the implementation, specification, audit brief, integration tests against Safe v1.5.0, adversarial test cases and installation verification tooling. Its audit brief records 1,118 non-comment source lines, 483 passing tests and 15 stateful invariant properties. These are documented results for that candidate, not a substitute for an external audit. The candidate is not yet externally audited or released for value-bearing production use.

Runtime Capital already owns the implementation work and can resolve findings directly. Development costs are already paid; the request covers the remaining external audit bill. The auditor has not been selected. Selection will use an eligible marketplace provider, a confirmed scope, remediation review and a public report, within the $20,000 gross ceiling.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- An independent Solidity audit of the exact agreed candidate commit: the lockdown and timelock contracts, their supporting components, fallback handler, PasswordVerifier and WebAuthnVerifier, and their integration with pinned dependencies, as specified in the public audit brief.
- Remediation and auditor verification of every medium, high and critical finding before production release, with dispositions for remaining findings in the public report.
- A tagged audited release, a deployment manifest identifying supported networks and verified contract code, and an installation guide covering all three Safe integration slots and emergency credential configuration.
- Deployment of the audited contracts on Ethereum mainnet and verification of a working installation used for real treasury custody. Runtime Capital supplies coordination, documentation and onboarding effort without a separate development or marketing fee.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- New contract features, a token, user incentives or a commercial product build.
- Re-auditing Safe itself or upstream dependencies independently of their integration with this guard.
- A frontend or hosted-service audit, Safe version migration, and unsupported network deployments.
- Claims to freeze third-party token allowances, prevent DeFi liquidations, or revoke signatures already valid before activation.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- Keep original guard code under MIT and the Safe-derived fallback handler under LGPL-3.0-only. The release has no protocol fee or token requirement.
- Runtime Capital maintains the released code and installation documentation at its own cost after the grant.
- Complete the independent audit, publish the audited release and establish verified production use on Ethereum mainnet within one month of funding. The expected work schedule is two weeks for the audit followed by two weeks for mainnet deployment and installation on operational Safes.
- Establish at least one verified installation of the audited release on an operational treasury Safe holding real assets and using the guard for actual custody.

initiatives.title: Saviour: Who can act through a Safe at one pinned block
initiatives.summary: Saviour reads an Ethereum mainnet Safe at one block and reports who can act through it beyond the owners. The report covers the Safe, its Delay module, and Roles v2.1.1 members, targets, and selectors taken from chain logs. A second person opens the same link and checks that the digest matches. Condition amounts stay unknown, and the report never says the Safe is safe.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
On 16 Nov 2026 a Safe lost about $6.45 million. [Cointelegraph](https://cointelegraph.com/news/safe-wallet-reportedly-loses-millions-after-key-compromise) put the transfer at about 4.39 million USDC and 1.72 million syrupUSDC, through a Zodiac Roles modifier, and quoted Zodiac's co-founder: the policy allowed the call, and the role member's key was most likely compromised. [Safe said no owner signed](https://coinmarketcap.com/academy/article/safe-multisig-zodiac-roles-key-compromise).

[Zodiac Roles](https://roles.gnosisguild.org) is where a team edits that policy. A co-signer still cannot hand someone a block-pinned link that a second person re-runs and matches.

Co-signers of mainnet Safes that use Delay or Roles v2.1.1 get that link. The page shows who can already act, and it leaves unread authority as unknown. The 16 Nov module is a Roles version this reader identifies and does not interpret. The loss shows the class of incident. This grant does not claim that loss would have been stopped.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
**Harshit Bainsla** builds and maintains Saviour. The work is solo.

Track record: [github.com/devhb1/Saviour](https://github.com/devhb1/Saviour) and [www.saviours.xyz](https://www.saviours.xyz). The repo is MIT, copyright 2026 Harshit Bainsla.

[Kesavi Web Solutions](https://kesaviwebsolutions.com/) has committed $2,500, which is 25% of this goal. No other funder pays for this scope.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
The reader is already on mainnet. Commit [`89f3902`](https://github.com/devhb1/Saviour/commit/89f3902) on [`main`](https://github.com/devhb1/Saviour) has the Safe and Delay reads, Roles v2.1.1 selectors from chain logs, a pin link whose digest ignores the RPC host, and a plain-language box that is dropped if it stamps the Safe as safe, invents a token amount, or claims a loss would have been prevented. The same read is on npm as [`@saviours/audit`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@saviours/audit).

A stranger can open [www.saviours.xyz/audit](https://www.saviours.xyz/audit) and the repo. One team proof, the Term Safe at block 26435999, is there so the read can be repeated. It does not count as an outside user.

The reader is built. This $10,000 pays for outside teams to use it, and for the hosted page to stay up.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- Bringing outside treasury teams onto the existing reader
- A public [pilots](https://www.saviours.xyz/pilots) page with the team or Safe, the block, the digest, the witness result, and the balance query
- Keeping [www.saviours.xyz/audit](https://www.saviours.xyz/audit) answering on Ethereum mainnet through the grant
- Charging those teams for a witnessed audit, and publishing a one-page plan of the hosted reader's monthly cost

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Interpreting Roles v1, including the module in the 16 Nov 2026 incident
- Computing token amounts from Roles conditions or allowances
- A Safe App, or an import from the Safe Transaction Service
- Any chain other than Ethereum mainnet
- Detecting a compromised key, holding keys, or blocking a signature inside Safe
- The archived ENS naming product

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- The auditor stays under the MIT license already in the repo.
- Harshit Bainsla keeps the hosted reader up for 12 months after the last milestone, with no further ask to the fund.
- Pinned target: at least 5 outside teams, on the terms in the adoption milestones.
- Condition amounts stay unknown, Roles v1 is named and not interpreted, and the report never says the Safe is safe.

initiatives.title: SCAR: Test security fixes against the real exploit before they ship
initiatives.summary: SCAR helps protocol teams and auditors check whether a smart-contract security fix blocks the known attack without breaking normal use. It replays the real exploit and its variants against the patched contract on a fork of Ethereum, checks normal use still works, and gives a verdict anyone can re-run before the fix ships or funds go back in. This grant pays for 24 test cases built from past Ethereum exploits, a public scoreboard that grades AI-written fixes on them, and four outside organizations using the check on eight real fixes of their own.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Protocol users are safer from the second drain: the same exploit working again after the team says it is fixed.

- The Verus bridge on Ethereum lost about $11.5 million on 18 May 2026. Most of it was returned for a bounty and put back into the same bridge on 8 July. On 23 July it lost $7.54 million through the same contract path and bug class ([CoinDesk](https://www.coindesk.com/tech/2026/07/23/bitcoin-ethereum-linked-protocols-lose-usd35-million-in-multiple-attacks-hours-apart)).
- TRM Labs counted a record 207 hacks in the first half of 2026, 125 of them exploiting smart-contract code ([TRM Labs](https://www.trmlabs.com/resources/blog/h1-2026-crypto-hacks-reach-record-high-as-losses-fall-below-usd-1-billion)).

Verus is why a fix gets re-tested before the money goes back in.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
**Farseen Shaikh**, founder of SCAR AI, works on it full time (github.com/FarseenSh). In this fund's first round, SCAR received $6,275 (linked). Its open datasets, including a 231,269-contract Solidity corpus, have over 1,800 Hugging Face downloads (linked). SunSec (DeFiHackLabs) used SCAR's retrieval model in auditing and credited it with higher recall in a first-place OneSavie Bastet Kaggle entry (linked).

An independent reviewer, named in the grant agreement, signs off every case and milestone. No other funder pays for this scope; E2B and Daytona credits cover part of the compute.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
- **Fix Verifier** (Apache-2.0), with four test cases today (one Ethereum mainnet exploit, three on BNB Chain). It grades a fix on security checks its author never sees, plus normal-use checks, and CI re-grades every control fix.
- **48 published receipts** for control fixes we wrote to test the checker. 26 stop the replayed exploit, yet 15 of those still fail: they leave another path open or break normal use. A replay-only check passes all 15.
- **Revision checks**, previewed on four public OpenZeppelin and Safe changes: 10 of 10 valid versions accepted, 6 of 6 planted faults rejected.

What is thin: one test case from Ethereum mainnet, and no outside reviewer or user of the verifier yet. The harness, receipts and CI exist, so this is not a from-scratch build.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- **24 test cases built from past exploits** on Ethereum mainnet or L2s with over $200 million secured on L2BEAT, 16 public and 8 private until the scoreboard freezes. Each packages the real exploit on frozen chain state, the related attack paths, normal-use checks, a working reference fix and two faulty fixes (one incomplete, one that breaks normal use), so the checker is tested on known answers.
- **A workflow teams run themselves**: Foundry import, command line, CI job and coding-agent adapter.
- **A public scoreboard** grading AI agents' fixes on the private test cases.
- **Onboarding**: intake template, self-serve guide, and hands-on setup of the checks for each adopter's first two fixes (fork, exploit replay, normal-use checks, reviewer sign-off).

Cost basis: one founder full time for 7 months on engineering, case building, onboarding and support ($45,000), 110 reviewer hours at $175 ($19,250), 12 exploit reproductions from outside contributors at $500 ($6,000), archive RPC, hosting and compute ($8,000), tools and bounties ($4,500), contingency ($7,250).

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Proofs or whole-contract certification
- Build systems other than Foundry
- A hosted commercial service
- Retrieval and model-training research
- Chains other than Ethereum and its L2s

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- New code under Apache-2.0, case write-ups under CC BY 4.0; third-party material keeps its own terms.
- Farseen maintains the funded release for 6 months after the last milestone at no further cost; after that, revenue from paid checks and support pays for it.
- A verdict never says "safe" or "audited": it states what was replayed and checked, with inputs and a hash anyone can re-run.
- Confidential adopter material goes only to the reviewer.
- Private test cases are published after the scoreboard freezes, with a tagged release.
- Pinned target: at least 4 outside organizations using the check on 8 real fixes.

initiatives.title: SEAL Audit Transparency: every DeFi protocol's audits, mapped to the code running onchain today
initiatives.summary: An open, sourced record of every Ethereum DeFi protocol over $1 million in TVL, about 400 today: what each one had audited, what was in scope, what is running onchain now, and what changed through upgrades since. Each live contract is rebuilt from its audited commit and compared to the deployed bytecode, so anyone can see which live code no public audit covers. It needs no cooperation from protocols or audit firms, so it can cover the whole ecosystem.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Users should know what they're trusting before they deposit. Today a protocol shows "audited by X", and that's where the information stops. It doesn't say how much of the live code the audit covered, whether the audit was three years ago and the code has been rewritten since, or whether the only change was one line. A determined user can piece this together for one protocol, but there's no public database that has it for every protocol in one place.

Ackee Blockchain found that 92 of 157 protocols on the Rekt list were hacked through unaudited or out-of-scope code, often while showing "audited by" logos ([Ackee, 2023](https://ackee.xyz/blog/why-we-need-to-start-using-erc-7512-onchain-audit-representation-right-now/)).

Afterwards:
- **Users and risk teams** can see, for any Ethereum DeFi protocol, which fund-holding contracts run code that no public audit covers, with every claim linked to its source.
- **Security researchers** get a list of post-audit changes no audit covers, ranked by TVL, as a place to start looking.
- **Protocols and audit firms** are accountable in public for what was actually reviewed and what shipped.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
- **SEAL (Security Alliance)** runs the project and publishes the results. SEAL is a nonprofit that shares threat intelligence and sets security standards for crypto. It runs SEAL 911, a free 24/7 incident hotline that has handled 3,300+ tickets; Safe Harbor, which lets whitehats step in to rescue funds during a live exploit; and SEAL Certifications, an operational security standard protocols are assessed against. Its frameworks and research are at [securityalliance.org](https://securityalliance.org/).
- **Dickson Wu** leads it: the method, the tooling and reviewing results. Dickson helps run SEAL's Safe Harbor and SEAL Certifications programs.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown: A working prototype already runs the full pipeline on Ethereum: it maps core contracts and proxies, collects public audits with their stated commit and scope, rebuilds the audited code and compares it to live bytecode. A public preview covers the 20 largest Ethereum DeFi protocols: [ethereum-audit-register-demo.dicksonwu.xyz](https://ethereum-audit-register-demo.dicksonwu.xyz). The grant pays to extend it to every protocol over $1 million, publish it and keep it current.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
Every Ethereum DeFi protocol over $1 million in TVL on DeFiLlama: DEXs, lending, liquid staking, restaking, stablecoins, bridges and the rest. Together they hold 99.9% of Ethereum DeFi TVL, and new protocols are added as they cross $1 million. For each one:
- Map the core contracts, resolve proxies to their current implementations, and record who can upgrade them.
- Collect the public audits and record the commit and scope each report states.
- Rebuild the audited commit with the deployed compiler settings and compare it to the live bytecode, accounting for metadata, immutables and linked libraries. Each difference is classed as cosmetic, covered by a later audit, or not covered by any public audit.
- Publish audit statistics: share of core contracts covered by an audit, number of audits, time since the last one, and auditor working days where reports state them.
- Roll contract results up into one protocol verdict, so an uncovered fund-holding contract can't hide behind the rest.
- A public site with every protocol page and its sources, plus the full dataset, free to query.
- A monthly refresh of every protocol that picks up new audits and upgrades, with a last-checked date on each record and a public corrections channel.

Some protocols and audit firms don't publish reports, keep repos private, or leave contracts unverified, so full coverage isn't possible everywhere. Where that blocks a comparison, the record says exactly what's missing, and those gaps are published too.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Rollup and L2 risk, which L2BEAT already does an excellent job covering.
- Other chains: this grant covers Ethereum mainnet.
- Protocols under $1 million in TVL. A protocol that falls below $1 million after it's added stays covered.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- **License:** the dataset under CC BY 4.0, with the method published.
- **Maintenance:** every covered protocol is refreshed monthly for at least 12 months after launch, and SEAL keeps the dataset running after that.

initiatives.title: SEAL Frameworks: Maintaining open security knowledge for Ethereum (Infra, AI and Front-end)
initiatives.summary: Frameworks turns practitioners' know-how into free, open Ethereum security guidance. This grant funds research, review and maintenance to complete AI, infrastructure and frontend sections for people and agents. Experienced external practitioners will steward subjects, contribute knowledge and improve the reference through recurring review and use in their own security work.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Frameworks has significant ongoing maintenance costs and no monetization: practical security know-how stays free for every team. Research, source checks, technical review, updates and releases recur as the reference grows and becomes agent-readable. This grant funds that capacity.

A developer workstation, cloud account or compromised frontend can put users' funds at risk. Chainalysis recorded over $3.4 billion in crypto theft in 2025, including the $1.5 billion Bybit theft. Sygnia traced the attack from a compromised developer workstation through reused AWS sessions to altered JavaScript served from Safe's S3 bucket, leading signers to approve a disguised transaction.

The Nx s1ngularity attack used AI command-line tools to search developer machines for credentials; investigators reported over 2,000 exposed secrets and about 1,700 affected users. Funded sections address developer AI, infrastructure access and frontend delivery. Frameworks publishes machine-readable guidance, extending the reference to agents.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
1. Matta (mattaereal), initiative lead. Leads SEAL Security Frameworks: sets its direction and scope, and does technical review. Founder of The Red Guild. https://github.com/mattaereal 

2. Sara (scode2277), co-maintainer. Maintains Frameworks day-to-day: content, reviews, contributor coordination, and releases. https://github.com/scode2277

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
SEAL is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit founded by samczsun. Frameworks has 30+ sections shaped by dozens of contributors. It periodically shares relevant TLP:GREEN information; DPRK/IT worker guidance is one of the things that draws on SEAL Intel. Frameworks coordinates with SEAL Certs to align overlapping guidance. Its site, contribution process, machine-readable exports, and releases already exist.

At proposal baseline, AI had seven short pages; frontend and most infrastructure pages were unpublished drafts on the development site. The grant funds completion, knowledge integration, and maintenance. The OPSEC Ratings Coalition initiative lists Frameworks as prior art.

Developing and maintaining authoritative security documentation demands years of dedicated research and significant institutional support, as demonstrated by foundational public goods like MDN, Wikipedia, the OWASP Top 10, and the NIST Cybersecurity Framework. While consuming these resources is seamless, sustaining them requires long-term commitment. Supporting Frameworks directly funds this critical security reference for the Web3 ecosystem while extending SEAL's current operational runway of 8.5 months.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
1. AI security: at least 4 new or substantively expanded pages covering coding-assistant permissions, secret separation, tool and MCP trust, and isolation, plus a team usage-policy template. Reuse existing DevSecOps isolation guidance.
2. Infrastructure: finish the cloud, identity and access management, zero trust and operating system security pages, covering account isolation, sessions, API keys, privileged access and secrets.
3. Frontend: finish the overview, web application security, common vulnerabilities and tools pages, with configurations for security headers, Content Security Policy, subresource integrity, hosting and CDN access.
4. Research, source checks, specialist review, configuration validation, and documented assumptions and limitations.
5. Recruit experienced external stewards for defined subjects; coordinate recurring reviews and integrate compatible, licensed guides with attribution.
6. Document external organizations' use of the guidance in existing Ethereum security work and upstream resulting improvements.
7. Maintain funded pages and shared publishing and release processes; update sources, resolve conflicts and publish corrections.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
1. Performing individual assessments, implementation engagements or onboarding for external teams.
2. A new assessment platform, rating system, certification, scanner or security product.
3. New content programs outside the three funded areas.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
1. Publish content under CC BY-SA 4.0, with source-license compatibility checked before external material is incorporated.
2. Keep grant scope, contributions, attribution, technical reviews, releases and maintenance records public.
3. Matta and Sara remain maintainers through the established review and release cycle.
4. Stewards take named responsibility for subjects across the funded areas and complete recurring technical reviews of the guidance.
5. Relevant experience is evidenced by published research, assessments, incident response, security operations or maintained guidance.
6. Counted organizations are independent of SEAL, The Red Guild and grant delivery. Grant-funded maintainers are excluded; each organization and its named steward count once.
7. Qualifying external use is a public record showing an independent organization applied funded guidance in its own completed Ethereum assessment or operational review, linking it to checks and conclusions. A citation alone does not qualify.
8. Contributors retain attribution. Funding confers no editorial approval or privileged access.
9. Generate machine-readable material from the reference and link it to source pages and releases.

initiatives.title: SEAL Intel: Scaling Actionable Threat Intelligence for Ethereum
initiatives.summary: SEAL collects threat intelligence through incident response, ecosystem reporting channels, and security research. This grant will connect those workflows into a shared pipeline that validates, enriches, and correlates Ethereum-relevant intelligence, delivering machine-readable feeds, urgent alerts, and actionable defensive recommendations. Over six months, SEAL will test these capabilities with independent Ethereum ecosystem organizations and measure intelligence quality, delivery speed, integration, and documented defensive actions.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Ethereum security teams face high volumes of fragmented threat information across incidents, malicious-domain lists, attacker infrastructure, private reporting channels, on-chain observations, and external research publications. As blockchain security has matured, attackers have increasingly targeted operational infrastructure, developers, credentials, and software supply chains alongside smart contracts, creating a growing need for intelligence that connects these threats to practical defensive actions. These sources differ in structure, reliability, and sharing restrictions. Teams must spend significant analyst time reconciling them before determining whether a threat affects their systems and what defensive action to take.

SEAL already has visibility into incidents and malicious campaigns across the Ethereum ecosystem. This initiative will make that intelligence easier to use through validated records with supporting evidence, relevant alerts delivered to affected teams, and recommendations that specify concrete defensive actions. Participating organizations will be able to integrate intelligence into their existing security tooling and contribute observations through controlled information-sharing channels.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
Security Alliance (SEAL) will deliver this initiative through its established SEAL Intel program, drawing on its existing intelligence, engineering, security research, and incident-response expertise.

- **Oskar (@blackbigswan) — SEAL Intel Lead:** Responsible for intelligence priorities, technical direction, analyst workflows, research coordination, and overall intelligence delivery. Oskar leads SEAL's existing threat intelligence operations and brings direct experience analyzing threats affecting Ethereum organizations.

His work will support intelligence analysis, enrichment, correlation, and defensive recommendations.

- **Peter Kacherginsky (@iphelix) — Security Research and Intelligence Contributor:** Peter brings cybersecurity expertise across traditional security and Web3. He operates BlockThreat, a security research publication covering blockchain threats, and will contribute specialized research and intelligence expertise on a limited part-time basis. Any use of BlockThreat intelligence will follow applicable permissions and data-sharing arrangements.
