His expertise in threat modeling, security frameworks, and practical blockchain security guidance will help translate observed attacker behavior into structured, actionable defensive recommendations.

- **Dickson Wu (@DicksonWuML) — On-Chain Security and Incident Response:** Dickson contributes to SEAL Safe Harbor, which supports secure asset recovery during critical protocol incidents. His experience in on-chain security and incident coordination will inform blockchain-specific threat analysis and recommendations for protocols and infrastructure providers.

- **Additional SEAL Engineering and Operations Contributors:** Existing SEAL personnel will support connector development, data normalization, intelligence automation, API/TAXII delivery, infrastructure, testing, and partner integrations. Individual assignments and time commitments will be finalized with the delivery team.

**Funding and relationships:** The initiative has a proposed total budget of $267,000, with $200,000 sought from TheDAO and $67,000 expected to be raised through external contributions. The Ethereum Foundation is a prospective funding source, but no contribution has been committed or received specifically for this initiative. SEAL operates existing intelligence and incident-response infrastructure and maintains relationships throughout the Ethereum ecosystem. Any previously funded work or overlapping expenditures will be disclosed to avoid duplicate reimbursement.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
SEAL Intel builds on an established operational threat intelligence program rather than creating a new intelligence organization from scratch. SEAL already receives threat information through incident response, ecosystem reporting channels, security research, and trusted relationships with blockchain organizations. The grant will fund the incremental engineering, automation, intelligence processing, and integrations needed to turn those existing capabilities into a more scalable intelligence service.

**Existing foundation and grant-funded additions**

| Existing SEAL capability | Additional work funded by this grant |
|---|---|
| Incident and intelligence intake through SEAL reporting channels | Connect selected intake workflows to a shared intelligence pipeline, preserving source provenance and sharing permissions |
| Existing analyst research and threat intelligence workflows | Automate selected collection, normalization, deduplication, enrichment, and correlation tasks |
| Existing OpenCTI-related intelligence capabilities | Build and document additional integrations, Ethereum-specific data conventions, and production workflows |
| Public security research, intelligence reports, and malicious-domain contributions | Produce consistent, evidence-linked records, actionable recommendations, and machine-readable distribution |
| Established relationships with ecosystem organizations | Support integrations and independently verified operational adoption of the new intelligence feeds |

**Existing operational capabilities and track record**

- **Ecosystem intelligence network:** SEAL maintains more than 100 communication channels and hotlines connecting DeFi protocols, centralized exchanges, infrastructure providers, and other blockchain organizations. These relationships provide direct visibility into incidents and emerging threats.

- **24/7 incident and intelligence intake:** SEAL operates `@seal_911_bot` and `@seal_tips_bot`, supporting incident reporting, intelligence submissions, initial response coordination, and information sharing.

- **Phishing detection and blocklisting:** SEAL reports identifying approximately 5,000–10,000 malicious frontends weekly and contributes intelligence to ecosystem phishing blocklists. Its integration with MetaMask's eth-phishing-detect helps malicious frontends become blocked rapidly after identification.

- **Malware and threat actor research:** SEAL investigates DPRK-linked threat actors, malware-as-a-service operations, social engineering campaigns, malicious infrastructure, and software supply-chain compromises. Research outputs include indicators of compromise, attacker tactics and techniques, campaign analysis, and coordinated defensive actions.

- **Public intelligence and research:** SEAL publishes threat research, incident analysis, and operational statistics through SEAL Radar and maintains public research repositories and datasets.

- **Existing intelligence infrastructure:** SEAL already conducts structured intelligence research and maintains OpenCTI-related capabilities for organizing and analyzing threat information.

These capabilities give SEAL a significant operational advantage: direct incident visibility, researchers who understand both traditional cybersecurity and Ethereum-specific threats, and established relationships with organizations positioned to act on intelligence.

**Why grant funding is needed**

While SEAL already collects and analyzes intelligence, many processes still require manual collection, reconciliation, enrichment, and distribution. This grant will connect existing workflows, automate repeatable processing tasks, improve intelligence quality and consistency, and provide integrations that enable security teams to consume and act on intelligence more efficiently.

**Public evidence and references**

- SEAL Radar: https://radar.securityalliance.org/
- SEAL GitHub: https://github.com/security-alliance
- Lazarus Group research: https://lazarus.group/
- Public Lazarus intelligence dataset: https://github.com/security-alliance/lazarus-group-data
- Binance incident research: https://radar.securityalliance.org/tradertraitor-vs-contagious-interview-a-look-at-binances-initial-incident-report/
- DPRK malware research: https://radar.securityalliance.org/vs-code-tasks-abuse-by-contagious-interview-dprk/
- Weekly operational statistics: https://radar.securityalliance.org/seal-weekly-stats-20-27-oct-2026/

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
SEAL Intel will expand its existing threat intelligence operations into an automated, analyst-validated service for Ethereum and its Layer 2 ecosystem. The grant funds new integrations, intelligence processing, distribution tools, and partner adoption—not the creation of a new intelligence team.

**1. Collection and normalization**

Build connectors for curated public and permissioned sources, including security research, malicious-domain feeds, incident reports, on-chain observations, and trusted reporting channels. Preserve source provenance, confidence, and sharing restrictions. Extract and deduplicate information from structured and unstructured reports, normalize it using STIX 2.1 with Ethereum-specific indicators (wallet addresses, contracts, transaction hashes, malicious dApp domains), and classify threats by category and affected participant type.

**2. Processing, correlation, and analyst review**

Automate enrichment and correlation against existing SEAL intelligence and incident observations, subject to permissions. Analysts review records before release for correctness (validity, source reliability, false positives), enrichment (supporting evidence and links to infrastructure, incidents, malware, and campaigns), and relevance (affected organizations, urgency, defensive actions). Outputs are evidence-linked, analyst-approved intelligence records. SEAL's differentiator is combining automation with direct incident visibility and researchers experienced in Ethereum threats; the technology reduces repetitive work so analysts can provide actionable guidance rather than raw indicator lists.

**3. Alerts, recommendations, and feeds**

Deliver flash alerts for active threats; tailored defensive recommendations for protocols, exchanges, wallets, and infrastructure providers; periodic campaign and threat reports; and authenticated TAXII 2.1 and REST feeds for integration into existing security tooling. Provide filtering by threat category, participant type, and authorized sharing level, plus API documentation and onboarding guidance.

**4. ISAC collaboration**

Connect selected existing SEAL reporting and ISAC workflows to enable two-way intelligence exchange. Approved participants can submit observations, receive relevant alerts, request context, and coordinate on shared threats. Apply contributor permissions, optional redaction or anonymization, and TLP 2.0 restrictions. Provide contributor feedback where confidentiality permits. This strengthens existing coordination rather than building a new messaging or incident-response platform.

**5. Security and quality**

Implement vetted access, role-based permissions, provenance, TLP-aware distribution, audit logs, and correction or withdrawal procedures for stale or inaccurate intelligence. Protect restricted sources and review automated outputs for false positives and malicious submissions.

**6. Pilot and verification**

Integrate independent Ethereum ecosystem organizations, gather operational feedback, and measure source coverage, extraction quality, analyst effort, alert delivery speed, feed/API usage, contributions, and documented defensive actions. An independent reviewer verifies the quantitative acceptance criteria specified separately in the milestones.

**Use of funds:** The proposed six-month $267,000 budget covers engineering ($108,000), intelligence analysis ($54,000), partner integration ($60,000), delivery management ($15,000), infrastructure ($18,000), and independent review ($12,000), subject to confirmation. Existing SEAL capabilities and previously funded work are excluded from duplicate reimbursement.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
The initiative does not include:

- Guaranteed prevention of all exploits, phishing campaigns, or security incidents.
- Replacement of participating organizations' existing security operations or incident-response teams.
- Unlimited custom threat investigations, security assessments, or consulting services for individual organizations.
- Automated changes to participant systems, including credential rotation, patching, or blocking.
- Development of an entirely new endpoint security, blockchain monitoring, messaging, or incident-response platform.
- Expansion into unrelated blockchain ecosystems beyond the agreed Ethereum and Layer 2 scope.
- Redistribution of restricted or confidential intelligence without authorization.
- Private donor services or features not expressly included in the approved grant scope and milestones.

The grant expands SEAL's existing intelligence capabilities and coordination workflows. It does not replace SEAL 911 or create a separate incident-response organization.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
SEAL will deliver the agreed grant-funded capabilities and provide independently verifiable evidence against the approved milestones. Evidence will include documented source integrations, intelligence-processing workflows, analyst review procedures, distribution mechanisms, and operational adoption by independent Ethereum ecosystem organizations.

**Long-term sustainability:** SEAL intends to maintain the capabilities developed through this initiative as part of its existing intelligence operations after the six-month grant period. Sustainability will be supported through continued ecosystem funding and a proposed enhanced Intel/ISAC donor offering, currently envisioned at $50,000 annually per participating organization. The proposed offering would provide participating organizations with access to SEAL Intel services, including invitation-only private intelligence briefings, quarterly threat intelligence reports, and relevant intelligence feeds and alerts. This model is prospective and does not represent committed revenue.

**Public-good outputs and access:** Grant-funded public-good deliverables will be distinguished from additional donor-supported services. Intelligence involving sensitive incidents, private sources, or confidential reporting will remain subject to contributor permissions, confidentiality requirements, and applicable TLP restrictions.

**Licensing:** SEAL will specify the licenses and publication commitments applicable to grant-funded software, documentation, schemas, and other deliverables in the final grant agreement. Restricted intelligence and confidential source material will not be publicly released where doing so would violate applicable permissions.

**Maintenance:** Named maintainers, the minimum post-grant support period, and the operating budget required to sustain the funded capabilities will be confirmed before the grant agreement is finalized.

**Measurement and accountability:** The initiative will be evaluated against agreed quantitative milestones covering source integration, normalization, automated extraction accuracy, analyst productivity, alert delivery, intelligence distribution, and independent partner adoption. Public evidence will be provided where appropriate, with sensitive information redacted or made available to the independent reviewer through approved access arrangements.

Any exceptions concerning source-code publication, restricted intelligence, or other standard grant requirements will be expressly disclosed and agreed before implementation.

initiatives.title: Shutter: Preparing encrypted mempools for inclusion in the earliest EIP possible
initiatives.summary:
EIP-8184, LUCID, proposes encrypting transactions as they move through Ethereum’s public mempool and revealing them only after their ordering has been committed.

The design has progressed significantly. The main remaining security barrier is the optionality problem: the party responsible for revealing a decryption key may have an opportunity to withhold it after a transaction has already been committed.

A promising approach is to use independent key publishers, with validators helping identify reliable providers. This would also enable a competitive marketplace for encryption and decryption service providers rather than relying on a single provider.

The goal of this initiative is to resolve the optionality problem, update the LUCID specification, obtain independent security review of optionality design, and formally propose EIP-8184 for inclusion in Ethereum’s I* hard fork.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Ethereum’s public mempool reveals transaction details before their order is finalized, creating opportunities for front-running, transaction copying, censorship, and other forms of harmful MEV.

More than $1.8 billion has extracted from Ethereum users through MEV since 2020, much of it through tactics including front-running and sandwich attacks. Encrypted mempools can reduce this attack surface by keeping transaction information hidden until ordering has been fixed.

LUCID provides a path to doing this at the Ethereum protocol level while preserving an open and permissionless transaction pipeline. Resolving optionality is an important remaining security requirement before LUCID can be proposed for inclusion in I*.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
The recipient is brainbot, a core contributor to Shutter Network.

- Jannik Luhn, Developer. Author of EIP-8105 and contributor to LUCID development.
- Luis Bezzenberger, Project Manager. Coordinates encrypted mempool development and ecosystem work.

Both have worked on encrypted mempools through Shutter Network for several years.

The team also helps coordinate the Encrypt the Mempool coalition, which brings together Ethereum researchers, client teams, builders, and infrastructure providers working to advance encrypted mempools for Ethereum.

brainbot receives monthly funding from Shutter DAO 0x36 for broader encrypted mempool work. That funding does not cover this milestone.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
brainbot and Shutter Network have years of encrypted mempool research and implementation experience. Jannik authored EIP-8105, and the team is actively contributing to EIP-8184.

Shutter has also deployed encrypted mempool technology on Gnosis Chain and previously launched a Shutterized OP Stack testnet on Sepolia. The work here builds directly on existing specifications, implementations, and relationships with Ethereum client teams.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- resolving the optionality problem
- defining the role and security model for independent key publishers
- developing the public threat model, economic analysis of key withholding, and test vectors for both execution and consensus layers
- obtaining independent security review of the optionality design
- revising EIP-8184
- technical review with Ethereum researchers and client teams
- preparing LUCID to be proposed for consideration in I*

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- guaranteeing acceptance or inclusion of EIP-8184 in I*, which is determined through Ethereum’s protocol upgrade process
- full production deployment on Ethereum Mainnet
- long-term operation of encryption or decryption service providers
- development of unrelated private order-flow or MEV mitigation systems

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- work funded by this initiative will be open source.
- brainbot will continue maintaining its contributions to EIP-8184 and coordinating LUCID development through its ongoing encrypted mempool work.
- Client implementations remain maintained by their respective upstream client teams.

initiatives.title: TEE Security Handbook: practical verification, failure analysis and recovery for Ethereum
initiatives.summary: Expand Bluethroat Labs' existing TEE Security Handbook with four reviewed engineering chapters, reusable security checklists and runnable examples. The work covers attestation verification, malicious-host interfaces, state recovery, and verification from source code to deployment. Funding also supports maintenance and documented use by independent Ethereum-facing teams.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Ethereum teams increasingly use TEEs for proving, signing and confidential execution. They need to establish more than whether an attestation has a valid signature: whether the workload is authorized, whether its inputs and host interfaces are safe, whether recovered state is current, and whether the deployed binary corresponds to reviewed source. The Handbook already explains TEE architectures and common failures; this expansion turns those foundations into checks engineers can execute.

[Taiko's postmortem](https://paragraph.com/@taiko-labs/taiko-security-incident-a-postmortem-and-next-steps) documents a debug-policy gap. Bluethroat's [published dstack research](https://bluethroatlabs.com/reveries/missing-tcb-status-check) addresses missing TCB-status enforcement. These cases demonstrate why authentic hardware evidence and safe application policy are separate concerns. The proposed chapters connect public incident analysis to rejection tests, review checklists and recovery exercises that Ethereum developers can apply to their own systems.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
**Rahul Saxena**, founder of Bluethroat Labs and the [Handbook's maintainer](https://bluethroatlabs.com/docs/contributors), leads technical research, reproduction validation and final editorial review. Phala's [security update](https://phala.com/posts/dstack-security-update-attestation-pipeline-hardening) publicly credits Rahul and Bluethroat for attestation-pipeline research and remediation collaboration.

**Wehi**, a Bluethroat Labs research intern, supports evidence collection, drafts, teaching examples and contribution records under Rahul's technical review. Funded contributions will be attributed in the public repository and release records.

Rahul operates the proposed recipient. Bluethroat has conducted security research involving Secret Network and collaborated on disclosures involving Phala/dstack. Existing Handbook contributors, including people identified on its contributors page as Coinbase-affiliated, are credited for past work; this proposal does not claim new participation or endorsement from them or their employers. The Handbook has been self-funded to date, and no external funding is committed to this proposed cycle. An independent technical reviewer will be appointed through the grant process; no reviewer is represented as already committed.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
The [public Handbook](https://bluethroatlabs.com/docs/executive-summary) already contains platform explanations, a Nitro workflow, implementation failure patterns and layered defenses. Bluethroat maintains that material and has published relevant original security research. The grant builds on an existing resource and delivery team instead of paying to establish one from scratch.

The Docusaurus migration is scheduled for September 16, 2026 and remains planned at submission. It will support version history, attributed contributions and an open contribution workflow. Existing content and that migration are not charged as new grant deliverables. The linked GitHub repository is the current website source; the migrated Handbook will identify its canonical content repository and licensing at publication.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- **Verifier engineering:** a practical acceptance-policy chapter covering debug state, measurements, TCB policy, collateral, freshness, key binding and failure behavior, with good/bad verification fixtures.
- **Malicious-host interfaces:** a casebook chapter covering concrete failures in host-controlled inputs or enclave interfaces, with an attacker-to-impact trace and vulnerable/fixed teaching example.
- **State continuity and recovery:** a chapter and exercise distinguishing authenticated storage, rollback, cloning, revocation and recovery after loss of the original host.
- **Source-to-deployment verification:** a pinned build walkthrough connecting reviewed source and build inputs to an attested deployment measurement, including an intentional mismatch.
- Four associated review checklists, independent review records, contribution/version records, corrections and six monthly maintenance updates.
- Documented use of the materials by independent Ethereum-facing teams, with a public evidence index and feedback-driven corrections.

The case material will draw on published Bluethroat research, cleared Secret Network lessons and public incident reports. Taiko is an initial verification-policy example. [Base Azul](https://blog.base.dev/introducing-base-azul) is a relevant comparison for proof-path and fallback assumptions. Any conclusion about a named implementation will identify the version and supporting evidence.

The planning allocation is $9,000 for Rahul's technical work, $4,000 for Wehi's research and writing, $4,000 for independent technical and milestone review, and $1,000 for test infrastructure and publication. These allocations support the milestone outcomes; they are not payments to users for reporting adoption.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- The corporate website redesign, other Bluethroat products and reimbursement for completed work.
- New vulnerability hunts or disclosure of confidential findings before clearance.
- A comprehensive audit, certification or security guarantee for every implementation discussed.
- A physical-hardware attack campaign or a commitment to cover the entire longer-term research backlog.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- **Open materials:** new grant-funded prose will be published under CC BY 4.0 and original example code under MIT. Third-party material retains its own license and attribution; existing contributions will not be relicensed without permission.
- **Deliverables:** at least 4 substantial engineering chapters, 4 associated checklists and 4 runnable examples or verification-fixture collections. Every chapter records author, reviewer, last-verified date, relevant revisions, evidence and limitations.
- **Maintenance:** Rahul remains lead maintainer. Six dated maintenance records will cover corrections, issues and releases during the grant. Afterward, Bluethroat will keep published releases publicly accessible and continue maintenance from its own capacity; further expansion depends on internal resources or additional funding. There is no committed follow-on sponsor or paid subscription model.
- **Adoption:** at least 6 independent Ethereum-facing teams document real use, with at least 2 publishing a follow-up after 30 days. No adopters are claimed as already committed.
- **Accountability:** each paid milestone has public evidence and an independent review record. Examples distinguish teaching simulations from hardware reproduction, and all security claims preserve their attacker assumptions.

initiatives.title: Trustblock: every public Ethereum and L2 audit tied to the contracts and commit it reviewed, free to look up
initiatives.summary: Trustblock indexes over 10,800 public audit reports from 60 security firms and shows them in an audit card on 26 block explorers, including Etherscan, and on Blockscout. This grant ties every Ethereum and L2 report to the repo, commit and deployed addresses it names, and makes every record free to look up on public pages and through a free API. For the 100 largest Ethereum and L2 protocols it closes the coverage gaps and shows, for each core contract, whether the live code matches the audited commit and who can upgrade it. Anyone about to sign, list collateral or integrate can then see which public report named that exact contract, with each finding in the firm's own words.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
- Users and protocols lose money to code nobody reviewed. ack3's H1 2026 incident dataset (Gattermayer, Kalivoda and Bašović, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13792) covers 135 DeFi incidents in the first half of 2026. Of the 68 where a pre-incident audit was found, 46 were hit through code outside every audit's scope, and out-of-scope paths account for 94.4% of those 68 incidents' losses.
- An "audited" badge does not say which contracts a report covered. That answer sits in PDFs on 60 firm websites, each with its own words for severity and status, and new reports appear every week.
- On Trustblock today, fewer than half of all reports name a deployed contract address (46.5%), and only about 1 in 5 protocol audits do (18.4%, 1,225 of 6,644). Many name a repository instead, so the link from a report to the live contract has to be made, and kept current: a report missing for three months is a gap a user cannot see.
- Every effort that compares deployed code with audits needs the same input first: which report reviewed which commit, which files and which addresses. This grant produces that input for every public Ethereum and L2 audit and makes it free to look up, record by record.
- Afterwards, a wallet user about to sign, a risk team listing collateral or an explorer visitor can look up which public reports named this exact contract and commit, with each finding's severity and status as the firm wrote it, or see that no report names it. Every record links to the firm's own PDF, so anyone can check it.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
- Bilel Seddik, CEO of Trustblock: product, data and partnerships (https://x.com/0xBilel).
- Reports arrive two ways: firms with verified accounts publish through the dashboard or the API, and Trustblock indexes the rest from firms' public sites and GitHub, attributed to the firm. No other funder pays for this scope.
- Relationships: Trustblock works with the security firms that publish on it, including Quantstamp, QuillAudits, Hacken, Zokyo, and ack3 (formerly Ackee Blockchain), whose incident dataset is cited above. Etherscan and Blockscout show Trustblock's card through their own integrations. None of them funds this work unless listed as a backer, and Trustblock does not rank or score firms.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
Already built, all public:
- A publishing platform for security firms: verified firm accounts publish reports, scope and findings through a dashboard or the API. Today it holds over 10,800 public audit reports from 60 firms, on more than 7,200 projects: https://app.trustblock.run
- Contract-level data: about 22,000 deployed contract addresses tied to reports, and over 5,100 reports that name a deployed contract address.
- Report files kept on IPFS: about 3,900 reports are kept only as our pinned IPFS copy, so they stay readable when a firm's page moves or disappears.
- An audit card on the contract pages of 26 block explorers, including Etherscan, and on Blockscout: open the Cards tab of the Uniswap token link above.
- A reading pipeline: new reports are read twice, blind, and a finding goes in only when both readings agree on its severity and the firm's own status word ("Mitigated" stays "Mitigated"). A third reading settles any disagreement.
- A free API tier, embeds for firms and projects, public project, firm and audit pages, and a sitemap and llms.txt for search engines and AI agents.
- Grants delivered: Starknet Foundation (25,000 USDC, 2024; Starknet support shipped in January 2025) and AngelHack x Polygon (80,000 POL, 2025; three milestones reported complete in December 2025).
- The platform, the explorer integrations and the reading pipeline are already paid for. What costs money every month is the reading itself: following 60 firms' sites, reading each new PDF twice, checking it, and keeping the card and API answering. This grant pays for the scope pinning, six months of that reading work on Ethereum and L2, and the open release, at a fraction of what a build from scratch would cost.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- Ethereum mainnet, and L2s holding at least $200 million on L2BEAT at the start date.
- Repo, commit and deployed addresses extracted from every Ethereum and L2 report on Trustblock and linked to the contracts, each marked "named in report" or "confirmed by firm".
- Every Ethereum and L2 record free to look up on public pages and through the free API tier, with a documented field format and a dated weekly log of what was added.
- Missing public reports added for the 100 largest Ethereum and L2 DeFi protocols by TVL, and for each of their core contracts (the deployed contracts the protocol lists on its own documentation's deployment page, up to 20 per protocol): the verified source compared with the audited commit (matches, differs with the changed files listed, or not verifiable), who can upgrade it (proxy admin, owner, multisig signers and threshold, timelock), and every upgrade since the audit.
- Six months of upkeep: every new public report from the indexed firms on an Ethereum or L2 project read twice, checked, pinned and added, and the card and API kept answering.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Alt-L1s and non-EVM chains, even where Trustblock covers them.
- Rebuilding contracts from source to compare bytecode, and the deployed-code comparison for protocols beyond the 100 largest.
- Reviewing or auditing code.
- Ranking, scoring or endorsing firms or protocols, or any statement that a contract carries no risk.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- Access: every Ethereum and L2 record stays free to read on Trustblock's public pages and through the free API tier, each linked to the firm's own report. The platform's code is not part of this grant.
- Free use: the explorer card and the free API tier stay free for display partners and non-commercial users.
- Maintenance: anything that breaks in the records or the free lookups is fixed within 30 days through month 6. After that, the records stay free to look up for at least 24 months.
- Accuracy: each report is read twice, blind, and each firm's status word is kept as written. Where we cannot read it, the field is marked unchecked, never guessed. A blind check of 100 findings per firm is published for the 5 firms holding the most Ethereum and L2 audits.
- Signed statements by firms, where they exist, are shown next to the record.

initiatives.title: ValOS: Keep ETH InfraOps Open, Secure & Resilient
initiatives.summary:
ValOS (Validator Operations Standard) is an open-source security standard, risk and controls framework, and collection of best practices for secure and resilient Ethereum node operations. Developed with contributors across staking operations, exchanges, risk, cybersecurity and assurance, ValOS evolved through two community releases, the first in 2024 and the full standard in Sep 2026.

The ValOS Operational Adoption Programme (VOAP) will drive adoption across two parts of the Ethereum ecosystem:
- Staking: Node operators and staking pools use ValOS to assess and improve operational security, while staking protocols use ValOS evidence in operator oversight and decisions.
- Security & Assurance: Auditors, ratings providers, monitoring platforms, risk providers, and other security parties incorporate ValOS into their existing security services and products.

Over 18 months, VOAP will coordinate these efforts, targeting 12 independently verifiable operational adoptions across 9 professional Ethereum node operators and 3 security and assurance providers, with mechanisms to maintain security and resilience over time.

Over 43% of the requested funding is directly contingent upon independently verified operational adoption outcomes.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
**ValOS is currently the only open-source standard for Ethereum validator operational security.** Other industry standards exist, but they restrict how people can use, modify or build upon them.

ValOS is free for anyone to adopt, adapt and extend, including for commercial use. This makes security controls accessible to more operators, while allowing auditors, monitoring platforms, ratings providers and other security companies to build their own tools and services to assess, monitor and improve infrastructure security.

**The ValOS standard has already been developed and gone through two rounds of updates and improvements. The next step is adoption.** The priority now is to put this work into practice, with organisations implementing security controls in their day-to-day operations to reduce risks, prevent failures and improve Ethereum infrastructure resilience.

**VOAP brings the same openness to adoption.** It helps operators implement ValOS security controls and security providers independently assess, monitor and support those practices. Together, they help ensure security improvements are not just documented, but implemented and maintained over time.

The programme will openly share adoption approaches, progress, challenges and lessons learned, while protecting confidential and security-sensitive information.

**Each adoption makes the next one easier.** Others can learn from what works, reuse proven security practices and build on previous work instead of starting from scratch. This allows security improvements made by one organisation to benefit others across Ethereum.

As more organisations adopt ValOS, their practical experience can also help improve the standard, keeping its security controls relevant as Ethereum infrastructure and risks evolve.

**The goal is not simply to have an open security standard, but to put it to work — building an open, community-driven security ecosystem where more operators implement stronger security controls, independent providers help maintain them, and shared learning makes Ethereum infrastructure safer and more resilient.**

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
**[Lionscraft](https://www.lionscraft.io/) has been the lead contributor, coordinator and maintainer of D.U.C.K. and subsequently ValOS since the initiative began in 2023.** Over nearly three years, Lionscraft has led the development, publication and ongoing improvement of the standard, its security controls, tools and best practices.

The initiative has involved contributions from 20 organisations across Ethereum staking, node operations, cybersecurity, risk and assurance. Lionscraft coordinated their participation, bringing together organisations with different expertise and levels of involvement. Some were major contributors to the standard and its supporting resources, while others provided specialist input, reviewed specific sections or contributed to individual controls and practices.

This experience is directly relevant to VOAP. Lionscraft has already demonstrated its ability to coordinate diverse independent organisations around a shared, open-source security framework, manage contributions and turn that collaboration into published outputs. **VOAP builds on this experience, shifting the focus from developing ValOS to driving its adoption across the Ethereum ecosystem.**

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
**ValOS is the result of nearly three years of development and industry collaboration, originally initiated and funded through Lido.**

Beginning with D.U.C.K. in November 2023, the initiative evolved through two phases of development, delivering an open-source security standard, risk and controls framework, assessment resources, toolkits and best practices for Ethereum validator operations. The full ValOS standard launched in September 2026.

The work has already delivered:

- **An open-source standard:** Published security risks, controls, mitigation practices and assessment guidance, available for anyone to use, adapt and extend.
- **Tools and best practices:** Existing resources that support operators in assessing and improving their security and resilience.
- **Industry collaboration:** Contributions from 20 organisations across staking operations, exchanges, cybersecurity, risk and assurance.
- **An independent assessment pathway:** Qualified third-party assessors can evaluate operators against ValOS. Lido will also subsidise part of the assessment costs for four early-adopter node operators.

With the standard, toolkits and best practices now established, the next phase is accelerating adoption across the wider Ethereum ecosystem.

VOAP will leverage existing resources, relationships and adoption pathways to minimise programme overhead and concentrate resources on real-world implementation. Of the $78,000 funding request, $34,000 is directly contingent upon independently verified operational adoption outcomes.

**Public documentation and prior work:** The initiative's development history is documented in the [original D.U.C.K. proposal on Lido Research](https://research.lido.fi/t/d-u-c-k-distributed-utilization-of-configurations-and-knowledge-proposal/5848), with its first published framework available in the [D.U.C.K. Knowledge Base](https://duck-initiative.gitbook.io/d.u.c.k.-knowledge-base). The subsequent development phase is documented in the [ValOS governance, assurance and adoption proposal](https://research.lido.fi/t/strengthen-d-u-c-k-governance-assurance-and-real-world-adoption/9849/4). Lido's continuing support for independent assessments is documented in the [early-adopter assessment subsidy proposal](https://research.lido.fi/t/proposal-funding-request-for-valos-early-adopter-assessment-subsidies/10657). The resulting open-source standard and its development history are available in the [ValOS GitHub repository](https://github.com/lidofinance/valos).

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
VOAP will deliver a coordinated, open adoption programme across Ethereum's staking and security and assurance ecosystems.

The programme will identify and develop adoption opportunities, recruit prospective adopters, facilitate ValOS integration into existing operations, products and services, and drive the ongoing application of security and resilience practices.

VOAP will prioritise adoption opportunities with credible implementation pathways, meaningful security benefits and the potential for wider ecosystem adoption.

The work is organised into three areas.

**1. Staking Ecosystem: Implementing ValOS in Validator Operations**

VOAP will drive adoption among infrastructure operators and staking organisations through two pathways:

- **Self-assessment:** Recruit and support operators to assess their security practices against ValOS, identify gaps, apply relevant controls and declare their alignment with the standard, without requiring paid third-party certification.
- **Independent assessment:** Connect operators with qualified external assurance providers and facilitate access to ValOS-based independent assessments.

VOAP will target operators of different sizes and staking affiliations, supporting adoption across the wider Ethereum staking ecosystem.

VOAP will also selectively engage staking protocols, pools and institutional stakers where there are credible opportunities to incorporate ValOS assurance evidence into operator selection, oversight and incentives.

The objective is to embed ValOS into how Ethereum staking organisations assess, manage and continuously improve their operational security and resilience.

**2. Security & Assurance Ecosystem: Integrating ValOS into Security Services**

VOAP will drive adoption among organisations that assess, secure, monitor and support Ethereum validator infrastructure. Potential adoption areas include:

- **Assurance & certification:** Integrate ValOS into independent security assessments, certification, control verification and ongoing assurance.
- **Ratings & risk intelligence:** Incorporate ValOS into validator security ratings, operator evaluations and risk analytics.
- **Security monitoring & detection:** Use ValOS risks and controls in monitoring, alerting and ongoing security oversight.
- **Infrastructure security technologies:** Build upon ValOS in validator security tooling, key management, distributed validator technology (DVT) and infrastructure protection services.
- **Incident response & resilience:** Incorporate ValOS into incident preparedness, response, recovery testing and operational resilience services.
- **Financial security & risk protection:** Use ValOS assurance evidence in underwriting, insurance, slashing protection and security-related risk decisions.

VOAP will prioritise integration opportunities based on their implementation feasibility, security impact and potential to extend the benefits of ValOS across multiple Ethereum infrastructure operators.

**Every VOAP-supported integration must address how security practices or assurance remain effective and relevant over time.** VOAP will make continuity a core requirement of its adoption partnerships, including suitable mechanisms for ongoing monitoring, periodic reviews, remediation follow-up or reassessment after material changes and incidents.

The specific mechanisms will be designed, implemented and maintained by the adopting organisations themselves.

The objective is to embed ValOS into the existing services and technologies that help Ethereum infrastructure prevent security failures, detect problems, respond, recover and improve.

**3. Open Adoption: Making Adoption Open, Collaborative and Reusable**

VOAP will operate as an **Open Adoption Programme**, allowing anyone in the Ethereum ecosystem to participate, propose adoption opportunities, contribute to integrations and build upon existing work.

VOAP will:

- **Maintain an open adoption register:** Publish opportunities, their proposed ValOS applications, progress, obstacles and next steps, so others can participate or pursue them independently.
- **Document adoption work as it happens:** Share outreach approaches, integration methods, decisions, outcomes and lessons learned, including unsuccessful efforts, while protecting confidential and security-sensitive information.
- **Publish reusable adoption resources:** Make non-confidential integration examples, practical guidance and relevant materials openly available so other organisations can adapt and extend them.
- **Enable community participation and continuity:** Allow external contributors to propose opportunities, contribute improvements and continue adoption efforts using existing ValOS infrastructure, without depending on Lionscraft.

**The result is an open, reusable body of adoption work that grows with each contribution.** Every adoption can make the next easier, while helping the Ethereum ecosystem independently expand, maintain and improve the use of ValOS.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Performing audits, security assessments or certification.
- Operating or securing third-party validator infrastructure.
- Building or maintaining partners' security products or services.
- Creating new assurance, ratings or certification standards.
- Routine ValOS governance, standards maintenance or publication of ValOS v2.
- Funding or administering existing Lido assessment subsidies.
- Adoption outside the Ethereum ecosystem.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- **Operational security adoption:** Drive real-world implementation of ValOS security controls among Ethereum infrastructure operators and integration into existing security and assurance services.
- **Verifiable adoption:** Deliver at least 12 independently verifiable operational adoptions across 9 professional Ethereum node operators and 3 security and assurance providers.
- **Diverse adoption:** Achieve operational adoption across operators of different sizes and staking affiliations, including at least 4 operators with at least 10,000 ETH staked each, at least 3 operators with fewer than 10,000 ETH staked each, and at least 3 Lido node operators, as specified in the adoption milestones.
- **Outcome-based funding:** Allocate $34,000, representing 43.6% of the requested funding, directly to independently verified operational adoption milestones.
- **Open adoption:** Publicly document adoption opportunities, approaches, progress, outcomes and lessons learned, making non-confidential materials openly available for others to reuse and extend.
- **Security and resilience continuity:** Ensure VOAP-supported adoptions address how operational security controls, assessments and assurance will be maintained, reviewed and improved over time.
- **Independent verification:** Provide evidence of completed adoption milestones for independent review, while protecting confidential information and security-sensitive findings.
- **Long-term sustainability:** Enable adopting organisations to maintain their own implementations and allow the wider Ethereum community to continue adoption efforts through existing ValOS infrastructure, independently of Lionscraft.

initiatives.title: Verity Labs: Securing Ethereum with Formal Verification
initiatives.summary: AI is making it faster to attack software, giving attackers a meaningful edge. Formal verification is widely considered the strongest security guarantee in software correctness. This grant aims to increase formal verification adoption across the Ethereum ecosystem with TVL secured as the ONLY success metric.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
AI is making it faster to attack software, giving attackers a meaningful edge. The answer is to put AI on the defending side too: AI that writes machine-checked proofs that a contract's stated properties hold, with humans only checking the theorems. Formal verification is widely considered the strongest guarantee of software correctness, and it is the one place where AI output can be checked mechanically rather than trusted.

This grant creates an open-source framework for Solidity verification (Verity, built on Lean 4, with an AI proof-writing skill) and increases formal verification adoption across the Ethereum ecosystem. Success is measured by the TVL covered by formally verified properties.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
The recipient is Verity Labs. This is a grant rather than an RFP because its team has spent the past few months doing unbounded formal-verification work with leading Ethereum protocols. Its public work covers 40+ protocols, among them popular names like Lido, Morpho, and Safe (see Existing work below).

This experience shows where real protocols need unbounded proofs, where modeling gaps block use, and what needs to become repeatable for developers and audit firms. The Ethereum Foundation has already funded part of Verity's product roadmap via a grant.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
- Verity Labs: https://veritylabs.dev and the Verity product page https://veritylabs.dev/projects/verity
- Verity compiler, MIT licensed: https://github.com/lfglabs-dev/verity
- verity-benchmark, the AI proof-generation benchmark built with ecosystem protocols: https://github.com/lfglabs-dev/verity-benchmark
- Technical docs, including the Solidity-to-Verity porting guide: https://veritylang.com
- Public verification case studies (Lido V3 vault solvency, Safe owner list invariants, Morpho, Balancer, 1inch, Pendle and others): https://veritylabs.dev/research
- Paper, "A Formally Verified Smart Contract Compiler in Lean 4", accepted at ETHReS 2026: https://veritylabs.dev/research/verity

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- Product work on Verity's compiler, Solidity coverage, reusable proof infrastructure, benchmark, documentation, developer onboarding, AI proof-writing skill, and a deterministic Solidity-to-Verity transpiler that reduces modeling gaps.
- Public releases that document supported workflows, trust assumptions, version pins, known limitations, and how teams and formal audit firms can use the tooling.
- Adoption through protocol teams using Verity in-house and formal audit firms using it in their own work.
- Measuring adoption primarily through the TVL of contracts whose stated properties are formally verified.

**What this pays for:**

This is not a program to select public contracts and publish formal verifications of them. It pays for two connected things:

- **Product work:** continue the open-source Verity tooling, benchmark, documentation, developer onboarding, AI proof-writing skill, and deterministic Solidity-to-Verity transpilation work.

- **Adoption work:** make Verity usable by protocol teams in-house and formal audit firms in their own work. Success is led by the value covered by the verified properties.

Our success will only be judged on adoption, cause that is the only things that matters.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- Verifying the Solidity compiler itself.
- A proprietary product, hosted-only workflow, or exclusive access for a single provider.
- Counting users or github stars as the main measure of adoption. We consider real impact in TVL.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
1. **Open to everyone.** Verity product code, benchmark artifacts, documentation, and CI are public under an OSI-approved license. No proprietary runtime, hosted service, account, or paid provider is needed to use the tooling or reproduce a proof.
2. **Reproducible.** A stranger can reproduce each headline product claim from a clean checkout, documented command, public CI, and version pins, without admitted proof gaps.
3. **TVL-led adoption.** Adoption evidence names the participating protocol team or formal audit firm, provides public confirmation of use, and gives the public TVL source and snapshot date for each value included in the aggregate.
4. **Clear scope on verified TVL.** Each reported verification states the code revision, properties proved, trust assumptions, and known limits in plain language.

initiatives.title: Wake: v5 Maintenance and AI-Assisted Fuzzing
initiatives.summary: ack3 will maintain Wake v5 and improve its AI-assisted fuzzing workflow for Solidity. The work covers compatibility updates, targeted code improvements, documentation, runnable examples, and resolution of GitHub issues raised by Wake users. Wake remains open source and usable independently of ack3's commercial audits.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Wake combines Solidity testing, fuzzing, static analysis, and code intelligence in a Python framework. Maintaining that stack requires continued work as Solidity, Python packages, EVM implementations, and Ethereum hard forks change. Unresolved compatibility problems and user-reported defects make security tests harder to reproduce and maintain.

AI can reduce the mechanical work involved in writing fuzz tests, as ack3 explains in [why AI-assisted smart contract testing belongs in Python](https://ack3.ai/research/why-ai-assisted-smart-contract-testing-belongs-in-python/), but useful tests still need explicit invariants, correct state models, and reviewable execution results. This initiative improves the parts of Wake that support that workflow. Developers and auditors will have a maintained Wake v5 release, clearer AI-assisted fuzzing paths, and public fixes for problems reported through GitHub.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
**ack3** does the work. [Michal Převrátil](https://github.com/michprev) is the author of Wake and leads its tooling work. [Naoki Yoshida](https://github.com/meditationduck) focuses on fuzz testing and making complex failures reproducible. [Jan Kalivoda](https://github.com/jaczkal) works on smart-contract security research and review methodology. [Josef Gattermayer](https://x.com/jgattermayer) provides project oversight.

The team built Wake and uses it in Ethereum security reviews. ack3 works with clients including [Lido](https://lido.fi/) and [Safe](https://safe.global/), and Wake fuzzing was used in the [public Lido NEST security work](https://ack3.ai/research/lido-nest-audit-summary/). The team's public track record is available at https://ack3.ai, https://github.com/ack3-ai/wake, and the linked fuzzing benchmark. No other funder currently pays for this scope.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
Wake is an existing open-source framework built and maintained by the team now operating as ack3. Wake v5 already provides Python-based Solidity testing, property-based fuzzing, [manually guided fuzzing](https://ack3.ai/research/introducing-manually-guided-fuzzing-a-new-approach-in-smart-contract-testing/), static-analysis detectors, typed Solidity representations, coverage, call tracing, and an EVM execution backend. Its documentation and releases are public.

ack3 also uses Wake in security work and has already tested AI-assisted fuzzing approaches. The linked benchmark records a concrete agent-written harness experiment, while the Wake documentation contains the testing and fuzzing foundations this initiative will extend. A new team would first need to learn the compiler pipeline, generated Python types, EVM backend, fuzzing runtime, static-analysis model, and release process. The $20,000 goal funds focused maintenance and improvements to the existing framework rather than a new framework build.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- Maintain the Wake v5 release line and address compatibility changes affecting Solidity compilation, Python support, EVM behavior, testing, fuzzing, and static analysis.
- Resolve GitHub issues that affect Wake reliability and usability, with fixes or documented resolutions linked from public issue threads.
- Improve Wake interfaces and workflows used for AI-assisted fuzz-test preparation and execution.
- Update documentation and publish runnable examples showing how AI-assisted fuzzing fits into Wake tests.
- Publish tagged releases and release notes for completed work.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- A fully autonomous audit system.
- A guarantee that fuzzing finds a fixed number of vulnerabilities or reaches a fixed coverage percentage.
- A Wake v6 rewrite or an unrelated replacement framework.
- Dedicated consulting, integration support, or developer onboarding as a milestone.
- Documentation of private user activity.
- New detector families unrelated to the maintenance and AI-assisted fuzzing scope.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- Grant-funded Wake code remains public under the repository's existing open-source license.
- Work, issues, fixes, tests, and releases are tracked in the public Wake repository.
- ack3 continues maintaining Wake after the grant because the team uses it in its own security-review work.
- The adoption target is based on public repositories outside ack3 running Wake fuzz tests created or materially updated through the grant-funded AI-assisted workflow.

initiatives.title: Walletbeat: Clear signing ratings, fixes and ecosystem adoption for hardware and software wallets
initiatives.summary: Walletbeat will rate hardware and software wallets on clear signing support and publish the results on our website. We'll work with teams to fix the checks they fail and expand clear signing support across the ecosystem.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Multisig thefts at [Bybit](https://www.theblock.co/post/343530/lazarus-appears-to-compromise-safe-developer-machine-in-lead-up-to-1-5-billion-bybit-hack-report) (February 2025, about $1.5 billion) and [Radiant Capital](https://decrypt.co/286728/radiant-capital-exploited-50-million) (October 2024, about $50 million) show that a compromised interface can display a routine transfer while the wallet signs a different transaction. Clear signing lets users understand the transaction payload in a human-readable way with hashes to compare against an independent source (e.g. "Deposit $100 into Aave" vs. an unintelligible hexadecimal string). As an industry, we can't expect to onboard the masses if the expectation is for them to decode raw transaction data themselves or otherwise lose their life savings.

As of October 8, 2026, none of the 32 hardware and software wallets listed passes Walletbeat's transaction legibility test.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
- **polymutex**, Walletbeat lead and core contributor: https://x.com/polymutex
- **0xMattmatt**, Walletbeat core contributor: https://x.com/0xmattmatt
- **REN2140**, Walletbeat contributor: https://x.com/REN2140_eth

No team member is affiliated with a rated wallet.

Other funding: https://beta.walletbeat.eth.limo/about

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
- A live transaction legibility rating, with a written methodology and benchmark transactions covering transactions of varying complexity (from simple token approvals to complex nested Safe multisend batch transactions).
- A public test page applying the benchmarks to any wallet: https://beta.walletbeat.eth.limo/test
- Six software wallets already tested for clear signing.
- A track record of wallet impact: https://github.com/walletbeat/walletbeat/blob/beta/resources/docs/impact/impact.md

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
- Clear signing ratings: readable benchmark transactions (ERC-7730), plus calldata and EIP-712 message hashes (ERC-8213).
- One device per rated hardware wallet, bought at retail (about 2,500 USD total).
- Retests of new releases, with results in the public impact log.
- Working with wallet teams to drive adoption.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- ERC-7730 descriptor files, or new clear signing technology such as on-device verifiers.
- Transaction simulation, scam warnings and other legibility checks.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- Code and data under the MIT license. Methodology and data public in the repository.
- Walletbeat maintains the ratings for 6 months after the last milestone at no further cost, funded by grants and donations.
- Pinned target: every listed hardware and software wallet rated on clear signing.
- Walletbeat accepts no payment from wallet teams for reviews or rating changes. A rating changes only when the wallet fixes its transaction legibility.

initiatives.title: Walnut: Source-Level Debugging for Solidity, ethdebug in solc
initiatives.summary: solc does not emit the debug information debuggers need, so every tool reverse-engineers compiler behavior and breaks when the compiler changes. This funds implementing the ethdebug format directly in solc, with debug data that survives the full optimizer pipeline so it works on production builds.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Debugging Solidity is a longstanding pain point, and the root cause is structural. The compiler (solc) does not emit the rich debug information debuggers need: variable types, scopes, and runtime locations. Without a standard for that data, every debugging tool reverse-engineers compiler behavior, which breaks whenever the compiler changes.

The 2025 Solidity Developer Survey (925 responses) re-confirmed this. The three most requested improvements, step-through debugging, variable and state inspection, and transaction replay, map directly to what a standard debug format enables. The need is sharpest in production, where deployed contracts are immutable and the cost of not understanding behavior is highest.

This RFP funds implementing the [ethdebug format](https://ethdebug.github.io/format/) directly in solc. The end state:
* solc emits standardized debug data covering storage variables, local variables, memory, calldata, and per-instruction context
* That data survives the full compilation pipeline, including all optimizer passes, so it works on production builds
* Debuggers, frameworks, monitoring tools, explorers, and agents can read one shared standard instead of reconstructing compiler internals

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
This RFP is a co-sponsorship opportunity brought by **Argot Collective** and **Walnut**. The ethdebug format is developed by Argot engineer Nicholas D'Andrea. The solc implementation is done by Walnut. We expect them to do this work.

This is not a competitive tender in the usual sense. The project is already in progress with the first three milestones funded and underway, so there is no open challenge window. A challenger just doesn’t make sense in this case.

Argot Collective is the anchor backer. A public goods nonprofit, Argot has committed up to $151,000 of the $279,000 project budget. This RFP raises the remaining $127,000: $85,500 to finish the project and additional $43,000 to ensure ecosystem adoption by every user of the solc compiler.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
* [ethdebug/format](https://github.com/ethdebug/format) is the open specification for EVM debug information, comparable in intent to DWARF for C and C++. It defines schemas for types, variable locations, runtime context, and compiler metadata.
* The implementation is underway at Walnut, with the first three milestones below funded by Argot.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
* The full six-milestone implementation of ethdebug in solc, from test infrastructure through the optimized production pipeline
* Complete debug data covering storage variables, local variables, memory, calldata, and per-instruction context
* Upstreaming the implementation into solc and documenting how tools consume the emitted data

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
* Building end-user debugger UIs. This funds the compiler-level data, not the tools that read it. Walnut is building soldb, the first ETHDebug consumer - a CLI-based debugger and tracer for Solidity.
* The ethdebug format specification itself, which Argot maintains separately.
* Ongoing maintenance beyond the grant period, beyond the maintenance plan required below.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
1. **Open source.** All work merged under solc's existing license, no closed-source dependencies.
2. **Upstream, not a fork.** Deliverables land in the official solc repository, or are open pull requests under active review by the Solidity team. A private fork does not count.
3. **Machine-checkable acceptance.** Debug data output is validated by an automated test suite in public CI against the ethdebug format schemas.
4. **Production coverage proven.** Final acceptance requires debug data demonstrated correct on optimized builds.
5. **Maintenance plan.** A documented plan for keeping ethdebug output current as solc and the optimizer evolve.

initiatives.title: Zealynx Defence: practical security training and help with suspicious messages
initiatives.summary: Build a paid training platform that helps Ethereum teams recognise deception, verify suspicious requests and practise safer decisions. One subscription includes an expanding course library and a case assistant that explains suspicious situations, suggests verification steps and recommends relevant training. Three free checks introduce the tool. TheDAO supports creation; customer subscriptions sustain delivery and updates.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
Ethereum security depends on the people controlling accounts, devices, software and signing permissions. Convincing messages, impersonation and malicious requests can persuade someone to bypass otherwise sound protections. The [FBI documents targeted social engineering against crypto employees](https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2024/PSA240903).

People need practical ways to verify requests, recognise uncertainty and respond safely. Zealynx Defence connects structured training with guidance when a suspicious situation actually happens. Learners practise decisions and demonstrate understanding on unfamiliar examples. Completion shows the skills assessed; it does not guarantee immunity from deception.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
Carlos Vendrell leads Zealynx's security work and Academy. Zealynx owns the platform and delivers the programme.

Earlier Academy support was 6.4466 ETH, valued at $12,008 when sent in [TheDAO's transparency record](https://thedao.fund/transparency/). Completed and previously funded work is excluded from this request.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
Academy Defence already provides simulated security drills. Zealynx also has sourced research on scams and attacks to inform the programme.

Reusing this foundation reduces development work. The grant funds the additional curriculum, assessment, reviewed case guidance and software needed to deliver a paid training service.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
**Multiple practical courses.** The initial library covers identity verification, account and device security, suspicious software requests, payments and signing, and incident response. It includes 30 reviewed case records and 12 practical exercises, with legitimate counterparts, explanations, corrective feedback and fresh assessments. The curriculum can grow as threats and learner needs change.

**A case assistant connected to training.** Users describe or paste a suspicious message or situation. The assistant explains supported warning signs, identifies missing information, suggests protective steps and recommends relevant lessons. It makes uncertainty explicit and does not declare something safe merely because it finds no known scam pattern.

**One paid subscription.** Access includes the standard paid course library, updates and a bounded assistant allowance. Individuals receive three free checks. Team access adds training assignment and completion records.

**Free educational resources.** Provide videos with Carlos's narration and Zealynx explanatory cards. Reviewed research also supports course updates, case guidance and newsletter material, with source dates and human review before publication.

The proposed fifteen-month schedule is approximately three months for the initial release, followed by twelve months to demonstrate paid adoption and sustainable operation.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown: Audits, guaranteed scam detection, automatic replies or transactions, continuous inbox monitoring, unlimited coaching and payment for completed work.

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- Maintain funded materials and essential corrections for twelve months from release. Customer revenue supports continuing operation and curriculum expansion.
- Publish new rights-cleared teaching handouts and assessment criteria under CC BY 4.0. Existing software and third-party material retain their licences.
- Preserve existing free and member rights. Protect private case inputs.
- Define the required core learning path and assessment rules before recruitment. Count distinct people, not course registrations or video views.

initiatives.title: ZKNOX: ZK Clear Signing, verifiable transaction display for hardware and software wallets
initiatives.summary: Hardware wallets sign bytes they cannot interpret, and clear signing today depends on a descriptor registry signed by the wallet vendor. This grant funds an open standard and toolchain in which the device verifies a zero-knowledge proof that the string it displays is the correct rendering of the bytes it signs, under rules the protocol itself commits on-chain. It ships an ERC draft, a compiler, an embedded verifier, Ledger and Kohaku integrations, five DeFi protocols including Safe, ZK clear signing of Tornado Cash, Privacy Pools and Railgun, policy-bound signing for AI agents, an independent review, and a second verifier that moves from Groth16 to a STARK streamed into the device.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.markdown:
- Bybit (2025, about USD 1.5B) and Radiant (2024, about USD 50M): compromised signing interfaces, hardware wallets that could not render a Safe delegatecall, signers approving a hash.
- ERC-7730 is a real improvement, and this builds on it. It also adds at the moment a single point of trust (the descriptor signing key and its review queue) and cannot express computed meaning: Safe `safeTxHash`, ERC-4337 `userOpHash`, shielded transfers.
- Protocols fund their own audits; the shared signing flow has no owner. The EF Trillion Dollar Security report lists blind signing among the main user-facing risks.

What people can do afterwards:

- **Semantic clear signing.** A proof attests a computation, so the device can show what a Safe hash commits to, what a batch does on net, or a shielded transfer bound to the commitment it signs. It closes a concrete attack: a compromised host swaps the commitment (Tornado), precommitment (Privacy Pools) or note key (Railgun) in a deposit for one it controls.
- **No registry, no permission.** Each contract compiles its rules with the open toolchain and publishes `h_rules` in its own storage or ENS name: nothing to submit, no per-vendor pipeline.
- **Policy-bound signing for AI agents.** The device signs an agent's proposal with no button press when the proof shows it fits a policy the user enrolled; a compromised agent gets no proof outside it.

sections.heading: The team
sections.markdown:
ZKNOX (Paris, 2025): 30+ open-source repositories, three hardware-wallet applications, three EIPs, public security analyses of privacy protocols and wallets, Ethereum Foundation grants, four hackathon prizes in two years including two first prizes, the latest at ETHGlobal Cannes 2026 for the proof of concept this grant starts from. Founders: Ledger co-founder and former CTO, an ex-Ledger cryptographer with fifteen years of embedded cryptography, a co-author of the Bandersnatch curve.

- Renaud Dubois, CTO: https://github.com/rdubois-crypto, https://dblp.org/pid/26/211.html
- Nicolas Bacca, CEO: https://github.com/btchip
- Simon Masson, CSO: https://github.com/simonmasson, https://dblp.org/pid/218/7096.html
- EIPs: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7885, https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-8051, https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-8052

Relationships: a Ledger co-founder; contributor to ethereum/kohaku (post-quantum account) and to Railgun's curve library; audited Railgun PPOI and Privacy Pools deposits. Other funding for this work: none.

sections.heading: Why a grant: what already exists
sections.markdown:
- ZKlarity (March 2026): clear-signing circuit for 13 Aave v3 actions and a Groth16 verifier running natively in a Ledger Nano S+ secure element, 2.8 s per verification: https://github.com/ZKNoxHQ/ZKlarity
- ETHGlobal Cannes 2026, first prize in the Ledger track: end-to-end demonstrator with an on-device storage proof checking the rules commitment in an ENS record.
- Streaming STARK verifier on the same device: a 97 KB proof streamed in 414 chunks with about 8 KB of RAM.
- Railgun joinsplit circuits in gnark with a test setup ceremony, and a Railgun signer on Nano S+.

The grant pays for generalisation, hardening, integrations, adoption and review of running code.

sections.heading: In scope
sections.markdown:
The prover (dapp, relayer or the user's wallet software) computes `readable` from `tx` and the protocol's rules and proves `h_tx = H(tx)`, `h_readable = H(readable)` and `readable = Render(rules, tx, context)` for rules identified by `h_rules`. The device recomputes both hashes from the bytes it signs and displays, verifies the proof and shows the string with a trust level, without parsing ABI or seeing private context. `h_rules` is anchored by the protocol (contract slot, registry or ENS record) and checked through a storage proof.

Deliverables:

- ERC draft with threat model, proof envelope, anchoring paths, trust indicator and agent policy envelope.
- ERC-7730-to-circuit compiler: all v1 field formats, nested calldata, `safeTxHash` and `userOpHash` binding, reproducible verification-key build, differential tests against viem and ethers.
- Embedded verifier v1.0 in C99 on BLS12-381 and BN254 for Nano S+, Nano X, Stax and Flex; self-hostable prover; Ledger app and Kohaku integrations.
- Five DeFi protocols end to end on the device: Aave v3, Safe (`execTransaction` with nested decoding and `safeTxHash` binding), Uniswap v3/v4, Lido, Morpho.
- Tornado Cash (`deposit`, `withdraw`), Privacy Pools (`deposit`, `withdraw`, `ragequit`) and Railgun (`shield`, `transact` spend authorisation, `unshield`) on the device: amounts, recipient, fee and change recomputed from the note plaintexts, and the commitment, precommitment or npk proven to derive from a note or key the wallet holds; circuits native to BN254; one negative vector per protocol where the host substitutes the commitment and the device refuses.
- Policy-bound signing for AI agents. A policy selects allowed protocols and functions with pinned addresses and constrains the rendered parameters (token in a set, amount at most a ceiling, recipient equal to the signer); the compiler turns it into one circuit with hash `h_policy`. The device verifies against (`h_tx`, `h_readable`, `h_policy`) and signs without a confirmation screen. Enrolment is a clear-signing event with a human (canonical policy text, `h_policy`, a signature cap); revocation is a button press. The ERC-8004 `agentWallet` is the device key, with `h_policy` published as Identity Registry metadata.
- Version 2: a hash-based STARK (KoalaBear, Poseidon2, FRI, Plonky3/SP1 format) replaces the verifier, streamed in phase order in 240-byte chunks with about 8 KB of RAM on the device. No trusted setup, so publishing rules is a single transaction by the contract owner; a pairing-free, plausibly post-quantum device; rules written as a Rust program compiled to an AIR.
- Independent review of the compiler, the privacy circuits and the embedded verifier; integration guides for wallet vendors and protocols.

sections.heading: Out of scope
sections.markdown:
- A descriptor registry or a vendor review pipeline: protocols anchor their own rules.
- Software wallets other than Kohaku and devices other than Ledger's (stretch goals).
- Privacy-protocol renderers under version 2: BN254 hashing is non-native in a 31-bit field, so they are evaluated only.
- Policies with time state (no trusted clock on the device).

sections.heading: Commitments
sections.markdown:
- Every deliverable under Apache-2.0 or MIT, built and tested in public CI.
- ZKNOX maintains the compiler, both verifiers and the Ledger and Kohaku integrations for 12 months after the last milestone at no further cost (security fixes, SDK updates, review of external pull requests) and runs the hosted prover for the same period; a Docker image allows self-hosting after that.
- Pinned targets: verification at most 3.0 s (BLS12-381) and 2.5 s (BN254) on Nano S+; 5 DeFi and 3 privacy protocols on the device; STARK verifier with no trusted setup, at most 16 KB of RAM and 128 KB of proof.
- No exception requested.

securityProblems.label: Development
securityProblems.description: Writing secure code: languages, compilers, debuggers, specifications, secure libraries and developer education.

securityProblems.label: Testing & verification
securityProblems.description: Finding bugs before deployment: fuzzing, formal verification, static analysis, audits and property testing.

securityProblems.label: Deployment & supply chain
securityProblems.description: Getting reviewed code onchain intact: reproducible builds, source verification, audit-to-bytecode mapping, release integrity.

securityProblems.label: Transaction construction
securityProblems.description: What the user is asked to sign: frontends, dApp integrity, simulation, intent and calldata decoding.

securityProblems.label: Signing & wallets
securityProblems.description: Key management and the signing moment: wallets, hardware wallets, clear signing, blind-signing prevention.

securityProblems.label: Runtime & protocol execution
securityProblems.description: Correct execution onchain and in clients: EVM, execution/consensus clients, mempool, L2 and bridge verification.

securityProblems.label: Monitoring
securityProblems.description: Continuous observation of deployed systems: onchain monitoring, alerts, dashboards and risk data.

securityProblems.label: Threat detection & intelligence
securityProblems.description: Identifying attackers and attacks: threat intelligence, phishing, address poisoning, malicious actors screening.

securityProblems.label: Incident response & disclosure
securityProblems.description: Acting on live incidents and bugs: war rooms, forensics, bug bounties, coordinated disclosure, whitehat rescues.

securityProblems.label: Recovery
securityProblems.description: Limiting and recovering losses: rescued-fund distribution, approvals revocation, emergency freezes, coercion protection.

securityProblems.label: Infrastructure & operational security
securityProblems.description: Operational and infrastructure security: OpSec practices, node operations, TEEs, data availability, archives, hiring screening.
