revisions.title: Defimon Rescue Agent: Autonomous Whitehat Rescues for Safe Harbor Protocols on Ethereum
revisions.summary: Defimon detects DeFi exploits in under a second and has returned over $2.5M to victims. This grant turns that into an autonomous rescue agent for the 33 protocols that adopted the SEAL Whitehat Safe Harbor: a rescue playbook per adopter, verified with the protocol, and an agent that identifies the root cause and the funds still at risk within minutes and moves the remaining funds straight to the protocol's registered recovery address, with no human in the loop. Safe Harbor bounties pay for running it after the grant.

sections.why:
Most exploits drain a protocol over several transactions, across minutes or hours. The funds still in the contract after the first transaction can be rescued, but only by someone who sees the attack at once, understands the bug fast enough to reuse it defensively, and has legal cover to do it. That almost never happens. The SEAL whitehat rescue list records 25 rescues worth about $80.7M since 2022, and only 5 of them were done under Safe Harbor, although 33 protocols holding $60.7B have adopted it (safeharbor.securityalliance.org). Whitehats hold back because reusing the attacker's path is legal risk, and because nobody runs rescue capacity as a standing service.

Who is safer: users of Safe Harbor adopters on Ethereum mainnet, Arbitrum One, OP Mainnet and Base (Aave, Lido, Sky, Uniswap, Pendle, Euler, Balancer, Polymarket and 25 others). From what: an exploit in progress, while part of the funds is still in the contract. What anyone can point to afterwards: at least 5 adopters that verified their rescue playbook and know Defimon as a responder, a published benchmark of minutes from attack transaction to root cause, a public incident log, and, when an exploit hits an adopter, funds returned to its on-chain recovery address, confirmed by the protocol and by SEAL 911.

The money at stake, from the DefiLlama hacks dataset (api.llama.fi/hacks, pulled November 11, 2026; DeFi protocols on Ethereum mainnet or an Ethereum L2, centralized exchanges excluded):

- 2025: 70 incidents, $447M lost, of which 56 contract-level exploits worth $364M.
- 2026 to date: 130 incidents, $557M lost, of which 111 contract-level exploits worth $414M.
- Three Safe Harbor adopters were exploited in the last 12 months: Balancer V2 ($128M, November 2025), Makina ($4.2M, 2026, $3.4M returned under Safe Harbor), Lazy Summer ($6M, 2026).

How much of that is rescuable: Decurity reconstructed the per-transaction drain timelines of 10 multi-transaction exploits from 2022 to 2026 (rescue-window.decurity.io). In 6 of the 10, more than 80% of the funds at risk were still on the contract 5 minutes after the first attacker transaction, and 6 of the 10 drains lasted longer than an hour. Where a bot acted inside that window (Squid, Foom), 81% to 82% of the funds at risk came back the same day; where nobody did (CrossCurve, $2.76M), less than 1% came back.

Why the rescue has to be autonomous: 49% of vulnerable contracts are exploited within 30 days of deployment and 85% of vulnerable proxy implementations within 30 days of the upgrade (time-to-hack.decurity.io). Incidents are spread evenly across all four 6-hour blocks of the UTC day, so a human responder misses most of the 5-minute windows, and a playbook written once goes stale at the adopter's next upgrade.
sections.in_scope:
- Covered chains: Ethereum mainnet, Arbitrum One, OP Mainnet and Base. These are the chains Defimon runs detection and rescue on today.
- A rescue playbook for every Safe Harbor adopter with at least $10M on a covered chain: recovery address and scoped assets read from the SafeHarborRegistry (0x326733493E143b8904716E7A64A9f4fb6A185a2c), bounty and identity terms, security contact, and a pre-written rescue execution path. A public index shows the terms; the execution paths stay private.
- Playbooks kept current: every implementation upgrade of an adopter's scoped contracts, which Defimon already detects, triggers a re-verification of that adopter's playbook within 7 days.
- Playbooks verified with the adopters themselves: recovery address, scoped contracts and security contact confirmed by the protocol, and Defimon introduced as a responder it should expect to hear from. Where an adopter's agreement requires Named identity (Aave, Sky, Euler, Balancer, Silo, Makina, Origin, Reserve and others), Decurity completes KYC and sanctions screening at payout, as the agreement requires.
- The root-cause agent benchmarked on replayed historic exploits, with the replay set and results published.
- Private transaction submission (Flashbots Protect or equivalent) and the go/no-go checklist from the SEAL Whitehat Rescue Guide: active or imminent exploit, independence from the attacker, net benefit, return within the agreement deadline, SEAL 911 notified.
- The rescue agent running against every covered adopter for 12 months, and a public incident log: every rescue-candidate event on an adopter is logged with acted or not acted, and why.
- Free rescue-grade alert feed for SEAL 911 members for the grant period.
- Outreach to protocols holding over $100M that have not adopted Safe Harbor, to add them to the registry.
sections.out_scope:
- Rescues on protocols that have not adopted Safe Harbor. Those are legal risk for the whitehat; a legal destination for such funds is the subject of the separate RFP "An Open Bug Bounty Program for All of Ethereum: White Hat Rescued Funds Distribution Service" on this board.
- Initiating an exploit, acting on a known vulnerability before an attack starts, or bug bounty reporting. Rescues start only during an active or imminent exploit.
- Any chain other than Ethereum mainnet, Arbitrum One, OP Mainnet and Base. Defimon also runs detection on Polygon PoS, BNB Chain, Avalanche and Hyperliquid, and nothing on those chains counts toward any deliverable or milestone.
- Tracing or freezing funds the attacker already moved, and negotiating with attackers.
sections.team:
Decurity does the work. The rescue is fully autonomous: Defimon's agent detects the exploit, identifies the vulnerable function and the funds still at risk, and moves them to the protocol's registered recovery address from the playbook, so the protocol holds its funds again before anyone at Decurity is awake. People do the follow-up, none of it time-critical: notifying SEAL 911 and the protocol's security contact, the incident log entry, and KYC where the agreement requires it for the bounty. Arseniy Reutov, CTO and co-founder, leads the program (QuickNode case study: https://www.quicknode.com/blog/real-time-defi-exploit-detection). Arseniy holds an ETHSecurity Badge and will abstain from rating and ranking this initiative.

Public cases where Defimon rescued funds or warned the team before the drain:

- Foom.cash, February 26, 2026: $1.84M rescued on Ethereum and returned the same day; Foom.cash paid a 10% security fee:
    - https://defimon.xyz/blog/foom-cash-whitehat-rescue-february-2026
- Squid Router, April 7, 2026: $512K rescued:
    - https://x.com/DefimonAlerts/status/2041530294369386806
- Veil.cash: 2.025 ETH rescued
    - https://x.com/Veildotcash/status/2025293773891404225
- Secured.finance: alert 45 minutes before the hack
    - https://x.com/DefimonAlerts/status/2096855557575458950
- Ajna.finance: team alerted one hour before the hack
    - https://x.com/DefimonAlerts/status/2093632180656263283
- Guru.fund: team alerted before 85% of funds were drained
    - https://x.com/DefimonAlerts/status/2080679061265739844
- Olas.network, Yam.finance: governance takeovers reported
    - https://x.com/DefimonAlerts/status/2096432367908933790
    - https://x.com/DefimonAlerts/status/2095019159847313766
- Kpk.io: proxy backdoor reported
    - https://x.com/DefimonAlerts/status/2079618207569133651
- CPIMP: several projects notified
    - https://x.com/DefimonAlerts/status/2003167362829418679

No other funder pays for this scope. Defimon's paid feed ($200 per month) and Signals channel ($50 per month) fund detection today; nothing funds standing rescue capacity.
sections.why_grant:
Everything the grant extends is live:

- Detection on Ethereum, Arbitrum, Optimism, Base and Polygon with an LLM-verified confirmed-attacks stream and early detection of attacker contracts, proxy upgrades and malicious governance proposals.
- An AI agent that, given an attack transaction, identifies the vulnerable function and the balances still exposed, and executes the rescue. Measured on real incidents: Squid Router was rescued 4 minutes after the first attacker transaction, $512K of $623K at risk (82%); Foom.cash 16 minutes after the first exploit transaction landed on Base, which included recognizing the same flaw in the separate Ethereum deployment, $1.84M of $2.26M at risk (81%).
- The operational experience of those rescues. Foom.cash also showed the gap this grant closes: the protocol had no Safe Harbor terms, no recovery address and no responder it knew, so the return relied on goodwill on both sides.

The grant pays for the part nobody funds: per-adopter rescue readiness (registry data, recovery addresses verified with the protocol, pre-written rescue paths), benchmarking the root-cause agent, private transaction submission, legal review of the runbook against the Safe Harbor terms, and running the agent and its follow-up process for 12 months. A from-scratch build of detection plus rescue capacity would cost several times this budget.
sections.commitments:
- The rescue runbook, the adopter index, the replay benchmark set and the incident log are published under CC BY 4.0. The rescue execution tooling stays closed, because it would help attackers as much as defenders.
- Every rescue under this program returns funds to the protocol's registered recovery address within the agreement deadline and is reported in the public incident log. Decurity keeps only the bounty the agreement defines. Rescues are rewarded by Safe Harbor bounties, never by this grant.
- Decurity keeps the rescue agent running against every covered adopter for at least 12 months after the last milestone, paid from Safe Harbor bounties and feed revenue, at no further cost to the fund.
- Decurity staff, affiliates and Decurity's own contracts never count toward any milestone.

revisions.title: Fund Echidna Development Through 2027
revisions.summary: Fund Gustavo Grieco, Echidna's creator and maintainer, to carry out Echidna's 2026 to 2027 roadmap during 2027: keep EVM execution current, improve campaign and worker architecture, strengthen symbolic verification, turn agent control into a dependable workflow and optimize execution performance. At minimum, the period produces three tagged maintenance or minor releases, at least two substantial roadmap outcomes delivered in tagged releases, three technical posts, and a public SKILL prompt and MCP workflow for AI agents.

sections.why:
Smart contracts can pass large unit test suites and still fail after an unexpected sequence of calls, actors, prices, timestamps, upgrades, or token behaviors. Echidna attacks that gap with stateless and stateful property-based testing. It generates transaction sequences from a contract ABI and searches for inputs that falsify user-defined properties or Solidity assertions.  
Echidna already combines coverage guidance, corpus mutation, source integration, automatic test minimization, Foundry reproducers, hevm cheatcodes, and optional symbolic execution. Its next challenge is reliability at the seams: EVM behavior changes, campaign and worker coordination, symbolic-execution edge cases, agent control and improved performance. Those are the areas that determine whether auditors can trust a long-running campaign and reproduce what it found.
sections.in_scope:
> * EVM and toolchain compatibility: hevm, Slither, new Foundry cheatcodes, crytic-compile, SMT solver configuration, packaging, and operating-system support  
> * Campaign and worker architecture and execution performance  
> * Symbolic execution for verification, exploration, and counterexample discovery, with bounds and unsupported cases reported plainly  
> * Continued development of the MCP integration so agents can inspect and direct live fuzzing campaigns  
> * A public versioned SKILL prompt that teaches an agent Echidna's capabilities  
> * Fixes and feedback sent upstream to hevm, Slither, and Foundry  
> * Support for users running long and complex campaigns, on Telegram, Discord, and GitHub

Six months of maintainer time at $8,000 a month, spread over the 12-month grant and including VPS capacity and frontier-model access, is $48,000.
sections.out_scope:
> * Rewriting Echidna in another language  
> * Building a general autonomous auditor or claiming that an LLM replaces a security engineer  
> * Writing a complete fuzzing harness or invariant suite for one protocol  
> * Performing an audit or formal-verification engagement for a specific protocol  
> * Supporting non-EVM chains except through the normal EVM-compatible stack
sections.team:
Gustavo Grieco does the work, in the public [Echidna repository](https://github.com/crytic/echidna).  
He was the lead developer of Echidna and the lead author of [the ISSTA 2020 paper](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3395363.3404366) that introduced it. He was a security engineer at Trail of Bits from September 2017 to April 2025, junior to principal, across blockchain audits, fuzzing, and tool development, and has been independent since. He has been [elected Audit Committee Technical Expert for the Arbitrum DAO since July 2025](https://snapshot.box/#/s:arbitrumfoundation.eth/proposal/0x131574819442cb6da293795ee9faeec4754a5af664b535b654b3d9d3d53f47e1). He co-authored the [Slither paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.09878) and echidna-parade, and before Echidna he built another fuzzer: [QuickFuzz](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2976002.2976017). Echidna lives in the crytic GitHub organization, which Trail of Bits runs. Even after he left Trail of Bits, Gustavo is still a volunteer to keep Echidna maintained.
sections.why_grant:
The recipient has the decisive head start. The work touches Echidna's Haskell engine, release process, hevm and Slither integrations, symbolic execution, Foundry compatibility, and the existing MCP preview. A new vendor would first spend months on implementation details and EVM edge cases.  
The [2026-2027 roadmap discussion](https://github.com/crytic/echidna/issues/1612) is the maintainer's planning thread, where users prioritize the goals. The 2.3 [releases](https://github.com/crytic/echidna/releases) added optional symbolic verification, multiple SMT solvers, Foundry reproducers, and an experimental MCP interface. The [public fuzzing campaigns list](https://github.com/perimetersec/public-fuzzing-campaigns-list) shows the tool in real audit work, and Recon Invariant Testing Extension and scfuzzbench are external users or integration targets.  
**Example roadmap outcomes**, to show the expected scope. The milestones name the class of outcome, so the issue can change.

> * Fork support like [issue \#1623](https://github.com/crytic/echidna/issues/1623): the relevant fork's execution-layer changes supported in hevm and Echidna, with fork-specific and conformance tests.  
> * Symbolic verification like [issue \#1625](https://github.com/crytic/echidna/issues/1625): difficult properties proved by combining fuzzing and symbolic execution, with replayable counterexamples.
sections.commitments:
> 1. **Open source and public development.** All grant-funded code, tests, documentation, and examples are published under AGPLv3 or another OSI-approved license, through public issues, pull requests, and tagged releases.  
> 2. **Roadmap delivery.** Each roadmap outcome ships in a tagged release whose notes explain the improvement and link to the test, reproducer, or benchmark behind it.  
> 3. **Substitution and 2026 carry-over.** A blocked roadmap item may be replaced by one of equal or greater security value and scope, with the reason, the replacement, and its acceptance evidence published first. Unfinished 2026 roadmap work counts if it happens in 2027, was not funded elsewhere, and is of comparable scope and importance.  
> 4. **Current EVM support.** Finalized EVM and toolchain changes in the work period are covered by public regression tests. No milestone depends on an Ethereum upgrade shipping on a fixed date: if a fork slips, the fork-dated target moves with it.  
> 5. **Honest output.** Agent controls are documented. Symbolic results state the mode, solver, bounds, timeout status, unsupported operations, and caveats, and incomplete analysis is never reported as verified. Release artifacts tie to public source tags, and installation paths are tested in CI.  
> 6. **Post-grant maintenance.** The recipient keeps maintaining Echidna after the grant (releases, triage, security reports, user support on the public channels), without follow-on funding and at a pace set by his other paid work.  
> 7. **Pinned targets, counted from the first payment.** EVM fidelity and campaign reliability: within 90 days after the next Ethereum mainnet fork activates. Symbolic verification and agent workflows: within 7 months. Roadmap completion and handoff: within 10 months. Adoption: within 12 months.

milestones.name: EVM fidelity and campaign reliability
criteria: A tagged release ships with a public changelog and installation artifacts, and every improvement in its release notes links to a test, reproducer, or benchmark

The release supports the execution-layer changes of the next Ethereum mainnet fork that activates in the grant period, with a public fork-specific test and a conformance test in hevm, by the pinned target in commitment 7\. If no fork activates, public regression tests cover the changes finalized for
A public reproducer, command included, shows the last 2026 release failing or unsupported on at least 1 newly supported execution-layer behavior where the 2027 release gives the expected result
At least 1 technical post explains a compatibility, performance, reliability, or reproducer improvement from this milestone

revisions.title: Echidna: Fund Development Through 2027
revisions.summary: Fund Gustavo Grieco, Echidna's creator and maintainer, to carry out Echidna's 2026 to 2027 roadmap during 2027: keep EVM execution current, improve campaign and worker architecture, strengthen symbolic verification, turn agent control into a dependable workflow and optimize execution performance. At minimum, the period produces three tagged maintenance or minor releases, at least two substantial roadmap outcomes delivered in tagged releases, three technical posts, and a public SKILL prompt and MCP workflow for AI agents.

sections.why:
Smart contracts can pass large unit test suites and still fail after an unexpected sequence of calls, actors, prices, timestamps, upgrades, or token behaviors. Echidna attacks that gap with stateless and stateful property-based testing. It generates transaction sequences from a contract ABI and searches for inputs that falsify user-defined properties or Solidity assertions.  
Echidna already combines coverage guidance, corpus mutation, source integration, automatic test minimization, Foundry reproducers, hevm cheatcodes, and optional symbolic execution. Its next challenge is reliability at the seams: EVM behavior changes, campaign and worker coordination, symbolic-execution edge cases, agent control and improved performance. Those are the areas that determine whether auditors can trust a long-running campaign and reproduce what it found.
sections.in_scope:
> * EVM and toolchain compatibility: hevm, Slither, new Foundry cheatcodes, crytic-compile, SMT solver configuration, packaging, and operating-system support  
> * Campaign and worker architecture and execution performance  
> * Symbolic execution for verification, exploration, and counterexample discovery, with bounds and unsupported cases reported plainly  
> * Continued development of the MCP integration so agents can inspect and direct live fuzzing campaigns  
> * A public versioned SKILL prompt that teaches an agent Echidna's capabilities  
> * Fixes and feedback sent upstream to hevm, Slither, and Foundry  
> * Support for users running long and complex campaigns, on Telegram, Discord, and GitHub

Six months of maintainer time at $8,000 a month, spread over the 12-month grant and including VPS capacity and frontier-model access, is $48,000.
sections.out_scope:
> * Rewriting Echidna in another language  
> * Building a general autonomous auditor or claiming that an LLM replaces a security engineer  
> * Writing a complete fuzzing harness or invariant suite for one protocol  
> * Performing an audit or formal-verification engagement for a specific protocol  
> * Supporting non-EVM chains except through the normal EVM-compatible stack
sections.team:
Gustavo Grieco does the work, in the public [Echidna repository](https://github.com/crytic/echidna).  
He was the lead developer of Echidna and the lead author of [the ISSTA 2020 paper](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3395363.3404366) that introduced it. He was a security engineer at Trail of Bits from September 2017 to April 2025, junior to principal, across blockchain audits, fuzzing, and tool development, and has been independent since. He has been [elected Audit Committee Technical Expert for the Arbitrum DAO since July 2025](https://snapshot.box/#/s:arbitrumfoundation.eth/proposal/0x131574819442cb6da293795ee9faeec4754a5af664b535b654b3d9d3d53f47e1). He co-authored the [Slither paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.09878) and echidna-parade, and before Echidna he built another fuzzer: [QuickFuzz](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2976002.2976017). Echidna lives in the crytic GitHub organization, which Trail of Bits runs. Even after he left Trail of Bits, Gustavo is still a volunteer to keep Echidna maintained.
sections.why_grant:
The recipient has the decisive head start. The work touches Echidna's Haskell engine, release process, hevm and Slither integrations, symbolic execution, Foundry compatibility, and the existing MCP preview. A new vendor would first spend months on implementation details and EVM edge cases.  
The [2026-2027 roadmap discussion](https://github.com/crytic/echidna/issues/1612) is the maintainer's planning thread, where users prioritize the goals. The 2.3 [releases](https://github.com/crytic/echidna/releases) added optional symbolic verification, multiple SMT solvers, Foundry reproducers, and an experimental MCP interface. The [public fuzzing campaigns list](https://github.com/perimetersec/public-fuzzing-campaigns-list) shows the tool in real audit work, and Recon Invariant Testing Extension and scfuzzbench are external users or integration targets.  
**Example roadmap outcomes**, to show the expected scope. The milestones name the class of outcome, so the issue can change.

> * Fork support like [issue \#1623](https://github.com/crytic/echidna/issues/1623): the relevant fork's execution-layer changes supported in hevm and Echidna, with fork-specific and conformance tests.  
> * Symbolic verification like [issue \#1625](https://github.com/crytic/echidna/issues/1625): difficult properties proved by combining fuzzing and symbolic execution, with replayable counterexamples.
sections.commitments:
> 1. **Open source and public development.** All grant-funded code, tests, documentation, and examples are published under AGPLv3 or another OSI-approved license, through public issues, pull requests, and tagged releases.  
> 2. **Roadmap delivery.** Each roadmap outcome ships in a tagged release whose notes explain the improvement and link to the test, reproducer, or benchmark behind it.  
> 3. **Substitution and 2026 carry-over.** A blocked roadmap item may be replaced by one of equal or greater security value and scope, with the reason, the replacement, and its acceptance evidence published first. Unfinished 2026 roadmap work counts if it happens in 2027, was not funded elsewhere, and is of comparable scope and importance.  
> 4. **Current EVM support.** Finalized EVM and toolchain changes in the work period are covered by public regression tests. No milestone depends on an Ethereum upgrade shipping on a fixed date: if a fork slips, the fork-dated target moves with it.  
> 5. **Honest output.** Agent controls are documented. Symbolic results state the mode, solver, bounds, timeout status, unsupported operations, and caveats, and incomplete analysis is never reported as verified. Release artifacts tie to public source tags, and installation paths are tested in CI.  
> 6. **Post-grant maintenance.** The recipient keeps maintaining Echidna after the grant (releases, triage, security reports, user support on the public channels), without follow-on funding and at a pace set by his other paid work.  
> 7. **Pinned targets, counted from the first payment.** EVM fidelity and campaign reliability: within 90 days after the next Ethereum mainnet fork activates. Symbolic verification and agent workflows: within 7 months. Roadmap completion and handoff: within 10 months. Adoption: within 12 months.

revisions.title: Independent Security Assurance for the EEZ Smart Contracts
revisions.summary: Fund an independent security audit and a standing bug bounty for the EEZ smart contracts through TheDAO Security Fund. EEZ is FOSS, and its security should be built the same way: open scrutiny from independently staffed teams, with every report, finding, and artifact published. A snapshot from the audit, continuous coverage from the bounty, and the final milestone pays only when chains adopt the reviewed contracts.

sections.why:
The Ethereum Economic Zone (EEZ) is fully decentralized and open protocol and  infrastructure for synchronous composability between Ethereum rollups. It is designed without centralized operators or trusted intermediaries and permisionless , which makes the security and correctness of its smart contracts fundamental to the security of the system as a whole. GnosisDAO has approved GIP-153, making Gnosis Chain the first governance-backed adopter, and the contracts are ready for audits and deployed on testnets.

Launching a new rollup or app chain via EEZ offers massive benefits. The network remains fully self-sovereign retaining its custom state transitions, prover schemes, and core architecture while EEZ provides a unified framework for synchronous composability with all other EEZ-connected networks, including Ethereum. We are in discussions with new projects, and with running app chains that want to tap Ethereum liquidity this way. The first thing they ask for is an independent security record.

The objective is to build security assurance through multiple complementary approaches rather than relying on a single audit or security provider. The resulting findings, specifications, tests, verification artifacts, and security tooling get published so they benefit both EEZ and the broader Ethereum ecosystem.

The primary step for the successful adoption of the EEZ is to verify its security and ensure that security is continuously maintained. We plan to achieve adoption by building upon these foundational pillars.
sections.in_scope:
**Expected Audit Process**

We expect the audit engagement to follow a clear and structured process:

**1. Scope & Kick-off**

Confirm the exact codebase, commit hash, components in scope, relevant dependencies, assumptions, and known areas of concern.

**2. System Understanding**

Review the protocol architecture, critical flows, privileged roles, trust assumptions, and key security properties before starting the detailed review. Understand how protocol messages, proof commitments, and execution on Ethereum L1 and participating rollups (L2s) fit together.

Identify which guarantees are enforced by the contracts and which depend on proof systems, off-chain components, or operational assumptions.

**3. Security Review**

Perform an independent manual review of the in-scope code and protocol documentation, supported by appropriate security tooling and testing techniques where relevant. Cross-chain behavior is a required part of this review.

In addition to contract security, assess:

Whether the contracts and protocol specification are consistent with each other.

Whether the specification is clear and sufficient for independent implementation.

Whether EEZ can provide the intended synchronous cross-chain interactions, including nested calls, static reads, failures, and rollback, and under which assumptions.

Whether the protocol abstractions and message format support different chain architectures, including EVM and non-EVM chains, and what adaptations or core changes are required.

**4. Findings & Preliminary Report**

Document validated findings with clear severity, impact, root cause, affected components, and recommended remediation. Critical issues should be communicated as soon as they are confirmed.

**5. Findings Review**

Walk through the findings with the development team to align on impact, assumptions, and the proposed remediation approach.

**6. Remediation Review**

Review the implemented fixes and verify that each issue has been properly addressed without introducing regressions.

**7. Final Report**

Deliver a final report covering the audited scope, methodology, findings, remediation status, remaining risks, and the final reviewed code version.

---
sections.out_scope:
- Rollup node software, provers, sequencers, and any off-chain infrastructure
- The internal economics of individual rollups connected to EEZ
- Re-auditing protocol changes made after the pinned commit
- Marketing, badges, or any public claim beyond what the published evidence supports
sections.existing:
- The protocol source and its contract-level specifications are public: eez-core-protocol, including specs for the core protocol, execution entries, the multi-prover design, and blob format under `docs/`.
- The repository tracks open security findings from internal review. Bidders start from a documented codebase, not a blank page.
sections.who:
Nobody is pre-selected. The winning bid can be a single coordinator subcontracting the work, a security firm partnering with a formal verification or tooling team, or a consortium. What matters is that the plan combines at least two complementary approaches performed by teams with no shared ownership, personnel, or financial ties.

To help Giveth judge the strongest bid, EEZ core contributors Eduardo Antuña and Jesús Ligero will be available as technical advisors during the selection process: they know the codebase best and can assess whether a proposed plan actually covers it.
sections.hard_req:
1. **Everything published.** The full audit report, findings, severity ratings, and fix reviews are released publicly; any test suites or tooling produced ship under an OSI license.
2. **Independent auditor.** The audit team has no shared ownership, personnel, or financial ties to the EEZ core contributors or to Gnosis, disclosed in writing.
3. **Verifiable acceptance.** Every milestone criterion below can be checked by a stranger from public evidence.
4. **Fixed target.** All work runs against one pinned commit. Any material protocol change during the engagement is documented in the public record.
5. **Bounty continuity.** The bug bounty runs on a named public platform with a published scope and payout table, and stays funded and open for at least 6 months after audit.

criteria: The first milestone we want to reach is having a comprehensive audit. This is crucial for the next steps, which are the bug bounty and adoption. By having a comprehensive audit, we will unlock this potential and strive to ensure the adoption of the protocol and establish a more secure coordination t

At least one full independent review of the in-scope contracts completed, combining at least two complementary approaches per the hard requirements
Complete report published: findings, severity ratings, and status
Every critical and high finding fixed or publicly acknowledged with rationale, and the fixes re-reviewed by the team that found them

milestones.name: Adoption with Bug Bounty Program
criteria: Following the detailed audit, our second milestone is launching a bug bounty program, which turns security into continuous coverage rather than a one-time snapshot giving researchers a  incentive to report the bugs audits inevitably miss. We have not yet determined the details of the bug bounty prog
A public bug bounty live on a named platform, covering the audited contracts at the pinned commit or a documented successor
Published scope and severity payout table, with a maximum payout of at least $10.000
The program funded and open for at least 6 months, shown on the platform's public page

revisions.title: EEZ Extends Ethereum: Making Its Contracts Safe for Chains to Adopt
revisions.summary:
EEZ extends Ethereum, and Ethereum's security with it. 

A Layer 2 stops being an isolated network behind a bridge, and a protocol deploys once instead of maintaining copies on every chain. This initiative funds the independent security audit of this Ethereum public good through TheDAO Security Fund. Gnosis separately funds a public Verification Sandbox where chain teams verify the audited contracts against their own stack. A public audit record, and a final milestone that pays only when external chains publish real verification results on the audited contracts.

sections.why:
**EEZ extends Ethereum, and Ethereum's security with it.** Some of the largest losses in Ethereum's history happened at its bridges: honeypots of locked funds guarded by small signer sets, most of them relying on reputation rather than contract logic or validity proofs, prioritizing UX over security, and that signer set becomes the security ceiling for every user behind it. The record shows it: the largest exploits in crypto's history are dominated by bridge signer and verifier compromises, Ronin, Poly Network, BNB Bridge, Wormhole, Nomad among them ([Rekt leaderboard](https://rekt.news/leaderboard/)). Async messages add a second problem: a transfer can get stuck halfway, and most cross-chain bugs live in that halfway state. EEZ ends both by making every Layer 2 a true extension of Ethereum instead of an isolated network behind a bridge: one account works everywhere, a contract keeps one address, and a cross-chain action either completes fully or does not happen at all. EEZ is able to achieve both: it maintains the exact security guarantees specified by the network, and it improves the UX of current reputation-based bridges. Securing the EEZ contracts is a security upgrade to Ethereum itself.

The clearest win is a smaller attack surface. Today a protocol deploys a copy of itself on every network it wants to reach, and duplication breeds bugs: version drift, per-chain initialization mistakes, maintenance across every copy. The Balancer v2 exploit drained the same duplicated code chain by chain. With EEZ a protocol can deploy once, on the network where it is easiest to control, audit, and secure, and every chain uses it through atomic cross-chain communication. One deployment, one audit, one patch, effective everywhere.

Concentration cuts both ways, and that is exactly why this audit is a shared responsibility. EEZ cannot weaken Ethereum L1 itself consensus does not depend on it. But every chain that adopts EEZ routes its cross-chain security through one contract set on Ethereum. A critical bug there would not be one chain's incident; it would be every connected chain's incident at once. The same design that removes per-bridge honeypots replaces many weak surfaces with one surface that must be strong. Infrastructure with a shared failure domain deserves shared, independent scrutiny before chains adopt it which is what this initiative funds. Shared risk requires shared security and shared funding.

How EEZ changes where security comes from:

- **Chosen by the chain, enforced on L1.** Each rollup declares the proof systems it accepts and the threshold that must agree, and every cross-chain action settles against that verification on Ethereum, designed for one aggregated proof per proof system per L1 block. Security is not bought with speed: a chain keeps the properties it chooses without giving up the UX of an instant call. Rollups that run based, like the first Gnosis deployment, go further: sequencing happens inside the L1 block itself, and anyone can rebuild the full chain from L1 data alone.
- **No half-done state.** A cross-chain call and its return value execute in one transaction. Everything commits or nothing does, so stuck funds and partial-state exploits are removed by design.
- **Verified, not trusted.** Every cross-chain outcome is precomputed and checked on L1 against the proof systems the rollup declared. Today that check is a single attestation signer re-executing the block window; the multi-prover design it plugs into is described below. A malicious operator cannot forge a result, only fail to produce one.
    - **No single proof system to break, by design.** With multiple proof systems and a threshold, one prover's bug does not compromise the chain. Verifying the live attestation pipeline, and the multi-prover design it plugs into, is in this audit's scope.

For users, this also means wallets can automate cross-chain sends, so funds sent to the right address on the wrong chain stop being a loss.

EEZ is not a dapp and not a product. It is an Ethereum public good: an open, permissionless protocol and  infrastructure for synchronous composability between Ethereum rollups. The core EEZ contract has no admin role. Each connected rollup keeps its own contract, whose owner sets the accepted proof systems, verification keys, and threshold; reviewing those privileged roles and how they can be locked down is part of this audit . EEZ is FOSS and has no token. That design puts the security of the whole system on its smart contracts, which is exactly what this initiative puts under independent review. The contracts are deployed on testnets and ready for audit.

The adoption signals are already public. GnosisDAO has approved GIP-153, making Gnosis Chain the first governance-backed adopter. Celo, Polygon, and Linea have stated they will test the audited contracts once the audit completes. 

Joseph Lubin has publicly spoken in support of the Ethereum Economic Zone ([post](https://x.com/etheconomiczone/status/2052390993610133513)). Every team in these conversations asks for the same thing first: an independent security record.

The design has been stress-tested in public. At ETHPrague 2026, Vitalik Buterin probed the worst case with Jordi Baylina, one chain's proof system breaking, and the answer held: damage stays confined to contracts that chose to trust the broken chain; users everywhere else are untouched ([fireside](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=prgWmgUbSVQ)). At Dappcon Berlin, Buterin named the risk EEZ prevents, interoperability "captured by centralized providers," and called EEZ "a quite helpful effort in that regard"([panel](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gfG-R8AOu0E)).
sections.in_scope:
**Expected Audit Process**

We expect the audit engagement to follow a clear and structured process, completed within 2 months of auditor selection. Selection follows TheDAO's process: full funding, a 30-day proposal window, then a 7-day decision. With funding closed by late October 2026, the report lands by late January 2027, leaving roughly ten weeks of the 6-month duration for the adoption milestone. That window is tight, which is why adoption criterion 1 carries a testnet fallback. The audit budget corresponds to 8 to 10 senior-auditor-weeks at prevailing protocol-audit rates plus remediation review; competitive bidding is the price check.

**1. Scope & Kick-off**

Confirm the exact codebase, commit hash, components in scope, relevant dependencies, assumptions, and known areas of concern.

**2. System Understanding**

Review the protocol architecture, critical flows, privileged roles, trust assumptions, and key security properties before starting the detailed review. Understand how protocol messages, proof commitments, and execution on Ethereum L1 and participating rollups (L2s) fit together.

**3. Security Review**

Perform an independent manual review of the in-scope code and protocol documentation, supported by appropriate security tooling and testing techniques where relevant. Cross-chain behavior is a required part of this review.

In addition to contract security, assess:

Whether the contracts match the protocol specification, and the specification is sufficient for independent implementation.

Whether EEZ delivers the intended synchronous cross-chain interactions (nested calls, static reads, failures, rollback) for EVM rollups, and under which assumptions. Non-EVM integration is a design question for the Verification Sandbox, not an audit deliverable.

**4. Findings & Preliminary Report**

Document validated findings with clear severity, impact, root cause, affected components, and recommended remediation. Critical issues should be communicated as soon as they are confirmed.

- A persistent public testnet running the audited contracts at the pinned commit or a documented successor
- A published conformance suite any chain can run against its own stack, with integration documentation

revisions.title: EEZ Extends Ethereum: Making Its Contracts Safe for Chains to Adopt
revisions.summary: EEZ extends Ethereum, and Ethereum's security with it. EEZ turns cross-chain execution into an Ethereum primitive: rollups and L1 call each other in one transaction, checked on Ethereum with no bridge in between, and a protocol deploys once instead of on every chain. This grant takes EEZ from audit to adoption: an independent audit and fixes, a testnet where outside chains can try the audited contracts, and a final payment only when an external chain or protocol decides to run EEZ on mainnet. Our mission is to deliver an open-source model, within a non-profit framework, that is secure enough for everyone to use; its adoption rests on shared risk, which requires shared security, shared funding, and shared collaboration.

sections.why:
Some of the largest losses in Ethereum's history happened at its bridges: honeypots of locked funds guarded by small signer sets that rely on reputation rather than contract logic or validity proofs, prioritizing UX over security. Ronin, Poly Network, BNB Bridge, Wormhole, and Nomad all sit near the top of the [Rekt leaderboard](https://rekt.news/leaderboard/), and each broke the layer that decides which cross-chain messages are valid. 

EEZ turns cross-chain execution into an Ethereum primitive. A contract on one rollup calls a contract on another rollup, or on L1, and uses the return value in the same transaction, with the result checked on Ethereum. That takes the bridge out of these flows:

* **Moving assets between rollups**, with no third-party contract holding pooled funds under a signer set.
* **Atomic multi-chain actions**, such as a swap funded from another rollup, which complete fully or revert.
* **One deployment serving every chain.** The Balancer v2 exploit drained the same duplicated code chain by chain. With EEZ a protocol deploys once, and a fix applies everywhere.

The clearest win is a smaller attack surface. Today a protocol deploys a copy of itself on every network it wants to reach, and duplication breeds bugs: version drift, per-chain initialization mistakes, maintenance across every copy. The Balancer v2 exploit drained the same duplicated code chain by chain. With EEZ a protocol can deploy once, on the network where it is easiest to control, audit, and secure, and every chain uses it through atomic cross-chain communication. 

Every Layer 2 becomes a true extension of Ethereum: one account and one contract address everywhere, with each network keeping the security guarantees it chooses and better UX than reputation-based bridges. Ethereum L1 stays as secure as it is today, since its consensus does not depend on EEZ. Every connected chain relies on one small contract set on Ethereum, which is easier to audit and monitor than many bridges; that shared risk calls for shared, independent review before chains adopt it, and this grant funds it.

How EEZ changes where security comes from:

* **Each chain picks its verification.** A rollup declares the proof systems it accepts and how many must agree, and every cross-chain action settles against that check on Ethereum. Rollups that run based, like the first Gnosis deployment, go further: sequencing happens inside the L1 block, and anyone can rebuild the chain from L1 data alone.
* **Results are checked on L1.** Every cross-chain outcome is computed ahead of time and checked on Ethereum, so a forged result fails and an operator can at most stall calls. Today one attestation signer runs the check by re-executing each block window; with several proof systems and a threshold, one prover's bug does not compromise the chain. The audit covers both.
* **Wallets** can route cross-chain sends automatically, so funds sent to the right address on the wrong chain stop being a loss.
* **No half-done state.** A cross-chain call and its return value execute in one transaction. Everything commits or nothing does, so stuck funds and partial-state exploits are removed by design.

EEZ is not a dapp and not a product. It is an Ethereum public good: an open, permissionless protocol and infrastructure for synchronous composability between Ethereum rollups. The core EEZ contract has no admin role. Each connected rollup keeps its own contract, whose owner sets the accepted proof systems, verification keys, and threshold; reviewing those privileged roles and how they can be locked down is part of this audit. That design puts the security of the whole system on its smart contracts, which is exactly what this initiative puts under independent review.

revisions.title: EEZ: Making Its Contracts Safe for Chains to Adopt
revisions.summary: EEZ extends Ethereum, and Ethereum's security with it. EEZ turns cross-chain execution into an Ethereum primitive: rollups and L1 call each other in one transaction, checked on Ethereum with no bridge in between, and a protocol deploys once instead of on every chain. This grant takes EEZ from audit to adoption: an independent audit and fixes, a testnet where outside chains can try the audited contracts, and a final payment only when outside chains and protocols run EEZ on mainnet. Our mission is to deliver an open-source model, within a non-profit framework, that is secure enough for everyone to use; its adoption rests on shared risk, which requires shared security, shared funding, and shared collaboration.

sections.why:
Some of the largest losses in Ethereum's history happened at its bridges: honeypots of locked funds guarded by small signer sets that rely on reputation rather than contract logic or validity proofs, prioritizing UX over security. Ronin, Poly Network, BNB Bridge, Wormhole, and Nomad all sit near the top of the [Rekt leaderboard](https://rekt.news/leaderboard/), and each broke the layer that decides which cross-chain messages are valid. 

EEZ turns cross-chain execution into an Ethereum primitive. A contract on one rollup calls a contract on another rollup, or on L1, and uses the return value in the same transaction, with the result checked on Ethereum. That takes the bridge out of these flows:

- Moving assets between rollups no longer needs a third-party contract holding pooled assets, so there is no bridge pool for an attacker to drain.
- Atomic multi-chain actions, such as a swap funded from another rollup, complete fully or revert together, within one L1 block, provided a builder includes the bundle.
- A smaller attack surface. Today a protocol copies itself onto every network it reaches, and duplication breeds bugs: version drift, per-chain initialization mistakes, maintenance across every copy. The Balancer v2 exploit drained the same code chain by chain. With EEZ a protocol deploys once, where it is easiest to audit and secure, and a fix applies everywhere. 

Every Layer 2 becomes a true extension of Ethereum: one account and one contract address across connected chains, with wallets routing sends so funds sent to the wrong chain can stop being lost. Ethereum L1 stays as secure as it is today, since its consensus does not depend on EEZ. What changes is the layer above it: cross-chain validity is decided by checks on Ethereum instead of by a signer set's reputation, the locked-fund pools that made bridges worth attacking disappear, and the code that can lose user money across chains collapses to one set that Ethereum can see and everyone can audit.

**What each rollup keeps.** Each rollup declares the proof systems it accepts and how many must agree, and every cross-chain outcome is checked on L1 against them; the composer that builds each bundle can at most stall calls. Based rollups, like the first Gnosis deployment, go further: sequencing happens inside the L1 block, and anyone can rebuild the chain from L1 data alone. Today one attestation signer runs the check by re-executing each block window, so until more proof systems are added, a chain's safety rests on that signer. The audit covers the signer, the multi-prover design it plugs into, and how each rollup locks its configuration down.

**What independently tested guarantees change.** Every rollup that adopts EEZ inherits the same contract set on Ethereum. Its cross-chain attack surface becomes that reviewed set plus its own configuration, instead of a bridge it built and audited alone. Every later adopter shares one review, and a fix reaches all of them at once. The same sharing is the risk: a flaw in the shared set is a flaw everywhere, which is why no chain should adopt it on the EEZ team's word alone. The audit turns these guarantees from a design claim into something a rollup can rely on; the testnet lets outside chains verify it, and mainnet adoption shows they did.

With audited EEZ, users and teams will be able to:

- Move assets between rollups with no third-party pool holding funds for an attacker to drain.
- Run atomic multi-chain actions, such as a swap funded from another rollup, that complete fully or revert together within one L1 block, provided a builder includes the bundle.
- Deploy a protocol once, where it is easiest to audit, and serve every connected chain from that one deployment, so a fix applies everywhere.
- Use one account and one contract address across connected chains, with wallets routing sends so funds sent to the wrong chain can stop being lost.
- Adopt a shared, independently audited contract set instead of building and auditing a bridge alone, with every later adopter sharing the same review and every fix reaching all of them at once.

EEZ is not a dapp and not a product. It is an Ethereum public good: an open, permissionless protocol for synchronous composability between Ethereum rollups. The core EEZ contract has no admin role. Each connected rollup keeps its own contract, whose owner sets the accepted proof systems, verification keys, and threshold. That design puts the security of the whole system on its smart contracts, which is exactly what this grant puts under independent review.
sections.in_scope:
* **Independent audit** of the EEZ core contracts at one pinned commit, including privileged roles, cross-chain behavior, and the single attestation signer live today with the multi-prover design it plugs into. Fixes by the EEZ team, re-review by the auditor. About 8 to 10 senior-auditor-weeks; report within 2 months of the auditor's appointment.
* **Integration environment:** the audited contracts on a public testnet, integration docs, a conformance suite, a reference integration, and a support channel. Celo, Polygon, and Linea build their own integrations; this grant pays none of that.
* **Integration support** for the first outside chain or protocol that goes to mainnet.
sections.out_scope:
* Rollup node software, provers, sequencers, and other off-chain infrastructure
* The internal economics of connected rollups
* Re-auditing changes made after the pinned commit
sections.team:
The EEZ Association does the work and is accountable for the outcome.

* [Jordi Baylina](https://x.com/jbaylina), core contributor
* [Friederike Ernst](https://x.com/tw_tter), co-initiator
* [Eduardo Antuña](https://x.com/eduadiez), core contributor
* [Jesús Ligero](https://x.com/JesusLigero3), core contributor
* [Armagan Ercan](https://x.com/epochzer0), coordinator

Other funding: Gnosis commits $30,000 to this goal and hosts the testnet nodes; the $10,000 milestone covers the contract deployment, documentation, conformance suite, and reference integration built on top.
sections.why_grant:
* The protocol is built and public at [eez-core-protocol](https://github.com/eez-association/eez-core-protocol): contracts, specifications under `docs/`, end-to-end test scenarios, and open findings from internal review. The contracts are prepared for devnets and ready for audit.
* GnosisDAO [approved GIP-153](https://snapshot.org/#/s:gnosis.eth/proposal/0x5522f4cbd034c966a08d6901b05c7ad7300041b3e0d75a0ad3da868af1a98b98), making Gnosis Chain the first governance-backed adopter.
* [Celo](https://celo.org/), [Polygon](https://polygon.technology/), and [Linea](https://linea.build/) have agreed in discussions with us to test the audited contracts.
* Vitalik Buterin stress-tested the design with Jordi Baylina at ETHPrague 2026 ([fireside](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=prgWmgUbSVQ)) and called EEZ "a quite helpful effort" at Dappcon Berlin ([panel](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gfG-R8AOu0E)). Joseph Lubin supports EEZ publicly ([post](https://x.com/etheconomiczone/status/2052390993610133513)).
sections.commitments:
* **License:** MIT, with a LICENSE file at the repository root.
* **Maintenance:** the EEZ Association maintains the contracts and the public security record after the grant; the testnet stays public for at least 12 months after the report.
* **Pinned target:** at least 2 outside chains and 4 dapps from the adoption lists run EEZ on mainnet within 6 months of the audit report. If the condition is met earlier, the adoption milestone is disbursed earlier.
* **Independent auditor:** we publish a shortlist of at least 2 firms and why we chose one; the auditor has no ties to the EEZ Association, its contributors, Gnosis, or ZisK.

criteria: At least 2 outside chains run the audited contracts on mainnet, from this list: Celo, Polygon, Linea, Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, Robinhood Chain, shown by deployment addresses and each chain's public announcement

revisions.title: ETH Daily Security: Getting Ethereum Users to the Tools That Protect Them
revisions.summary: Ethereum security builders ship good tools, and most users never hear about them. ETH Daily is moving from a general news briefing to a dedicated security publication, and uses its existing audience to send users to anti-phishing tools. Every tool link is a unique invite link, so each wallet that takes a security action is counted and verified.

sections.why:
Builders keep shipping tools that stop attacks: approval revokers, wallets that check signatures and transactions. A tool only protects the users who find it, and users have no single place to learn what exists. They scramble to search X, GitHub and Reddit.

Wallet drainers took $494 million from 332,000 addresses in 2024 and $83.85 million from 106,106 wallets in 2025 (Scam Sniffer annual reports, drops.scamsniffer.io). Users who revoke bad approvals, check signatures and verify addresses avoid these attacks.
sections.in_scope:
- ETH Daily becomes a dedicated Ethereum security publication for the grant period
- A public hub of security tools and guides on token approvals, wallet signatures and address poisoning
- A unique, trackable invite link for each listed tool
- Guides and podcast episodes that send the audience to the hub
- A published neutrality policy
sections.out_scope:
- Building security tools
- Onboarding tool teams: we bring users to teams that already exist
- Coverage of chains other than Ethereum
sections.team: ETH Daily (pseudonymous): solo producer of a daily Ethereum news podcast, newsletter and social feed for over 4 years. Track record: https://x.com/ethdaily
sections.why_grant: The distribution exists: 10,000 combined newsletter and podcast subscribers and 26,000 combined followers on X, Lens and Farcaster (https://ethdaily.io/ads). Four years of coverage and a security archive are public. Nobody else funds this scope, which is why the price is $2,900 a month.
sections.commitments:
- Guides published under CC BY 4.0
- Paid referrals and sponsored listings are disclosed inline and never change what we recommend
- The hub is maintained for 12 months after the last milestone at no further cost
- Pinned target: at least 100 verified wallets completing a security action

criteria: At least 100 distinct wallets completed a security action through the tracking links (revoked an approval or activated a listed tool), with duplicates, staff and automated wallets excluded.
The count verified by the technical reviewer from the link logs
At least 2 outside tool teams confirm activations in writing, 1 of them a wallet from this list: Ambire, Rabby, MetaMask, Ledger, Trust Wallet

milestones.name: Sustainability
criteria: At least $1,500 of sponsorship or referral revenue, not counting grants, received from at least 2 outside projects, shown on a revenue note and verified by the technical reviewer

revisions.title: EthSec: AI Security Review of the Ethereum Ecosystem
revisions.summary: EthSec will run Argus, its AI security system (https://ethsecurity.org/content/argus/), as an ongoing review of the Ethereum ecosystem: all Ethereum DeFi, all Ethereum layer 2s, and base-layer and client code. This grant pays $200,000 for Argus token credits used in that work. EthSec will publish a report; when appropriate, that report is an aggregate findings report without technical details. Adoption is acknowledgment from the affected teams. A public acknowledgment is not required, but EthSec will ask for one where possible. After the grant, EthSec keeps running the reviews from its own budget, which it intends to keep raising money for.

sections.why:
The problem is larger than DeFi protocol losses alone. Argus covers the Ethereum ecosystem: DeFi on Ethereum, Ethereum layer 2s, and the base-layer clients that run the network.

As of 13 November 2026, Ethereum DeFi has about $39.4 billion locked (https://defillama.com/chain/ethereum). Ethereum layer 2s secure about $35.1 billion (https://l2beat.com/scaling/tvs). Those figures move day to day; they show the scale of funds that sit on live contracts, on layer 2s, and behind the clients that process them.

Losses span more than one layer. Immunefi's 2026 Ecosystem Vulnerability Scoreboard puts DeFi protocol losses at $680 million in 2025, and says 89% of those losses came from protocol logic exploits (https://immunefi.com/blog/research/the-ecosystem-vulnerability-scoreboard-6-years-of-defi-loss-data/). One of those incidents, the Balancer V2 composable stable pools exploit, lost $128 million across Ethereum and several layer 2s. That same report keeps centralized exchange failures separate: exchanges absorbed over $1.6 billion in infrastructure-class losses in 2025, led by the $1.5 billion Bybit compromise. revisions.title: ForensIQ: Faster Ethereum Incident Response Through Evidence Reconstruction
revisions.summary: ForensIQ is building an open-source module that connects off-chain incident evidence (logs, files, transaction hashes) with Ethereum activity to reconstruct attack timelines, trace fund flows, and flag transfers to attributed exchange addresses. It replaces the manual handoffs between logs, block explorers, and attribution tools with one evidence-linked workflow that produces a verified response package faster. The grant funds the missing connective layer on top of ForensIQ's existing MVP (case management, Crystal and Etherscan integrations), not a rebuild of the platform. Success is measured through pilots with protocol, exchange, and law-enforcement investigators, tracking time to a verified timeline and correctness rather than a promised percentage improvement.

sections.why:
During an Ethereum security incident, time is a critical resource. Responders need to establish what happened, identify the affected assets, follow the funds, and prepare the evidence needed for their next action. Every manual handoff between logs, transaction views, attribution results, and investigation notes consumes part of that response window. Funds can move again while the team is still assembling its first coherent account.

This initiative funds an open-source module that reduces the work between receiving incident evidence and producing a verified response package. It connects off-chain evidence with Ethereum activity, reconstructs the attack timeline, maps supported fund movements, and flags transfers to attributed exchange addresses. The intended users are protocol and exchange security teams, incident-response firms, and law-enforcement investigators.

**Less time assembling evidence. More time to act on it.**
sections.in_scope:
- Ethereum mainnet, native ETH movements, and ERC-20 transfers; support for relevant execution traces must be documented against the selected data provider.
- Two or three log formats chosen with pilot users during the first month, plus supporting file evidence with stable source references.
- A shared timeline with normalized timestamps, original timestamps retained, and explicit handling of unknown time zones or uncertain ordering.
- Fund-flow views linking transfers to transaction hashes and addresses, with documented tracing assumptions.
- Crystal attribution integration and Etherscan transaction-data integration, with documented access requirements.
- Incremental case updates and configurable polling alerts for supported transfers to addresses attributed to exchanges, including source, retrieval time, and uncertainty. Provider delays and polling intervals are visible.
- Evidence-linked attack hypotheses, human-reviewed containment recommendations for agreed scenarios, and an exportable investigation package. Exchange action remains at the recipient exchange's discretion.
- Standalone deployment, public documentation, reproducible test fixtures, and independent pilot evaluation.

**What this pays for:**

Consider an illustrative investigation: a team provides access logs, incident files, and suspicious transaction hashes. The module places relevant events on one timeline, links each finding to its source, traces supported transfers, and checks available address attribution. If funds reach an address attributed to an exchange, the investigator gets an alert and an evidence package to review for an escalation request. The team can start reviewing supported findings while the broader investigation continues.

The funded contribution is the connection between those steps: evidence normalization, traceable correlations, incremental updates, and a consistent response export. Existing blockchain intelligence supplies attribution. AI helps organize evidence and propose explanations; an investigator verifies conclusions and chooses actions. Recommendations will cover a small set of incident scenarios agreed with pilot users, rather than promise a reliable diagnosis for every attack.

Success means shorter time to a verified timeline and a usable escalation package, with correctness measured alongside speed. Pilot results will establish whether and where the module saves time; no improvement percentage is claimed in advance.

The open-source core will ingest supported logs and supplied Ethereum data, produce timelines and fund-flow views, and export evidence without a ForensIQ account. Commercial attribution is an optional enrichment using the operator's own credentials. Without it, exchange identity can remain unknown. Public fixtures allow the complete workflow to be evaluated without purchasing third-party access.

**On the milestone plan:**

The six-month plan allocates roughly four months to development and two to pilots and refinement. Pilot recruitment and data-access arrangements start in month one. The proposed cost basis is $120,000 for team work ($20,000 per month), $10,000 for infrastructure and external services, and $5,000 for independent review, all included in the milestone amounts. Team work covers backend and data integration, AI/evidence analysis, investigator-led validation, and pilot delivery. Staffing allocations will be fixed in the final plan; these figures do not imply four full-time hires. Service costs and reviewer fees must be validated before contracting. Payments are tied to acceptance, not monthly payroll.
sections.out_scope:
- Other chains and L2s, cross-chain bridge tracing, and claims to resolve movement through mixers.
- A proprietary address-labeling database or redistribution of third-party data without permission.
- Universal log ingestion, autonomous remediation, automatic freeze-request submission, or guaranteed recovery.
sections.team:
The proposed recipient is the ForensIQ team, backed by HackenProof. The proposer reports an existing MVP with user and role management, case creation, file uploads, AI file analysis, and integrations with Crystal and Etherscan. These components provide a head start; the grant pays for the additional investigation module and its validation, not rebuilding the SaaS foundation.

The head start combines working ingestion and analysis components with existing blockchain integrations and access to prospective pilot users through HackenProof. Reuse should let the team spend the grant on cross-source reconstruction, response exports, and field validation. revisions.title: ForensIQ: Faster Ethereum Incident Response Through Evidence Reconstruction
revisions.summary: ForensIQ is building an open-source module that connects off-chain incident evidence (logs, files, transaction hashes) with Ethereum activity to reconstruct attack timelines, trace fund flows, and flag transfers to attributed exchange addresses. It replaces the manual handoffs between logs, block explorers, and attribution tools with one evidence-linked workflow that produces a verified response package faster. The grant funds the missing connective layer on top of ForensIQ's existing MVP (case management, Crystal and Etherscan integrations), not a rebuild of the platform. Success is measured through pilots with protocol, exchange, and law-enforcement investigators, tracking time to a verified timeline and correctness rather than a promised percentage improvement.

sections.why:
During an Ethereum security incident, time is a critical resource. Responders need to establish what happened, identify the affected assets, follow the funds, and prepare the evidence needed for their next action. Every manual handoff between logs, transaction views, attribution results, and investigation notes consumes part of that response window. Funds can move again while the team is still assembling its first coherent account.

This initiative funds an open-source module that reduces the work between receiving incident evidence and producing a verified response package. It connects off-chain evidence with Ethereum activity, reconstructs the attack timeline, maps supported fund movements, and flags transfers to attributed exchange addresses. The intended users are protocol and exchange security teams, incident-response firms, and law-enforcement investigators.

**Less time assembling evidence. More time to act on it.**
sections.in_scope:
- Ethereum mainnet, native ETH movements, and ERC-20 transfers; support for relevant execution traces must be documented against the selected data provider.
- Two or three log formats chosen with pilot users during the first month, plus supporting file evidence with stable source references.
- A shared timeline with normalized timestamps, original timestamps retained, and explicit handling of unknown time zones or uncertain ordering.
- Fund-flow views linking transfers to transaction hashes and addresses, with documented tracing assumptions.
- Crystal attribution integration and Etherscan transaction-data integration, with documented access requirements.
- Incremental case updates and configurable polling alerts for supported transfers to addresses attributed to exchanges, including source, retrieval time, and uncertainty. Provider delays and polling intervals are visible.
- Evidence-linked attack hypotheses, human-reviewed containment recommendations for agreed scenarios, and an exportable investigation package. Exchange action remains at the recipient exchange's discretion.
- Standalone deployment, public documentation, reproducible test fixtures, and independent pilot evaluation.

**What this pays for:**

Consider an illustrative investigation: a team provides access logs, incident files, and suspicious transaction hashes. The module places relevant events on one timeline, links each finding to its source, traces supported transfers, and checks available address attribution. If funds reach an address attributed to an exchange, the investigator gets an alert and an evidence package to review for an escalation request. The team can start reviewing supported findings while the broader investigation continues.

The funded contribution is the connection between those steps: evidence normalization, traceable correlations, incremental updates, and a consistent response export. Existing blockchain intelligence supplies attribution. AI helps organize evidence and propose explanations; an investigator verifies conclusions and chooses actions. Recommendations will cover a small set of incident scenarios agreed with pilot users, rather than promise a reliable diagnosis for every attack.

Success means shorter time to a verified timeline and a usable escalation package, with correctness measured alongside speed. Pilot results will establish whether and where the module saves time; no improvement percentage is claimed in advance.

The open-source core will ingest supported logs and supplied Ethereum data, produce timelines and fund-flow views, and export evidence without a ForensIQ account. Commercial attribution is an optional enrichment using the operator's own credentials. Without it, exchange identity can remain unknown. Public fixtures allow the complete workflow to be evaluated without purchasing third-party access.

**On the milestone plan:**

The six-month plan allocates roughly four months to development and two to pilots and refinement. Pilot recruitment and data-access arrangements start in month one. The proposed cost basis is $120,000 for team work ($20,000 per month), $10,000 for infrastructure and external services, and $5,000 for independent review, all included in the milestone amounts. Team work covers backend and data integration, AI/evidence analysis, investigator-led validation, and pilot delivery. Staffing allocations will be fixed in the final plan; these figures do not imply four full-time hires. Service costs and reviewer fees must be validated before contracting. Payments are tied to acceptance, not monthly payroll.

- A proprietary address-labeling database or redistribution of third-party data without permission.
- Universal log ingestion, autonomous remediation, automatic freeze-request submission, or guaranteed recovery.
