sections.commitments:
LeakDetectAI commits to releasing all grant-funded, non-sensitive software, detection tooling, benchmark suites, test cases, documentation, and integration examples under an OSI-approved open-source license, preferably Apache-2.0, with source code and development history publicly available in the project's GitHub repositories. Any existing components with different licenses will retain their original licenses, and their licensing compatibility will be reviewed before integration. No grant-funded core functionality will be made exclusively available through a proprietary service.

We commit to maintaining the open-source repositories after the grant period, including preserving documentation, addressing critical bugs, reviewing community contributions, and keeping the detection and regression-testing infrastructure usable. We will make reasonable efforts to coordinate ongoing maintenance with the relevant Ethereum wallet, agent-framework, and open-source maintainers. The project will also document installation, testing, and integration procedures so that other developers can independently use and extend the work without depending on the original team.

Evidence will consist of publicly verifiable issues, maintainer-reviewed fixes, merged pull requests or downstream commits, and regression tests, subject to responsible-disclosure requirements. These projects are pinned adoption targets for engagement and evaluation, not claimed partnerships or guaranteed commitments from their maintainers. Where a target has no reproducible vulnerability within the project's scope, or its maintainers decline participation, we will document the outcome and pursue another relevant Ethereum wallet or agent framework with equivalent adoption potential.

We will not use confidentiality as a reason to withhold non-sensitive grant-funded deliverables or the evidence needed to verify completed security improvements.

revisions.title: LeakDetectAI: Detecting and Eliminating Side-Channel Vulnerabilities in Ethereum Wallets and AI Agents
revisions.summary: LeakDetectAI strengthens Ethereum security by identifying and helping eliminate side-channel vulnerabilities in wallets and AI agent frameworks. The project will develop and validate detection capabilities against real-world Ethereum use cases, then work directly with ecosystem teams to remediate confirmed vulnerabilities. Its primary outcome is measurable security improvements: upstream fixes, merged patches, and regression tests across Ethereum wallets and agent infrastructure.

sections.why:
Ethereum wallets, hardware wallets, and AI-agent frameworks increasingly handle cryptographic keys, transaction signing, and sensitive authorization workflows. However, developers lack accessible, reproducible ways to identify and remediate side-channel vulnerabilities in these real-world applications. Conventional security testing often focuses on functional correctness, smart-contract vulnerabilities, and known attack patterns, leaving weaknesses arising from observable execution behaviour, such as timing and other information leakage, insufficiently tested. This creates an attack surface that can expose sensitive information and undermine the security of wallets and agent-driven transactions.

LeakDetectAI closes this gap by enabling Ethereum developers and maintainers to test real wallet and agent workflows, reproduce actionable side-channel vulnerabilities, and implement and verify mitigations. Afterwards, participating projects will be able to incorporate repeatable side-channel security testing and regression checks into their development processes, identify weaknesses before deployment, and demonstrate that fixes have addressed them. Through adoption by Ethereum wallet developers, agent-framework teams, and Layer 2 ecosystems, the initiative will deliver concrete security improvements: stronger protection of wallet keys, safer transaction signing and authorization, and reduced exposure of AI-agent workflows to attacks exploiting observable execution behaviour.

revisions.title: LeakDetectAI: Detecting and Eliminating Side-Channel Vulnerabilities in Ethereum Wallets and AI Agents
revisions.summary: LeakDetectAI strengthens Ethereum security by identifying and helping eliminate side-channel vulnerabilities in wallets and AI agent frameworks. The project will develop and validate detection capabilities against real-world Ethereum use cases, then work directly with ecosystem teams to remediate confirmed vulnerabilities. Its primary outcome is measurable security improvements: upstream fixes, merged patches, and regression tests across Ethereum wallets and agent infrastructure.

sections.why:
Ethereum wallets, hardware wallets, and AI-agent frameworks increasingly handle cryptographic keys, transaction signing, and sensitive authorization workflows. However, developers lack accessible, reproducible ways to identify and remediate side-channel vulnerabilities in these real-world applications. Conventional security testing often focuses on functional correctness, smart-contract vulnerabilities, and known attack patterns, leaving weaknesses arising from observable execution behaviour, such as timing and other information leakage, insufficiently tested. This creates an attack surface that can expose sensitive information and undermine the security of wallets and agent-driven transactions.

LeakDetectAI closes this gap by enabling Ethereum developers and maintainers to test real wallet and agent workflows, reproduce actionable side-channel vulnerabilities, and implement and verify mitigations. Afterwards, participating projects will be able to incorporate repeatable side-channel security testing and regression checks into their development processes, identify weaknesses before deployment, and demonstrate that fixes have addressed them. Through adoption by Ethereum wallet developers, agent-framework teams, and Layer 2 ecosystems, the initiative will deliver concrete security improvements: stronger protection of wallet keys, safer transaction signing and authorization, and reduced exposure of AI-agent workflows to attacks exploiting observable execution behaviour.
sections.in_scope:
LeakDetectAI will deliver the adoption of an open-source security testing and remediation capability across Ethereum wallets, hardware wallets, AI-agent frameworks, and Layer 2 ecosystems. The funding will support the integration of LeakDetectAI into the actual security-testing and development workflows of participating projects, collaboration with their maintainers to identify and reproduce exploitable side-channel weaknesses, and engineering support to implement and verify fixes. The central deliverable is not simply a tool that detects potential information leakage, but demonstrable security improvements in Ethereum projects that use it.

Adoption will be pursued across six areas. First, LeakDetectAI will be adopted for desktop, mobile, and hardware-wallet security testing, covering real-world key-management, transaction-signing, and authorization workflows. The work will engage relevant wallet developers and hardware-wallet testing environments to identify reproducible weaknesses, provide actionable remediation guidance, and support fixes and regression tests. Second, the existing Ethereum field deployments, including the Ethereum Layer 1 and 2 based hardware-wallet testing workflow using Ledger, will be used to apply LeakDetectAI in practical environments. The objective is to translate findings from these deployments into documented, actionable security improvements in the participating applications and their associated workflows.

Third, adoption will extend across Ethereum agent and protocol ecosystems, including relevant teams and applications within Optimism and Arbitrum. LeakDetectAI will be applied to agent execution, transaction authorization, signing, and protocol-integrated workflows, with participating developers supported in reproducing and remediating confirmed weaknesses. Fourth, we will work with Ethereum wallet developers, with prospective targets including MetaMask, Rabby Wallet, and Safe, to identify side-channel vulnerabilities affecting wallet security and support maintainers in implementing fixes. Fifth, we will engage Ethereum agent-framework developers, with prospective targets including Coinbase AgentKit and ElizaOS, to identify weaknesses in agent execution and transaction workflows and support code-level remediation and regression testing. These are prospective adoption targets, not confirmed commitments; engagement and remediation will be pursued in coordination with the relevant maintainers.

The sixth area will consolidate these efforts into ecosystem-wide adoption and verified security remediation. We target adoption by at least three named Ethereum wallet or agent-framework projects and at least three implemented security improvements in participating codebases, including wallet and agent-framework environments. Each counted improvement must be linked to a reproducible weakness identified through LeakDetectAI and supported by verifiable evidence of remediation, such as a merged patch, released fix, downstream code change, or equivalent maintainer-confirmed implementation, together with a regression test or repeatable validation showing that the weakness has been addressed. Deliverables will include documented integrations, vulnerability reproduction reports, remediation records, regression tests, and a public adoption report, subject to responsible-disclosure requirements.

The $70,000 requested will fund the adoption work required to achieve these outcomes: deployment and testing across desktop, mobile, and hardware-wallet environments; integration into existing Ethereum field deployments; engagement with Ethereum and Layer 2 agent and protocol teams; direct collaboration with wallet and agent-framework maintainers; vulnerability reproduction and remediation support; implementation of security fixes and regression tests; and independent verification and documentation of the resulting improvements. Of the total request, $60,000 (Milestones B to D) pays only on outside teams using LeakDetectAI and merging its fixes. This allocation will support the engineering effort and maintainer coordination needed to move identified vulnerabilities through to implemented fixes.

The success of the initiative will be measured by security improvements in real Ethereum projects, rather than downloads, user counts, demonstrations, or the number of testing runs. By completion, participating projects will have used LeakDetectAI to identify actionable side-channel weaknesses and address them through implemented fixes and regression tests. This will make Ethereum safer by reducing opportunities for attackers to exploit observable execution behaviour to infer sensitive information, strengthening the protection of wallet keys and signing operations, improving transaction authorization security, and reducing the exposure of AI-agent workflows to side-channel attacks. All non-sensitive tooling, remediation guidance, and verification evidence will be published as reusable open-source resources so that other Ethereum developers can adopt the same protections.
sections.out_scope:
LeakDetectAI will not undertake general-purpose privacy research, academic research without a direct Ethereum security application, or the development of new foundational machine-learning or side-channel analysis algorithms unrelated to the project's defined objectives. The initiative is not intended to build a general-purpose privacy auditing platform, surveillance or user-monitoring system, or a commercial security product. It will not cover non-Ethereum ecosystems, or other unrelated blockchain networks; the scope is strictly limited to Ethereum, its Layer 2 ecosystems, and the wallets and agent frameworks serving them.

The grant will not fund the development of new wallets, blockchain protocols, consensus clients, agent frameworks, or general-purpose AI infrastructure. It will not include broad penetration-testing engagements, smart-contract auditing unrelated to the identified side-channel risks, formal verification of entire applications, or remediation of vulnerabilities outside the project's defined threat model. It will also not fund speculative vulnerability research that cannot be connected to a concrete Ethereum security risk or actionable remediation.

Finally, the project will not publicly disclose exploitable vulnerabilities before maintainers have had a reasonable opportunity to address them. Sensitive findings, exploit details, and affected code will be handled through responsible-disclosure processes. Funding is specifically for the development and application of Ethereum-focused detection capabilities, vulnerability validation, maintainer-supported remediation, and independently verifiable improvements to Ethereum wallet and agent security; activities outside these boundaries are excluded.
sections.team:
LeakDetectAI is led by Manu Gupta, Project Lead, and Dr. Pritha Gupta, Research Lead. Together, they bring complementary experience in open-source infrastructure, decentralized systems, AI, cryptography, side-channel analysis, and automated security testing.

Manu Gupta: Project Lead | Open-Source Security and P2P Maintainer
Manu brings over 20 years of open-source engineering experience, with a track record spanning decentralized networking, cryptographic infrastructure, distributed systems, and security engineering. He is a Technical Lead and Maintainer in the libp2p ecosystem and has contributed to IPFS, IPLD, and Multiformats, including work across Go, Rust, JavaScript, and Python implementations, interoperability, protocol specifications, and network security. For LeakDetectAI, he leads project delivery, Ethereum and wallet ecosystem integration, open-source development, adoption by external projects, and coordination with maintainers to turn identified vulnerabilities into verified fixes.
Profile: https://github.com/seetadev

Dr. Pritha Gupta: Adoption and Research Lead | AI, Cryptography and Side-Channel Security
Dr. Pritha Gupta brings research experience in AI, cryptography, side-channel analysis, and automated security testing, including work associated with Ruhr-Universität Bochum and Software Innovation Campus Paderborn. She leads the technical methodology underpinning LeakDetectAI, including adversarial inference experiments, machine-learning and neural architecture search (NAS) pipelines, detection methodology, and security benchmarks. She also supports the translation of research capabilities into reproducible testing workflows and practical adoption by wallet and agent developers.
Research profile: https://sec4ai-ai4sec.github.io/

Existing funding and technical foundation
LeakDetectAI has previously received community support through the Giveth / Ethereum Security Quadratic Funding round, including community contributions and matching-pool support. This provides an initial community-backed funding foundation. The present request is for dedicated funding to support Ethereum ecosystem adoption, integrations, remediation engineering, and verification of security improvements. No additional grant amount or funding commitment is being represented here beyond that community support.

The initiative builds on existing side-channel analysis and automated security-testing work, including AutoSCA, developed in the context of Achelos. AutoSCA demonstrates the practical application of automated analysis and machine learning to identify cryptographic side-channel vulnerabilities, including Bleichenbacher-style TLS vulnerabilities. The underlying research direction is documented in the ACM AISec paper, Automated Detection of Side Channels in Cryptographic Protocols: DROWN the ROBOTs! LeakDetectAI extends this technical direction to Ethereum wallets, transaction signing, hardware-wallet workflows, and AI-agent applications.

- AutoSCA: https://github.com/achelos/AutoSCA
- Achelos: https://www.achelos.de/en/
- Implementation and user stories: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-ljLPgrw-DY&t=388s
- Workshops at Devcon: https://leak-detect-tooling.lovable.app/devcon

Existing ecosystem relationships and deployment context

The project builds on relationships and technical work across security tooling, Ethereum applications, decentralized infrastructure, and AI-agent ecosystems. These relationships provide potential pathways for practical validation and adoption, while not implying that every organisation listed has committed to adopt LeakDetectAI.

Achelos / AutoSCA: Existing technical alignment with automated side-channel analysis tooling.
Park Pro Token: Field-testing partner and token deployment. LeakDetectAI-related testing includes live Park Pro Token workflows using a Ledger hardware wallet, with wallet, signing, and cross-chain activity providing a practical environment for evaluating potential leakage.

Diagnosity: Health-AI observability pilot and field-deployment context.

Agent0 (ERC-8004): Alignment with trustless agent discovery, reputation, and validation workflows.

Aave and Morpho: Existing engagement contexts around enterprise and Health-AI observability, respectively.

Thales Security team, led by Vibhor Bijoy: Security research and advisory relationship.

Aspiring Investments Corp: Deployment relationship.

Samagra: Public-sector deployment experience.

SAP BTP and Joule team: Enterprise AI-agent observability engagement.

libp2p, IPFS, IPLD, and Multiformats: Existing open-source technical relationships and contributions in decentralized networking, content-addressed storage, and interoperable data infrastructure.

Public AI: Alignment with open and verifiable AI infrastructure.

Davos Economic Forum Committee, New Delhi: Policy and global security dialogue.

Relevant links:

- https://park-token-deploy.vercel.app/
- https://samagragovernance.in/
- https://libp2p.io/
- https://ipfs.tech/
- https://github.com/multiformats
- https://github.com/ipld
- https://publicai.co/
- http://www.aspiringapps.com/

The team’s delivery model combines research-led vulnerability analysis with open-source engineering and direct ecosystem engagement. Manu leads the adoption and remediation effort with wallet, agent, and infrastructure maintainers, while Dr. Gupta leads the technical methodology and validation. The requested funding will support this team in moving from existing capabilities and field-testing contexts to verified security fixes in Ethereum projects.

revisions.title: LeakDetectAI: Detecting and Eliminating Side-Channel Vulnerabilities in Ethereum Wallets and AI Agents
revisions.summary: LeakDetectAI is an AI-powered security initiative that detects and helps eliminate side-channel vulnerabilities that can expose private keys, signing secrets, cryptographic operations, and sensitive transaction data across Ethereum wallets, protocols, and autonomous AI agents. The project will deploy LeakDetectAI in real-world Ethereum security workflows, working directly with ecosystem developers and maintainers to identify, reproduce, and remediate vulnerabilities. Its success will be measured through independently verifiable adoption, maintainer-accepted vulnerabilities, merged fixes, and regression tests across the Ethereum ecosystem.

sections.why:
Ethereum wallets, protocols, and autonomous AI agents handle sensitive information, including private keys, signing secrets, cryptographic operations, and transaction data. Yet timing variations and other side-channel signals can expose this information even when software behaves as designed. Conventional security testing often overlooks these vulnerabilities because it focuses on functional correctness rather than unintended information leakage.

LeakDetectAI closes this gap by bringing AI-powered side-channel detection into real-world Ethereum security workflows. It enables developers and security teams to identify and reproduce hidden vulnerabilities, validate fixes, and introduce regression tests that prevent them from returning. This makes it possible to detect and remediate security weaknesses that conventional testing may miss, strengthening the protection of Ethereum wallets, protocols, and AI agents.
sections.in_scope:
LeakDetectAI will deliver the adoption of an open-source security testing and remediation capability across Ethereum wallets, hardware wallets, AI-agent frameworks, and Layer 2 ecosystems. The funding will support the integration of LeakDetectAI into the actual security-testing and development workflows of participating projects, collaboration with their maintainers to identify and reproduce exploitable side-channel weaknesses, and engineering support to implement and verify fixes. The central deliverable is not simply a tool that detects potential information leakage, but demonstrable security improvements in Ethereum projects that use it.

Adoption will be pursued across six areas. First, LeakDetectAI will be adopted for desktop, mobile, and hardware-wallet security testing, covering real-world key-management, transaction-signing, and authorization workflows. The work will engage relevant wallet developers and hardware-wallet testing environments to identify reproducible weaknesses, provide actionable remediation guidance, and support fixes and regression tests. Second, the existing Ethereum field deployments, including the Ethereum Layer 1 and 2 based hardware-wallet testing workflow using Ledger, will be used to apply LeakDetectAI in practical environments. The objective is to translate findings from these deployments into documented, actionable security improvements in the participating applications and their associated workflows.

Third, adoption will extend across Ethereum agent and protocol ecosystems, including relevant teams and applications within Optimism and Arbitrum. LeakDetectAI will be applied to agent execution, transaction authorization, signing, and protocol-integrated workflows, with participating developers supported in reproducing and remediating confirmed weaknesses. Fourth, we will work with Ethereum wallet developers, with prospective targets including MetaMask, Rabby Wallet, and Safe, to identify side-channel vulnerabilities affecting wallet security and support maintainers in implementing fixes. Fifth, we will engage Ethereum agent-framework developers, with prospective targets including Coinbase AgentKit and ElizaOS, to identify weaknesses in agent execution and transaction workflows and support code-level remediation and regression testing. These are prospective adoption targets, not confirmed commitments; engagement and remediation will be pursued in coordination with the relevant maintainers.

The sixth area will consolidate these efforts into ecosystem-wide adoption and verified security remediation. We target adoption by at least three named Ethereum wallet or agent-framework projects and at least three implemented security improvements in participating codebases, including wallet and agent-framework environments. Each counted improvement must be linked to a reproducible weakness identified through LeakDetectAI and supported by verifiable evidence of remediation, such as a merged patch, released fix, downstream code change, or equivalent maintainer-confirmed implementation, together with a regression test or repeatable validation showing that the weakness has been addressed. Deliverables will include documented integrations, vulnerability reproduction reports, remediation records, regression tests, and a public adoption report, subject to responsible-disclosure requirements.

The $60,000 requested will fund the adoption work required to achieve these outcomes: deployment and testing across desktop, mobile, and hardware-wallet environments; integration into existing Ethereum field deployments; engagement with Ethereum and Layer 2 agent and protocol teams; direct collaboration with wallet and agent-framework maintainers; vulnerability reproduction and remediation support; implementation of security fixes and regression tests; and independent verification and documentation of the resulting improvements. Of the total request, $50,000 (Milestones B to D) pays only on outside teams using LeakDetectAI and merging its fixes. This allocation will support the engineering effort and maintainer coordination needed to move identified vulnerabilities through to implemented fixes.

The success of the initiative will be measured by security improvements in real Ethereum projects, rather than downloads, user counts, demonstrations, or the number of testing runs. By completion, participating projects will have used LeakDetectAI to identify actionable side-channel weaknesses and address them through implemented fixes and regression tests. This will make Ethereum safer by reducing opportunities for attackers to exploit observable execution behaviour to infer sensitive information, strengthening the protection of wallet keys and signing operations, improving transaction authorization security, and reducing the exposure of AI-agent workflows to side-channel attacks. All non-sensitive tooling, remediation guidance, and verification evidence will be published as reusable open-source resources so that other Ethereum developers can adopt the same protections.
sections.out_scope:
LeakDetectAI will not undertake general-purpose privacy research, academic research without a direct Ethereum security application, or the development of new foundational machine-learning or side-channel analysis algorithms unrelated to the project's defined objectives. The initiative is not intended to build a general-purpose privacy auditing platform, surveillance or user-monitoring system, or a commercial security product. It will not cover non-Ethereum ecosystems, or other unrelated blockchain networks; the scope is strictly limited to Ethereum, its Layer 2 ecosystems, and the wallets and agent frameworks serving them.

The grant will not fund the development of new wallets, blockchain protocols, consensus clients, agent frameworks, or general-purpose AI infrastructure. It will not include broad penetration-testing engagements, smart-contract auditing unrelated to the identified side-channel risks, formal verification of entire applications, or remediation of vulnerabilities outside the project's defined threat model. It will also not fund speculative vulnerability research that cannot be connected to a concrete Ethereum security risk or actionable remediation.

Finally, the project will not publicly disclose exploitable vulnerabilities before maintainers have had a reasonable opportunity to address them. Sensitive findings, exploit details, and affected code will be handled through responsible-disclosure processes. Funding is specifically for the development and application of Ethereum-focused detection capabilities, vulnerability validation, maintainer-supported remediation, and independently verifiable improvements to Ethereum wallet and agent security; activities outside these boundaries are excluded.

Deliverables will include documented integrations, vulnerability reproduction reports, remediation records, regression tests, and a public adoption report, subject to responsible-disclosure requirements.

The $60,000 requested will fund the adoption work required to achieve these outcomes: deployment and testing across desktop, mobile, and hardware-wallet environments; integration into existing Ethereum field deployments; engagement with Ethereum and Layer 2 agent and protocol teams; direct collaboration with wallet and agent-framework maintainers; vulnerability reproduction and remediation support; implementation of security fixes and regression tests; and independent verification and documentation of the resulting improvements. Of the total request, $50,000 (Milestones B to D) pays only on outside teams using LeakDetectAI and merging its fixes. This allocation will support the engineering effort and maintainer coordination needed to move identified vulnerabilities through to implemented fixes.

The success of the initiative will be measured by security improvements in real Ethereum projects, rather than downloads, user counts, demonstrations, or the number of testing runs. By completion, participating projects will have used LeakDetectAI to identify actionable side-channel weaknesses and address them through implemented fixes and regression tests. This will make Ethereum safer by reducing opportunities for attackers to exploit observable execution behaviour to infer sensitive information, strengthening the protection of wallet keys and signing operations, improving transaction authorization security, and reducing the exposure of AI-agent workflows to side-channel attacks. All non-sensitive tooling, remediation guidance, and verification evidence will be published as reusable open-source resources so that other Ethereum developers can adopt the same protections.
sections.out_scope:
LeakDetectAI will not undertake general-purpose privacy research, academic research without a direct Ethereum security application, or the development of new foundational machine-learning or side-channel analysis algorithms unrelated to the project's defined objectives. The initiative is not intended to build a general-purpose privacy auditing platform, surveillance or user-monitoring system, or a commercial security product. It will not cover non-Ethereum ecosystems, or other unrelated blockchain networks; the scope is strictly limited to Ethereum, its Layer 2 ecosystems, and the wallets and agent frameworks serving them.

The grant will not fund the development of new wallets, blockchain protocols, consensus clients, agent frameworks, or general-purpose AI infrastructure. It will not include broad penetration-testing engagements, smart-contract auditing unrelated to the identified side-channel risks, formal verification of entire applications, or remediation of vulnerabilities outside the project's defined threat model. It will also not fund speculative vulnerability research that cannot be connected to a concrete Ethereum security risk or actionable remediation.

Finally, the project will not publicly disclose exploitable vulnerabilities before maintainers have had a reasonable opportunity to address them. Sensitive findings, exploit details, and affected code will be handled through responsible-disclosure processes. Funding is specifically for the development and application of Ethereum-focused detection capabilities, vulnerability validation, maintainer-supported remediation, and independently verifiable improvements to Ethereum wallet and agent security; activities outside these boundaries are excluded.
sections.team:
LeakDetectAI is led by Manu Gupta, Project Lead, and Dr. Pritha Gupta, Research Lead. Together, they bring complementary experience in open-source infrastructure, decentralized systems, AI, cryptography, side-channel analysis, and automated security testing.

Manu Gupta: Project Lead | Open-Source Security and P2P Maintainer
Manu brings over 20 years of open-source engineering experience, with a track record spanning decentralized networking, cryptographic infrastructure, distributed systems, and security engineering. He is a Technical Lead and Maintainer in the libp2p ecosystem and has contributed to IPFS, IPLD, and Multiformats, including work across Go, Rust, JavaScript, and Python implementations, interoperability, protocol specifications, and network security. For LeakDetectAI, he leads project delivery, Ethereum and wallet ecosystem integration, open-source development, adoption by external projects, and coordination with maintainers to turn identified vulnerabilities into verified fixes.
Profile: https://github.com/seetadev

Dr. Pritha Gupta: Adoption and Research Lead | AI, Cryptography and Side-Channel Security
Dr. Pritha Gupta brings research experience in AI, cryptography, side-channel analysis, and automated security testing, including work associated with Ruhr-Universität Bochum and Software Innovation Campus Paderborn. She leads the technical methodology underpinning LeakDetectAI, including adversarial inference experiments, machine-learning and neural architecture search (NAS) pipelines, detection methodology, and security benchmarks. sections.why_grant:
LeakDetectAI has an existing open-source foundation in automated side-channel analysis, machine-learning-based leakage detection, and hardware-wallet security testing. This is not a proposal to build side-channel analysis from scratch: the team has already published and made available the underlying research code and experimentation infrastructure. Public work includes:

Hardware-wallet testing and Ethereum/Web3 security: https://github.com/SEC4AI-AI4SEC/autosca-hw-wallet-tester 
The active development repository for automated side-channel security testing, including hardware-wallet analysis.

Deep-learning side-channel analysis: https://github.com/SEC4AI-AI4SEC/deep-learning-sca
An existing research and reproducibility codebase for automated side-channel analysis.

Quantitative information-leakage detection: https://github.com/SEC4AI-AI4SEC/AutoMLQuantILDetect 
An existing package applying AutoML and information-theoretic methods to detect and quantify leakage.

Project resources and demonstrations: LeakDetectAI project github site, project dashboard and and public research discussions: 
https://github.com/SEC4AI-AI4SEC/deep-learning-sca/discussions/3 and https://x.com/libp2p/status/2119770702907871743 

Partners: https://leak-detect-tooling.lovable.app/#partners 
Giveth Update: https://leak-detect-tooling.lovable.app/#giveth 
Devcon Update: https://leak-detect-tooling.lovable.app/devcon 
 
Prior ecosystem validation: LeakDetectAI was selected for the Ethereum Security Quadratic Funding round, with support from Giveth and TheDAO Security Fund. The selection and community discussion are publicly documented at https://x.com/manusheel/status/2054083699298472238 and https://github.com/SEC4AI-AI4SEC/deep-learning-sca/discussions/3

sections.commitments:
LeakDetectAI commits to releasing all grant-funded, non-sensitive software, detection tooling, benchmark suites, test cases, documentation, and integration examples under an OSI-approved open-source license, preferably Apache-2.0, with source code and development history publicly available in the project's GitHub repositories. Any existing components with different licenses will retain their original licenses, and their licensing compatibility will be reviewed before integration. No grant-funded core functionality will be made exclusively available through a proprietary service.

We commit to maintaining the open-source repositories after the grant period, including preserving documentation, addressing critical bugs, reviewing community contributions, and keeping the detection and regression-testing infrastructure usable. We will make reasonable efforts to coordinate ongoing maintenance with the relevant Ethereum wallet, agent-framework, and open-source maintainers. The project will also document installation, testing, and integration procedures so that other developers can independently use and extend the work without depending on the original team.

For ecosystem adoption, we commit to pursuing the named targets MetaMask, Rabby, Trust Wallet, Safe, Coinbase AgentKit, and ElizaOS. The adoption objective is verified remediation in at least three named projects, including at least one Ethereum wallet and one agent framework. Evidence will consist of publicly verifiable issues, maintainer-reviewed fixes, merged pull requests or downstream commits, and regression tests, subject to responsible-disclosure requirements. These projects are pinned adoption targets for engagement and evaluation, not claimed partnerships or guaranteed commitments from their maintainers. Where a target has no reproducible vulnerability within the project's scope, or its maintainers decline participation, we will document the outcome and pursue another relevant Ethereum wallet or agent framework with equivalent adoption potential.

We are not requesting an exception to the open-source licensing or public-goods commitments. The only qualification is that existing third-party components retain their original licenses and security-sensitive vulnerability details may remain confidential until responsible disclosure permits publication. We will not use confidentiality as a reason to withhold non-sensitive grant-funded deliverables or the evidence needed to verify completed security improvements.

revisions.title: Reproducible Ethereum clients: official releases that anyone can rebuild and check against the public source code
revisions.summary:
Ethereum runs on client software such as Geth, Lighthouse and Prysm, which node operators download from each client's repositories.
Today, operators have to trust that each download was built from the public source code untampered.
This proposal aims to make the 12 main clients reproducible: anyone can rebuild a release from its source, and get exactly the same binary as the one in the repository.
We work with the client teams to achieve reproducibility, and we publish a webpage explaining how anyone can verify a release themselves.

sections.why:
- **Who is safer:** validators and node operators who run official client releases, and the users who rely on them.
- **From what:** an attacker who breaks into a client team's build machine or release account and ships a tampered release, while the public source code still looks clean. The xz-utils backdoor in 2024 worked this way: the malicious code was only in the release files, not in the public repository [1].
- **What anyone can point to afterwards:** official client releases that rebuild from source to exactly the same file, the accepted fixes in each client's repository, and a public webpage that explains how to repeat the check.

We found no client whose official releases are checked by anyone outside its own team. Two clients check their own builds, some say their builds are reproducible without anyone verifying it, and the rest have done part of the work or none. No tampered client release is known so far. These clients secure all staked ETH.
sections.in_scope:
- Fixes to each client's build process, so its official Linux release can be rebuilt exactly from source. We contribute them to the client's own repository.
- A public webpage that explains the work and, for each client, how anyone can verify a release themselves.
- Working with each client team until the fixes are accepted. This is where most of the effort goes.

By official release we mean the file operators download from the client's release page.

The 12 clients: Geth, Nethermind, Besu, Erigon, Reth and Nimbus-eth1 (execution), and Prysm, Lighthouse, Teku, Nimbus, Lodestar and Grandine (consensus).
sections.out_scope:
- Reviewing the client source code itself. This work proves that a release matches its source, not that the source is free of bugs.
- Operating systems other than Linux.
- A service that rebuilds and checks every new release automatically (this is an initiative itself).
- L2 clients and validator tooling.
sections.team:
- [Vivi Andersson](https://github.com/vivi365), engineer: PhD student at KTH. Built Geth Rebuild, a tool that checks whether official Geth releases match their source code [2].
- [Sofia Bobadilla](https://sofiabobadilla.github.io/), coordinator and engineer: PhD student at KTH and member of mab.xyz, works on Ethereum and smart contract security.
- [Raphina Liu](https://github.com/Stamp9), engineer: PhD student at KTH. Took part in Ethereum Protocol Fellowship cohort 7.
- [Julien Malka](https://luj.fr/), engineer: postdoc at KTH. Studies build reproducibility across whole software distributions, and showed how one tampered build tool can infect an entire Linux distribution [8].
- [Martin Monperrus](https://www.monperrus.net/martin/), advisor: Professor of Software Technology at KTH.
- [Javier Ron](https://github.com/javierron), advisor: postdoc at KTH. Researches how running several different clients keeps Ethereum resilient [4].
- [Aman Sharma](https://github.com/algomaster99), engineer: PhD student at KTH. Studies why building the same software twice gives different files, and how to fix it [3].

Other funding: CHAINS, a KTH research project financed by the Swedish Foundation for Strategic Research, funds the PhD research of the four KTH students. It does not pay for this engineering work, so this grant pays for the engineers' time. The Ethereum Foundation funded our earlier research on client diversity [5].
sections.why_grant:
Our team has already done this for Geth, the most used execution client, and has studied the problem at scale:

- **Geth:** Geth Rebuild checks whether an official Geth release matches its source code [2]. While building it, Vivi Andersson reported two problems to the Geth team: file paths from the build machine were left inside the release, and the wrong compiler version was used. The Geth team fixed its builds in 2024 and tagged her on the fix [6][7].
- **Attacks on build tools:** with Julien Malka, we showed that a single tampered build tool can silently spread to nearly all the software of a Linux distribution [8]. It is the kind of attack that hides in the build, not in the source code.
- **Java clients:** our published study of thousands of Java packages explains the common reasons builds differ and provides a tool that removes some of them [3]. The clients Besu and Teku are written in Java.

What is missing is the same work for the other 11 clients: finding what makes their releases differ and getting the fixes accepted. Some client teams have started on their own, such as Reth and Lighthouse [9][10], but none has yet reached an official release that anyone outside the team can rebuild and check.

**References:**

[1] Report of the xz-utils backdoor. https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2024/03/29/4

[2] Geth Rebuild: Verifiable Builds for Go Ethereum. https://www.diva-portal.org/smash/record.jsf?pid=diva2%3A1908608

[3] Causes and Canonicalization of Unreproducible Builds in Java. https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21679

[4] Proving and Rewarding Client Diversity to Strengthen Resilience of Blockchain Networks. https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.18401

[5] Ethereum Foundation 2024 Academic Grants. https://blog.ethereum.org/2025/01/17/academic-grants-recipients

[6] Geth issue on reproducible builds. https://github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/issues/28987

[7] Geth fix for reproducible builds. https://github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/pull/30321

[8] Trusting-Trust Attack against an Entire Linux Distribution through Binary Manipulation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24888

[9] Reth: reproducible build profile. https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/10459

[10] Lighthouse: reproducible builds. https://github.com/sigp/lighthouse/pull/6799
sections.commitments:
- MIT license for the webpage, the how-to guides and any scripts. Fixes use each client's own license.
- The fixes live in the client repositories, where the client teams maintain them.
- MAB maintains the webpage and the how-to guides for 12 months after the last milestone.

milestones.name: Execution clients reproducible
criteria: At least 5 execution client teams publish official Linux releases that rebuild from source to exactly the same file, for 2 releases in a row. The technical reviewer repeats the rebuild.
Each of those teams has accepted our fixes into its repository or, where none were needed, links to our how-to guide from its documentation or release notes.

milestones.name: Consensus clients reproducible
criteria: At least 5 consensus client teams publish official Linux releases that rebuild from source to exactly the same file, for 2 releases in a row. The technical reviewer repeats the rebuild.
Each of those teams has accepted our fixes into its repository or, where none were needed, links to our how-to guide from its documentation or release notes.

milestones.name: Public webpage and how-to guides
criteria: A public webpage explains the work in plain language and shows, for each of the 12 clients, the result of our rebuild and the release it was done on.
A how-to guide for each reproducible client is published on the page, so anyone can verify a release themselves.

sections.in_scope:
- Fixes to each client's build process, so its official Linux release can be rebuilt exactly from source. We contribute them to the client's own repository.
- A public webpage that explains the work and, for each client, how anyone can verify a release themselves.
- Working with each client team until the fixes are accepted. This is where most of the effort goes.

By official release we mean the file operators download from the client's release page.

sections.out_scope:

- Operating systems other than Linux.

- L2 clients and validator tooling.

sections.why_grant:
Our team has already done this for Geth, the most used execution client, and has studied the problem at scale:

revisions.title: Reusable Security Workflows for Triage of Vulnerability Reports
revisions.summary: This initiative will research, develop and validate reusable workflows for Ethereum vulnerability triage and patch validation. Rather than building another standalone AI security agent, we will investigate how existing tools, agent skills, automated checks and human review can support trustworthy decisions. Audit firms, bounty platforms and protocol teams will be able to adapt the open workflows to their own tools and infrastructure. Independent teams will test them on real security work.

sections.why:
- **Who is safer:** Ethereum and L2 protocol users whose security teams must investigate reported vulnerabilities and assess proposed fixes.
- **From what:** False or inconclusive vulnerability reports, ineffective fixes, regressions that disrupt legitimate transactions, and new vulnerabilities introduced during repair.
- **What anyone can point to afterwards:** Openly documented workflows, reproducible evaluations on Ethereum incidents, and evidence that independent auditing teams used the workflows on real findings.
sections.in_scope:
- Workflow specifications for three decisions: whether a vulnerability is reproducible, whether a patch stops the exploit while preserving expected behavior, and whether a patch introduces security regressions.
- Explicit inputs, outputs, verification steps, uncertainty states, escalation criteria and evidence formats for each workflow.
- Portable agent skills and reference examples that can be adapted to different models, agent frameworks, and existing auditor toolchains.
- Reproducible empirical evaluation on public Ethereum cases, including failure analysis and comparisons with existing individual-tool approaches.
- Hands-on integration and feedback with independent audit firms and security teams using real Ethereum or L2 findings.
sections.out_scope:
- Building a hosted service or requiring teams to adopt one agent framework or vendor.
- Guaranteeing that all workflows outperform existing practice; negative and inconclusive findings will be documented.
sections.team:
- **Sofia Bobadilla, lead:** PhD student at KTH, member of CHAINS and mab.xyz, with expertise on smart contract security, particularly on exploit validation, automated vulnerability repair and transaction replay. Homepage: https://sofiabobadilla.github.io/
- **Martin Monperrus, advisor:** Professor of Software Technology at KTH and co-founder of mab.xyz. Homepage: https://www.monperrus.net/martin/

Other funding: WASP (Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation) and the Swedish Foundation for Strategic Research support Sofia's PhD research. This grant supports applied workflow research, portable implementation examples, reproducible evaluation and external adoption, distinct from the existing research funding.
sections.why_grant:
Our team has already published research and developed open tools addressing three stages of smart contract vulnerability response:

- **Behavior preservation:** PonDeReplay, our open-source replay framework, compares patched contract behavior with historical Ethereum transactions [1]. This mechanism is key for revealing unintended effects; for example, a tested guard that stops an attack on Yearn yDAI also blocks 88 legitimate keeper calls [2].
- **Exploit validation:** PoCo studies how AI agents turn vulnerability reports into runnable Foundry proofs of concept and how to verify that those tests actually demonstrate the reported issue [3].
- **Patch effectiveness:** Our study of automated smart contract fixes evaluated whether patches stopped real exploits, showing why passing conventional checks is not sufficient evidence of security [4].

These results are publicly available, and our work on exploit validation and automated repair has been peer-reviewed. Our findings have also informed AI-related guidance for Ethereum Foundation grants [5].

The missing piece is not another standalone agent or replay tool, but independently evaluated guidance for combining these checks in real audits. We will study which workflows improve decisions across different setups, where they fail, and when human review is necessary. We will publish reusable specifications, integration examples, and evidence of adoption by independent auditing teams.

**References:**

[1] PonDeReplay (open-source replay framework).
https://github.com/ASSERT-KTH/PonDeReplay

[2] Smart Contract Invariants Protect Against Cybercriminals.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13191

[3] PoCo: Agentic Proof-of-Concept Exploit Generation for Smart Contracts.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.02780

[4] Do Automated Fixes Truly Mitigate Smart Contract Exploits?
https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.04600

[5] Ethereum PhD Fellowship on AI-Powered Protocol Security: Research, Auditing, and Vulnerability Detection.
https://web.archive.org/web/20260211213355/https://esp.ethereum.foundation/rounds/phdfp26/phdfp-rfpd1
sections.commitments:
- MIT for code and agent skills; CC BY 4.0 for workflow specifications, public benchmarks and published evaluation results.
- Sofia Bobadilla will maintain the published reference materials and fix reproducibility-breaking issues for 18 months after the final milestone.
- Public benchmarks will use public incidents. Confidential adopter cases can be validated using redacted evidence supplied to the independent technical reviewer.

milestones.name: Research and release reusable security workflows
criteria: Publish at least 3 reusable workflows covering vulnerability validation, patch assessment, and regression checks. Each includes decision criteria, an integration example or agent skill, and clear guidance for human review. The technical reviewer checks the public release.
Evaluate the workflows on at least 15 public Ethereum or L2 cases, publishing reproducible tests, results, and failures. The technical reviewer checks the evidence and reruns the evaluation.

milestones.name: Independent adoption and improvement
criteria: At least 3 independent security teams outside KTH, CHAINS and mab.xyz use a workflow in their own setup on a real Ethereum or L2 finding. A technical reviewer verifies public or confidential redacted evidence of use.
Publish at least 1 updated workflow release incorporating external feedback, with integration guidance and a public change log. The technical reviewer checks the release.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.02780

https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.04600

revisions.title: Formally Verified EVM for Ethereum
revisions.summary: Nethermind will formally verify the complete Amsterdam EVM used in its zkVM guest, from Ethereum semantics through compiled .NET CIL to optimised RISC-V code. The proof will be reproducible and tied to the guest's exact build. Nethermind's regular Ethereum client shares EVM code with the guest; a published overlap manifest will identify which proved methods also appear unchanged in production builds. Adoption targets at least 20% of independently observed Ethereum execution-layer nodes running a release containing that shared implementation.

sections.why:
A zkVM proves that a guest program executed, but cannot establish that the guest implements Ethereum's rules correctly. An incorrect opcode, gas charge or state transition can produce a valid cryptographic proof of an invalid Ethereum result. The same implementation errors can affect ordinary execution clients.

This project will establish machine-checked correctness of Nethermind's Amsterdam zk-EVM, including its native RISC-V implementation, against an independent Lean specification. Nethermind's production EVM shares code with the guest. Publishing the exact verified overlap and measuring deployment of a release containing that code will show wider use, including validator infrastructure, RPC providers and personal nodes. Production-only branches and the regular client's native JIT code remain outside the proof.
sections.in_scope:
- Extend EVMYulLean to the complete Amsterdam EVM: opcodes, gas, nested calls, creation, memory, transient storage, state changes, reversions and exceptional outcomes.
- Extend LeanCIL to cover the zkVM interpreter's reachable CIL instructions and runtime operations, then prove the complete Amsterdam EVM-owned CIL implementation against that specification.
- Prove optimised RISC-V refinement for the zkVM EVM code using `il2rv64`, and compose the specification-to-CIL-to-RISC-V theorem.
- Verify precompile invocation, charging, inputs, outputs and failure behaviour against explicit external contracts.
- Publish reproducible proofs, build identities, coverage manifests and an independently checkable comparison of EVM methods in zkVM and regular Nethermind builds.
- Support public measurement of independent Ethereum execution nodes running a production release containing the documented shared EVM implementation.
sections.out_scope:
- Formal verification of the entire regular Nethermind EVM build or its .NET JIT-generated native code. Differing production CIL is not covered by the zkVM proof.
- Proofs of precompile internal algorithms, witness and SSZ processing, tries, complete block orchestration, zkVM provers or the full guest.
- Wider execution-client, consensus-client, L2-plugin and non-Ethereum verification.

LeanCIL verifies a supported subset of compiled CIL, not the full EVM, and its model targets .NET 10 while the guest builds with .NET 11. - Cover the complete Amsterdam zkVM EVM interpreter, including precompile invocation; publish all runtime and external-host assumptions.

criteria: Publish complete Amsterdam EVM semantics in Lean, including every opcode family, gas and precompile-call boundary; the independent reviewer checks the public coverage manifest.

revisions.summary: Nethermind will extend LeanCIL to verify the Amsterdam EVM in its zkVM guest. The proof will link Ethereum's rules in Lean to compiled .NET CIL and optimised RISC-V. Nethermind will check EthLib definitions before reuse and publish proofs tied to the guest's exact build, identifying methods shared with the regular client. Adoption requires two independent operators publishing mainnet block proofs for 30 consecutive days and 20% of observed Ethereum execution nodes running a release with the shared methods.

sections.why:
A zkVM proves that a guest program ran. It cannot show whether the program implements Ethereum correctly. Wrong opcode results, gas charges or state updates can produce valid proofs of invalid Ethereum results. Bugs in EVM code shared with the regular client may also affect ordinary nodes.

Nethermind will prove its Amsterdam EVM against an independently reviewed Lean specification, through CIL and optimised RISC-V. The team will check EthLib definitions against Ethereum specifications and fixtures before reuse. A public manifest will identify proved methods that also appear unchanged in regular-client builds. The proof excludes production-only methods and JIT-generated code.

LeanCIL could also help verify C# components of other Ethereum projects. Nethereum provides .NET libraries for transaction signing, wallets and EVM interaction, alongside tooling for Solidity development in VS Code. Applying LeanCIL to Nethereum would require separate work beyond this grant.
sections.in_scope:
- Extend EVMYulLean to Amsterdam using reviewed EthLib definitions and lemmas. Check fork rules, gas charges and state changes against Ethereum specifications and fixtures.

- Extend `il2rv64` to prove that the optimised RISC-V code matches the compiled CIL, then compose the refinement proofs.
- Prove precompile dispatch, gas charges, return data and failures under explicit contracts, excluding their algorithms.

- Measure independent Ethereum nodes running a release containing those methods.

LeanCIL is being built to verify compiled .NET code, including Nethermind's EVM. It proves supported CIL methods and composes contracts. Its instruction model, runtime support and proof automation do not yet cover the full EVM. This grant funds the missing capabilities and the EVM proofs.

EVMYulLean and `il2rv64` provide starting points for the other proof stages. EthLib defines and proves EVM rules in Lean, with some Amsterdam gaps. Nethermind will review these components before reuse, reducing duplicate work.

- Nethermind will maintain LeanCIL and the EVM correctness proofs after the grant and update coverage for later Ethereum forks.
- Prove the complete Amsterdam zkVM EVM, including precompile invocation, and publish trusted assumptions and external contracts.

- Describe regular-client benefits only for identical, proof-covered methods. Exclude duplicate node observations and known Nethermind-operated nodes from adoption counts.

milestones.name: Verified zkVM EVM CIL
criteria: Publish LeanCIL conformance tests for all CIL instructions and modelled runtime operations used by the EVM, with documented external-contract exclusions. The reviewer checks coverage.
LeanCIL proves every EVM-owned method reachable from the interpreter against compiled bytes and metadata. The reviewer reproduces CI checks rejecting unproved paths and altered builds.

milestones.name: Verified zkVM RISC-V refinement
criteria: `il2rv64` proves that the RISC-V code for all EVM-owned methods matches their CIL. Public CI ties certificates to CIL and machine-code hashes.
The reviewer reproduces checks and audits runtime, ABI, linker and precompile assumptions.

milestones.name: Composed EVM theorem and shared-code evidence
criteria: Publish a Lean-checked theorem connecting Amsterdam semantics to CIL and RISC-V. The reviewer reproduces the proof.
Publish a CIL comparison of the guest and regular client. The reviewer checks identical proved methods, excluded differences and production release mapping.

milestones.name: Independent Ethereum zkVM and node adoption
criteria: At least 2 operators independent of Nethermind publish Ethereum mainnet block proofs with the proof-covered Nethermind guest for 30 days. The reviewer checks independence, proof records and build identities.

At least 20% of independently observed, synced Ethereum mainnet execution nodes advertise a Nethermind release containing documented shared EVM methods. The reviewer checks crawler records, distinct identities and exclusion of Nethermind-operated nodes.
The reviewer matches counted builds to the shared-method manifests and zkVM proofs, identifying production code outside the proof.

revisions.title: DPRK IT Worker Screening for the Ethereum Ecosystem
revisions.summary: NorthScan will provide approved Ethereum organizations with a controlled service for screening GitHub profiles for behavioral, identity and network signals associated with DPRK IT worker activity. The six-month pilot will combine automated assessments with selected human review, practical integration resources and measurable adoption across the ecosystem. The grant will also validate a sustainable freemium and paid-access model for trusted organizations.

sections.why:
Ethereum organizations often evaluate remote contributors through fragmented checks that miss coordinated GitHub activity, fabricated professional identities and network patterns associated with DPRK IT worker operations. General KYC and background-check services rarely provide this GitHub-specific threat context.

After this pilot, approved organizations will be able to submit a public GitHub profile before hiring, funding or granting technical access and receive a structured, evidence-based assessment with confidence levels and selected human review. This will support better-informed decisions while treating the results as risk signals rather than definitive attribution.
sections.in_scope:
* A secure, access-controlled screening API for approved organizations. It will accept a public GitHub username or profile URL and return a structured JSON assessment containing relevant behavioral, identity and network signals, supporting evidence and confidence levels.

* Production-ready pilot infrastructure, including API-key authentication, rate limiting, usage logging, credential revocation, persistent database hosting and a documented process for escalating selected assessments to human review.

* Public integration resources: API documentation, JSON schema, synthetic examples and a lightweight open-source SDK that participating organizations can use from their own environments.

* A controlled pilot with at least 10 independent Ethereum ecosystem organizations, at least 100 non-test profile assessments and at least 10 participant-submitted cases receiving human analyst review.

* Demonstrated technical adoption, with at least five participating organizations using the documented API or SDK from their own environments and at least three participants providing documented feedback.

* A whitelisted freemium model for trusted organizations, including a small allowance of free screenings, proposed paid tiers and access safeguards.

* Commercial validation of the service, including a concise sustainability plan and evidence of initial organizations paying for screening capacity.

* A concise public GitHub screening guide describing defensive indicators and appropriate interpretation of results without disclosing NorthScan’s private detection logic, database or sensitive intelligence.

The funding pays for engineering and security hardening, hosting and database infrastructure, API and SDK development, documentation, pilot onboarding and support, human analyst time, participant coordination, and validation of a sustainable operating model beyond the grant.
sections.out_scope:
* No public dashboard or unsupervised access to NorthScan’s internal intelligence platform.

* No public release of NorthScan’s private source code, intelligence database, detection rules, scoring methodology or sensitive investigative material.

* No ATS, HRIS, KYC provider, identity-verification or background-check integration during this grant.

* No access to private GitHub accounts or repositories, compromised credentials or non-public platform data. Assessments use publicly available information.

* No mass collection or enrichment of personal information, broad email discovery, wallet tracing or continuous monitoring of every assessed profile.

* No public bulk IOC feed or commitment to produce recurring threat-intelligence reports. Public reporting is limited to the concise screening guide and approved aggregate pilot findings.

* No unlimited human investigations. Human review is limited to the cases specified in the milestones.

* No automated hiring rejection, legal determination or definitive attribution of a person to the DPRK. NorthScan provides evidence-based risk signals to support decisions made by participating organizations.

* No 24/7 incident-response service, guaranteed detection of every DPRK IT worker or guaranteed prevention of infiltration.
sections.team:
NorthScan is led by Heiner García Pérez, an independent cyber threat intelligence researcher specializing in DPRK IT worker activity, OSINT, HUMINT, financial crime and GitHub-based investigations. Heiner will lead the research, product direction, screening methodology, pilot operations, human reviews and participant support. Limited specialist support may be contracted for discrete engineering or infrastructure tasks, but Heiner remains accountable for every milestone.

Relevant work and track record:

* NorthScan: https://northscan.co/
* About NorthScan: https://northscan.co/about
* The GitHub Diaries: https://northscan.co/articles/github-diaries
* ANY.RUN investigation, Part 1: https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/lazarus-group-it-workers-investigation/
* ANY.RUN investigation, Part 2: https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/lazarus-group-it-workers-investigation-part-two/
* Insomni’hack presentation: https://insomnihack.ch/talks/smile-youre-on-camera-livestreaming-from-north-koreas-it-workers-laptop-farm/
* Security Alliance contribution: https://radar.securityalliance.org/from-north-korean-it-workers-to-it-recruiters/

NorthScan previously received approximately $2,000 in community funding through Giveth and a prior TheDAO-supported initiative. The remaining development and research have primarily been self-funded, and there is no other committed funding for the work described in this proposal.

NorthScan owns and operates the private screening platform, intelligence registry and detection methodology used for this initiative. ANY.RUN and BCA LTD were research collaborators on the linked investigations but are not recipients of this grant. NorthScan does not own or maintain GitHub, Giveth, TheDAO, ANY.RUN or Security Alliance codebases, and no external organization named above controls the proposed service.
sections.why_grant:
NorthScan is not starting from a concept. A working private intelligence platform already stores and connects GitHub accounts, public commit-email observations, sources and provenance; performs GitHub profile lookups; preserves profile snapshots; maps follower and following networks; identifies network communities and evidence similarities; and supports analyst review and exportable assessments. The underlying database, investigative rules and detection logic are private, but designated TheDAO curators can receive a supervised live walkthrough without receiving access to the source code or intelligence database.

This foundation was developed from more than two years of direct research into DPRK IT worker operations. Public evidence of that work includes:

* NorthScan research: https://northscan.co/
* The GitHub Diaries: https://northscan.co/articles/github-diaries
* ANY.RUN investigation, Part 1: https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/lazarus-group-it-workers-investigation/
* ANY.RUN investigation, Part 2: https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/lazarus-group-it-workers-investigation-part-two/
* Security Alliance contribution: https://radar.securityalliance.org/from-north-korean-it-workers-to-it-recruiters/

The grant therefore pays to harden and adapt an existing research platform into a controlled screening service: secure API access, documentation, a lightweight SDK, pilot operations, selected human review and adoption validation. The $50,000 price is below a from-scratch build because the core platform, intelligence corpus, investigative methodology and working GitHub-analysis workflows already exist. Public release of the internal codebase, database or detection logic is not included because these are NorthScan’s core security and investigative assets.
sections.commitments:
Licensing

* The lightweight client SDK and synthetic integration examples will be published under the MIT License.
* The API documentation, JSON schema and public GitHub screening guide will be published under CC BY 4.0.
* Published materials will remain publicly accessible after the grant.

Maintenance

* NorthScan will maintain the published SDK, documentation and examples for at least 12 months after the final milestone, including critical security, compatibility and documentation fixes.
* The hosted screening service will remain available to approved organizations for at least six months after the final milestone while the validated freemium and paid-access model supports longer-term operation.
* This maintenance commitment does not include major new features, unlimited screenings, unlimited human investigations or 24/7 support.

Pinned targets

The milestone amounts and acceptance targets are fixed as submitted. In particular, the adoption payment remains conditional on evidence of at least 10 participating organizations, 100 non-test assessments, 10 human-reviewed cases, five organizations using the API or SDK from their own environments, and documented feedback from three participants. Targets will not be reduced or materially reinterpreted without prior written approval from TheDAO.

Requested exception

NorthScan’s internal platform source code, intelligence database, detection rules, scoring methodology and sensitive investigative material will remain private and proprietary. The hosted API will remain restricted to approved organizations rather than becoming permissionless or publicly accessible, because unrestricted access could expose investigative methods, enable evasion or create privacy and abuse risks.

milestones.name: Name: Secure Screening Service and Pilot Readiness
criteria: An authenticated screening endpoint accepts a public GitHub username or profile URL and returns a structured JSON assessment.
Each assessment includes relevant behavioral, identity and network signals, confidence levels and supporting public evidence.
API-key authentication, rate limiting, usage logging and credential revocation are implemented.
Persistent database infrastructure and reliable pilot hosting are configured.
A documented workflow exists for escalating selected assessments to human analyst review.

NorthScan provides designated TheDAO curators with a private live walkthrough of its existing internal platform and the new screening workflow, without disclosing its database, source code or detection logic.
The service is ready to issue credentials to approved pilot participants by the end of Month 2.

milestones.name: Pilot Launch and Public Integration Resources
criteria: The screening API is available for onboarding approved pilot participants.
A lightweight client SDK is published in a public GitHub repository under the MIT License.
API documentation, a JSON schema and synthetic integration examples are published.
Participant onboarding, authentication, usage and API-key revocation instructions are completed.
A concise GitHub screening guide is published under CC BY 4.0, describing defensive indicators, limitations and appropriate interpretation of results.
Published documentation explains that assessments provide risk signals rather than definitive attribution or automated hiring decisions.

milestones.name: Whitelisted Freemium and Sustainability Model
criteria: A documented eligibility and approval process is established for organizations requesting access.
A controlled freemium tier is implemented, providing each approved organization with three free screening requests.
Published pilot pricing is established for additional automated assessments and optional human review.
A basic paid-access and usage-tracking workflow is implemented and tested without exposing payment or customer information.
A sustainability plan documents expected hosting, maintenance and analyst costs and explains how paid usage can support the service after the grant.
Access, abuse prevention, data handling, retention and credential-revocation terms are documented.

milestones.name: Proven Adoption by Ethereum Ecosystem Organizations
criteria: At least 10 independent Ethereum ecosystem organizations use the NorthScan service for real contributor, contractor or technical-access screening, with each organization submitting at least five non-test requests.
Participating organizations request and receive at least 100 non-test GitHub profile assessments through the pilot.
At least 10 participant-submitted assessments receive human analyst review and are delivered back to the requesting organizations.
At least five participating organizations use the published SDK or documented API from their own environments to submit screening requests.
At least three participating organizations provide documented feedback describing their use of the service, its usefulness, limitations or desired improvements.
At least three participating organizations purchase additional screening capacity at the published pilot price.
TheDAO receives anonymized usage records or private participant confirmations sufficient to verify these adoption results without publicly identifying screened individuals.

sections.in_scope:
1. Publish the graph specification: node and relationship semantics, incident surface
   roles, confidence levels, and primary-cause assessment rules.
   Include JSON schemas, TypeScript interfaces, migration guidance, and examples.

   hypotheses.

   assertions. Record reviewer identities, dates, disagreements, and corrections.

   counts and loss totals.

probabilities of future compromise.

revisions.title: Onay: Local signing companion
revisions.summary:
Ethereum is built to be verifiable, and verification is cheap. Yet most users still sign transactions without independently checking what they are approving. A second sanity check on the tx is a low-hanging fruit and Onay makes that second check seamless: it verifies the transaction locally, explains what it does, and lets the user compare against their wallet before signing.
Onay is a local desktop app with a thin browser extension that sits between the dapp and the wallet. It intercepts the signing request, verifies chain state through an embedded Helios light client, recompiles and verifies the source code locally, simulates the transaction, renders its intent in readable form with ERC-7730 clear signing, and finally displays the ERC8213 calldata digest for an equivalence check.

sections.why:
Ethereum is built around verification. In practice, transaction signing still depends heavily on blind trust.
Before approving a transaction, a user typically trusts an RPC for chain state, a verification service or explorer for the ABI, the dapp for what the action means, and often a remote tx simulator for what the transaction will do. The wallet eventually asks the user to approve bytes, but the context that makes those bytes understandable usually comes from external systems, if it comes at all.
Independent verification is already possible, easy, and cheap. So why not add a second or third factor check to what you are about to sign, and check if they agree on everything? We are used to have 2FA in every parts of our lives but not in the most sensitive step in crypto.
The problem is usability. Doing it properly today means stitching together several tools and manual checks, so almost nobody does it for ordinary transactions. 
Onay turns that into a second sanity check that can run on every signing request. It independently reconstructs the facts the user needs before approving: the chain state, the code actually deployed, the contracts reached during execution, and the human-readable intent of the transaction. 
The application does not hold any keys and is view only. So it can safely leverage a multitude of services and display any information that will enrich the signing process. It does this locally, without replacing the wallet or taking custody of keys. 
This gives hardware-wallet users, multisig signers, treasury operators, and ordinary Ethereum users a practical way to compare what a dapp is asking them to sign against an independently verified view.
Ethereum already makes verification possible. Onay makes it easy enough to actually use.
Onay puts every security-relevant fact through the user's own machine, or highlights what’s missing:

- Chain state is proof-verified by a local Helios client where the chain supports it (Ethereum, the OP Stack family, Linea), and read from an RPC the user chooses everywhere else, with a permanent notice about the trust that implies.
- Sourcify's verification claim is not trusted blindly. The app downloads the sources, recompiles them with the pinned solc binary, and compares the result byte for byte with the on-chain code.
- The transaction runs in a local EVM to reconstruct the call tree, so every contract it touches goes through the two checks above, and ERC-7730 descriptors turn the verified ABI into readable intent. It does full ABI decoding with NatSpec comments when clear-signing is not possible.
- After confirmation the app shows the ERC-8213 digest. A wallet that implements the standard shows the same hash, which proves the wallet received exactly the bytes the user reviewed, and that the dapp or the transport was not compromised in between.

Afterwards a multisig signer, a treasury operator or any hardware wallet user can check what they sign with no trusted intermediary and no hosted service.
sections.in_scope:
Release 1 is the transaction verifier. This grant pays for:

- **The extension.** A hand-written, zero-dependency script that wraps the page's EIP-1193 provider, catches eth_sendTransaction and signing requests, and forwards them to the app over native messaging. The host manifest allows only this extension, the channel is sealed with X25519 keys exchanged on first approval, and the app verifies the browser binary before accepting.
- **The app.** Helios light-client state for supported chains and user-chosen RPC state for every other EVM chain, the local EVM call-tree reconstruction, the local verification gate over every contract in the tree, ERC-7730 rendering, the confirm-or-reject review, and the ERC-8213 digest display after confirmation.

revisions.title: Ostros: an open-source hardware wallet on Crossbar's security chip, against screen implants and blind signing
revisions.summary: Ostros is Crossbar's hardware wallet, open from the chip to the apps. It runs on Daric, Crossbar's open-core RISC-V security chip, and the Rust-based Xous operating system. This grant adds chip attestation, clear signing, a recovery phrase a screen implant cannot read, an owner check that firmware and chip are genuine, an independent security review, and an app loader for outside security apps. The grant is paid out as wallets add Ostros support, owners verify their own devices, and outside teams build security apps on it.

sections.why:
- **Screen implants.** In October 2026, Ledger confirmed a hidden implant in at least one device sold through a reseller. It read the recovery phrase off the screen during setup and sent it out over a mobile network. Reported losses exceed $86 million (BleepingComputer, Ledger).
- **Blind signing.** In February 2025, Bybit lost about $1.5 billion after its Safe signers approved a malicious upgrade they could not read on their devices (BlockSec).

- **Attestation:** each Ostros can prove it carries a genuine Daric chip, set up in a new factory personalization flow. The split recovery phrase and the app loader both build on it.

- **Web companion:** connects Ostros to any Ethereum app through WalletConnect.
  - Technical: USB or Bluetooth. The device decodes and displays each request itself, so the companion never decides what the owner sees.
- **Owner verification:** a public guide and tool to rebuild the firmware, match its hash and check the attestation.

sections.why_grant:
