revisions.title: An Open Bug Bounty Program for All of Ethereum: White Hat Rescued Funds Distribution Service
revisions.summary: Our industry's security holes fund North Korea's weapons programs, scam compounds full of trafficked people, and countless cybercriminals. Black hats find exposed money and take it, while white hats who find the same holes warn the team and hope the money stays there long enough to be rescued; with AI speeding up attacks, that is a losing strategy. This RFP funds a legal entity that takes what white hats rescue, gives them legal cover, pays them without KYC, and earns its fee only when owners get their money back. Our goal is an army of white hats rescuing money everywhere they can, in effect an open bug bounty on all of Ethereum.

sections.why:
This protects people whose funds sit in exploitable contracts or on leaked keys: a white hat who finds them can take them first and send them somewhere lawful. Today we leave that money on the table for the worst people in the world. White hats hold back because they want legal cover first, someone else to do the work of returning the money second, and pay third. Give them a destination they trust and they will rescue funds like mad, many just for the lulz.

- North Korea takes billions from our industry ([FBI](https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA250226)). UN monitors found crypto theft brings in as much as half of its foreign income and helps bankroll its nuclear program ([NK News](https://www.nknews.org/2024/03/north-korea-relies-on-crypto-theft-for-up-to-half-of-foreign-income-un-report)).
- At least 220,000 people may be held in scam compounds in Myanmar and Cambodia alone, forced to run scams that include crypto fraud ([UN News](https://news.un.org/en/story/2023/08/1140187)).
- Anthropic measured the value AI agents could exploit from real, previously hacked contracts doubling roughly every 1.3 months ([Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/research/smart-contracts)). You fight AI with AI, once white hats have somewhere safe to send what they find.
sections.in_scope:
Legal setup (a new entity or an existing one), custody, an owner portal and a public case page, plus case work through month 12: outreach that brings rescuers' cases in, the operator's own rescues, intake, owner searches, ownership checks and returns. That covers known owners (a protocol, company or token holders), paid back within weeks, and unknown owners (weak or leaked keys), paid as they prove their claims.

The ideal service gives white hats legal cover when they hand funds over and pays their bounties without KYC. Where the law stops short of that, propose the design that gets closest and say where it falls short; once this RFP is funded, we pick the proposal that works and comes closest. The fee design here is a starting idea too: the team picks the legal structure, custody setup and tools, and may propose any design that solves the same problem, as long as owners pay for their rescue, the rescuer's bounty and operator's fee come only from returns, and unclaimed funds stay open to claims.
sections.out_scope:
- Rescues that need red-teaming or breaking into someone's computer or systems, this is not accecptable: rescues must start from public information, such as open-source code, onchain data or keys already published
- Tracing and freezing stolen funds
- Assets on chains other than Ethereum and its L2s
sections.existing:
- [SEAL Whitehat Safe Harbor](https://frameworks.securityalliance.org/safe-harbor/whitehat/) lets a white hat step in only during an exploit under way or imminent, on a protocol that adopted it, for a bounty usually 10% capped at $1 million ([SEAL](https://securityalliance.org/safe-harbor)). A good start with a narrow use: a white hat may not act on a known hole before an attacker does.
- [DART](https://assetrecovery.io/) (Digital Asset Recovery Technologies) and the independent Crypto Recovery Trust it works with are the closest model: a Wyoming statutory trust with an independent trustee takes crypto from white hats, gives them legal cover and returns it to verified original owners where the law allows.
- About 70,500 ETH from TheDAO's 2016 refund contracts is still unclaimed a decade later ([thedao.fund](https://thedao.fund)): even a famous refund never reaches every owner.
- [Kleros](https://kleros.io/) arbitration, for disputed claims.

This RFP aims to go further than Safe Harbor: if a white hat can take exposed money, they should.
sections.who:
Nobody is pre-selected. A winning team pairs legal operations with BD and outreach people that white hats and incident-response groups already trust, since adoption pays only when rescuers hand funds over and owners are found. It needs no onchain engineering expertise.

Drafted with TheDAO Security Fund; the idea was built by Griff Green from conversations with SEAL 911, DART, TheDAO's lawyers and other teams. DART has a clear head start and may bid, as may TheDAO's lawyers.
sections.hard_req:
1. Victims pay for their rescue with a haircut on the return or a fee to collect it. That funds an equal rescuer bounty and operator fee, paid only on returns to verified owners: An example payout scheme could be: 2% each of the first $10 million, 0.25% to $100 million, 0.06% to $1 billion and 0.01% above (about $200,000 each at $10 million, $425,000 at $100 million and $1 million at $1 billion). Tiers apply per case, and a case is one incident with all its related addresses, chains and staged returns. Rates may rise case by case, within a published ceiling and set before the case is accepted, when few owners are likely to come forward. The proposal shows how the fee sustains the service after the grant, even with few claims and zero yield.
2. Published rules for proving ownership, including for leaked or weak keys (a signature from the exposed key proves nothing on its own), and a dispute path to a neutral arbiter.
3. A licensed firm's legal opinion covers custody, money transmission, sanctions, unclaimed property, how far rescuers can be paid without KYC, and what protection rescuers get when they hand funds over. Every return and bounty is sanctions-screened.
4. Funds nobody claims become an endowment: once they count as lost or abandoned under applicable law or a rule the operator publishes before the rescue, the operator may stake them or earn other low-risk yield and keep that yield, but every claim stays open and the principal stays available to pay it for at least 7 years from the rescue.
5. Rescued funds, including any staked under Hard requirement 4, sit only in audited code, such as an unmodified Safe, or with an independent trustee or regulated custodian, kept apart per case and from the operator's own funds, and the operator can't move them alone.
6. A public case page lists every deposit, return and endowment balance, each valued in USD at its block by a published onchain query: Chainlink feed, else relevant DEX TWAP (e.g. Uniswap v3 TWAP); anything else counts as $0.
7. Rescuers may stay unnamed in public. Where the law requires identity checks for bounties, the proposal says which checks and why, and the legal opinion in Hard requirement 3 confirms them. Owners' identities and evidence stay with the operator; the technical reviewer inspects counted case files and keeps no copies.
8. Code is open source, under a license the bidder states.
9. A case counts only if the funds were rescued after the award starts and its case page links the onchain trail from exploited contract or leaked address to owner. The technical reviewer also confirms the owner had the funds before the incident, no protocol could have recovered the funds itself, the owner is not the operator, its staff or an affiliate, the exposed contract or key was not deployed or funded by the rescuer, the operator or their affiliates, counted rescuers are not each other's staff or affiliates, and in each adoption milestone at most one counted rescuer is the operator or tied to it. Milestones count what owners receive, after bounty, fee and gas.

milestones.name: Legal setup
criteria: Entity registered or an existing one in place, and Hard requirement 3's legal opinion issued, both confirmed by the technical reviewer.

milestones.name: Service live
criteria: Custody, owner portal and case page live on Ethereum mainnet and the L2s the proposal names, with Hard requirements 1, 2 and 4 published there and every custody address meeting Hard requirement 5 listed on the case page, confirmed by the technical reviewer

milestones.name: First returns
criteria: At least $1,000,000 returned to verified owners from at least 2 counted cases handed over by 2 different rescuers, each case returning at least $250,000, summed from the onchain returns on the case page and confirmed by the technical reviewer

milestones.name: Returns at scale
criteria: At least $10,000,000 returned to verified owners in total, from at least 5 counted cases handed over by at least 3 different rescuers, each rescuer's cases returning at least $500,000, summed from the onchain returns on the case page and confirmed by the technical reviewer
At least 1 counted case referred by an incident-response group that takes hack reports from the public and is not tied to the operator, confirmed by that group to the technical reviewer

revisions.title: An Open Bug Bounty Program for All of Ethereum: White Hat Rescued Funds Distribution Service
revisions.summary: Our industry's security holes fund North Korea's weapons programs, scam compounds full of trafficked people, and countless cybercriminals. Black hats find exposed money and take it, while white hats who find the same holes warn the team and hope the money stays there long enough to be rescued; with AI speeding up attacks, that is a losing strategy. This RFP funds a legal entity that takes what white hats rescue, gives them legal cover, pays them without KYC, and earns its fee only when owners get their money back. Our goal is an army of white hats rescuing money everywhere they can, in effect an open bug bounty on all of Ethereum.

sections.why:
This protects people whose funds sit in exploitable contracts or on leaked keys: a white hat who finds them can take them first and send them somewhere lawful. Today we leave that money on the table for the worst people in the world. White hats hold back because they want legal cover first, someone else to do the work of returning the money second, and pay third. Give them a destination they trust and they will rescue funds like mad, many just for the lulz.

- North Korea takes billions from our industry ([FBI](https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA250226)). UN monitors found crypto theft brings in as much as half of its foreign income and helps bankroll its nuclear program ([NK News](https://www.nknews.org/2024/03/north-korea-relies-on-crypto-theft-for-up-to-half-of-foreign-income-un-report)).
- At least 220,000 people may be held in scam compounds in Myanmar and Cambodia alone, forced to run scams that include crypto fraud ([UN News](https://news.un.org/en/story/2023/08/1140187)).
- Anthropic measured the value AI agents could exploit from real, previously hacked contracts doubling roughly every 1.3 months ([Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/research/smart-contracts)). You fight AI with AI, once white hats have somewhere safe to send what they find.
sections.in_scope:
Legal setup (a new entity or an existing one), custody, an owner portal and a public case page, plus case work through month 12: outreach that brings rescuers' cases in, the operator's own rescues, intake, owner searches, ownership checks and returns. That covers known owners (a protocol, company or token holders), paid back within weeks, and unknown owners (weak or leaked keys), paid as they prove their claims.

The ideal service gives white hats legal cover when they hand funds over and pays their bounties without KYC. Where the law stops short of that, propose the design that gets closest and say where it falls short; once this RFP is funded, we pick the proposal that works and comes closest. The fee design here is a starting idea too: the team picks the legal structure, custody setup and tools, and may propose any design that solves the same problem, as long as owners pay for their rescue, the rescuer's bounty and operator's fee come only from returns, and unclaimed funds stay open to claims.
sections.out_scope:
- Rescues that need red-teaming or breaking into someone's computer or systems, this is not accecptable: rescues must start from public information, such as open-source code, onchain data or keys already published
- Tracing and freezing stolen funds
- Assets on chains other than Ethereum and its L2s
sections.existing:
- [SEAL Whitehat Safe Harbor](https://frameworks.securityalliance.org/safe-harbor/whitehat/) lets a white hat step in only during an exploit under way or imminent, on a protocol that adopted it, for a bounty usually 10% capped at $1 million ([SEAL](https://securityalliance.org/safe-harbor)). A good start with a narrow use: a white hat may not act on a known hole before an attacker does.
- [DART](https://assetrecovery.io/) (Digital Asset Recovery Technologies) and the independent Crypto Recovery Trust it works with are the closest model: a Wyoming statutory trust with an independent trustee takes crypto from white hats, gives them legal cover and returns it to verified original owners where the law allows.
- About 70,500 ETH from TheDAO's 2016 refund contracts is still unclaimed a decade later ([thedao.fund](https://thedao.fund)): even a famous refund never reaches every owner.
- [Kleros](https://kleros.io/) arbitration, for disputed claims.

This RFP aims to go further than Safe Harbor: if a white hat can take exposed money, they should.

revisions.title: Independent Attestations for the ERC-7730 Descriptors of Ethereum's 100 Most-Used Contracts
revisions.summary: Pay one established security firm to review, under its own name, the ERC-7730 clear signing descriptors for the 100 most-used verified Ethereum contracts and publish a signed attestation for each one, so wallets can trust what they render. The registry holds 739 descriptors, 166 carry an attestation, every one of those is signed by a single firm, and none of the top 100 contracts has an attested descriptor. Payment lands on published attestations and on a wallet that acts on them.

sections.why:
Clear Signing (ERC-7730) is the Ethereum standard for showing users a human-readable summary of what they are about to sign, instead of raw calldata. Descriptors for each contract live in the open registry at github.com/ethereum/clear-signing-erc7730-registry, and wallets read them. A wrong descriptor is worse than none: the user sees a confident summary that does not match what the contract does. The registry's own reviewing guide says its pull request review is a plausibility check, and that the trust layer is the signed attestation an auditor publishes after verifying the descriptor against the contract's source. Wallets choose which attesters to trust and can refuse to render a descriptor nobody has attested. Bybit lost about $1.5 billion in February 2025 after its signers approved a Safe transaction whose displayed contents differed from what they signed ([Bybit incident timeline](https://www.bybit.com/en/learn/this-week-in-bybit/bybit-security-incident-timeline), [NCC Group analysis](https://www.nccgroup.com/research/in-depth-technical-analysis-of-the-bybit-hack/)).

Attestation lags far behind authoring. On 2026-10-31 the registry had 739 descriptors and 166 attestations, all signed by one firm under Ethereum Foundation funding. Sourcify's live dashboard at erc7730.sourcify.dev ranks verified mainnet contracts by calls that are not plain ETH or standard token transfers: the top 100 carry 75% of those calls, 20 of them have a descriptor, and 0 of those descriptors are attested. Descriptor authoring for the rest is under way through the clear signing working group. Nobody is funded to verify and sign the result, and no second firm has put its name behind any descriptor.
sections.in_scope:
This RFP pays one security firm for verification and signature. The firm's reputation is the deliverable: every attestation is published under the firm's own key and name.

- Review each descriptor for a target contract against the registry's auditor guide
- Publish an EAS offchain attestation (ERC-8176 schema) for each descriptor that passes, as a PR to the registry's sigs folder
- For each descriptor that fails, post the defects on the registry PR or as an issue, and attest the corrected version once it is merged
- Re-attest within 30 days when an attested descriptor changes, so the registry's dropped-attestations list stays empty for this batch
- Publish a batch page: each target contract, its descriptor, review status, defects found, attestation UID and date

The target set is the top 100 verified contracts on erc7730.sourcify.dev by calls that are not filtered out (ETH, standard token transfers, closed source, bots etc) 7-day window, archived on the day the firm starts (based on final agreement with argot to allow for small manual fixes to the list). Descriptors for those contracts are written by others; the firm attests what exists and what lands during the engagement.

The submitter is allowed to update the list (with consent from TheDAO at milestones after 30 contracts attested and 80 contracts attested).
sections.out_scope:
- Writing descriptors. The firm does not attest a descriptor it authored.
- Contracts without verified source, and contracts outside the agreed list
- Wallet-side code, schema changes, registry tooling
sections.existing:
- The registry's auditor guide (auditors/README.md): the 5-step review, the ERC-8176 hash, the EAS schema, and the sigs folder format, built on the clearsig CLI (github.com/Cyfrin/clearsig)
- The 166 attestations already in the registry, as the format and bar to match
- Sourcify's clear-signing library, which lets a wallet name trusted attesters and fall back to raw calldata when no trusted attestation exists
sections.who:
Nobody is pre-selected. We want one firm whose whole business is security and whose name a wallet would accept as a trusted attester: a smart contract audit firm, or a firm in monitoring or incident response with published Ethereum work. Today one firm signs every attestation in the registry; this RFP adds a second, independent name. A strong bid shows at least 3 years of published Ethereum security work, names the reviewers who will sign, and names a wallet it will work with on the adoption milestone.

Co-drafted by the submitter with TheDAO Security Fund. The submitter is a listed co-author of ERC-7730, convened the clear signing working group meetings until the Ethereum Foundation took over that role. The submitter and his employer will not bid on this initiative.
sections.hard_req:
1. **Security firm, in public.** The bidder is a company whose primary business is security, with at least 3 years of published Ethereum security work and at least 20 public audit or incident reports, linked in the bid.
2. **By the book.** Every review follows the registry's auditor guide in full, and no attestation is issued for a descriptor that formats a function whose displayed intent the guide says v2 cannot express.
3. **Under its own name.** Attestations are signed with a key the firm publicly declares as its own, in ERC-8176 format, merged into the registry's sigs folder.
4. **Independent.** The firm attests no descriptor it wrote, and discloses any commercial relationship with a protocol whose descriptor it reviews.
5. **Defects in public.** Every failed review is posted on the registry PR or as a registry issue before any attestation of the corrected version.
6. **Maintenance.** For 12 months after the last milestone, the firm re-attests within 30 days any descriptor in the batch that changes.

milestones.name: First 30 attested
criteria: The archived top-100 list and the batch page published, with review status per contract
At least 30 contracts from the list carry an attestation by the firm merged into the registry's sigs folder, linked by PR

milestones.name: Batch attested
criteria: At least 80 contracts from the list carry an attestation by the firm merged into the registry's sigs folder, linked by PR
Every defect the firm found is posted on the registry PR or as a registry issue, linked from the batch page

milestones.name: Wallets act on the attestations
criteria: At least 1 wallet from this list names the firm as a trusted attester in a production release, shown in the wallet's public release notes or documentation: MetaMask, Rabby, Trust Wallet, Ledger, Trezor, Ambire etc.

revisions.title: Community Fuzzing Tooling for Ethereum Ecosystem Projects
revisions.summary: The Ethereum ecosystem is lacking a solution for scalable, continuous, and compute-intensive fuzzing campaigns for projects. For each project to subscribe to their own solution would be costly and could have diminishing returns over time to make it a worthwhile investment of time, money, and human capital. We are requesting proposals from applicants who have developed or can develop tools to orchestrate fuzzing at scale, assign compute resources efficiently, and flex these resources up and down in an agile manner so that any team can orchestrate their own fuzzing campaign for themselves. A self-serve model. This RFP would fund the construction and maintenance of such a tool.

sections.why:
Security review has shifted a great deal of effort onto LLM-assisted tooling over the last eighteen months. That shift has been productive and remains accessible to teams through frontier models and private tools, but it is also incomplete. They are weakest precisely where fuzzing is strongest, particularly on regression detection and avoidance as developers ship new or harden existing code.

**Current state:**

Many teams know the above, but very few run fuzzing continuously. The reasons are mostly operational:

- Compute: Meaningful fuzzing is measured in sustained core hours. Most teams cannot justify that as a standing line item for a single codebase, so it never gets budgeted.
- Time: Someone has to write harnesses that generate inputs structured enough to reach deep code rather than bouncing off input validation.
- Software: Teams that do try usually run a fuzzer in GitHub Actions or a similarly time-boxed CI runner, yielding a few minutes of fuzzing per commit. That is only enough to replay an existing corpus and generate suitable code coverage.
sections.in_scope:
- A documented CLI or front-end UI
- Running continuous fuzzing campaigns across multiple tenants in a secure manner
- Ability to allocate compute across multiple projects and scale it up and down efficiently and on demand
- Capability to hand off harnesses, corpora, and knowledge to users
- Documentation so teams can maximally self-serve

**On the milestone plan:**

Amounts below are shown as a share of the awarded budget, with an indicative figure at a $150,000 award.
sections.out_scope:
- Manual audits and code review. This program funds fuzzing infrastructure.
- Authorship of harnesses and tests
- Publishing exploit detail or proof-of-concept code for anything still unpatched
- A guaranteed bug count. Fuzzing finds what it finds; the commitment is to compute and process.
- Triage of findings
- Incident response
- Any other professional services
sections.existing: None named.
sections.who:
The strongest bidder is a team that has run continuous fuzzing at scale before, over months rather than for the duration of an audit, and can show the following evidence: campaigns sustained, coverage figures, bugs found and disclosed. Proposals should be explicit about:

- Coverage of languages and frameworks
- Compute: State the sustained core hours you can field and where they come from
- User Experience: How does the user access the tool? Is it via service request only? A CLI? A dedicated User Interface? Briefly describe the user flow as it will exist should the grant be awarded.

The proposal will likely be best served by a single grant recipient, but the RFP can certainly be considered for multiple participants if that best serves the needs of the ecosystem.
sections.hard_req:
1. Aggregated results measured and published: Aggregate and abstracted statistics for coverage, findings, etc., updated at least quarterly on a public page. Bug counts alone are not an acceptable measure of a fuzzing program.
2. Siloed User Experience: Users may only see their own findings for security purposes. This must be available to be considered for the grant.
3. No user lock-in: Harnesses must build and run on standard open source fuzzing tooling. Every project keeps its harnesses, corpus, and documentation under an open license at no further cost, and must be able to keep running them without paying the grantee anything.

criteria: Specs and timeline provided for tool to go live
Intake form for grantor and grantee to gauge interest and sequencing is live
Ability for first project/users to potentially onboard

criteria: Onboarding flows are available and open
7+ projects have self-onboarded and begun a campaign

revisions.title: RFP: No More Lost Bug Reports, a Verified Security Contact for Every Ethereum Project Worth Attacking
revisions.summary: A valid bug report that cannot find its owner waits for an attacker to find the same bug. Of the 50 largest DeFi entries on Ethereum by DeFiLlama, 37 serve no security.txt on the website DeFiLlama lists for them, and only 2 publish an encryption key. This RFP funds the outreach to get every project with real value at stake to publish a verified contact, plus one open lookup for researchers and their bug-hunting agents.

sections.why:
Users are safer when valid reports reach a team that can fix them.

- Our count, November 23, 2026, checks the website DeFiLlama lists for each entry. Many of these teams run bug bounties; what is missing is a contact researchers can find, with a key to encrypt to.

Afterwards anyone can count the contacts projects published themselves, and the technical reviewer confirms how many valid reports reached them.
sections.in_scope:
We pay for the outcome: every Ethereum and L2 project with real value at stake publishes an encrypted contact it controls, findable in one query. The real work is outreach. The design is the bidder's.

- Getting projects to publish: security.txt, SECURITY.md with GitHub private vulnerability reporting, an onchain record such as ERC-5437, or another route.
- One open directory of those records that people and agents can query.
- Bidders may add a way for projects to recognize known researchers.
- Coverage of protocols, L2s, client teams and widely used libraries, where shared bugs land.
sections.out_scope:
- Running bug bounties.
- Validating or handling reports (the companion bug broker RFP).
- Emergency response to live hacks ([SEAL 911](https://securityalliance.org/seal-911) does that).
- Publishing anything about a project's vulnerabilities.
sections.existing:
- [RFC 9116](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116): security.txt, with a field for an encryption key.
- Hand-kept lists go stale. [Trail of Bits' list](https://github.com/trailofbits/blockchain-security-contacts) of about 250 entries across all chains and categories was last updated in February 2025, and OpenZeppelin's [Security Registry](https://github.com/ethereum-lists/contracts) took its last entry in February 2022.
- [ERC-5437](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-5437): an onchain security contact with an encryption key, status Stagnant. OpenZeppelin recommends a `@custom:security-contact` tag in contract source ([SECURITY.md](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/SECURITY.md)).
- [SEAL Safe Harbor](https://github.com/security-alliance/safe-harbor): adopters register agreements onchain, and each agreement carries contact details.
- [RFP: Directory of Value](https://initiatives.thedao.fund/initiative/directory-of-value) on this board maps what holds value. Bidders may attach contacts to it but must not depend on it.
sections.who:
A team good at relentless, polite outreach that researchers already trust: a security collective, block explorer, bug bounty platform or audit firm. Nobody is pre-selected.

Drafted by TheDAO Security Fund from a conversation with EthSec (ethsecurity.org) and Consensys. EthSec may bid. TheDAO Security Fund and Giveth will not bid.
sections.hard_req:
1. **Verified means project-controlled.** An entry shows as verified only when it matches a record the project publishes itself: security.txt on its domain, SECURITY.md in its repository, an onchain record from its admin or governance address, or another record only the project can publish. Anything else shows as unverified.
2. **Walk-away test.** Entries re-verify automatically from those records, the data is open, and anyone can run the indexer.
3. **Encrypted to count.** Only verified entries with a private channel count toward milestones: a published encryption key, or a private reporting form the project controls, such as [GitHub private vulnerability reporting](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/security-advisories/working-with-repository-security-advisories/configuring-private-vulnerability-reporting-for-a-repository).
4. **A maintained home.** A named organization commits to run it after the grant. Queries stay free, since charging would block the outcome.
5. **Outside means unaffiliated.** An outside team shares no owner, staff or funding relationship with the selected team. Affiliates count toward no criterion.
6. Ethereum and L2 projects only.

revisions.title: RFP: Hunt Down Every Ethereum Team Until It Publishes a security.txt and Joins a Web of Trust
revisions.summary: Ethereum is permissionless, so teams publish security contacts many ways or not at all, and researchers and their AI agents cannot reliably find where a bug goes or how to encrypt it. Of the 50 largest DeFi entries on Ethereum, 37 serve no security.txt, and only 2 publish one with an encryption key. AI is finding bugs fast, so this needs solving now. This RFP pays one person or a small team to get every team to publish one standard and to build, on what SEAL and other groups already have, a private web of trust that reaches each team's security lead fast.

sections.why:
Researchers need one clear pathway to every team. A report that never reaches the team leaves users exposed until an attacker finds the same bug.

- Researchers now hunt with AI agents. An agent can route and encrypt a report automatically only when every team publishes the same machine-readable record in the same place. AI can also chain low-severity bugs into critical ones, so every finding needs a route.
- The worst bugs need more than a public address: every extra hop is a chance to leak. In a web of trust a finding goes straight to a verified security lead, who knows the sender is real amid AI-generated junk reports.
- Our count (November 23, 2026) checked the website DeFiLlama lists for each entry.
sections.in_scope:
Bidders have complete freedom in how they get there, including their own milestones, within the hard requirements below. What matters is three outcomes: one agreed standard for what teams publish and where; every Ethereum and L2 team with real value at stake publishing it; and a private web of trust that reaches those teams' security leads fast. - Build the web of trust with SEAL: start from the contacts SEAL and other groups already have, verify each team's security lead and a backup on a video call, connect them over encrypted channels, let members vouch for researchers so teams know a report is real, and keep it current with call-tree drills.

revisions.title: OPSEC Ratings Coalition to Build & Maintain an "L2Beat for OPSEC"
revisions.summary: Fund a coordinator to bring at least six OPSEC auditing firms together around a single, industry-agreed rating standard: an A / AA / AAA tier a team earns, displays, and renews every six months to a year, the way the community demands a smart contract audit; we hope this encourages OPSEC audits. Firms already running OPSEC audits become the accredited raters, applying one shared scoring template inside their existing flow and publishing tiers only, never a team's detailed report or score. A simple public board shows who is rated; teams with unacceptable OPSEC simply don't appear. The real work is social: getting the audit community to co-own one standard and stand up a lightweight, self-sustaining membership body that keeps it credible and pays to keep it going.

revisions.title: OPSEC Ratings Coalition to Build & Maintain an "L2Beat for OPSEC"
revisions.summary: Fund a single coordinator to bring at least six OPSEC auditing firms together around one industry-agreed rating standard: an A / AA / AAA tier a team earns and renews yearly, with a six-month check-in and automatic suspension when its security posture changes. The firms already running OPSEC audits become the accredited raters, apply one shared scoring template inside their existing flow and publish tiers only, never a team's report or score. Rated teams pay a fixed fee into a membership body that owns the standard and the board once the coordinator hands off. A simple public board shows who is rated; teams with unacceptable OPSEC simply don't appear.

sections.why:
Your keys, your devices, your multisig process, your access controls... these are just as important as your smart contracts. Every serious team already invests in OPSEC, and OPSEC audits happen all the time. But all of that work is invisible. There is no public signal that tells users, investors or partners who is actually running a tight ship.

We want to change that with a single OPSEC rating the whole industry agrees on. Think of a Moody's rating: people want one because everyone recognizes what it means. Teams that earn an A, AA or AAA get their tier on a public board. That's it, just the tier. We will never publish what a team is missing (a public list of weaknesses is a gift to attackers), and teams with unacceptable OPSEC simply don't make the board... which says something all by itself.
sections.in_scope:
Let's be clear about what this RFP is: **a coordination effort.** The money here pays for a social exercise, getting the community of OPSEC auditing firms around one table to agree on one standard. The website is the easy part.

Three roles, and only one of them gets this money:

| Role | Who | Funded by this RFP? |
|---|---|---|
| Rated teams | Protocol, L2 and infra teams whose OPSEC gets scored and who appear on the board with their tier | No, they pay a fixed fee for their own assessment |
| Accredited raters | The 6+ existing OPSEC auditing firms that agree the scoring template and issue tiers inside their existing audit flow | No, the membership body pays them per rating from the fee pool |
| Coordinator | The single party that convenes the firms, gets them to sign one standard, builds the board and stands up the membership body | Yes, this is the recipient |

What we expect to come out of it:

- One scoring template and tier definitions (A / AA / AAA), agreed on by **at least 6 OPSEC auditing companies**. Roughly speaking, an A team follows best practices and we don't expect them to have incidents. AAA is wild: secure beyond what's reasonable.
- The firms already doing OPSEC audits become the raters. They add exactly one step to the audits they already run: apply the scoring template, issue the tier. The first batch of accredited raters is the same group that built the standard, so they have skin in the game from day one.
- A simple public board of rated teams, their tiers, a valid-until date and a last check-in date. Honestly, this part could probably be vibe coded in a weekend. The value is the standard and the names on it.
- A membership body that ends up owning all of it. The accredited firms form a cooperative professional body, one firm, one vote. It maintains the standard, certifies new raters, runs a small verification committee (paid something modest like $2,000 per member per cycle) that spot-checks a share of ratings, and takes over the standard, the board and the name from the coordinator no later than six months after this grant ends.
- A funding model that outlives the grant: issuer-pays, the same model the Moody's analogy comes from. Rated teams pay a fixed fee for their assessment (think $2,000 to $5,000 on top of an audit they were buying anyway), and the fee is the same whether they get a AAA or nothing. Fees go to the membership body, not to the rater. The body pays raters from the pool and funds the verification committee from it. Rough math: 30 teams a year at $3,000 is $90,000 a year, enough for the committee and a lean secretariat. The budget is sized for 12 to 18 months of runway on purpose, because fee revenue is thin until enough teams are on the board that being absent is conspicuous.
- Ratings that go stale on events, not on a calendar. A rating is valid for 12 months. At the six-month mark the team files a short self-attestation and its rater does a check-in (not a full audit), or the rating lapses. A disclosed incident or a material change (signer set, leadership, treasury or infrastructure migration) suspends the rating automatically until the team is re-rated. The scoring template itself changes through a defined process no more than once a year, so nobody is chasing a moving target.

Bidders are welcome to propose a different path to get there. The goal is what's fixed: a decentralized rating system that many OPSEC auditing companies co-own, with a real shot at sustaining itself long after this money is spent.

**In scope**

- Coordinating at least 6 OPSEC auditing companies to agree on one scoring template and the A / AA / AAA tier definitions
- Onboarding those firms as the first accredited raters, with whatever materials they need to run the template inside their existing audit flow
- A simple public board of rated teams and their tiers, with valid-until and last check-in dates... tiers only, no details, no gaps
- Standing up the membership body: the charter (one firm, one vote), how raters get certified, the verification committee, the fixed fee schedule and the pooled funding model
- The 12-month rating cycle with the six-month check-in and the event-based suspension process
- The handoff: transferring the standard, the board and the name to the membership body

- Performing the underlying OPSEC audits (the accredited firms do that)
- Publishing any team's specific weaknesses, unmet controls, or the reasons behind a tier

sections.existing: - [Security Frameworks by SEAL](https://frameworks.securityalliance.org/): the Security Alliance's open framework covering operational security, infrastructure, DevOps, incident response and more. Bidders should read it before proposing a scoring template.
sections.who:
Nobody is pre-selected. Once the RFP is fully funded there will be an open bidding process, and the winner gets picked through the process below. The dream candidate is a credible coordinator in the security community: someone who can bring 6+ OPSEC auditing firms to the same table and get them all to sign the same document. (If you have ever tried to get six companies to agree on anything, you know that's the real work here.)

Ideally the coordinator is not an OPSEC auditing firm, because whoever holds the pen on the standard walks away with an edge over the firms they convened. That is a preference, not a requirement, and it will weigh in selection. An audit firm that coordinates takes no rater role during the grant and no ownership of the board. The best pitch a bidder can make is simple: here is why the other firms can trust me to run this.
sections.hard_req:
1. **Six firms minimum.** At least 6 OPSEC auditing companies formally agree to the scoring template and tier definitions, and commit to issuing ratings with it.
2. **Tiers only.** The public board shows a team's tier, its valid-until date and its last check-in, and nothing more. No gaps, no unmet controls, no explanations.
3. **Open and versioned.** The scoring template and tier definitions are public, open source and versioned, with changes dated and attributable, revised through a defined change process no more than once a year.
4. **Tool-agnostic.** Every tier is reachable no matter which tools or frameworks a team uses. No vendor's product is ever required.
5. **One firm, one vote.** Every founding firm gets equal governance rights in the membership body, regardless of who convened whom.
6. **Neutral name.** The standard and the board are not branded after the coordinator or any single firm.
7. **Mandatory handoff.** The standard, the board, the name and any secretariat function transfer to the membership body no later than six months after the final milestone. The coordinator keeps no veto and no unilateral control.
8. **Fixed fees, pooled.** Rated teams pay a fixed, outcome-independent fee. Fees flow to the membership body, which pays raters from the pool and funds the verification committee from it. No tier-contingent pricing, no "we'll get you to AA" upsell.

revisions.title: No Rating, No Listing: An L2BEAT for OpSec With Teeth
revisions.summary: Every team says it takes OpSec seriously, and nobody can check. This RFP funds a coordinator to get at least 6 OpSec audit firms onto one A / AA / AAA rating, show tiers on a public board (every gap stays private) and hand it to a body the firms own. Then the rating gets teeth: protocols, bridges, L2s, wallets and exchanges make a current tier a condition of doing business.

sections.why:
Your keys, your devices, your multisig process, your access controls... these matter as much as your smart contracts:

- Bybit lost nearly $1.5B in ETH in February 2025 after attackers took over one Safe developer's computer ([Chainalysis](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/bybit-exchange-hack-february-2025-crypto-security-dprk/)).
- KelpDAO lost about $292M in April 2026 through compromised RPC nodes, "not a smart contract hack" ([Chainalysis](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/kelpdao-bridge-exploit-april-2026/)).

Serious teams already buy OpSec audits, and all of that work is invisible. Think of a Moody's rating: people want one because everyone recognizes what it means. Teams that earn an A, AA or AAA get their tier on a public board. That's it, just the tier (a public list of weaknesses is a gift to attackers).

A rating only matters if missing it costs something, the way no bank works with a firm that fails compliance. Once the exchanges, protocols, bridges, L2s and wallets that move the money require a current tier, weak OpSec costs a team its listings and integrations, and users are safer from stolen keys, hijacked laptops, tricked signers and poisoned infrastructure.

Each policy applied at least once, confirmed privately by the organization to the technical reviewer

revisions.title: Production-Ready Local-First Safe UI
revisions.summary: This RFP funds a production-ready, local-first Safe multisig UI, deployed to IPFS with reproducible builds, that anyone can run with nothing but an RPC endpoint and a wallet. It is an independent way to execute transactions if Safe for any reason becomes unreachable, and a tool to cross-check every hash before signers approve.

sections.why:
A Safe is a contract on Ethereum. Its owners and threshold are on-chain, and anyone can execute a transaction once it carries enough owner signatures to meet the threshold. In the standard flow, everything before that step happens off-chain, through the hosted Safe{Wallet} frontend that Safe Labs operates and the Safe Transaction Service behind it. Self-hosting that stack means running the Client Gateway, the Transaction Service and a tracing archive node for internal-transaction indexing, so few teams do.

In July 2024, WazirX lost roughly $235M from a Safe multisig managed through Liminal Custody, whose interface showed a routine transfer while the signatures authorized a malicious contract upgrade. In October 2024, malware on the computers of Radiant Capital's signers showed a clean transaction while their hardware wallets received different calldata; the signers signed blind instead of checking the domain and message hash on the device, and lost roughly $50M. In February 2025, malicious JavaScript in the hosted Safe{Wallet} frontend showed Bybit's signers one transaction while their hardware wallets signed another, and roughly $1.5B left the Safe. These incidents are different manifestations of the same underlying problem: the software presenting a transaction to a signer cannot be treated as a trusted part of the signing boundary.

Assume Safe's hosted frontend and Transaction Service disappear tomorrow. A non-technical multisig signer should still be able to:

- open this UI from a local copy or the IPFS release
- connect a hardware wallet
- rebuild the transaction from the Safe's on-chain state (owners, threshold, nonce, contract version) and the parameters they were sent, then recompute its hashes locally
- verify exactly what they are signing
- exchange signatures with the other owners through ordinary files or links
- execute the transaction using only a JSON-RPC endpoint

No Safe account, Safe backend, project-operated server, indexer or technical help required. That is Vitalik's walkaway test.
sections.in_scope:
This RFP pays for finishing, hardening and maintaining a local-first Safe UI with minimal dependencies and trivial deployment. Optimise for the least technical signer rather than the developer running the UI. Deliverables:

- Ethereum Mainnet, Safe contract versions v1.3.0 and v1.4.1 at minimum
- Production hardening of an existing codebase, or a fresh build
- The full lifecycle against one standard JSON-RPC endpoint: load a Safe from chain state, propose, sign, exchange signatures, execute, manage owners and threshold, arbitrary contract calls
- Signature exchange without a server: signed transaction packages exported and imported through ordinary files or shareable links, with nested Safe (EIP-1271) support and approveHash as the on-chain alternative
- Verification: enter or import a transaction's full SafeTx parameters and recompute the EIP-712 domain hash, message hash and safeTxHash locally, with calldata decoded offline from a bundled selector database or a user-supplied ABI
- Hardware wallet signing on Ledger and Trezor at minimum, over WebUSB or WebHID or through a vendor library bundled with the app
- A command-line tool or local API that returns the hashes and decoded calldata for a given Safe address, chain ID and transaction parameters, for scripts and AI agents
- Reproducible IPFS builds with fixed import settings, an ENS name whose contenthash resolves to the current release, and docs for running locally and verifying a build
- 12 months of maintenance after the first tagged release (expected within 3 months of funding), and a business plan for the years after
sections.out_scope:
- Full Safe{Wallet} parity (Safe Apps, swaps, staking, onramps)
- Hosted backends or indexers, including a team-run web server for this UI (the IPFS and ENS release is in scope)
- Chains beyond Ethereum Mainnet
- Mobile apps
- New smart contracts
sections.existing:
- [localsafe.eth](https://github.com/Cyfrin/localsafe.eth) (Cyfrin, MIT), live at [localsafe.eth.limo](https://localsafe.eth.limo). Its README calls it "still a project in early development": Safe v1.4.1 only, no transaction history; last release v0.3.1, June 18, 2026.
- [Eternal Safe](https://github.com/eternalsafe/wallet) (GPL-3.0), a Safe{Wallet} fork (app v1.26.2) that needs only an RPC URL. Received a Safe Grants Program grant; maintained by Devan Non; signature "smart links" are encoded rather than encrypted; v1.4.1 by default.
- [Safe's own monorepo](https://github.com/safe-global/safe-wallet-monorepo) (GPL-3.0). Self-hosting it means the [Client Gateway](https://github.com/safe-global/safe-client-gateway), the [Transaction Service](https://github.com/safe-global/safe-transaction-service) and a tracing archive node ([Safe docs](https://docs.safe.global/core-api/api-overview)).
- Hash-verification tools: [safe-tx-hashes-util](https://github.com/pcaversaccio/safe-tx-hashes-util), [OpenZeppelin Safe Utils](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/safe-utils), [Cyfrin safe-hash](https://tools.cyfrin.io/safe-hash). They verify hashes only.

A bid built on another codebase should show it meets these hard requirements with fewer runtime dependencies.
sections.who:
Nobody is pre-selected. Teams that have already shipped Safe frontends or signing tools, including the people behind localsafe.eth and Eternal Safe, will be judged on that record, and the budget is $120,000 either way. Safe contributors are welcome to bid or to co-fund.

Co-drafted by Griff Green and pcaversaccio, both Curators of TheDAO Security Fund. pcaversaccio maintains [safe-tx-hashes-util](https://github.com/pcaversaccio/safe-tx-hashes-util), listed above.
sections.hard_req:
1. **Open source.** An OSI-approved license, MIT or GPL-3.0 expected, and a public repository from the first commit of funded work.
2. **RPC only, nothing project-operated.** Every flow works against a standard JSON-RPC endpoint. Runtime dependencies are minimised, with no dependency on a hosted SaaS, proprietary API, mandatory backend, indexer, telemetry service, analytics provider or project-operated infrastructure, and no analytics or telemetry in the UI.
3. **Signature exchange without a server.** Signed transaction packages export and import through ordinary files or shareable links. Imported signatures are checked against the transaction's safeTxHash and the Safe's current owner set before they are accepted: signature recovery for EOA owners, an isValidSignature call for contract owners. Off-chain signatures work for nested Safes through EIP-1271, and on-chain approval through approveHash is supported as an alternative.
4. **Hardware wallets.** Ledger and Trezor at minimum, over WebUSB or WebHID or through a bundled vendor library. Before signing, the UI shows the EIP-712 domain hash, message hash and safeTxHash. The device shows the domain hash and the message hash, and the signer matches those against the UI and an independent hash tool. Vendor libraries are bundled and served with the app, with no popup, iframe or metadata fetched from a vendor's servers and no separate bridge daemon to install.
5. **Undecodable calldata stays unverified.** Calldata the UI cannot decode is shown as raw bytes with an unverified label, never as safe to sign.
6. **Verifiable builds.** Reproducible from a tagged commit to the published IPFS CID with fixed import settings, by an unaffiliated user without the team's infrastructure; the ENS contenthash resolves to the current release.
7. **Trivial deployment.** Open a local copy or the IPFS release, connect a hardware wallet, and work. Nothing to install beyond that.

revisions.title: Production-Ready Local-First Safe UI
revisions.summary: This RFP funds a production-ready, local-first Safe multisig UI, deployed to IPFS with reproducible builds, that anyone can run with nothing but an RPC endpoint and a wallet. It is an independent way to execute transactions if Safe for any reason becomes unreachable, and a tool to cross-check every hash before signers approve.

sections.why:
A Safe is a contract on Ethereum. Its owners and threshold are on-chain, and anyone can execute a transaction once it carries enough owner signatures to meet the threshold. In the standard flow, everything before that step happens off-chain, through the hosted Safe{Wallet} frontend that Safe Labs operates and the Safe Transaction Service behind it. Self-hosting that stack means running the Client Gateway, the Transaction Service and a tracing archive node for internal-transaction indexing, so few teams do.

In July 2024, WazirX lost roughly $235M from a Safe multisig managed through Liminal Custody, whose interface showed a routine transfer while the signatures authorized a malicious contract upgrade. In October 2024, malware on the computers of Radiant Capital's signers showed a clean transaction while their hardware wallets received different calldata; the signers signed blind instead of checking the domain and message hash on the device, and lost roughly $50M. In February 2025, malicious JavaScript in the hosted Safe{Wallet} frontend showed Bybit's signers one transaction while their hardware wallets signed another, and roughly $1.5B left the Safe. These incidents are different manifestations of the same underlying problem: the software presenting a transaction to a signer cannot be treated as a trusted part of the signing boundary.

Assume Safe's hosted frontend and Transaction Service disappear tomorrow. A non-technical multisig signer should still be able to:

- open this UI from a local copy or the IPFS release
- connect a hardware wallet
- rebuild the transaction from the Safe's on-chain state (owners, threshold, nonce, contract version) and the parameters they were sent, then recompute its hashes locally
- verify exactly what they are signing
- exchange signatures with the other owners through ordinary files or links
- execute the transaction using only a JSON-RPC endpoint

No Safe account, Safe backend, project-operated server, indexer or technical help required. That is Vitalik's walkaway test.
sections.in_scope:
This RFP pays for finishing, hardening and maintaining a local-first Safe UI with minimal dependencies and trivial deployment. Optimise for the least technical signer rather than the developer running the UI. Deliverables:

- Ethereum Mainnet, Safe contract versions v1.3.0 and v1.4.1 at minimum
- Production hardening of an existing codebase, or a fresh build
- The full lifecycle against one standard JSON-RPC endpoint: load a Safe from chain state, propose, sign, exchange signatures, execute, manage owners and threshold, arbitrary contract calls
- Signature exchange without a server: signed transaction packages exported and imported through ordinary files or shareable links, with nested Safe (EIP-1271) support and approveHash as the on-chain alternative
- Verification: enter or import a transaction's full SafeTx parameters and recompute the EIP-712 domain hash, message hash and safeTxHash locally, with calldata decoded offline from a bundled selector database or a user-supplied ABI
- Hardware wallet signing on Ledger and Trezor at minimum, over WebUSB or WebHID or through a vendor library bundled with the app
- A command-line tool or local API that returns the hashes and decoded calldata for a given Safe address, chain ID and transaction parameters, for scripts and AI agents
- Reproducible IPFS builds with fixed import settings, an ENS name whose contenthash resolves to the current release, and docs for running locally and verifying a build
- 12 months of maintenance after the first tagged release (expected within 3 months of funding), and a business plan for the years after
sections.out_scope:
- Full Safe{Wallet} parity (Safe Apps, swaps, staking, onramps)
- Hosted backends or indexers, including a team-run web server for this UI (the IPFS and ENS release is in scope)
- Chains beyond Ethereum Mainnet
- Mobile apps
- New smart contracts
sections.existing:
- [localsafe.eth](https://github.com/Cyfrin/localsafe.eth) (Cyfrin, MIT), live at [localsafe.eth.limo](https://localsafe.eth.limo). Its README calls it "still a project in early development": Safe v1.4.1 only, no transaction history; last release v0.3.1, June 18, 2026.
- [Eternal Safe](https://github.com/eternalsafe/wallet) (GPL-3.0), a Safe{Wallet} fork (app v1.26.2) that needs only an RPC URL. Received a Safe Grants Program grant; maintained by Devan Non; signature "smart links" are encoded rather than encrypted; v1.4.1 by default.
- [Safe's own monorepo](https://github.com/safe-global/safe-wallet-monorepo) (GPL-3.0). Self-hosting it means the [Client Gateway](https://github.com/safe-global/safe-client-gateway), the [Transaction Service](https://github.com/safe-global/safe-transaction-service) and a tracing archive node ([Safe docs](https://docs.safe.global/core-api/api-overview)).

A bid built on another codebase should show it meets these hard requirements with fewer runtime dependencies.
sections.who:
Nobody is pre-selected. Teams that have already shipped Safe frontends or signing tools, including the people behind localsafe.eth and Eternal Safe, will be judged on that record, and the budget is $120,000 either way. Safe contributors are welcome to bid or to co-fund.

Co-drafted by Griff Green and pcaversaccio, both Curators of TheDAO Security Fund. pcaversaccio maintains [safe-tx-hashes-util](https://github.com/pcaversaccio/safe-tx-hashes-util), listed above.
sections.hard_req:
1. **Open source.** An OSI-approved license, MIT or GPL-3.0 expected, and a public repository from the first commit of funded work.
2. **RPC only, nothing project-operated.** Every flow works against a standard JSON-RPC endpoint. Runtime dependencies are minimised, with no dependency on a hosted SaaS, proprietary API, mandatory backend, indexer, telemetry service, analytics provider or project-operated infrastructure, and no analytics or telemetry in the UI.
3. **Signature exchange without a server.** Signed transaction packages export and import through ordinary files or shareable links. Imported signatures are checked against the transaction's safeTxHash and the Safe's current owner set before they are accepted: signature recovery for EOA owners, an isValidSignature call for contract owners. 8. **A maintenance and business plan in the proposal.** Who maintains the UI for the 12 months after the first tagged release, and how it is paid for after that.
9. **Public evidence for every milestone.** Recordings, transaction hashes, CIDs, test runs and named parties confirming, all published.

Vendor libraries are bundled and served with the app, with no popup, iframe or metadata fetched from a vendor's servers and no separate bridge daemon to install.

6. **Verifiable builds.** Reproducible from a tagged commit to the published IPFS CID with fixed import settings, by an unaffiliated user without the team's infrastructure; the ENS contenthash resolves to the current release.
7. **Trivial deployment.** Open a local copy or the IPFS release, connect a hardware wallet, and work. Nothing to install beyond that.
8. **A maintenance and business plan in the proposal.** Who maintains the UI for the 12 months after the first tagged release, and how it is paid for after that.
9. **Public evidence for every milestone.** Recordings, transaction hashes, CIDs, test runs and named parties confirming, all published.

criteria: A public repository under an OSI-approved license with a tagged release, and a published recording of the complete lifecycle on a v1.3.0 Safe and on a v1.4.1 Safe on Mainnet, using only the local or IPFS UI, one named public JSON-RPC endpoint and hardware wallets, with the browser's network panel showing no other network requests and a Mainnet transaction hash for each

A published recording on a 2-of-3 Mainnet Safe: signer 1 constructs and exports the transaction; signer 2 imports it from a file or link, verifies the hashes on a Ledger, signs and exports the package again; signer 3 imports that package, verifies on a Trezor and signs; an independent machine imports the final package and executes; transaction hash published; no machine contacts the Safe Transaction Service
A published recording of off-chain Safe signatures created, exported, imported, validated and used without the Transaction Service, including a nested Safe signing through EIP-1271

A recorded recovery test: an operator unaffiliated with the team, starting from only the Safe address, a JSON-RPC endpoint and the exported artifacts, obtains the UI from the tagged source or the IPFS release and executes a previously signed transaction; transaction hash published

Published automated tests, passing in public CI, for a stale nonce, two transactions competing for one nonce, an already-executed transaction, a cancelled or replaced transaction, and an imported signature that belongs to a different transaction

revisions.title: RFP: Stop Patches From Becoming Exploits, Coordinated Fixes for Shared Ethereum Code
revisions.summary: Every public fix is also a public description of the bug. Ethereum's clients, rollup stacks and most-forked contracts share code across many teams, and the first team to push a fix tells attackers where to look in all the others. This RFP funds a coordinator that finds everyone running the vulnerable code, warns them privately and gets them patched before the fix goes public.

sections.why:
Users of every chain and protocol running shared code are safer when all its operators patch before attackers can read the fix.

- Geth shipped a pre-announced fix for CVE-2021-39137 on August 24, 2021. Three days later it was exploited on mainnet, splitting off nodes that had not upgraded. Geth's [postmortem](https://github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/blob/master/docs/postmortems/2021-08-22-split-postmortem.md) calls that disclosure decision "dangerous" in hindsight, and its [disclosure policy](https://geth.ethereum.org/docs/developers/geth-developer/disclosures) keeps the option to patch silently.
- Vyper fixed a broken reentrancy lock in v0.3.1 (December 2021) without realizing its impact, and protocols on the old versions were not explicitly notified ([Vyper](https://hackmd.io/@vyperlang/HJUgNMhs2)). In July 2023 attackers took $69.3M from Curve pools compiled with them ([CertiK](https://www.certik.com/resources/blog/2qbPMcyJpR5UfoKrcjWxlQ-vyper-incident-anaylsis)).
- In December 2023 a flaw in how ERC-2771 and Multicall combine affected thousands of contracts. thirdweb and OpenZeppelin warned teams privately, and several pools holding almost 90 ETH were hacked before OpenZeppelin's full public disclosure ([OpenZeppelin](https://www.openzeppelin.com/news/secure-implementations-vulnerable-integrations)).
- In a 2024 study, a GPT-4 agent exploited 87% of 15 disclosed vulnerabilities when handed the public advisory, and 7% without it ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.08144)). Rollup stacks are the next case: L2BEAT lists 38 Ethereum L2s built on the OP Stack alone ([L2BEAT](https://l2beat.com/scaling/summary)).
sections.out_scope:
- Finding bugs.
- Whitehat rescues.
- Protocol upgrades decided through Ethereum's governance process.
- Findings only one team must fix (the companion bug broker RFP).
sections.existing:
- [linux-distros](https://oss-security.openwall.org/wiki/mailing-lists/distros): Linux distributions' private embargo list (14 days at most), with public release on [oss-security](https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/).
- [CERT/CC VINCE](https://sei.cmu.edu/news/certcc-releases-vince-software-vulnerability-collaboration-platform): one shared case space for many vendors.
- [Project Zero's Reporting Transparency trial](https://projectzero.google/2025/07/reporting-transparency.html) (2025) targets the "upstream patch gap" between an upstream fix and its arrival downstream.
- [Ethereum Foundation public disclosures](https://github.com/ethereum/public-disclosures): the EF cross-checks client bug bounty reports, shares them with affected client teams, and aims to publish them in 90 days. Bids say how they extend or work beside it.
- The ERC-2771 response above, as a worked case.
- [SEAL 911](https://securityalliance.org/seal-911), for attacks under way.
sections.who:
A team that client, rollup and protocol security leads already trust with embargoed information: a security alliance, an incident-response firm or a consortium of those leads. Nobody is pre-selected.

Drafted by TheDAO Security Fund from a conversation with EthSec (ethsecurity.org) and Consensys. TheDAO Security Fund and Giveth will not bid.
sections.hard_req:
1. Embargo terms are published and signed by every enrolled team.
2. Notices go only to teams running the affected code.
3. A public log records each coordinated fix after release (what, when, share patched), never before.
4. Bids name the shared code they cover first (clients, rollup stacks, widely forked contracts or libraries) and why.
5. Running costs come from enrolled L2s and protocols, or from a named home that funds it. Client teams are not expected to pay.
6. **Outside means unaffiliated.** An outside team shares no owner, staff or funding relationship with the selected team. Affiliates count toward no criterion.
7. Ethereum and L2s only.

milestones.name: Network and drill
criteria: At least 10 outside teams sign the embargo terms, at least 4 of them Ethereum client teams, L2s over $200M on L2BEAT, or protocols holding over $100M onchain (value query linked), signed terms shown to the technical reviewer
One past public incident replayed, with the list of affected deployments checked by the technical reviewer

milestones.name: First coordinated fixes
criteria: At least 3 high or critical bugs in shared code fixed under embargo, each affecting at least 3 outside teams, confirmed by those teams to the technical reviewer

At least 90% of the affected teams, on a list hash-committed before the first notice and checked by the technical reviewer after release, had the fix deployed or a mitigation in place by the time the fix or its details went public

milestones.name: At scale
criteria: At least 10 coordinated fixes in total, each high or critical on the coordinator's published rubric and affecting at least 3 outside teams, on the public log and checked by the technical reviewer
At least 25 enrolled teams, at least 10 of them Ethereum client teams, L2s over $200M on L2BEAT, or protocols holding over $100M onchain (value query linked), checked by the technical reviewer
Across all 10, at least 90% of listed affected teams had the fix deployed or a mitigation in place by the time the fix or its details went public, checked by the technical reviewer

milestones.name: Sustainability
criteria: At least $15,000 in fees or contributions from at least 3 enrolled L2s or protocols, confirmed by the technical reviewer, plus a plan to run 12 months past the grant

revisions.summary: Ethereum is permissionless, so when a bug turns up in shared code nobody knows who else runs it or where. sections.in_scope:
The answer is the bidder's. Each bid states a hypothesis and a plan of attack for three problems:

1. Who else has it: find who runs the vulnerable code (forks, deployments, chains, node operators) on Ethereum and its L2s.
2. A warning they trust: warn them privately, through a channel where each side can verify the other, so they act.
3. Going public in the age of AI: stage fixes so they land in public repositories without exposing the bug early, release them together, then push operators to update.

The work starts by hand. The selected team runs real disclosures alongside the teams fixing each bug, races to reach every other affected team before the fix is public, then systematizes what worked. The target clock is 24 hours from bug confirmed to every affected team notified. Example hypothesis: a dependency map built before any bug lets one person list every affected team inside that clock.

The lasting output is an open, broad disclosure standard (process, comms templates, when and how to go public), informed by SEAL 911 and the cases run. Bugs can come from any source; bids say where. The selected team may use the companion security-contact directory and may pass researcher payment to the companion bug broker.

revisions.title: Safe Lockdown Guard: An Emergency Freeze for Kidnapping and Coercion
revisions.summary: Kidnapping and physical coercion can force Safe owners to authorize transfers with perfectly valid signatures. Safe Lockdown Guard gives them a separate emergency action: freeze guarded transfers with a credential that cannot spend funds. Runtime Capital has built and published the open-source audit candidate; this $14,000 request funds the remaining independent audit cost, with a final milestone tied to verified use on Ethereum mainnet. The audit, fixes and installation documentation will be public for every compatible Safe operator.

sections.why:
A Safe verifies signatures, not whether its owners signed freely. Physical coercion can turn a valid signing quorum into an attack path. Treasury operators need a separate emergency action that can interrupt transfers without giving another party custody or spending authority.

The guard lets a registered emergency credential start an on-chain freeze. With the required configuration, it blocks owner and module transfers and new ERC-1271 signature validation during the incident. A restricted recovery path lets owners replace a compromised signer with a pre-approved recovery owner. Normal operation resumes after the configured lockdown and recovery periods. An optional transaction delay provides time to activate the freeze before a coerced transaction executes. The contracts have no team administrator or privileged unlock key. The protection has documented boundaries, including existing token allowances and previously valid signatures; it does not guarantee an attacker's behaviour or a person's physical safety.

- Deployment of the audited contracts on Ethereum mainnet and verification of a working installation used for real treasury custody. Runtime Capital supplies coordination, documentation and onboarding effort without a separate development or marketing fee.

revisions.title: Saviour: Who can act through a Safe at one pinned block
revisions.summary: Saviour reads an Ethereum mainnet Safe at one block and reports who can act through it beyond the owners. The report covers the Safe, its Delay module, and Roles v2.1.1 members, targets, and selectors taken from chain logs. A second person opens the same link and checks that the digest matches. Condition amounts stay unknown, and the report never says the Safe is safe.

sections.why:
On 16 Nov 2026 a Safe lost about $6.45 million. [Cointelegraph](https://cointelegraph.com/news/safe-wallet-reportedly-loses-millions-after-key-compromise) put the transfer at about 4.39 million USDC and 1.72 million syrupUSDC, through a Zodiac Roles modifier, and quoted Zodiac's co-founder: the policy allowed the call, and the role member's key was most likely compromised. [Safe said no owner signed](https://coinmarketcap.com/academy/article/safe-multisig-zodiac-roles-key-compromise).

Zodiac App is where a team edits that policy. A co-signer still cannot hand someone a block-pinned link that a second person re-runs and matches.

Co-signers of mainnet Safes that use Delay or Roles v2.1.1 get that link. The page shows who can already act, and it leaves unread authority as unknown. The 16 Nov module is a Roles version this reader identifies and does not interpret. The loss shows the class of incident. This grant does not claim that loss would have been stopped.
sections.in_scope:
- Bringing outside treasury teams onto the existing reader
- A public pilots page with the team or Safe, the block, the digest, the witness result, and the balance query
- Keeping www.saviours.xyz/audit answering on Ethereum mainnet through the grant
- Charging those teams for a witnessed audit, and publishing a one-page plan of the hosted reader's monthly cost
sections.out_scope:
- Interpreting Roles v1, including the module in the 16 Nov 2026 incident
- Computing token amounts from Roles conditions or allowances
- A Safe App, or an import from the Safe Transaction Service
- Any chain other than Ethereum mainnet
- Detecting a compromised key, holding keys, or blocking a signature inside Safe
- The archived ENS naming product
sections.team:
**Harshit Bainsla** builds and maintains Saviour. The work is solo.

Track record: [github.com/devhb1/Saviour](https://github.com/devhb1/Saviour) and [www.saviours.xyz](https://www.saviours.xyz). The repo is MIT, copyright 2026 Harshit Bainsla.

Ai Green Bubble has committed $3,000, which is 25% of this goal. No other funder pays for this scope.
sections.why_grant:
The reader is already on mainnet. Commit `f896213` on `main` has the Safe and Delay reads, Roles v2.1.1 selectors from chain logs, a pin link whose digest ignores the RPC host, and a plain-language box that is dropped if it stamps the Safe as safe, invents a token amount, or claims a loss would have been prevented.

A stranger can open [www.saviours.xyz/audit](https://www.saviours.xyz/audit) and the repo. One team proof, the Term Safe at block 26435999, is there so the read can be repeated. It does not count as an outside user.

The reader is built. This $12,000 pays for outside teams to use it, and for the hosted page to stay up.

- Condition amounts stay unknown, Roles v1 is named and not interpreted, and the report never says the Safe is safe.

revisions.title: SCAR: Test security fixes against the real exploit before they ship
revisions.summary: A security fix can stop the published attack and still leave money exposed, or close the hole and break normal use. SCAR checks a fix the way an attacker would: it forks Ethereum at the block before a real exploit, runs that exploit against the patched contract, and confirms normal use still works. This grant pays for 24 reviewed Ethereum incident cases, a public scoreboard for AI-written fixes, and getting audit firms, bounty platforms and protocols to use the check.

sections.why:
Protocol users are safer from the second drain: the same exploit working again after the team says it is fixed.

- The Verus bridge on Ethereum lost about $11.5 million on 18 May 2026. Most of it was returned for a bounty and put back into the same bridge on 8 July. On 23 July it lost $7.54 million through the same contract path and bug class ([CoinDesk](https://www.coindesk.com/tech/2026/07/23/bitcoin-ethereum-linked-protocols-lose-usd35-million-in-multiple-attacks-hours-apart)).
- TRM Labs counted a record 207 hacks in the first half of 2026, 125 of them exploiting smart-contract code ([TRM Labs](https://www.trmlabs.com/resources/blog/h1-2026-crypto-hacks-reach-record-high-as-losses-fall-below-usd-1-billion)).

Verus is why a fix gets re-tested before the money goes back in. After this grant, any team can run the exploit and the variants a reviewer would write against its own fix, and get a verdict anyone can re-run: solved, not solved or inconclusive.
sections.in_scope:
- **24 incident cases** on Ethereum mainnet or L2s with over $200 million secured on L2BEAT, 16 public and 8 private until the scoreboard freezes. Each has the real exploit on frozen chain state, a working reference fix, and two near-miss fixes (one incomplete, one that breaks normal use).
- **A workflow teams run themselves**: Foundry import, command line, CI job and coding-agent adapter.
- **A public scoreboard** grading AI agents' fixes on the private cases, with appeals.
