revisions.title: Audit Transparency for Ethereum: every DeFi protocol's audits, mapped to the code running onchain today
revisions.summary: An open, sourced record of every Ethereum DeFi protocol over $1 million in TVL, about 400 today: what each one had audited, what was in scope, what is running onchain now, and what changed through upgrades since. Each live contract is rebuilt from its audited commit and compared to the deployed bytecode, so anyone can see which live code no public audit covers. It needs no cooperation from protocols or audit firms, so it can cover the whole ecosystem.

sections.why:
Users should know what they're trusting before they deposit. Today a protocol shows "audited by X", and that's where the information stops. It doesn't say how much of the live code the audit covered, whether the audit was three years ago and the code has been rewritten since, or whether the only change was one line. A determined user can piece this together for one protocol, but there's no public database that has it for every protocol in one place.

Ackee Blockchain found that 92 of 157 protocols on the Rekt list were hacked through unaudited or out-of-scope code, often while showing "audited by" logos ([Ackee, 2023](https://ackee.xyz/blog/why-we-need-to-start-using-erc-7512-onchain-audit-representation-right-now/)).

Afterwards:
- **Users and risk teams** can see, for any Ethereum DeFi protocol, which fund-holding contracts run code that no public audit covers, with every claim linked to its source.
- **Security researchers** get a list of post-audit changes no audit covers, ranked by TVL, as a place to start looking.
- **Protocols and audit firms** are accountable in public for what was actually reviewed and what shipped.
sections.in_scope:
Every Ethereum DeFi protocol over $1 million in TVL on DeFiLlama: DEXs, lending, liquid staking, restaking, stablecoins, bridges and the rest. Together they hold 99.9% of Ethereum DeFi TVL, and new protocols are added as they cross $1 million. For each one:
- Map the core contracts, resolve proxies to their current implementations, and record who can upgrade them.
- Collect the public audits and record the commit and scope each report states.
- Rebuild the audited commit with the deployed compiler settings and compare it to the live bytecode, accounting for metadata, immutables and linked libraries. Each difference is classed as cosmetic, covered by a later audit, or not covered by any public audit.
- Publish audit statistics: share of core contracts covered by an audit, number of audits, time since the last one, and auditor working days where reports state them.
- Roll contract results up into one protocol verdict, so an uncovered fund-holding contract can't hide behind the rest.
- A public site with every protocol page and its sources, plus the full dataset, free to query.
- A monthly refresh of every protocol that picks up new audits and upgrades, with a last-checked date on each record and a public corrections channel.

Some protocols and audit firms don't publish reports, keep repos private, or leave contracts unverified, so full coverage isn't possible everywhere. Where that blocks a comparison, the record says exactly what's missing, and those gaps are published too.
sections.out_scope:
- Rollup and L2 risk, which L2BEAT already does an excellent job covering.
- Other chains: this grant covers Ethereum mainnet.
- Protocols under $1 million in TVL. A protocol that falls below $1 million after it's added stays covered.
sections.team:
- **SEAL (Security Alliance)** runs the project and publishes the results. SEAL is a nonprofit that shares threat intelligence and sets security standards for crypto. It runs SEAL 911, a free 24/7 incident hotline that has handled 3,300+ tickets; Safe Harbor, which lets whitehats step in to rescue funds during a live exploit; and SEAL Certifications, an operational security standard protocols are assessed against. Its frameworks and research are at [securityalliance.org](https://securityalliance.org/).
- **Dickson Wu** leads it: the method, the tooling and reviewing results. Dickson helps run SEAL's Safe Harbor and SEAL Certifications programs.
sections.why_grant: A working prototype already runs the full pipeline on Ethereum: it maps core contracts and proxies, collects public audits with their stated commit and scope, rebuilds the audited code and compares it to live bytecode. A public preview covers the 20 largest Ethereum DeFi protocols: [ethereum-audit-register-demo.dicksonwu.xyz](https://ethereum-audit-register-demo.dicksonwu.xyz). The grant pays to extend it to every protocol over $1 million, publish it and keep it current.
sections.commitments:
- **License:** the dataset under CC BY 4.0, with the method published.
- **Maintenance:** every covered protocol is refreshed monthly for at least 12 months after launch, and SEAL keeps the dataset running after that.

revisions.title: SEAL Security Frameworks: Maintaining open security knowledge for Ethereum (scope: Infra, AI and Front-end)
revisions.summary: Frameworks turns practitioners' know-how into free, open Ethereum security guidance. This grant funds research, review and maintenance to complete AI, infrastructure and frontend sections for people and agents. Experienced external practitioners will steward subjects, contribute knowledge and improve the reference through recurring review and use in their own security work.

sections.why:
Frameworks has significant ongoing maintenance costs and no monetization: practical security know-how stays free for every team. Research, source checks, technical review, updates and releases recur as the reference grows and becomes agent-readable. This grant funds that capacity.

A developer workstation, cloud account or compromised frontend can put users' funds at risk. Chainalysis recorded over $3.4 billion in crypto theft in 2025, including the $1.5 billion Bybit theft. Sygnia traced the attack from a compromised developer workstation through reused AWS sessions to altered JavaScript served from Safe's S3 bucket, leading signers to approve a disguised transaction.

The Nx s1ngularity attack used AI command-line tools to search developer machines for credentials; investigators reported over 2,000 exposed secrets and about 1,700 affected users. Funded sections address developer AI, infrastructure access and frontend delivery. Frameworks publishes machine-readable guidance, extending the reference to agents.
sections.in_scope:
1. AI security: at least 4 new or substantively expanded pages covering coding-assistant permissions, secret separation, tool and MCP trust, and isolation, plus a team usage-policy template. Reuse existing DevSecOps isolation guidance.
2. Infrastructure: finish the cloud, identity and access management, zero trust and operating system security pages, covering account isolation, sessions, API keys, privileged access and secrets.
3. Frontend: finish the overview, web application security, common vulnerabilities and tools pages, with configurations for security headers, Content Security Policy, subresource integrity, hosting and CDN access.
4. Research, source checks, specialist review, configuration validation, and documented assumptions and limitations.
5. Recruit experienced external stewards for defined subjects; coordinate recurring reviews and integrate compatible, licensed guides with attribution.
6. Document external organizations' use of the guidance in existing Ethereum security work and upstream resulting improvements.
7. Maintain funded pages and shared publishing and release processes; update sources, resolve conflicts and publish corrections.
sections.out_scope:
1. Performing individual assessments, implementation engagements or onboarding for external teams.
2. A new assessment platform, rating system, certification, scanner or security product.
3. New content programs outside the three funded areas.
sections.team:
1. Matta (mattaereal), initiative lead. Leads SEAL Security Frameworks: sets its direction and scope, and does technical review. Founder of The Red Guild. https://github.com/mattaereal 

2. Sara (scode2277), co-maintainer. Maintains Frameworks day-to-day: content, reviews, contributor coordination, and releases. https://github.com/scode2277
sections.why_grant:
SEAL is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit founded by samczsun. Frameworks has 30+ sections shaped by dozens of contributors. It periodically shares relevant TLP:GREEN information; DPRK/IT worker guidance is one of the things that draws on SEAL Intel. Frameworks coordinates with SEAL Certs to align overlapping guidance. Its site, contribution process, machine-readable exports, and releases already exist.

At proposal baseline, AI had seven short pages; frontend and most infrastructure pages were unpublished drafts on the development site. The grant funds completion, knowledge integration, and maintenance. The OPSEC Ratings Coalition initiative lists Frameworks as prior art.

revisions.title: SEAL Intel: Scaling Blockchain Threat Intelligence - Enhancing Reporting and Recommendation Capabilities for Ethereum Infinite Garden
revisions.summary:
Security Alliance (SEAL) proposes expanding its existing intelligence program into an automated threat intelligence and response capability for Ethereum and its L2 ecosystem. The project will improve collection, enrichment, correlation, and distribution of threat data, delivering actionable alerts and intelligence feeds to security teams. The goal is to help ecosystem participants recognize emerging threats and act faster.
The goal is to deliver relevant, timely and properly structured intelligence to blockchain companies for the purpose of boosting their security posture. Incidents such as the most recent Binance exchange hack, continuous and ever-evolving social engineering and malware campaigns as well as LLM-scaled vulnerability research conducted by hackers leave little room for error and require fast adaptation capability by SOC teams across the whole industry.
SEAL and its initiative - SEAL Intel - is extremely well positioned to provide such intelligence based on indicators collected through real incidents occurring in the EVM ecosystem.

sections.why:
Ethereum security teams face high volumes of fragmented threat information across incidents, malicious domains, attacker infrastructure, and external research. Turning these signals into timely, relevant warnings often requires manual collection, validation, and analyst effort.

This initiative would help teams move from scattered indicators to actionable intelligence: correlated threats, relevant exposure information, and alerts that can inform preventive action and incident response.

For a long time the blockchain industry security gap was related to smart contracts security. However, we observe a significant shift in malicious campaigns targeting underlying infrastructure and operational security of cryptocurrency companies, developers and users. Mitigating such threats is reliant on receiving actionable intelligence and exact recommendations extracted from real-life cases SEAL is processing daily.

Web2 security firms often lack necessary context and/or observability pipelines to provide intelligence relevant to the Web3 ecosystem. Similarly, the pricing range and availability of classic security vendors is often carving out a considerable number of Web3 companies from provider’s services.

SEAL Intel is an initiative that can help to close this gap. SEAL is a well recognized security organization within blockchain space with an operational intel distribution network, 24/7 availability and broad spectrum of expertise relevant for Web3 threat intelligence. SEAL and their contributors are also well-aligned with blockchain principles.
sections.in_scope:
Automated pipelines for better  ingestion and normalization of selected Ethereum-relevant intelligence sources with the goal of providing tailored recommendations, flash alerting, real-time data streams and better coordination across otherwise fragmented entities. Our goal is to scale our Information Sharing and Analysis Center (ISAC) capabilities by offering more complete services as well as better coordination between participants of ISAC programme. Additional services will include invitation  only in depth private briefings and  quarterly reports from SEAL Intel experts.

WORKSTREAMS

• Collection and normalization: Ethereum threat intelligence is currently fragmented on three fronts:

1. Sources: it is scattered across open-source feeds, security firms, on-chain monitoring, vulnerability disclosures, social channels, private groups, and partner ISACs/CERTs, with no single point of aggregation. A single aggregation point, with automated connectors pulling from a curated and regularly reviewed source set, so participants no longer have to monitor each source themselves.
2. Structure: it arrives as free-text reports, chat messages, spreadsheets, and incompatible feed schemas. Normalization to one common schema (STIX 2.1), extended for Ethereum-specific indicators such as addresses, contracts, transaction hashes, and malicious dApp domains. Automated extraction turns unstructured reports into structured records.
3. Breadth: it spans smart contract exploits, phishing and drainer campaigns, infrastructure and supply-chain compromise, and state-linked actor activity, which no single team tracks completely. A shared taxonomy that classifies every item by threat category and affected participant type, so coverage gaps become visible and each participant can filter to what concerns them.


• Processing and analysis: Automation deduplicates, enriches, and correlates at volume, but nothing is distributed without analyst review. Human-in-the-loop curation is a hard requirement, covering three checks:

1. Correctness: validating indicators and claims, and scoring source reliability and confidence, so that false positives do not reach participants.
2. Enrichment: adding the context, attribution, and links to known campaigns that automated tooling misses.
3. Relevance: judging which participants an item matters to and how urgently, so that they receive only what they can act on.

The finished product of this stage is intelligence a Web3 organization can act on. Each item is verified and merged into a single analyst-approved record. Analysts who understand how Ethereum protocols, infrastructure, and attackers operate then add the context that generic threat feeds lack: who is affected, how the threat plays out on-chain and off-chain, and what specific steps to take. Because the pipeline automates the volume work and the ISAC sits inside the ecosystem, close to both the sources and the affected teams, this reaches participants while they can still act on it. Flash alerts, data feeds, and tailored recommendations are all produced from these records, so every service carries the same accuracy, relevance, and concrete guidance.

• Dissemination: Tiered products matched to urgency and audience:

1. flash alerts for active threats
2. tailored recommendations by participant profile (e.g. protocol, infrastructure provider, wallet, exchange)
3. periodic sector summaries
4. machine-readable feeds via API/TAXII for direct integration into participants' tooling

• Member contribution and coordination: The core of the ISAC is two-way exchange: participants contribute as well as consume, and the ISAC connects them to each other.

1. Submission: low-friction channels (portal, API, secure messaging) for reporting incidents, indicators, and observations.
2. Protected sharing: optional anonymization and redaction of attributing details, with TLP marking chosen by the submitter, so that sharing does not expose the reporting organization.
3. Requests for information: participants can query the ISAC and, through it, other participants, for example to ask whether anyone else is seeing the same activity.
4. Incident coordination: for threats that affect several participants, the ISAC convenes the affected parties, maintains a shared picture of the situation, and synchronizes response and disclosure.
5. Community structures: trusted working groups by segment or topic, and liaison with external bodies (other ISACs, CERTs, security response groups), so that coordination reaches beyond the membership.
6. Feedback to contributors: confirming what was done with a submission and what it led to, which sustains the incentive to share.

•Trust and governance: Vetted membership, role-based access, TLP 2.0 marking enforced end to end, redaction of attributing details, audit logs of access and sharing, and quality checks for false positives and stale indicators.

• Pilot and iteration: Phased integrations with a defined cohort of Ethereum ecosystem partners, with structured feedback on relevance, timeliness, and actionability used to tune sources, scoring, and products.

• Measurement and evidence: Metrics that show the ISAC works, with documentation and milestone evidence for each deliverable:

1. participation: active participants and contribution rate
2. speed: time from detection to dissemination
3. use: feed and API consumption, and alerts acted upon
4. quality: false-positive rate
sections.out_scope:
• Guaranteed prevention of all exploits or phishing campaigns.
• Full replacement of participant security operations or incident response teams.
• Unlimited custom research and consulting for individual organizations.
• Expansion to unrelated chains unless separately funded.
• Features and private donor services not expressly included in agreed grant milestones.
sections.team: Security Alliance (SEAL) will lead delivery through its existing Intel program. @blackbigswan is a lead of the SEAL threat intelligence initiative; Joe Dobson (ex-Mandiant) contributes security research and lends his expertise to structuring actionable threat intelligence offerings tailored for enterprise and government organizations; Peter Kacherginsky contributes limited part-time extensive security expertise from both Web2 and Web3 world he operates a well-known security newsletter BlockThreat. BlockThreat onchain data  now will also be available as part of SEAL Intel intelligence.
sections.why_grant:
SEAL already operates a threat intelligence function, maintains intelligence workflows and OpenCTI-related capabilities, and supports ecosystem security through SEAL 911 and related programs. The proposed work expands an operating program rather than starting a new intelligence team from scratch.

SEAL is maintaining a +100 channels (hotlines) with multiple participants of the blockchain ecosystem, including DeFi protocols, centralized exchanges and infrastructure providers. We provide on-demand insight into malicious campaigns spotted by entities that participate in hotlines channels.

We operate a 24/7 support ticket pipeline through @seal_911_bot and @seal_tips_bot - helping individual users and companies with initial incident response, on-chain tracing and coordination across industry.

Our weekly (public) threat intel reports provide a view into the scope of SEAL’s operations. With the future scaling we want to move from the “informative” nature of the initiative into the “actionable” stage - issuing direct recommendations based on modeled attack patterns and trends observed.

We are the main contributor to phishing domain blocklists in the ecosystem. Detecting between five to ten thousand malicious front ends weekly. Upon detection, our integration with MetaMask operated eth-phishing-detect blocklist allows us to render front end lures inoperational within minutes after detection.

revisions.title: SEAL Intel: Scaling Actionable Threat Intelligence for Ethereum
revisions.summary:
Security Alliance (SEAL) proposes expanding its existing intelligence program into an automated threat intelligence and response capability for Ethereum and its Layer 2 ecosystem. The initiative will strengthen the collection, normalization, enrichment, correlation, and distribution of intelligence gathered through real-world incidents, security research, and ecosystem partnerships.

By combining automation with expert human analysis, SEAL Intel will deliver verified indicators of compromise, actionable threat alerts, machine-readable intelligence feeds, and tailored defensive recommendations. The goal is to help Ethereum organizations identify emerging threats earlier, understand how attackers operate, and take preventive action before similar attacks spread across the ecosystem.

The initiative will also strengthen SEAL's Information Sharing and Analysis Center (ISAC) capabilities, enabling trusted participants to exchange intelligence, coordinate responses, and improve their collective security posture.

sections.why:
Ethereum security threats increasingly extend beyond smart contract vulnerabilities to the infrastructure, developers, employees, and operational systems supporting blockchain organizations. Social engineering, malware, compromised developer environments, supply-chain attacks, and increasingly sophisticated AI-assisted campaigns require security teams to identify and respond to threats quickly. Yet relevant intelligence remains fragmented across incident reports, malicious-domain lists, security vendors, on-chain monitoring, private reporting channels, and external research. Traditional security intelligence providers often lack the Web3-specific context needed to connect these signals to real-world blockchain threats, while the cost of enterprise intelligence services can limit access for smaller organizations.

SEAL Intel aims to close this gap by transforming intelligence gathered through real incidents into verified, actionable information that Ethereum organizations can use to protect themselves. By automating collection, enrichment, correlation, and distribution while preserving expert analyst review, SEAL will deliver timely alerts, machine-readable feeds, and tailored defensive recommendations. Rather than simply receiving isolated indicators or retrospective reports, participating organizations will be able to understand how emerging threats operate, determine whether their infrastructure is exposed, and take preventive action. The initiative will also strengthen coordination and two-way intelligence sharing across SEAL's existing ecosystem network.
sections.in_scope:
The initiative will expand SEAL Intel's existing capabilities into a more automated, scalable, and coordinated threat intelligence service for Ethereum and its Layer 2 ecosystem. Grant funding will support intelligence collection and normalization, automated processing and correlation, analyst workflows, actionable intelligence delivery, ISAC coordination, and independently verifiable partner adoption.

**1. Intelligence Collection and Normalization**

Ethereum threat intelligence is fragmented across sources, formats, and threat categories. SEAL will address these challenges through:

**Source aggregation:** Automated connectors will collect relevant intelligence from a curated set of open-source feeds, security firms, on-chain monitoring systems, vulnerability disclosures, social channels, private reporting groups, and partner ISACs/CERTs. Sources will be reviewed for reliability, relevance, and sharing permissions.

**Data normalization:** Intelligence arriving as free-text reports, chat messages, spreadsheets, and incompatible feed formats will be normalized using STIX 2.1, with documented conventions for Ethereum-specific indicators including wallet addresses, smart contracts, transaction hashes, and malicious dApp domains. Automated extraction will transform supported unstructured reports into records suitable for further analysis.

**Threat classification:** Intelligence will be categorized across smart contract exploits, phishing and wallet-draining campaigns, malware, social engineering, infrastructure and supply-chain compromises, and state-linked threat actor activity. Classification by threat category and affected participant type will help identify coverage gaps and improve relevance filtering.

**2. Automated Processing, Enrichment, and Correlation**

The initiative will automate repeatable intelligence-processing tasks while retaining human-in-the-loop review before intelligence is released through the proposed analyst-approved workflows.

Processing will include:

- **Correctness:** Validate indicators and intelligence claims, assess source reliability, and assign confidence levels to reduce false positives.
- **Enrichment:** Connect indicators to relevant malware, infrastructure, incidents, campaigns, and threat actors where supported by evidence.
- **Correlation:** Identify relationships between newly ingested intelligence, existing SEAL records, and observations collected through incident-response and reporting channels.
- **Relevance:** Determine which participant types are affected, the urgency of the threat, and the defensive actions organizations should consider.

The resulting intelligence records will combine structured indicators with supporting context explaining how threats operate, their potential impact, and relevant defensive measures.

**3. Actionable Intelligence and Recommendations**

SEAL will expand beyond primarily informative intelligence reporting to provide more actionable outputs derived from observed attacker behavior and real-world incidents.

Analyst-approved recommendations will be tailored to relevant participant profiles, including DeFi protocols, centralized exchanges, wallet providers, infrastructure operators, security firms, government organizations, and institutional participants.

Recommendations may include investigating malicious infrastructure, blocking suspicious domains, reviewing authentication controls, rotating compromised credentials, examining software dependencies, or implementing additional monitoring.

The objective is to help organizations understand not only what threat indicators exist, but also how the underlying attack operates and what they can do to reduce exposure.

**4. Intelligence Distribution and Alerting**

SEAL will develop tiered intelligence products matched to urgency and audience:

- **Flash alerts:** Timely notifications concerning active or emerging threats.
- **Tailored defensive recommendations:** Actionable guidance relevant to specific organization types and infrastructure.
- **Periodic intelligence reports:** Research covering significant campaigns, attacker trends, emerging techniques, and defensive recommendations.
- **Machine-readable intelligence feeds:** Authenticated REST API and TAXII 2.1 endpoints allowing organizations to integrate intelligence into existing security tooling.

These outputs will draw from consistent, validated intelligence records to improve accuracy and relevance across reporting and distribution channels.

**5. ISAC Participation and Two-Way Intelligence Sharing**

The initiative will strengthen SEAL's Information Sharing and Analysis Center (ISAC) by supporting both intelligence distribution and participant contributions.

Planned capabilities include:

- **Intelligence submission:** Approved channels for participants to submit incidents, indicators, and observations through secure messaging, APIs, or other supported interfaces.
- **Protected sharing:** Appropriate anonymization, redaction, contributor permissions, and TLP 2.0 markings to protect sensitive information.
- **Requests for information:** Mechanisms for participants to request context or determine whether others are observing similar threats.
- **Incident coordination:** Facilitation of information sharing and coordinated responses when threats affect multiple organizations.
- **Community collaboration:** Trusted working groups and liaison with other ISACs, CERTs, and security organizations.
- **Contributor feedback:** Information about how submitted intelligence was processed and whether it contributed to released intelligence.

**6. Trust, Security, and Governance**

The expanded intelligence service will incorporate vetted participation, role-based access, source attribution, TLP 2.0 information handling, redaction, access and sharing audit logs, and processes for identifying false positives or stale indicators.

Appropriate safeguards will address unauthorized access, malicious submissions, intelligence corrections, and restricted redistribution.

**7. Partner Pilot and Performance Measurement**

SEAL will conduct phased integrations with independent Ethereum ecosystem organizations to evaluate the operational usefulness of its feeds, alerts, and recommendations.

Performance will be measured through:

- **Participation:** Active organizations, integrations, and intelligence contributions.
- **Speed:** Time from detection to validation and dissemination.
- **Usage:** Feed/API consumption and documented defensive actions.
- **Quality:** False-positive rates, relevance, and participant feedback.

The six-month delivery plan will cover initial ingestion and normalization, operational analyst workflows and alerting, and a partner adoption pilot. The specific acceptance criteria and funding allocations are detailed in the milestones.

**Grant-Funded Resources**

The proposed $267,000 budget supports engineering, intelligence analysis, partner integrations, delivery management, infrastructure, and independent technical verification. The current planning model allocates $108,000 to engineering, $54,000 to intelligence analysis, $60,000 to partner integration, $15,000 to delivery management, $18,000 to infrastructure, and $12,000 to independent review. These allocations remain subject to validation against actual staffing commitments and project costs.
sections.out_scope:
The initiative does not include:

- Guaranteed prevention of all exploits, phishing campaigns, or security incidents.
- Replacement of participating organizations' existing security operations or incident-response teams.
- Unlimited custom investigations, security assessments, or consulting engagements.
- Automated modification of participant systems, including credential rotation, patching, or blocking.
- Development of an entirely new endpoint security, blockchain monitoring, or phishing-takedown platform.
- Expansion into unrelated blockchain ecosystems beyond the agreed Ethereum and Layer 2 scope.
- Redistribution of restricted intelligence without appropriate authorization.
- Private donor services or features not expressly included in the agreed grant scope and milestones.

The initiative expands SEAL's existing intelligence capabilities and does not replace SEAL 911 or create a separate incident-response organization.

Security Alliance (SEAL) will deliver this initiative through its established threat intelligence program, drawing on experienced security researchers, engineers, and incident-response specialists across its existing operations.

Oskar (@blackbigswan) — SEAL Intel Lead: Leads SEAL's threat intelligence initiative, overseeing intelligence priorities, technical direction, analyst workflows, research coordination, and the development of actionable intelligence capabilities for Ethereum ecosystem participants.

Joe Dobson — Security Research and Threat Intelligence: Formerly of Mandiant, Joe contributes expertise in cybersecurity research, malware analysis, and the development of actionable threat intelligence products and workflows tailored to enterprise and government security organizations.

Peter Kacherginsky — Security Research and Intelligence Contributor: Peter brings extensive cybersecurity expertise spanning traditional security and Web3. He operates BlockThreat, a recognized security research publication, and contributes specialized research and intelligence expertise on a limited part-time basis. Relevant BlockThreat on-chain intelligence is expected to become available through SEAL Intel, subject to applicable data-sharing permissions.

Matta (@mattaereal) — Security Frameworks and Technical Research: Matta leads SEAL Security Frameworks and is the founder of The Red Guild. revisions.title: SEAL Intel: Scaling Actionable Threat Intelligence for Ethereum
revisions.summary: SEAL already collects threat intelligence through incident response, ecosystem reporting channels, and security research. This grant will connect those workflows into a shared pipeline that validates, enriches, and correlates Ethereum-relevant intelligence, delivering machine-readable feeds, urgent alerts, and actionable defensive recommendations. Over six months, SEAL will test these capabilities with independent Ethereum ecosystem organizations and measure intelligence quality, delivery speed, integration, and documented defensive actions.

sections.why:
Ethereum security teams face high volumes of fragmented threat information across incidents, malicious-domain lists, attacker infrastructure, private reporting channels, on-chain observations, and external research publications. These sources differ in structure, reliability, and sharing restrictions. Teams must spend significant analyst time reconciling them before determining whether a threat affects their systems and what defensive action to take.

SEAL already has visibility into incidents and malicious campaigns across the Ethereum ecosystem. This initiative will make that intelligence easier to use through validated records with supporting evidence, relevant alerts delivered to affected teams, and recommendations that specify concrete defensive actions. Participating organizations will be able to integrate intelligence into their existing security tooling and contribute observations through controlled information-sharing channels.
sections.in_scope:
SEAL Intel will expand its existing intelligence operations into a shared, automated, and analyst-validated threat intelligence capability for Ethereum and its Layer 2 ecosystem. The grant will fund collection and normalization, automated processing and correlation, actionable intelligence distribution, secure ISAC collaboration, and independently verified adoption.

**1. Intelligence Collection and Normalization**

Ethereum threat intelligence is fragmented across three dimensions:

- **Sources:** Intelligence is scattered across open-source feeds, security firms, on-chain monitoring, vulnerability disclosures, social channels, private reporting groups, and ISACs/CERTs. SEAL will build automated connectors to aggregate intelligence from curated sources, preserving provenance and sharing permissions.
- **Structure:** Information arrives as reports, chat messages, spreadsheets, and incompatible feed formats. SEAL will normalize supported intelligence using STIX 2.1, with conventions for Ethereum-specific indicators such as wallet addresses, contracts, transaction hashes, and malicious dApp domains. Automated extraction will convert unstructured reports into usable records.
- **Breadth:** Threats span smart contract exploits, phishing and wallet drainers, malware, social engineering, infrastructure and supply-chain compromises, and state-linked actors. A shared taxonomy will classify intelligence by threat category and affected participant type, improving filtering and identifying coverage gaps.

**2. Automated Processing and Analysis**

SEAL will automate collection, deduplication, enrichment, and correlation while maintaining human-in-the-loop analyst review before intelligence is distributed.

Analysts will evaluate intelligence across three dimensions:

- **Correctness:** Validate indicators and claims, assess source reliability, assign confidence levels, and reduce false positives.
- **Enrichment:** Connect indicators to supporting evidence, attacker infrastructure, malware, incidents, and known campaigns.
- **Relevance:** Determine which organizations are affected, the urgency of the threat, and appropriate defensive actions.

Automated correlation will connect new intelligence with existing SEAL records and observations gathered through incident-response and reporting channels.

The output will be structured, evidence-linked, analyst-approved intelligence explaining what was observed, how the threat operates, who may be affected, and what actions to consider.

**SEAL's advantage** is combining automation with direct incident visibility, specialized Ethereum security expertise, and established relationships with organizations positioned to act on intelligence. Automation handles repetitive processing while experienced researchers provide the context that generic intelligence feeds often lack.

**3. Actionable Intelligence and Distribution**

SEAL will produce intelligence products matched to threat urgency and participant needs:

- **Flash alerts:** Timely notifications about active or emerging threats.
- **Tailored recommendations:** Concrete defensive guidance for protocols, exchanges, wallets, infrastructure providers, security firms, government organizations, and institutions.
- **Periodic intelligence reports:** Analysis of significant campaigns, attacker techniques, emerging
sections.out_scope:
The initiative does not include:

- Guaranteed prevention of all exploits, phishing campaigns, or security incidents.
- Replacement of participating organizations' existing security operations or incident-response teams.
- Unlimited custom investigations, security assessments, or consulting engagements.
- Automated modification of participant systems, including credential rotation, patching, or blocking.
- Development of an entirely new endpoint security, blockchain monitoring, or phishing-takedown platform.
- Expansion into unrelated blockchain ecosystems beyond the agreed Ethereum and Layer 2 scope.
- Redistribution of restricted intelligence without appropriate authorization.
- Private donor services or features not expressly included in the agreed grant scope and milestones.

The initiative expands SEAL's existing intelligence capabilities. It does not replace SEAL 911 or establish a separate incident-response organization.

sections.why_grant:
SEAL Intel builds on an established operational threat intelligence program rather than creating a new intelligence organization from scratch. SEAL already receives threat information through incident response, ecosystem reporting channels, security research, and trusted relationships with blockchain organizations. The grant will fund the incremental engineering, automation, intelligence processing, and integrations needed to turn those existing capabilities into a more scalable intelligence service.

**Existing foundation and grant-funded additions**

| Existing SEAL capability | Additional work funded by this grant |
|---|---|
| Incident and intelligence intake through SEAL reporting channels | Connect selected intake workflows to a shared intelligence pipeline, preserving source provenance and sharing permissions |
| Existing analyst research and threat intelligence workflows | Automate selected collection, normalization, deduplication, enrichment, and correlation tasks |
| Existing OpenCTI-related intelligence capabilities | Build and document additional integrations, Ethereum-specific data conventions, and production workflows |
| Public security research, intelligence reports, and malicious-domain contributions | Produce consistent, evidence-linked records, actionable recommendations, and machine-readable distribution |
| Established relationships with ecosystem organizations | Support integrations and independently verified operational adoption of the new intelligence feeds |

**Existing operational capabilities and track record**

- **Ecosystem intelligence network:** SEAL maintains more than 100 communication channels and hotlines connecting DeFi protocols, centralized exchanges, infrastructure providers, and other blockchain organizations. These relationships provide direct visibility into incidents and emerging threats.

- **24/7 incident and intelligence intake:** SEAL operates `@seal_911_bot` and `@seal_tips_bot`, supporting incident reporting, intelligence submissions, initial response coordination, and information sharing.

- **Phishing detection and blocklisting:** SEAL reports identifying approximately 5,000–10,000 malicious frontends weekly and contributes intelligence to ecosystem phishing blocklists. Its integration with MetaMask's eth-phishing-detect helps malicious frontends become blocked rapidly after identification.

- **Malware and threat actor research:** SEAL investigates DPRK-linked threat actors, malware-as-a-service operations, social engineering campaigns, malicious infrastructure, and software supply-chain compromises. Research outputs include indicators of compromise, attacker tactics and techniques, campaign analysis, and coordinated defensive actions.

- **Public intelligence and research:** SEAL publishes threat research, incident analysis, and operational statistics through SEAL Radar and maintains public research repositories and datasets.

- **Existing intelligence infrastructure:** SEAL already conducts structured intelligence research and maintains OpenCTI-related capabilities for organizing and analyzing threat information.

These capabilities give SEAL a significant operational advantage: direct incident visibility, researchers who understand both traditional cybersecurity and Ethereum-specific threats, and established relationships with organizations positioned to act on intelligence.

**Why grant funding is needed**

While SEAL already collects and analyzes intelligence, many processes still require manual collection, reconciliation, enrichment, and distribution. This grant will connect existing workflows, automate repeatable processing tasks, improve intelligence quality and consistency, and provide integrations that enable security teams to consume and act on intelligence more efficiently.

Before development begins, SEAL will document the existing implementation, identify missing capabilities, and distinguish new grant-funded work from previously funded deliverables and operating costs.

Connect selected existing SEAL reporting and ISAC workflows to enable two-way intelligence exchange. Implement vetted access, role-based permissions, provenance, TLP-aware distribution, audit logs, and correction or withdrawal procedures for stale or inaccurate intelligence. Protect restricted sources and review automated outputs for false positives and malicious submissions.

Integrate independent Ethereum ecosystem organizations, gather operational feedback, and measure source coverage, extraction quality, analyst effort, alert delivery speed, feed/API usage, contributions, and documented defensive actions. sections.why:
Ethereum security teams face high volumes of fragmented threat information across incidents, malicious-domain lists, attacker infrastructure, private reporting channels, on-chain observations, and external research publications. These sources differ in structure, reliability, and sharing restrictions. Teams must spend significant analyst time reconciling them before determining whether a threat affects their systems and what defensive action to take.

SEAL already has visibility into incidents and malicious campaigns across the Ethereum ecosystem. sections.in_scope:
SEAL Intel will expand its existing threat intelligence operations into an automated, analyst-validated service for Ethereum and its Layer 2 ecosystem. The grant funds new integrations, intelligence processing, distribution tools, and partner adoption—not the creation of a new intelligence team.

**1. Collection and normalization**

Build connectors for curated public and permissioned sources, including security research, malicious-domain feeds, incident reports, on-chain observations, and trusted reporting channels. Preserve source provenance, confidence, and sharing restrictions. Extract and deduplicate information from structured and unstructured reports, normalize it using STIX 2.1 with Ethereum-specific indicators (wallet addresses, contracts, transaction hashes, malicious dApp domains), and classify threats by category and affected participant type.

**2. Processing, correlation, and analyst review**

Automate enrichment and correlation against existing SEAL intelligence and incident observations, subject to permissions. Analysts review records before release for correctness (validity, source reliability, false positives), enrichment (supporting evidence and links to infrastructure, incidents, malware, and campaigns), and relevance (affected organizations, urgency, defensive actions). Outputs are evidence-linked, analyst-approved intelligence records. SEAL's differentiator is combining automation with direct incident visibility and researchers experienced in Ethereum threats; the technology reduces repetitive work so analysts can provide actionable guidance rather than raw indicator lists.

**3. Alerts, recommendations, and feeds**

Deliver flash alerts for active threats; tailored defensive recommendations for protocols, exchanges, wallets, and infrastructure providers; periodic campaign and threat reports; and authenticated TAXII 2.1 and REST feeds for integration into existing security tooling. Provide filtering by threat category, participant type, and authorized sharing level, plus API documentation and onboarding guidance.

**4. ISAC collaboration**

Connect selected existing SEAL reporting and ISAC workflows to enable two-way intelligence exchange. Approved participants can submit observations, receive relevant alerts, request context, and coordinate on shared threats. Apply contributor permissions, optional redaction or anonymization, and TLP 2.0 restrictions. Provide contributor feedback where confidentiality permits. This strengthens existing coordination rather than building a new messaging or incident-response platform.

**5. Security and quality**

Implement vetted access, role-based permissions, provenance, TLP-aware distribution, audit logs, and correction or withdrawal procedures for stale or inaccurate intelligence. Protect restricted sources and review automated outputs for false positives and malicious submissions.

**6. Pilot and verification**

Integrate independent Ethereum ecosystem organizations, gather operational feedback, and measure source coverage, extraction quality, analyst effort, alert delivery speed, feed/API usage, contributions, and documented defensive actions. An independent reviewer verifies the quantitative acceptance criteria specified separately in the milestones.

sections.why_grant:
SEAL Intel builds on an established operational threat intelligence program rather than creating a new intelligence organization from scratch. SEAL already receives threat information through incident response, ecosystem reporting channels, security research, and trusted relationships with blockchain organizations. The grant will fund the incremental engineering, automation, intelligence processing, and integrations needed to turn those existing capabilities into a more scalable intelligence service.

**Existing foundation and grant-funded additions**

| Existing SEAL capability | Additional work funded by this grant |
|---|---|
| Incident and intelligence intake through SEAL reporting channels | Connect selected intake workflows to a shared intelligence pipeline, preserving source provenance and sharing permissions |
| Existing analyst research and threat intelligence workflows | Automate selected collection, normalization, deduplication, enrichment, and correlation tasks |
| Existing OpenCTI-related intelligence capabilities | Build and document additional integrations, Ethereum-specific data conventions, and production workflows |
| Public security research, intelligence reports, and malicious-domain contributions | Produce consistent, evidence-linked records, actionable recommendations, and machine-readable distribution |
| Established relationships with ecosystem organizations | Support integrations and independently verified operational adoption of the new intelligence feeds |

**Existing operational capabilities and track record**

- **Ecosystem intelligence network:** SEAL maintains more than 100 communication channels and hotlines connecting DeFi protocols, centralized exchanges, infrastructure providers, and other blockchain organizations. These relationships provide direct visibility into incidents and emerging threats.

- **24/7 incident and intelligence intake:** SEAL operates `@seal_911_bot` and `@seal_tips_bot`, supporting incident reporting, intelligence submissions, initial response coordination, and information sharing.

- **Phishing detection and blocklisting:** SEAL reports identifying approximately 5,000–10,000 malicious frontends weekly and contributes intelligence to ecosystem phishing blocklists. Its integration with MetaMask's eth-phishing-detect helps malicious frontends become blocked rapidly after identification.

- **Malware and threat actor research:** SEAL investigates DPRK-linked threat actors, malware-as-a-service operations, social engineering campaigns, malicious infrastructure, and software supply-chain compromises. Research outputs include indicators of compromise, attacker tactics and techniques, campaign analysis, and coordinated defensive actions.

- **Public intelligence and research:** SEAL publishes threat research, incident analysis, and operational statistics through SEAL Radar and maintains public research repositories and datasets.

- **Existing intelligence infrastructure:** SEAL already conducts structured intelligence research and maintains OpenCTI-related capabilities for organizing and analyzing threat information.

These capabilities give SEAL a significant operational advantage: direct incident visibility, researchers who understand both traditional cybersecurity and Ethereum-specific threats, and established relationships with organizations positioned to act on intelligence.

**Why grant funding is needed**

While SEAL already collects and analyzes intelligence, many processes still require manual collection, reconciliation, enrichment, and distribution. This grant will connect existing workflows, automate repeatable processing tasks, improve intelligence quality and consistency, and provide integrations that enable security teams to consume and act on intelligence more efficiently.

Before development begins, SEAL will document the existing implementation, identify missing capabilities, and distinguish new grant-funded work from previously funded deliverables and operating costs.

**Public evidence and references**

- SEAL Radar: https://radar.securityalliance.org/
- SEAL GitHub: https://github.com/security-alliance
- Lazarus Group research: https://lazarus.group/
- Public Lazarus intelligence dataset: https://github.com/security-alliance/lazarus-group-data
- Binance incident research: https://radar.securityalliance.org/tradertraitor-vs-contagious-interview-a-look-at-binances-initial-incident-report/
- DPRK malware research: https://radar.securityalliance.org/vs-code-tasks-abuse-by-contagious-interview-dprk/
- Weekly operational statistics: https://radar.securityalliance.org/seal-weekly-stats-20-27-oct-2026/
sections.commitments:

milestones.name: Data ingestion and normalization
criteria: 100% of ingested items are stored as STIX 2.1 bundles, including Ethereum-specific indicators such as addresses, contracts, transaction hashes, and malicious dApp domains.

milestones.name: Correlation, analyst workflows and alert delivery
criteria: Median analyst time required to produce a report through the new workflow is at least 50% lower than the manual baseline, measured using 10 reports against five baseline reports timed at the beginning of the grant.

criteria: At least six independent organizations, representing at least three participant types, each retrieve intelligence from the feed or API on at least 20 days within a 30-day period, verified through access logs.

milestones.name: Data ingestion and normalization
criteria: 100% of ingested items are stored as STIX 2.1 bundles, including Ethereum-specific indicators such as addresses, contracts, transaction hashes, and malicious dApp domains.

milestones.name: Correlation, analyst workflows and alert delivery
criteria: Median analyst time required to produce a report through the new workflow is at least 50% lower than the manual baseline, measured using 10 reports against five baseline reports timed at the beginning of the grant.

criteria: At least six independent organizations, representing at least three participant types, each retrieve intelligence from the feed or API on at least 20 days within a 30-day period, verified through access logs.

revisions.title: SEAL Intel: Scaling Actionable Threat Intelligence for Ethereum
revisions.summary: SEAL collects threat intelligence through incident response, ecosystem reporting channels, and security research. This grant will connect those workflows into a shared pipeline that validates, enriches, and correlates Ethereum-relevant intelligence, delivering machine-readable feeds, urgent alerts, and actionable defensive recommendations. Over six months, SEAL will test these capabilities with independent Ethereum ecosystem organizations and measure intelligence quality, delivery speed, integration, and documented defensive actions.

sections.why:
Ethereum security teams face high volumes of fragmented threat information across incidents, malicious-domain lists, attacker infrastructure, private reporting channels, on-chain observations, and external research publications. As blockchain security has matured, attackers have increasingly targeted operational infrastructure, developers, credentials, and software supply chains alongside smart contracts, creating a growing need for intelligence that connects these threats to practical defensive actions. These sources differ in structure, reliability, and sharing restrictions. Teams must spend significant analyst time reconciling them before determining whether a threat affects their systems and what defensive action to take.

SEAL already has visibility into incidents and malicious campaigns across the Ethereum ecosystem. This initiative will make that intelligence easier to use through validated records with supporting evidence, relevant alerts delivered to affected teams, and recommendations that specify concrete defensive actions. Participating organizations will be able to integrate intelligence into their existing security tooling and contribute observations through controlled information-sharing channels.
sections.in_scope:
SEAL Intel will expand its existing threat intelligence operations into an automated, analyst-validated service for Ethereum and its Layer 2 ecosystem. The grant funds new integrations, intelligence processing, distribution tools, and partner adoption—not the creation of a new intelligence team.

**1. Collection and normalization**

Build connectors for curated public and permissioned sources, including security research, malicious-domain feeds, incident reports, on-chain observations, and trusted reporting channels. Preserve source provenance, confidence, and sharing restrictions. Extract and deduplicate information from structured and unstructured reports, normalize it using STIX 2.1 with Ethereum-specific indicators (wallet addresses, contracts, transaction hashes, malicious dApp domains), and classify threats by category and affected participant type.

**2. Processing, correlation, and analyst review**

Automate enrichment and correlation against existing SEAL intelligence and incident observations, subject to permissions. Analysts review records before release for correctness (validity, source reliability, false positives), enrichment (supporting evidence and links to infrastructure, incidents, malware, and campaigns), and relevance (affected organizations, urgency, defensive actions). Outputs are evidence-linked, analyst-approved intelligence records. SEAL's differentiator is combining automation with direct incident visibility and researchers experienced in Ethereum threats; the technology reduces repetitive work so analysts can provide actionable guidance rather than raw indicator lists.

**3. Alerts, recommendations, and feeds**

Deliver flash alerts for active threats; tailored defensive recommendations for protocols, exchanges, wallets, and infrastructure providers; periodic campaign and threat reports; and authenticated TAXII 2.1 and REST feeds for integration into existing security tooling. Provide filtering by threat category, participant type, and authorized sharing level, plus API documentation and onboarding guidance.

**4. ISAC collaboration**

Connect selected existing SEAL reporting and ISAC workflows to enable two-way intelligence exchange. Approved participants can submit observations, receive relevant alerts, request context, and coordinate on shared threats. Apply contributor permissions, optional redaction or anonymization, and TLP 2.0 restrictions. Provide contributor feedback where confidentiality permits. This strengthens existing coordination rather than building a new messaging or incident-response platform.

**5. Security and quality**

Implement vetted access, role-based permissions, provenance, TLP-aware distribution, audit logs, and correction or withdrawal procedures for stale or inaccurate intelligence. Protect restricted sources and review automated outputs for false positives and malicious submissions.

**6. Pilot and verification**

Integrate independent Ethereum ecosystem organizations, gather operational feedback, and measure source coverage, extraction quality, analyst effort, alert delivery speed, feed/API usage, contributions, and documented defensive actions. An independent reviewer verifies the quantitative acceptance criteria specified separately in the milestones.

**Use of funds:** The proposed six-month $267,000 budget covers engineering ($108,000), intelligence analysis ($54,000), partner integration ($60,000), delivery management ($15,000), infrastructure ($18,000), and independent review ($12,000), subject to confirmation. Existing SEAL capabilities and previously funded work are excluded from duplicate reimbursement.
sections.out_scope:
The initiative does not include:

- Guaranteed prevention of all exploits, phishing campaigns, or security incidents.
- Replacement of participating organizations' existing security operations or incident-response teams.
- Unlimited custom threat investigations, security assessments, or consulting services for individual organizations.
- Automated changes to participant systems, including credential rotation, patching, or blocking.
- Development of an entirely new endpoint security, blockchain monitoring, messaging, or incident-response platform.
- Expansion into unrelated blockchain ecosystems beyond the agreed Ethereum and Layer 2 scope.
- Redistribution of restricted or confidential intelligence without authorization.
- Private donor services or features not expressly included in the approved grant scope and milestones.

The grant expands SEAL's existing intelligence capabilities and coordination workflows. It does not replace SEAL 911 or create a separate incident-response organization.

milestones.name: Data ingestion and normalization
criteria: 100% of ingested items are stored as STIX 2.1 bundles, including Ethereum-specific indicators such as addresses, contracts, transaction hashes, and malicious dApp domains.

milestones.name: Correlation, analyst workflows and alert delivery

revisions.summary: SEAL collects threat intelligence through incident response, ecosystem reporting channels, and security research. sections.why:
Ethereum security teams face high volumes of fragmented threat information across incidents, malicious-domain lists, attacker infrastructure, private reporting channels, on-chain observations, and external research publications. As blockchain security has matured, attackers have increasingly targeted operational infrastructure, developers, credentials, and software supply chains alongside smart contracts, creating a growing need for intelligence that connects these threats to practical defensive actions. These sources differ in structure, reliability, and sharing restrictions. Teams must spend significant analyst time reconciling them before determining whether a threat affects their systems and what defensive action to take.

SEAL already has visibility into incidents and malicious campaigns across the Ethereum ecosystem. This initiative will make that intelligence easier to use through validated records with supporting evidence, relevant alerts delivered to affected teams, and recommendations that specify concrete defensive actions. Participating organizations will be able to integrate intelligence into their existing security tooling and contribute observations through controlled information-sharing channels.
sections.in_scope:
SEAL Intel will expand its existing threat intelligence operations into an automated, analyst-validated service for Ethereum and its Layer 2 ecosystem. The grant funds new integrations, intelligence processing, distribution tools, and partner adoption—not the creation of a new intelligence team.

**1. Collection and normalization**

Build connectors for curated public and permissioned sources, including security research, malicious-domain feeds, incident reports, on-chain observations, and trusted reporting channels. Preserve source provenance, confidence, and sharing restrictions. Extract and deduplicate information from structured and unstructured reports, normalize it using STIX 2.1 with Ethereum-specific indicators (wallet addresses, contracts, transaction hashes, malicious dApp domains), and classify threats by category and affected participant type.

**2. Processing, correlation, and analyst review**

Automate enrichment and correlation against existing SEAL intelligence and incident observations, subject to permissions. Analysts review records before release for correctness (validity, source reliability, false positives), enrichment (supporting evidence and links to infrastructure, incidents, malware, and campaigns), and relevance (affected organizations, urgency, defensive actions). Outputs are evidence-linked, analyst-approved intelligence records. SEAL's differentiator is combining automation with direct incident visibility and researchers experienced in Ethereum threats; the technology reduces repetitive work so analysts can provide actionable guidance rather than raw indicator lists.

**3. Alerts, recommendations, and feeds**

Deliver flash alerts for active threats; tailored defensive recommendations for protocols, exchanges, wallets, and infrastructure providers; periodic campaign and threat reports; and authenticated TAXII 2.1 and REST feeds for integration into existing security tooling. Provide filtering by threat category, participant type, and authorized sharing level, plus API documentation and onboarding guidance.

**4. ISAC collaboration**

Connect selected existing SEAL reporting and ISAC workflows to enable two-way intelligence exchange. Approved participants can submit observations, receive relevant alerts, request context, and coordinate on shared threats. Apply contributor permissions, optional redaction or anonymization, and TLP 2.0 restrictions. Provide contributor feedback where confidentiality permits. This strengthens existing coordination rather than building a new messaging or incident-response platform.

**5. Security and quality**

Implement vetted access, role-based permissions, provenance, TLP-aware distribution, audit logs, and correction or withdrawal procedures for stale or inaccurate intelligence. Protect restricted sources and review automated outputs for false positives and malicious submissions.

**6. Pilot and verification**

Integrate independent Ethereum ecosystem organizations, gather operational feedback, and measure source coverage, extraction quality, analyst effort, alert delivery speed, feed/API usage, contributions, and documented defensive actions. An independent reviewer verifies the quantitative acceptance criteria specified separately in the milestones.

**Use of funds:** The proposed six-month $267,000 budget covers engineering ($108,000), intelligence analysis ($54,000), partner integration ($60,000), delivery management ($15,000), infrastructure ($18,000), and independent review ($12,000), subject to confirmation. Existing SEAL capabilities and previously funded work are excluded from duplicate reimbursement.

criteria: 100% of ingested items are stored as STIX 2.1 bundles, including Ethereum-specific indicators such as addresses, contracts, transaction hashes, and malicious dApp domains.

revisions.title: Preparing encrypted mempools for inclusion in the earliest EIP possible
revisions.summary:
EIP-8184, LUCID, proposes encrypting transactions as they move through Ethereum’s public mempool and revealing them only after their ordering has been committed.

The design has progressed significantly. The main remaining security barrier is the optionality problem: the party responsible for revealing a decryption key may have an opportunity to withhold it after a transaction has already been committed.

A promising approach is to use independent key publishers, with validators helping identify reliable providers. This would also enable a competitive marketplace for encryption and decryption service providers rather than relying on a single provider.

The goal of this initiative is to resolve the optionality problem and complete the remaining specification and implementation work needed to propose LUCID for inclusion in Ethereum’s I* hard fork.

sections.why:
Ethereum’s public mempool reveals transaction details before their order is finalized, creating opportunities for front-running, transaction copying, censorship, and other forms of harmful MEV.

More than $1.8 billion has extracted from Ethereum users through MEV since 2020, much of it through tactics including front-running and sandwich attacks. Encrypted mempools can reduce this attack surface by keeping transaction information hidden until ordering has been fixed.

LUCID provides a path to doing this at the Ethereum protocol level while preserving an open and permissionless transaction pipeline. Resolving optionality is an important remaining security requirement before LUCID can be proposed for inclusion in I*.
sections.in_scope:
- resolving the optionality problem
- defining the role and security model for independent key publishers
- revising EIP-8184
- drafting the execution layer specification
- drafting the consensus layer specification
- developing client implementations
- testing the updated design under adversarial conditions
- technical review with Ethereum researchers and client teams
- coordinating cryptographers on post-quantum threshold encryption and maintaining a public index of the field (e.g. extending the existing PQ threshold knowledge graph), so that LUCID's key-encapsulation path has a documented migration story
- preparing LUCID to be proposed for consideration in I*
sections.out_scope:
- guaranteeing acceptance or inclusion of EIP-8184 in I*, which is determined through Ethereum’s protocol upgrade process
- full production deployment on Ethereum Mainnet
- long-term operation of encryption or decryption service providers
- development of unrelated private order-flow or MEV mitigation systems
sections.team:
The recipient is brainbot, a core contributor to Shutter Network.

- Jannik Luhn, Developer. Author of EIP-8105 and contributor to LUCID development.
- Luis Bezzenberger, Project Manager. Coordinates encrypted mempool development and ecosystem work.

Both have worked on encrypted mempools through Shutter Network for several years.

The team also helps coordinate the Encrypt the Mempool coalition, which brings together Ethereum researchers, client teams, builders, and infrastructure providers working to advance encrypted mempools for Ethereum.

brainbot receives monthly funding from Shutter DAO 0x36 for broader encrypted mempool work. That funding does not cover these milestones.
sections.why_grant:
brainbot and Shutter Network have years of encrypted mempool research and implementation experience. Jannik authored EIP-8105, and the team is actively contributing to EIP-8184.

Shutter has also deployed encrypted mempool technology on Gnosis Chain and previously launched a Shutterized OP Stack testnet on Sepolia. The work here builds directly on existing specifications, implementations, and relationships with Ethereum client teams.
sections.commitments:
- Prototype work funded by this initiative will be open source.
- brainbot will continue maintaining its contributions to EIP-8184 and coordinating LUCID development through its ongoing encrypted mempool work.
- Client implementations remain maintained by their respective upstream client teams.

milestones.name: 1. Expand LUCID with key publisher whitelisting and prepare EIP for I
criteria: Revised EIP-8184 includes validator governance of the key publisher set, public threat model and protocol design, comparison of alternatives, economic model of key withholding, and test vectors for both layers.
Review takes place with researchers and client teams through AllCoreDevs and Encrypt the Mempool calls, with remaining blockers published.
LUCID / EIP-8184 is formally brought into Ethereum’s I* protocol-upgrade process for consideration by core developers and client teams.
Independent security review of the optionality design.
The pull request proposing LUCID / EIP-8184 for inclusion in I* is merged into the I* Meta EIP, with the public pull request and Meta EIP providing evidence.

milestones.name: 2. Implement and test
criteria: Open-source prototype published in one EL client and one CL client, plus a reference key publisher.
Single-client devnet demonstrates the LUCID flow and adversarial tests covering key withholding, late reveals, invalid keys, publisher outages, and PTC vote splits.
Public report documents latency, overhead, and security findings.

milestones.name: 3. Post-quantum threshold encryption
criteria: PQ threshold knowledge graph v2 published with wider coverage and consistent attributes for assumptions, sizes, setup, batching, and suitability for LUCID.
Open-source implementation and benchmarks published for one cutting-edge scheme, compared against BLT25, PQ BEAT-MEV, and TACET.
Short public note documents how LUCID could move to a post-quantum scheme later.
