revisions.title: Securing Ethereum with Formal Verification
revisions.summary: AI is making it faster to attack software, giving attackers a meaningful edge. Formal verification is widely considered the strongest security guarantee in software correctness. This grant aims to increase formal verification adoption across the Ethereum ecosystem with TVL secured as its main success metric.

sections.why:
AI is making it faster to attack software, giving attackers a meaningful edge. The answer is to put AI on the defending side too: AI that writes machine-checked proofs that a contract's stated properties hold, with humans only checking the theorems. Formal verification is widely considered the strongest guarantee of software correctness, and it is the one place where AI output can be checked mechanically rather than trusted.

This grant creates an open-source framework for Solidity verification (Verity, built on Lean 4, with an AI proof-writing skill) and increases formal verification adoption across the Ethereum ecosystem. Success is measured by the TVL covered by formally verified properties.

The Ethereum Foundation has already pledged $100,000 USD of the $300,000 USD budget for the Verity product foundation. The remaining $200,000 USD finishes the product and pays for adoption, so every dollar donated here builds on money already committed.
sections.in_scope:
- Product work on Verity's compiler, Solidity coverage, reusable proof infrastructure, benchmark, documentation, developer onboarding, AI proof-writing skill, and a deterministic Solidity-to-Verity transpiler that reduces modeling gaps.
- Public releases that document supported workflows, trust assumptions, version pins, known limitations, and how teams and formal audit firms can use the tooling.
- Adoption through protocol teams using Verity in-house and formal audit firms using it in their own work.
- Measuring adoption primarily through the TVL of contracts whose stated properties are formally verified.

**What this pays for:**

This is not a program to select public contracts and publish formal verifications of them. It pays for two connected things:

- **Product work:** continue the open-source Verity tooling, benchmark, documentation, developer onboarding, AI proof-writing skill, and deterministic Solidity-to-Verity transpilation work already defined in the Ethereum Foundation funded grant.
- **Adoption work:** make Verity usable by protocol teams in-house and formal audit firms in their own work. Success is led by the value covered by the verified properties.

The total program budget is $300,000 USD. It combines the $100,000 USD Ethereum Foundation pledge for the Verity product foundation with $200,000 USD raised through TheDAO Security Fund's Second Round.
sections.out_scope:
- Verifying the Solidity compiler itself.
- A proprietary product, hosted-only workflow, or exclusive access for a single provider.
- Counting users or github stars as the main measure of adoption. We consider real impact in TVL.
sections.team:
The recipient is Verity Labs. This is a grant rather than an RFP because its team has spent the past few months doing unbounded formal-verification work with leading Ethereum protocols. Its public work covers 40+ protocols, among them popular names like Lido, Morpho, and Safe (see Existing work below).

This experience shows where real protocols need unbounded proofs, where modeling gaps block use, and what needs to become repeatable for developers and audit firms. The Ethereum Foundation has already funded part of Verity's product roadmap and everything is public.
sections.why_grant:
- Verity Labs: https://veritylabs.dev and the Verity product page https://veritylabs.dev/projects/verity
- Verity compiler, MIT licensed: https://github.com/lfglabs-dev/verity
- verity-benchmark, the AI proof-generation benchmark built with the Ethereum Foundation and ecosystem protocols: https://github.com/lfglabs-dev/verity-benchmark
- Technical docs, including the Solidity-to-Verity porting guide: https://veritylang.com
- Public verification case studies (Lido V3 vault solvency, Safe owner list invariants, Morpho, Balancer, 1inch, Pendle and others): https://veritylabs.dev/research
- Paper, "A Formally Verified Smart Contract Compiler in Lean 4", accepted at ETHReS 2026: https://veritylabs.dev/research/verity
sections.commitments:
1. **Open to everyone.** Verity product code, benchmark artifacts, documentation, and CI are public under an OSI-approved license. No proprietary runtime, hosted service, account, or paid provider is needed to use the tooling or reproduce a proof.
2. **Reproducible.** A stranger can reproduce each headline product claim from a clean checkout, documented command, public CI, and version pins, without admitted proof gaps.
3. **TVL-led adoption.** Adoption evidence names the participating protocol team or formal audit firm, provides public confirmation of use, and gives the public TVL source and snapshot date for each value included in the aggregate.
4. **Clear scope on verified TVL.** Each reported verification states the code revision, properties proved, trust assumptions, and known limits in plain language.

milestones.name: Building the Verity product
criteria: A public, versioned Verity release records the delivered compiler stabilization and bug fixes, Solidity feature coverage, reusable EVM proof infrastructure, and exact source revisions.

A deterministic Solidity-to-Verity transpiler is public. For its supported Solidity subset, it produces reproducible Verity output without an LLM in the translation path, documents unsupported patterns, and has public regression tests.
A public verity-benchmark release contains fixed implementations, formal specifications, editable Lean proof files, and target theorems, with checks that reject incomplete or admitted proofs.

Public developer material covers beginner onboarding, supported workflows, trust assumptions, version pins, known limitations, an AI proof-writing skill, and use by in-house teams and formal audit firms.
Public compiler and benchmark research materials are published, and developer onboarding includes a workshop or talk at EthCC, Devcon, or a similar venue.
A public maintenance plan names the maintainer, release process, and post-grant sustainability path.

milestones.name: $1B TVL covered by Verity-verified properties
criteria: At least $1 billion in TVL total (from at least 3 different protocols) is counted on a stated public snapshot date across contracts whose selected properties are formally verified with Verity, whether protocol teams use it in-house or formal audit firms use it in their own work.
The protocol team or formal audit firm publicly confirms its use of Verity for the stated contract revision and properties.
A public metrics page lists the counted systems, snapshot dates, TVL sources, aggregate covered TVL, and the limits of the measurement.

milestones.name: $5B TVL covered by Verity-verified properties
criteria: At least $5 billion in TVL (from at least 10 different protocols) is counted on a public snapshot date across contracts formally verified with Verity, whether used in-house by protocol teams or by formal audit firms.

revisions.summary: AI is making it faster to attack software, giving attackers a meaningful edge. Formal verification is widely considered the strongest security guarantee in software correctness. This grant aims to increase formal verification adoption across the Ethereum ecosystem with TVL secured as the ONLY success metric.

sections.why:
AI is making it faster to attack software, giving attackers a meaningful edge. The answer is to put AI on the defending side too: AI that writes machine-checked proofs that a contract's stated properties hold, with humans only checking the theorems. Formal verification is widely considered the strongest guarantee of software correctness, and it is the one place where AI output can be checked mechanically rather than trusted.

This grant creates an open-source framework for Solidity verification (Verity, built on Lean 4, with an AI proof-writing skill) and increases formal verification adoption across the Ethereum ecosystem. Success is measured by the TVL covered by formally verified properties.
sections.in_scope:
- Product work on Verity's compiler, Solidity coverage, reusable proof infrastructure, benchmark, documentation, developer onboarding, AI proof-writing skill, and a deterministic Solidity-to-Verity transpiler that reduces modeling gaps.
- Public releases that document supported workflows, trust assumptions, version pins, known limitations, and how teams and formal audit firms can use the tooling.
- Adoption through protocol teams using Verity in-house and formal audit firms using it in their own work.
- Measuring adoption primarily through the TVL of contracts whose stated properties are formally verified.

**What this pays for:**

This is not a program to select public contracts and publish formal verifications of them. It pays for two connected things:

- **Product work:** continue the open-source Verity tooling, benchmark, documentation, developer onboarding, AI proof-writing skill, and deterministic Solidity-to-Verity transpilation work.

- **Adoption work:** make Verity usable by protocol teams in-house and formal audit firms in their own work. Success is led by the value covered by the verified properties.

Our success will only be judged on adoption, cause that is the only things that matters.
sections.out_scope:
- Verifying the Solidity compiler itself.
- A proprietary product, hosted-only workflow, or exclusive access for a single provider.
- Counting users or github stars as the main measure of adoption. We consider real impact in TVL.
sections.team:
The recipient is Verity Labs. This is a grant rather than an RFP because its team has spent the past few months doing unbounded formal-verification work with leading Ethereum protocols. Its public work covers 40+ protocols, among them popular names like Lido, Morpho, and Safe (see Existing work below).

This experience shows where real protocols need unbounded proofs, where modeling gaps block use, and what needs to become repeatable for developers and audit firms. The Ethereum Foundation has already funded part of Verity's product roadmap via a grant.
sections.why_grant:
- Verity Labs: https://veritylabs.dev and the Verity product page https://veritylabs.dev/projects/verity
- Verity compiler, MIT licensed: https://github.com/lfglabs-dev/verity
- verity-benchmark, the AI proof-generation benchmark built with ecosystem protocols: https://github.com/lfglabs-dev/verity-benchmark
- Technical docs, including the Solidity-to-Verity porting guide: https://veritylang.com
- Public verification case studies (Lido V3 vault solvency, Safe owner list invariants, Morpho, Balancer, 1inch, Pendle and others): https://veritylabs.dev/research
- Paper, "A Formally Verified Smart Contract Compiler in Lean 4", accepted at ETHReS 2026: https://veritylabs.dev/research/verity
sections.commitments:
1. **Open to everyone.** Verity product code, benchmark artifacts, documentation, and CI are public under an OSI-approved license. No proprietary runtime, hosted service, account, or paid provider is needed to use the tooling or reproduce a proof.
2. **Reproducible.** A stranger can reproduce each headline product claim from a clean checkout, documented command, public CI, and version pins, without admitted proof gaps.
3. **TVL-led adoption.** Adoption evidence names the participating protocol team or formal audit firm, provides public confirmation of use, and gives the public TVL source and snapshot date for each value included in the aggregate.
4. **Clear scope on verified TVL.** Each reported verification states the code revision, properties proved, trust assumptions, and known limits in plain language.

milestones.name: $1B TVL covered by Verity-verified properties

A public metrics page lists the counted systems, snapshot dates, TVL sources, aggregate covered TVL, and the limits of the measurement.

milestones.name: $5B TVL covered by Verity-verified properties
criteria: At least $5 billion in TVL is counted on a public snapshot date across contracts formally verified with Verity, whether used in-house by protocol teams or by formal audit firms.

revisions.title: Wake v5 Maintenance and AI-Assisted Fuzzing
revisions.summary: ack3 will maintain Wake v5 and improve its AI-assisted fuzzing workflow for Solidity. The work covers compatibility updates, targeted code improvements, documentation, runnable examples, and resolution of GitHub issues raised by Wake users. Wake remains open source and usable independently of ack3's commercial audits.

sections.why:
Wake combines Solidity testing, fuzzing, static analysis, and code intelligence in a Python framework. Maintaining that stack requires continued work as Solidity, Python packages, EVM implementations, and Ethereum hard forks change. Unresolved compatibility problems and user-reported defects make security tests harder to reproduce and maintain.

AI can reduce the mechanical work involved in writing fuzz tests, but useful tests still need explicit invariants, correct state models, and reviewable execution results. This initiative improves the parts of Wake that support that workflow. Developers and auditors will have a maintained Wake v5 release, clearer AI-assisted fuzzing paths, and public fixes for problems reported through GitHub.
sections.in_scope:
- Maintain the Wake v5 release line and address compatibility changes affecting Solidity compilation, Python support, EVM behavior, testing, fuzzing, and static analysis.
- Resolve GitHub issues that affect Wake reliability and usability, with fixes or documented resolutions linked from public issue threads.
- Improve Wake interfaces and workflows used for AI-assisted fuzz-test preparation and execution.
- Update documentation and publish runnable examples showing how AI-assisted fuzzing fits into Wake tests.
- Publish tagged releases and release notes for completed work.
sections.out_scope:
- A fully autonomous audit system.
- A guarantee that fuzzing finds a fixed number of vulnerabilities or reaches a fixed coverage percentage.
- A Wake v6 rewrite or an unrelated replacement framework.
- Dedicated consulting, integration support, or developer onboarding as a milestone.
- Documentation of private user activity.
- New detector families unrelated to the maintenance and AI-assisted fuzzing scope.
sections.team:
**ack3** does the work. Michal Převrátil leads Wake engineering and published ack3's 2026 comparison of Wake, Foundry, Echidna, and an agent-written harness. Josef Gattermayer leads ack3 and provides technical and project oversight. ack3's security researchers use Wake in Solidity reviews and test releases against real audit workflows.

The team's public track record is available at https://ack3.ai, https://github.com/ack3-ai/wake, and the linked fuzzing benchmark. No other funder currently pays for this scope.
sections.why_grant:
Wake is an existing open-source framework built and maintained by the team now operating as ack3. Wake v5 already provides Python-based Solidity testing, property-based fuzzing, manually guided fuzzing, static-analysis detectors, typed Solidity representations, coverage, call tracing, and an EVM execution backend. Its documentation and releases are public.

ack3 also uses Wake in security work and has already tested AI-assisted fuzzing approaches. The linked benchmark records a concrete agent-written harness experiment, while the Wake documentation contains the testing and fuzzing foundations this initiative will extend. A new team would first need to learn the compiler pipeline, generated Python types, EVM backend, fuzzing runtime, static-analysis model, and release process. The $20,000 goal funds focused maintenance and improvements to the existing framework rather than a new framework build.
sections.commitments:
- Grant-funded Wake code remains public under the repository's existing open-source license.
- Work, issues, fixes, tests, and releases are tracked in the public Wake repository.
- ack3 continues maintaining Wake after the grant because the team uses it in its own security-review work.
- The adoption target is based on public GitHub issues from users outside ack3, with reporter confirmations visible on the issue threads.

milestones.name: Wake v5 maintenance release
criteria: A tagged Wake v5 maintenance release is published in https://github.com/ack3-ai/wake with release notes linking the included fixes and compatibility changes.
Public CI passes the supported Python and Solidity test matrix at the tagged release commit.

milestones.name: AI-assisted fuzzing improvements
criteria: AI-assisted fuzzing improvements are included in a tagged Wake v5 release, with their implementation and tests public in https://github.com/ack3-ai/wake.
Wake documentation publishes one end-to-end AI-assisted fuzzing workflow and at least two runnable Solidity fuzzing examples.
Each published example runs successfully in public CI at the release commit.

milestones.name: External-user issue resolution
criteria: At least 8 GitHub issues opened by accounts outside ack3 are closed with linked code changes or documented resolutions.
At least 4 of those issue reporters publicly confirm on the issue thread that they tested the current Wake v5 resolution.
Public release notes link every qualifying issue and reporter confirmation.

revisions.title: Clear signing: ratings, fixes and ecosystem adoption for hardware and software wallets
revisions.summary: Walletbeat will rate hardware and software wallets on clear signing support and publish the results on our website. We'll work with teams to fix the checks they fail and expand clear signing support across the ecosystem.

sections.why:
Multisig thefts at [Bybit](https://www.theblock.co/post/343530/lazarus-appears-to-compromise-safe-developer-machine-in-lead-up-to-1-5-billion-bybit-hack-report) (February 2025, about $1.5 billion) and [Radiant Capital](https://decrypt.co/286728/radiant-capital-exploited-50-million) (October 2024, about $50 million) show that a compromised interface can display a routine transfer while the wallet signs a different transaction. Clear signing lets users understand the transaction payload in a human-readable way with hashes to compare against an independent source (e.g. "Deposit $100 into Aave" vs. an unintelligible hexadecimal string). As an industry, we can't expect to onboard the masses if the expectation is for them to decode raw transaction data themselves or otherwise lose their life savings.

As of October 8, 2026, none of the 32 hardware and software wallets listed passes Walletbeat's transaction legibility test.
sections.in_scope:
- Clear signing ratings: readable benchmark transactions (ERC-7730), plus calldata and EIP-712 message hashes (ERC-8213).
- One device per rated hardware wallet, bought at retail (about 2,500 USD total).
- Retests of new releases, with results in the public impact log.
- Working with wallet teams to drive adoption.
sections.out_scope:
- ERC-7730 descriptor files, or new clear signing technology such as on-device verifiers.
- Transaction simulation, scam warnings and other legibility checks.
sections.team:
- **polymutex**, Walletbeat lead and core contributor: https://x.com/polymutex
- **0xMattmatt**, Walletbeat core contributor: https://x.com/0xmattmatt
- **REN2140**, Walletbeat contributor: https://x.com/REN2140_eth

No team member is affiliated with a rated wallet.

Other funding: https://beta.walletbeat.eth.limo/about
sections.why_grant:
- A live transaction legibility rating, with a written methodology and benchmark transactions covering transactions of varying complexity (from simple token approvals to complex nested Safe multisend batch transactions).
- A public test page applying the benchmarks to any wallet: https://beta.walletbeat.eth.limo/test
- Six software wallets already tested for clear signing.
- A track record of wallet impact: https://github.com/walletbeat/walletbeat/blob/beta/resources/docs/impact/impact.md
sections.commitments:
- Code and data under the MIT license. Methodology and data public in the repository.
- Walletbeat maintains the ratings for 6 months after the last milestone at no further cost, funded by grants and donations.
- Pinned target: every listed hardware and software wallet rated on clear signing.
- Walletbeat accepts no payment from wallet teams for reviews or rating changes. A rating changes only when the wallet fixes its transaction legibility.

criteria: At least 11 hardware and 16 software wallets rated on the clear signing checks of Walletbeat's transaction legibility rating, with a reference for every tested field, verified by an independent reviewer

criteria: At least 4 software wallet teams release a version that changes at least one failed clear signing check to a pass, 2 of them from this list: MetaMask, Rabby, Phantom, Base App, Rainbow, Uniswap Wallet, Zerion, OKX
The independent reviewer verifies each fix from Walletbeat's retest and the team's public credit or direct confirmation

criteria: At least 3 hardware wallet vendors release firmware that changes at least one failed clear signing check to a pass, at least 1 of them Ledger or Trezor

revisions.title: Source-Level Debugging for Solidity: ethdebug in solc
revisions.summary: solc does not emit the debug information debuggers need, so every tool reverse-engineers compiler behavior and breaks when the compiler changes. This funds implementing the ethdebug format directly in solc, with debug data that survives the full optimizer pipeline so it works on production builds.

sections.why:
Debugging Solidity is a longstanding pain point, and the root cause is structural. The compiler (solc) does not emit the rich debug information debuggers need: variable types, scopes, and runtime locations. Without a standard for that data, every debugging tool reverse-engineers compiler behavior, which breaks whenever the compiler changes.

The 2025 Solidity Developer Survey (925 responses) re-confirmed this. The three most requested improvements, step-through debugging, variable and state inspection, and transaction replay, map directly to what a standard debug format enables. The need is sharpest in production, where deployed contracts are immutable and the cost of not understanding behavior is highest.

This RFP funds implementing the [ethdebug format](https://ethdebug.github.io/format/) directly in solc. The end state:
* solc emits standardized debug data covering storage variables, local variables, memory, calldata, and per-instruction context
* That data survives the full compilation pipeline, including all optimizer passes, so it works on production builds
* Debuggers, frameworks, monitoring tools, explorers, and agents can read one shared standard instead of reconstructing compiler internals
sections.in_scope:
* The full six-milestone implementation of ethdebug in solc, from test infrastructure through the optimized production pipeline
* Complete debug data covering storage variables, local variables, memory, calldata, and per-instruction context
* Upstreaming the implementation into solc and documenting how tools consume the emitted data
sections.out_scope:
* Building end-user debugger UIs. This funds the compiler-level data, not the tools that read it. Walnut is building soldb, the first ETHDebug consumer - a CLI-based debugger and tracer for Solidity.
* The ethdebug format specification itself, which Argot maintains separately.
* Ongoing maintenance beyond the grant period, beyond the maintenance plan required below.
sections.team:
This RFP is a co-sponsorship opportunity brought by **Argot Collective** and **Walnut**. The ethdebug format is developed by Argot engineer Nicholas D'Andrea. The solc implementation is done by Walnut. We expect them to do this work.

This is not a competitive tender in the usual sense. The project is already in progress with the first three milestones funded and underway, so there is no open challenge window. A challenger just doesn’t make sense in this case.

**Argot Collective is the anchor backer.** A public goods nonprofit, Argot has committed up to $150,000 of the $278,000 project budget. This RFP raises the remaining $127,000:  $85,500 to finish the project and additional $42,000 to ensure ecosystem adoption by every user of the solc compiler.
sections.why_grant:
* [ethdebug/format](https://github.com/ethdebug/format) is the open specification for EVM debug information, comparable in intent to DWARF for C and C++. It defines schemas for types, variable locations, runtime context, and compiler metadata.
* The implementation is underway at Walnut, with the first three milestones below funded by Argot.
sections.commitments:
1. **Open source.** All work merged under solc's existing license, no closed-source dependencies.
2. **Upstream, not a fork.** Deliverables land in the official solc repository, or are open pull requests under active review by the Solidity team. A private fork does not count.
3. **Machine-checkable acceptance.** Debug data output is validated by an automated test suite in public CI against the ethdebug format schemas.
4. **Production coverage proven.** Final acceptance requires debug data demonstrated correct on optimized builds.
5. **Maintenance plan.** A documented plan for keeping ethdebug output current as solc and the optimizer evolve.

milestones.name: Testing and validation infrastructure
criteria: Automated test and validation infrastructure for ethdebug output in place, running in public CI

milestones.name: Internal debug data specification
criteria: Internal specification for how solc represents and propagates debug data, published for review

milestones.name: Yul serialization
criteria: Debug info survives compilation round-trips through Yul, demonstrated by automated tests in public CI

milestones.name: Full unoptimized pipeline
criteria: solc emits ethdebug-format debug data for unoptimized builds, covering storage variables, local variables, memory, calldata, and per-instruction context
Output validates against the ethdebug schemas in an automated public CI check
Implementation is merged into solc, or is an open pull request under active review by the Solidity team, linkable by URL
A published walkthrough showing a debugger or test harness consuming the emitted data on a sample contract

milestones.name: Optimized pipeline
criteria: Debug data extended through all optimizer passes, correct on optimized production builds
Public test suite demonstrates debug data accuracy on optimized builds, with results published
Implementation merged into solc, or an open pull request under active review, linkable by URL
Published maintenance plan for keeping ethdebug output current across future solc and optimizer changes

milestones.name: Adoption evidence
criteria: soldb debugs optimized production builds end-to-end (tracing, source-level stepping, variable inspection) using solc's ETHDebug output alone - no source-map fallback. Results published and reproducible: pinned solc/soldb versions, sample contracts, run instructions.

Integration engagement underway with at least 3 of the 5 providers (Tenderly, Foundry, Hardhat, Medusa, Remix) - anywhere from confirmed interest to active work. Each engagement is evidenced in writing and names an indicative, non-binding timeframe (e.g. a target quarter).

revisions.title: Zealynx Defence: paid security training and practical help with suspicious messages
revisions.summary: Build a paid training programme that helps Ethereum teams verify suspicious requests and practise safer decisions. One subscription includes the paid course library and a case assistant that explains suspicious messages, suggests verification steps and recommends training. Three free checks introduce the tool. TheDAO supports creation; subscriptions sustain delivery and updates.

sections.why:
An attacker can reach Ethereum assets through the people controlling accounts, devices and signing permissions. The [FBI](https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2024/PSA240903) documents tailored social engineering against crypto employees. Teams need people who can verify a request and respond appropriately, including when a convincing message lacks enough evidence to trust it.

We will teach those decisions through practice and a fresh assessment, then provide guidance when a new situation arises. Completion will demonstrate scoped skills, not certify that someone cannot be deceived.
sections.in_scope:
One foundation course covering verification, accounts, devices, payments, signing and escalation; 30 reviewed case records; 12 exercises with legitimate counterparts and fresh assessment. These establish an expandable curriculum rather than a fixed list of scams.

A text-based case assistant explains supported patterns, uncertainty and protective steps, and recommends lessons. Team assignment and completion records support onboarding. Shared research becomes professional briefs, exercises, assistant references and newsletter material, with source dates and human review before publication.

Adapt suitable channel videos into free platform resources, with Carlos's narration and Zealynx explanatory cards instead of the primate character, reusing rights-cleared material.
sections.out_scope: Audits, guaranteed scam detection, automatic actions, continuous inbox monitoring, unlimited coaching and payment for completed work.
sections.team: Carlos Vendrell leads Zealynx's security work and Academy. Zealynx owns the platform and delivers the programme. Earlier Academy support was 6.4466 ETH, valued at $12,008 when sent in [TheDAO's transparency record](https://thedao.fund/transparency/); previously funded work is excluded.
sections.why_grant: Academy Defence already provides simulated security drills. Our Primate explain hacks channel supplies sourced scam and hack research. Reusing these assets reduces new work; the grant funds structured learning, assessment, reviewed guidance and additional software.
sections.commitments:
- Maintain funded materials and essential corrections for 12 months from release; customer revenue supports subsequent operation.
- Publish new rights-cleared teaching handouts and assessment criteria under CC BY 4.0; existing software and third-party material retain their licences.
- Preserve existing free/member rights and private case inputs. Pin assessment, payment and distinct-person verification rules before recruitment.

milestones.name: Reviewed course and assessment
criteria: Independent reviewer accepts the complete course, 30 sourced records, 12 exercises and fresh-task assessment rubric.
Publish the incremental-work and prior-funding reconciliation.

milestones.name: Case assistant and hosted delivery
criteria: Independent reviewer reproduces the learner/team journey and accepts privacy controls and assistant guidance against an agreed 80-case test set, with a sanitised report.

milestones.name: Paid learning and sustainable operation
criteria: 500 distinct paying outside Ethereum/L2 learners complete the course and fresh assessment; independent review excludes staff, bots, duplicates, refunds and grant-paid seats.
Three consecutive months of earned customer revenue after fulfilment costs cover ongoing labour, support and maintenance; independent review excludes grants and unearned subscription billings.

revisions.title: Zealynx Defence: practical security training and help with suspicious messages
revisions.summary: Build a paid training platform that helps Ethereum teams recognise deception, verify suspicious requests and practise safer decisions. One subscription includes an expanding course library and a case assistant that explains suspicious situations, suggests verification steps and recommends relevant training. Three free checks introduce the tool. TheDAO supports creation; customer subscriptions sustain delivery and updates.

sections.why:
Ethereum security depends on the people controlling accounts, devices, software and signing permissions. Convincing messages, impersonation and malicious requests can persuade someone to bypass otherwise sound protections. The [FBI documents targeted social engineering against crypto employees](https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2024/PSA240903).

People need practical ways to verify requests, recognise uncertainty and respond safely. Zealynx Defence connects structured training with guidance when a suspicious situation actually happens. Learners practise decisions and demonstrate understanding on unfamiliar examples. Completion shows the skills assessed; it does not guarantee immunity from deception.
sections.in_scope:
**Multiple practical courses.** The initial library covers identity verification, account and device security, suspicious software requests, payments and signing, and incident response. It includes 30 reviewed case records and 12 practical exercises, with legitimate counterparts, explanations, corrective feedback and fresh assessments. The curriculum can grow as threats and learner needs change.

**A case assistant connected to training.** Users describe or paste a suspicious message or situation. The assistant explains supported warning signs, identifies missing information, suggests protective steps and recommends relevant lessons. It makes uncertainty explicit and does not declare something safe merely because it finds no known scam pattern.

**One paid subscription.** Access includes the standard paid course library, updates and a bounded assistant allowance. Individuals receive three free checks. Team access adds training assignment and completion records.

**Free educational resources.** Provide videos with Carlos's narration and Zealynx explanatory cards. Reviewed research also supports course updates, case guidance and newsletter material, with source dates and human review before publication.

The proposed fifteen-month schedule is approximately three months for the initial release, followed by twelve months to demonstrate paid adoption and sustainable operation.
sections.out_scope: Audits, guaranteed scam detection, automatic replies or transactions, continuous inbox monitoring, unlimited coaching and payment for completed work.
sections.team:
Carlos Vendrell leads Zealynx's security work and Academy. Zealynx owns the platform and delivers the programme.

Earlier Academy support was 6.4466 ETH, valued at $12,008 when sent in [TheDAO's transparency record](https://thedao.fund/transparency/). Completed and previously funded work is excluded from this request.
sections.why_grant:
Academy Defence already provides simulated security drills. Zealynx also has sourced research on scams and attacks to inform the programme.

Reusing this foundation reduces development work. The grant funds the additional curriculum, assessment, reviewed case guidance and software needed to deliver a paid training service.
sections.commitments:
- Maintain funded materials and essential corrections for twelve months from release. Customer revenue supports continuing operation and curriculum expansion.
- Publish new rights-cleared teaching handouts and assessment criteria under CC BY 4.0. Existing software and third-party material retain their licences.
- Preserve existing free and member rights. Protect private case inputs.
- Define the required core learning path and assessment rules before recruitment. Count distinct people, not course registrations or video views.

milestones.name: Six complete courses, ready for independent testing
criteria: Deliver six initial courses: verifying identities and requests; protecting accounts and recovery methods; device, download and malicious-software risks; recognising manipulation in work and personal communications; verifying payments and signing requests; responding to suspected compromise. Each course contains lessons, a worked example, two interactive exercises with explanations and corrective feedback, and an assessment using unfamiliar examples. These are the initial courses, with later expansion supported by customer revenue.
All six courses are accessible in a test account, with saved progress.
All twelve exercises work, including plausible legitimate requests, not just obvious scams.
Thirty sourced case records support the teaching, each with its source, observation date and reviewed defensive guidance.
An independent reviewer checks every course and exercise against a published checklist. Critical factual errors or unsafe guidance must be corrected before acceptance.
Publish an inventory identifying the new work and excluding previously funded work.

milestones.name: Working paid platform and case assistant
criteria: Deliver the hosted product connecting courses, assessments and case guidance. The independent reviewer demonstrates that an individual can join, purchase access, take courses, resume progress and complete an assessment.
The independent reviewer demonstrates that a team manager can assign training and see completion records, while private case submissions remain inaccessible to the manager.
The independent reviewer demonstrates that a new account receives exactly three free case checks, followed by the published paid allowance.

revisions.title: Zealynx Defence: practical security training and help with suspicious messages
revisions.summary: Build a paid training platform that helps Ethereum teams recognise deception, verify suspicious requests and practise safer decisions. One subscription includes an expanding course library and a case assistant that explains suspicious situations, suggests verification steps and recommends relevant training. Three free checks introduce the tool. TheDAO supports creation; customer subscriptions sustain delivery and updates.

sections.why:
Ethereum security depends on the people controlling accounts, devices, software and signing permissions. Convincing messages, impersonation and malicious requests can persuade someone to bypass otherwise sound protections. The [FBI documents targeted social engineering against crypto employees](https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2024/PSA240903).

People need practical ways to verify requests, recognise uncertainty and respond safely. Zealynx Defence connects structured training with guidance when a suspicious situation actually happens. Learners practise decisions and demonstrate understanding on unfamiliar examples. Completion shows the skills assessed; it does not guarantee immunity from deception.
sections.in_scope:
**Multiple practical courses.** The initial library covers identity verification, account and device security, suspicious software requests, payments and signing, and incident response. It includes 30 reviewed case records and 12 practical exercises, with legitimate counterparts, explanations, corrective feedback and fresh assessments. The curriculum can grow as threats and learner needs change.

**A case assistant connected to training.** Users describe or paste a suspicious message or situation. The assistant explains supported warning signs, identifies missing information, suggests protective steps and recommends relevant lessons. It makes uncertainty explicit and does not declare something safe merely because it finds no known scam pattern.

**One paid subscription.** Access includes the standard paid course library, updates and a bounded assistant allowance. Individuals receive three free checks. Team access adds training assignment and completion records.

sections.out_scope: Audits, guaranteed scam detection, automatic replies or transactions, continuous inbox monitoring, unlimited coaching and payment for completed work.

revisions.title: ZK Clear Signing: verifiable transaction display for hardware and software wallets
revisions.summary: Hardware wallets sign bytes they cannot interpret, and clear signing today depends on a descriptor registry signed by the wallet vendor. This grant funds an open standard and toolchain in which the device verifies a zero-knowledge proof that the string it displays is the correct rendering of the bytes it signs, under rules the protocol itself commits on-chain. It ships an ERC draft, a compiler, an embedded verifier, Ledger and Kohaku integrations, five DeFi protocols including Safe, ZK clear signing of Tornado Cash, Privacy Pools and Railgun, policy-bound signing for AI agents, an independent review, and a second verifier that moves from Groth16 to a STARK streamed into the device.

sections.why:
- Bybit (2025, about USD 1.5B) and Radiant (2024, about USD 50M): compromised signing interfaces, hardware wallets that could not render a Safe delegatecall, signers approving a hash.
- ERC-7730 is a real improvement, and this builds on it. It also adds at the moment a single point of trust (the descriptor signing key and its review queue) and cannot express computed meaning: Safe `safeTxHash`, ERC-4337 `userOpHash`, shielded transfers.
- Protocols fund their own audits; the shared signing flow has no owner. The EF Trillion Dollar Security report lists blind signing among the main user-facing risks.

What people can do afterwards:

- **Semantic clear signing.** A proof attests a computation, so the device can show what a Safe hash commits to, what a batch does on net, or a shielded transfer bound to the commitment it signs. It closes a concrete attack: a compromised host swaps the commitment (Tornado), precommitment (Privacy Pools) or note key (Railgun) in a deposit for one it controls.
- **No registry, no permission.** Each contract compiles its rules with the open toolchain and publishes `h_rules` in its own storage or ENS name: nothing to submit, no per-vendor pipeline.
- **Policy-bound signing for AI agents.** The device signs an agent's proposal with no button press when the proof shows it fits a policy the user enrolled; a compromised agent gets no proof outside it.
sections.in_scope:
The prover (dapp, relayer or the user's wallet software) computes `readable` from `tx` and the protocol's rules and proves `h_tx = H(tx)`, `h_readable = H(readable)` and `readable = Render(rules, tx, context)` for rules identified by `h_rules`. The device recomputes both hashes from the bytes it signs and displays, verifies the proof and shows the string with a trust level, without parsing ABI or seeing private context. `h_rules` is anchored by the protocol (contract slot, registry or ENS record) and checked through a storage proof.

Deliverables:

- ERC draft with threat model, proof envelope, anchoring paths, trust indicator and agent policy envelope.
- ERC-7730-to-circuit compiler: all v1 field formats, nested calldata, `safeTxHash` and `userOpHash` binding, reproducible verification-key build, differential tests against viem and ethers.
- Embedded verifier v1.0 in C99 on BLS12-381 and BN254 for Nano S+, Nano X, Stax and Flex; self-hostable prover; Ledger app and Kohaku integrations.
- Five DeFi protocols end to end on the device: Aave v3, Safe (`execTransaction` with nested decoding and `safeTxHash` binding), Uniswap v3/v4, Lido, Morpho.
- Tornado Cash (`deposit`, `withdraw`), Privacy Pools (`deposit`, `withdraw`, `ragequit`) and Railgun (`shield`, `transact` spend authorisation, `unshield`) on the device: amounts, recipient, fee and change recomputed from the note plaintexts, and the commitment, precommitment or npk proven to derive from a note or key the wallet holds; circuits native to BN254; one negative vector per protocol where the host substitutes the commitment and the device refuses.
- Policy-bound signing for AI agents. A policy selects allowed protocols and functions with pinned addresses and constrains the rendered parameters (token in a set, amount at most a ceiling, recipient equal to the signer); the compiler turns it into one circuit with hash `h_policy`. The device verifies against (`h_tx`, `h_readable`, `h_policy`) and signs without a confirmation screen. Enrolment is a clear-signing event with a human (canonical policy text, `h_policy`, a signature cap); revocation is a button press. The ERC-8004 `agentWallet` is the device key, with `h_policy` published as Identity Registry metadata.
- Version 2: a hash-based STARK (KoalaBear, Poseidon2, FRI, Plonky3/SP1 format) replaces the verifier, streamed in phase order in 240-byte chunks with about 8 KB of RAM on the device. No trusted setup, so publishing rules is a single transaction by the contract owner; a pairing-free, plausibly post-quantum device; rules written as a Rust program compiled to an AIR.
- Independent review of the compiler, the privacy circuits and the embedded verifier; integration guides for wallet vendors and protocols.
sections.out_scope:
- A descriptor registry or a vendor review pipeline: protocols anchor their own rules.
- Software wallets other than Kohaku and devices other than Ledger's (stretch goals).
- Privacy-protocol renderers under version 2: BN254 hashing is non-native in a 31-bit field, so they are evaluated only.
- Policies with time state (no trusted clock on the device).
sections.team:
ZKNOX (Paris, 2025): 30+ open-source repositories, three hardware-wallet applications, three EIPs, public security analyses of privacy protocols and wallets, Ethereum Foundation grants, four hackathon prizes in two years including two first prizes, the latest at ETHGlobal Cannes 2026 for the proof of concept this grant starts from. Founders: Ledger co-founder and former CTO, an ex-Ledger cryptographer with fifteen years of embedded cryptography, a co-author of the Bandersnatch curve.

- Renaud Dubois, CTO: https://github.com/rdubois-crypto, https://dblp.org/pid/26/211.html
- Nicolas Bacca, CEO: https://github.com/btchip
- Simon Masson, CSO: https://github.com/simonmasson, https://dblp.org/pid/218/7096.html
- EIPs: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7885, https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-8051, https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-8052

Relationships: a Ledger co-founder; contributor to ethereum/kohaku (post-quantum account) and to Railgun's curve library; audited Railgun PPOI and Privacy Pools deposits. Other funding for this work: none.
sections.why_grant:
- ZKlarity (March 2026): clear-signing circuit for 13 Aave v3 actions and a Groth16 verifier running natively in a Ledger Nano S+ secure element, 2.8 s per verification: https://github.com/ZKNoxHQ/ZKlarity
- ETHGlobal Cannes 2026, first prize in the Ledger track: end-to-end demonstrator with an on-device storage proof checking the rules commitment in an ENS record.
- Streaming STARK verifier on the same device: a 97 KB proof streamed in 414 chunks with about 8 KB of RAM.
- Railgun joinsplit circuits in gnark with a test setup ceremony, and a Railgun signer on Nano S+.

The grant pays for generalisation, hardening, integrations, adoption and review of running code.
sections.commitments:
- Every deliverable under Apache-2.0 or MIT, built and tested in public CI.
- ZKNOX maintains the compiler, both verifiers and the Ledger and Kohaku integrations for 12 months after the last milestone at no further cost (security fixes, SDK updates, review of external pull requests) and runs the hosted prover for the same period; a Docker image allows self-hosting after that.
- Pinned targets: verification at most 3.0 s (BLS12-381) and 2.5 s (BN254) on Nano S+; 5 DeFi and 3 privacy protocols on the device; STARK verifier with no trusted setup, at most 16 KB of RAM and 128 KB of proof.
- No exception requested.

The prover (dapp, relayer or the user's wallet software) computes `readable` from `tx` and the protocol's rules and proves `h_tx = H(tx)`, `h_readable = H(readable)` and `readable = Render(rules, tx, context)` for rules identified by `h_rules`. The device recomputes both hashes from the bytes it signs and displays, verifies the proof and shows the string with a trust level, without parsing ABI or seeing private context. `h_rules` is anchored by the protocol (contract slot, registry or ENS record) and checked through a storage proof.

Deliverables:

- ERC draft with threat model, proof envelope, anchoring paths, trust indicator and agent policy envelope.
- ERC-7730-to-circuit compiler: all v1 field formats, nested calldata, `safeTxHash` and `userOpHash` binding, reproducible verification-key build, differential tests against viem and ethers.
- Embedded verifier v1.0 in C99 on BLS12-381 and BN254 for Nano S+, Nano X, Stax and Flex; self-hostable prover; Ledger app and Kohaku integrations.
- Five DeFi protocols end to end on the device: Aave v3, Safe (`execTransaction` with nested decoding and `safeTxHash` binding), Uniswap v3/v4, Lido, Morpho.
- Tornado Cash (`deposit`, `withdraw`), Privacy Pools (`deposit`, `withdraw`, `ragequit`) and Railgun (`shield`, `transact` spend authorisation, `unshield`) on the device: amounts, recipient, fee and change recomputed from the note plaintexts, and the commitment, precommitment or npk proven to derive from a note or key the wallet holds; circuits native to BN254; one negative vector per protocol where the host substitutes the commitment and the device refuses.
- Policy-bound signing for AI agents. A policy selects allowed protocols and functions with pinned addresses and constrains the rendered parameters (token in a set, amount at most a ceiling, recipient equal to the signer); the compiler turns it into one circuit with hash `h_policy`. The device verifies against (`h_tx`, `h_readable`, `h_policy`) and signs without a confirmation screen. Enrolment is a clear-signing event with a human (canonical policy text, `h_policy`, a signature cap); revocation is a button press. The ERC-8004 `agentWallet` is the device key, with `h_policy` published as Identity Registry metadata.
- Version 2: a hash-based STARK (KoalaBear, Poseidon2, FRI, Plonky3/SP1 format) replaces the verifier, streamed in phase order in 240-byte chunks with about 8 KB of RAM on the device. No trusted setup, so publishing rules is a single transaction by the contract owner; a pairing-free, plausibly post-quantum device; rules written as a Rust program compiled to an AIR.
- Independent review of the compiler, the privacy circuits and the embedded verifier; integration guides for wallet vendors and protocols.
sections.out_scope:
- A descriptor registry or a vendor review pipeline: protocols anchor their own rules.
- Software wallets other than Kohaku and devices other than Ledger's (stretch goals).
- Privacy-protocol renderers under version 2: BN254 hashing is non-native in a 31-bit field, so they are evaluated only.
- Policies with time state (no trusted clock on the device).
sections.team:
ZKNOX (Paris, 2025): 30+ open-source repositories, three hardware-wallet applications, three EIPs, public security analyses of privacy protocols and wallets, Ethereum Foundation grants, four hackathon prizes in two years including two first prizes, the latest at ETHGlobal Cannes 2026 for the proof of concept this grant starts from. Founders: Ledger co-founder and former CTO, an ex-Ledger cryptographer with fifteen years of embedded cryptography, a co-author of the Bandersnatch curve.

- Renaud Dubois, CTO: https://github.com/rdubois-crypto, https://dblp.org/pid/26/211.html
- Nicolas Bacca, CEO: https://github.com/btchip
- Simon Masson, CSO: https://github.com/simonmasson, https://dblp.org/pid/218/7096.html
- EIPs: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7885, https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-8051, https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-8052

Relationships: a Ledger co-founder; contributor to ethereum/kohaku (post-quantum account) and to Railgun's curve library; audited Railgun PPOI and Privacy Pools deposits. Other funding for this work: none.
sections.why_grant:
- ZKlarity (March 2026): clear-signing circuit for 13 Aave v3 actions and a Groth16 verifier running natively in a Ledger Nano S+ secure element, 2.8 s per verification: https://github.com/ZKNoxHQ/ZKlarity
- ETHGlobal Cannes 2026, first prize in the Ledger track: end-to-end demonstrator with an on-device storage proof checking the rules commitment in an ENS record.
- Streaming STARK verifier on the same device: a 97 KB proof streamed in 414 chunks with about 8 KB of RAM.
- Railgun joinsplit circuits in gnark with a test setup ceremony, and a Railgun signer on Nano S+.

The grant pays for generalisation, hardening, integrations, adoption and review of running code.
sections.commitments:
- Every deliverable under Apache-2.0 or MIT, built and tested in public CI.
- ZKNOX maintains the compiler, both verifiers and the Ledger and Kohaku integrations for 12 months after the last milestone at no further cost (security fixes, SDK updates, review of external pull requests) and runs the hosted prover for the same period; a Docker image allows self-hosting after that.
- Pinned targets: verification at most 3.0 s (BLS12-381) and 2.5 s (BN254) on Nano S+; 5 DeFi and 3 privacy protocols on the device; STARK verifier with no trusted setup, at most 16 KB of RAM and 128 KB of proof.
- No exception requested.

milestones.name: Specification, compiler and privacy circuits
criteria: ERC draft with threat model, proof envelope, anchoring paths, trust indicator, agent policy envelope and design decision record published on Ethereum Magicians
Compiler covers 100% of ERC-7730 v1 field formats, nested calldata depth at least 2, `safeTxHash` and `userOpHash` binding, shown by the public test suite in CI
Verification-key hash reproducible bit-exact from source, and at least 10,000 differential fuzz cases per field format against viem and ethers passing, both in public CI
At least 5 DeFi protocols compiled (Aave v3, Safe, Uniswap v3/v4, Lido, Morpho) with at least 50 functions, listed in the repository
Tornado Cash and Privacy Pools circuits pass mainnet test vectors and reject 1 substitution vector per protocol in CI
Policy compiler with canonical policy text; an Aave v3 plus Morpho yield policy compiled, policy text and `h_policy` reproducible bit-exact in CI

milestones.name: Embedded verifier and Railgun
criteria: Verifier v1.0 on BLS12/381 and BN254 runs on Nano S+, Nano X, Stax and Flex, at most 3.0 s (BLS12/381) and 2.5 s (BN254) on Nano S+, reproduced by the technical reviewer on a device. Min 2.5s.
On-device storage-proof anchor check and trust indicator shown in a recorded device session
Railgun circuits verified on the device before the EdDSA-Poseidon/FROST signer signs, 1 substitution vector rejected, in a recorded device session
Policy-signer mode on the same devices (persistent `h_policy`, signature counter, no confirmation screen), unattended verification at most 3.0 s, in a recorded device session

milestones.name: Integrations and adoption
criteria: Self-hostable prover published (browser proving at most 5 s for 1 KB of calldata, measured in CI); 5 DeFi and 3 privacy protocols end to end on mainnet, 1 recorded device session per privacy protocol, reproduced by the technical reviewer
Reference agent signing only through the device on mainnet, 4 out-of-policy proposals refused, agent registered under ERC-8004 with `h_policy` published, checked on a public explorer
Independent review report public with 0 open high or critical findings
Ledger ships the verifier in an app listed in its public app catalog, checked by the technical reviewer
The verification path merged upstream in ethereum/kohaku, shown by the merged pull request
At least 5 protocols publish `h_rules` on-chain or on ENS, at least 1 of them from Aave v3, Safe, Uniswap, Lido, Morpho, checked on a public explorer
At least 1 privacy protocol team (Railgun or Privacy Pools) merges the rendering circuits into its SDK or wallet, shown by the merged pull request
At least 1 wallet vendor and 2 protocols listed as ERC co-authors in its header

milestones.name: Version 2, streamed STARK
criteria: Streaming STARK verifier hardened on Nano S+, Nano X, Stax and Flex, RAM working set at most 16 KB, measured and published in the repository
STARK transport specification added to the ERC draft, and Rust rendering-program toolchain with program commitments reproducible bit-exact in CI
At least 1 DeFi protocol rendered and verified under STARK on the device, proof at most 128 KB, verification at most 10 s on Nano S+, reproduced by the technical reviewer
Privacy renderers evaluated under version 2 with measured proof sizes published
